Delivery and adherence of biomarker‐guided antibiotic treatment protocols in the ADAPT ‐Sepsis clinical trial: an in‐trial descriptive process evaluation of daily procalcitonin‐ and C‐reactive protein‐guided protocols
items.abstract: Introduction Biomarker‐guided antibiotic protocols using daily procalcitonin or C‐reactive protein have been proposed to optimise antibiotic duration in sepsis. This pre‐planned process evaluation of the ADAPT‐Sepsis trial examined delivery and clinician adherence to procalcitonin‐ and C‐reactive protein‐guided protocols. Methods An embedded descriptive process evaluation was conducted within the multicentre ADAPT‐Sepsis trial including 2760 adults across 41 UK critical care units. Patients were assigned to procalcitonin‐guided, C‐reactive protein‐guided or standard care. Algorithm‐generated recommendations (strong stop, suggest stop or standard care) were relayed to research staff and clinicians who remained blinded to group allocation. Adherence was defined as stopping biomarker sampling after advice. Advice timings, frequencies, adherence rates and reasons for non‐adherence were recorded and analysed. Results Among 2760 patients, strong stop advice occurred earlier in those allocated to the procalcitonin‐guided group compared with the C‐reactive protein‐guided group (mean difference ‐1.7 days, 95%CI ‐2.5 to ‐0.9, p < 0.001). C‐reactive protein guidance generated a higher proportion of standard care advice (mean difference ‐9.1%, 95%CI ‐10.9% to ‐7.3%, p < 0.001). Overall advice adherence was greater in patients allocated to the C‐reactive protein group than those allocated to the procalcitonin group (mean difference ‐6.8%, 95%CI ‐9.0 to ‐4.5, p < 0.001), driven by the higher proportion of standard care advice and later stronger stop advice with higher adherence (mean difference ‐14.3%, 95%CI ‐21.8 to ‐6.8, p < 0.001). Reasons for advice non‐adherence included fixed‐duration microbiology guidance, illness severity, continuing fever and elevation of routine inflammatory markers, which did not differ between groups. Discussion A C‐reactive protein‐guided discontinuation protocol achieved higher clinician adherence, probably because its recommendations aligned more closely with established prescribing norms. In contrast, procalcitonin guidance produced earlier and more frequent stop signals, offering greater potential to reduce antibiotic exposure but requiring clinicians to accept earlier discontinuation than usual practice.

items.title: Optimum timing of cerebral computed tomography angiography for determination of death using neurological criteria: a retrospective sensitivity cohort study
items.abstract: Introduction Cerebral computed tomography angiography (CTA) is increasingly incorporated into national guidelines to confirm cerebral circulatory arrest during the determination of death using neurological criteria. However, implementation remains limited due to studies showing variable sensitivity. Clinical observations suggest the time elapsed from the onset of initial signs of brainstem areflexia, defined as the appearance of fixed and dilated pupils and loss of cough and gag reflexes, significantly influences CTA sensitivity. This study aimed to evaluate the impact of this time interval on test sensitivity. Methods We retrospectively assessed 118 intensive care unit patients undergoing determination of death using neurological criteria. Cerebral CTA was used to confirm cerebral circulatory arrest based on a four‐point scoring system. Patients were categorised according to the time elapsed from the onset of initial signs of brainstem areflexia to the investigation. Results Cerebral CTA did not confirm cerebral circulatory arrest in 15/118 (13%) patients, yielding an overall sensitivity of 87.3% (95%CI 79.6–92.5%). Notably, 93.3% (95%CI 66.0–99.7%) of false‐negative results occurred within 12 h of the onset of initial signs of brainstem areflexia. Patients were secondarily stratified into early (≤ 12 h) and late (> 12 h) groups, revealing a significantly higher sensitivity in the late group (67.4%, 95%CI 51.3–80.5% vs. 98.7%, 95%CI 91.8–100%, p < 0.001). Discussion The sensitivity of cerebral CTA increases with the time elapsed after the onset of initial signs of brainstem areflexia. We recommend delaying cerebral CTA until at least 12 h after the onset of initial signs of brainstem areflexia, and, in case of inconclusive results, test repetition at least 12 h later. Further work is required to confirm our findings and increase diagnostic confidence.

items.title: Pain management after total shoulder arthroplasty: a systematic review and procedure‐specific postoperative pain management ( PROSPECT ) recommendations
items.abstract: Introduction Total shoulder arthroplasty is associated with moderate‐to‐severe postoperative pain. The aim of this systematic review was to assess the available literature and provide PROSPECT (PROcedure SPECific Postoperative Pain ManagemenT) recommendations for optimal pain management after total shoulder arthroplasty. Methods A systematic review utilising PROSPECT methodology was performed. Randomised controlled trials and systematic reviews published in the English language that assessed postoperative pain using analgesic, anaesthetic and surgical interventions were identified from databases. Results Of the 1809 articles identified, 30 randomised controlled trials and seven systematic reviews/meta‐analyses met our inclusion criteria. Interventions that improved postoperative pain relief included: paracetamol and non‐steroidal anti‐inflammatory drugs; dexamethasone; interscalene brachial plexus block and, as an alternative, local infiltration analgesia. Conflicting evidence was found for continuous interscalene brachial plexus block (catheter) or liposomal bupivacaine for interscalene block or local infiltration analgesia. No evidence was found for a specific surgical technique. Discussion In the absence of contraindication, the analgesic regimen should include: paracetamol; a non‐steroidal anti‐inflammatory drug administered peri‐operatively and continued postoperatively; intravenous dexamethasone (8–10 mg); and postoperative opioids for rescue analgesia. As a regional technique, an interscalene brachial plexus block with a single‐bolus injection of long‐acting local anaesthetic (bupivacaine or ropivacaine), but not liposomal bupivacaine, should be provided. In case of contraindications or absence of expertise, local infiltration analgesia is a reasonable alternative. Further studies are required to investigate the analgesic benefit of a continuous infusion for the interscalene brachial plexus block.

items.title: Salmon calcitonin prescribing for acute phantom limb pain after amputation
items.abstract: Salmon calcitonin prescribing for acute phantom limb pain after amputation Phantom limb pain is common after amputation and remains difficult to treat.Salmon calcitonin has been used for acute phantom limb pain for several decades and has several plausible analgesic mechanisms, including modulation of serotonergic and endogenous opioid signalling [1], but its clinical role remains uncertain.Existing evidence is limited to small, heterogeneous studies using different doses, routes and treatment schedules, and there is no established prescribing standard [2-4].Contemporary practice is therefore described poorly, and it is unclear which regimen should be taken forward for definitive evaluation.We sought primarily to characterise real-world prescribing of salmon calcitonin for acute postoperative phantom limb pain at a tertiary Australian hospital and to describe changes in pain scores, opioid requirements and patient-reported symptoms during treatment.The study was not designed to determine efficacy.We conducted a single-centre retrospective observational cohort study using an acute pain service database.The study was approved by the local Human Research Ethics Committee with waiver of written informed consent.Between January 2020 and December 2023, adults who received salmon calcitonin for phantom limb pain within 7 days of elective or emergency surgical amputation were eligible.Patients undergoing repeat treatment episodes within 3 months of a previous calcitonin course and those with calcitonin prescribed for indications other than acute phantom limb pain were not eligible.We recorded: concurrent analgesic therapies; calcitonin timing, dose, route and duration; adverse effects; and documented patient-reported symptom resolution.Visual analogue pain scores and oral morphine equivalent daily dose were recorded before calcitonin and after treatment completion.Continuous outcomes were assessed over time using linear mixed-effects models with patient-level random intercepts and time as a fixed effect.

items.title: Interpreting bispectral index monitoring during remimazolam and propofol anaesthesia: a reply
items.abstract: We thank Wang et al. [1] for their thoughtful comments on our study [2]. We agree that the bispectral index (BIS) may not be an ideal or fully validated measure of anaesthetic depth during remimazolam-based anaesthesia. Clinically, adequate remimazolam anaesthesia may occur at BIS values higher than those typically seen with propofol, which is consistent with published evidence [3] and our clinical experience. We used BIS as one reference for anaesthetic depth, not as the sole basis for drug administration. Anaesthetic titration also considered haemodynamic responses; clinical signs; surgical stimulation; and the judgement of the attending anaesthetist. Because there is currently no validated monitoring index designed specifically for remimazolam-based sedation or anaesthesia, a BIS of 40–60 was used only as a reference range, not as proof of equivalent hypnotic depth between remimazolam and propofol. The remimazolam infusion was adjusted within the protocol-specified range according to the overall clinical condition of patients, rather than simply to target BIS below a fixed threshold. We also agree that anaesthetic dose and exposure may influence emergence quality and delirium-related outcomes. This issue is acknowledged in the limitations section of the discussion. The relationships among remimazolam dose, drug exposure, BIS values and recovery profile require further study. Importantly, this limitation does not change the main clinical conclusion of our trial. Our study was designed to compare two clinically used anaesthetic regimens in older patients undergoing lung resection, not to perform a pharmacological experiment under strictly matched electroencephalographic or exposure conditions. Under the regimen studied, remimazolam anaesthesia without routine flumazenil reversal, guided by BIS, haemodynamics and clinical assessment, did not meet the prespecified non-inferiority criterion compared with propofol for postoperative delirium, with excess events mainly occurring during emergence. Thus, our findings should be interpreted as showing that the remimazolam-based regimen used in our trial was associated with less favourable emergence period neurocognitive outcomes than the propofol-based regimen. The findings also suggest that anaesthetists should pay close attention to emergence quality, recovery trajectory and early neurocognitive status when using remimazolam in older patients having thoracic surgery.

items.title: Liberal vs. conventional pre‐operative clear fluid fasting policies in children: a systematic review and meta‐analysis of randomised and non‐randomised studies
items.abstract: Introduction Pre‐operative clear fluid fasting in children aims to reduce the risk of pulmonary aspiration. Recent studies have shown the safety of shorter clear fluid fasting durations. However, because pulmonary aspiration is rare, it remains uncertain whether the incidence differs between the liberal (< 2 h) and conventional (≥ 2 h) clear fluid fasting policies. Methods We conducted a systematic review and meta‐analysis, performing comprehensive searches across five databases. We included studies with patients aged < 18 y who underwent general anaesthesia or sedation for surgery or procedures. Primary outcome was pulmonary aspiration and secondary outcome was vomiting without pulmonary aspiration. We performed meta‐analyses to estimate pooled incidences according to fasting policy (< 2 h vs. ≥ 2 h). Results We included 33 studies involving 580,197 patients. Twenty‐nine studies (579,737 patients) reported pulmonary aspiration. The pooled incidence of pulmonary aspiration was 0.03% (95%CI 0.01–0.09%) with conventional fasting policies and 0.03% (95%CI 0.01–0.09%) with liberal policies. Risk ratios were available from 14 studies (475,399 patients) and showed no difference in pulmonary aspiration between policies (risk ratio 0.77, 95%CI 0.40–1.47). Seventeen studies (344,653 patients) reported vomiting; the pooled incidence was 0.99% (95%CI 0.27–3.51%) with conventional policies and 0.76% (95%CI 0.18–3.14%) with liberal policies. The certainty of evidence was very low for both outcomes. Discussion Pulmonary aspiration is rare in children, and similar incidences of aspiration and vomiting were observed under liberal and conventional clear fluid fasting policies. The results should be interpreted cautiously due to the very low certainty of evidence.

items.title: Development and temporal validation of a simple CT-based body surface landmark approach for optimising central venous catheter tip position in the superior vena cava
items.abstract: BACKGROUND Accurate positioning of central venous catheter (CVC) tips is essential to avoid complications, yet consistent appropriate placement within the superior vena cava remains challenging without a simple method for depth adjustment. OBJECTIVES To develop and temporally validate a simple computed tomography-based (CT-based) body surface landmark approach for estimating optimal insertion depth (OID) and to assess its impact on appropriate catheter tip positioning. DESIGN Single-centre prospective observational cohort study. SETTING Tertiary care hospital in Japan; February 2017 to June 2019. PATIENTS Adult patients undergoing surgery requiring CVC placement via the right internal jugular vein with preoperative chest CT. After exclusions, 86 patients were included in the derivation cohort and 100 in the validation cohort. INTERVENTION In the derivation cohort, insertion depth was determined by the attending anaesthesiologist; in the validation cohort, it was determined using a model derived from the derivation cohort. MAIN OUTCOME MEASURE The primary outcome was the proportion of appropriately placed catheter tips. RESULTS The final model retained the insertion point-to-body surface landmark distance (ILD), defined using a body surface landmark corresponding to the CT-identified midpoint of Zone B, as the sole predictor: OID (cm) = 0.64 × ILD + 3.64. The proportion of appropriately placed catheter tips was higher in the validation cohort than in the derivation cohort (92.0% (95% CI, 85.0 to 95.9%) vs. 73.3% (95% CI, 63.1 to 81.5%); P < 0.001). Model-guided placement was associated with increased likelihood of appropriate positioning (adjusted odds ratio 4.68 (95% CI, 1.97 to 12.27)). Model performance showed good calibration and moderate explanatory ability ( R 2 approximately 50%) in both cohorts. CONSLUSIONS A CT-based body surface landmark approach was associated with improved consistency of appropriate CVC tip placement and enables patient-specific estimation of insertion depth. TRIAL REGISTRY UMIN Clinical Trials Registry (UMIN000026252).

items.title: Postoperative delirium and 1-year functional decline, institutionalization and mortality
items.abstract: BACKGROUND Postoperative delirium is a common and serious complication in older surgical patients and has been associated with increased morbidity, healthcare costs, long-term functional decline and mortality. OBJECTIVE To determine whether postoperative delirium is associated with functional status, quality of life, institutionalisation and mortality at 1 year after surgery in a large multicentre surgical cohort. DESIGN Prospective multicentre observational study. SETTING Forty-three hospitals in Spain. Surgical patients were recruited in November 2023 and assessed for delirium 48 h after surgery, with follow-up at 1 year. PATIENTS, OTHER PARTICIPANTS A total of 2442 adult surgical patients undergoing elective or urgent procedures requiring hospital admission. Postoperative delirium was assessed using the Confusion Assessment Method (CAM), CAM for the Intensive Care Unit (CAM-ICU) or the telephone-administered 4AT according to clinical setting. INTERVENTIONS None. MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES Functional status and quality of life at 1 year assessed using the 12-item World Health Organization Disability Assessment Schedule (WHODAS 2.0). Secondary outcomes included institutionalisation and mortality. RESULTS After excluding 81 deaths and 462 nonresponders, the 1-year telephone follow-up was completed for 1899 patients. Postoperative delirium within the first 48 h was independently associated with a 4.6-point higher WHODAS score at 1 year: adjusted mean difference = 4.60 [95% confidence interval (CI), 1.57 to 7.64, P = 0.003]. Delirium was also associated with increased institutionalisation and higher mortality: odds ratio (OR) 2.5 (95% CI, 1.07 to 5.84, P = 0.03), and (16.7 vs. 3.1%; P < 0.001), including 30-day, 60-day, and 365-day mortality (all P < 0.001), respectively. CONCLUSIONS Postoperative delirium is independently associated with long-term functional decline, loss of independence, institutionalisation and increased 1-year mortality. These findings highlight delirium as a key perioperative complication and support prevention strategies and structured long-term follow-up after surgery. TRIAL REGISTRATION ClinicalTrials.gov (identifier: NC-T06127901).

items.title: Antibiotic prophylaxis with vancomycin and gentamicin and the occurrence of acute kidney injury after cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass
items.abstract: BACKGROUND Vancomycin combined with gentamicin (VGA) is used as an alternative antibiotic prophylaxis in cardiac surgery when cephalosporins are contraindicated. However, the nephrotoxic potential of this combination raises concerns regarding postoperative acute kidney injury (AKI). OBJECTIVE This study aimed to evaluate the association between VGA prophylaxis and AKI occurrence in patients undergoing cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB), while accounting for preoperative risk factors. DESIGN Retrospective single-centre study. AKI was defined according to KDIGO criteria within 7 postoperative days. PATIENTS Of the 8895 eligible patients between April 2013 and December 2021, 8198 were included. Subgroup analyses were performed according to preoperative AKI risk status (high-risk: insulin-dependent diabetes, cirrhosis, acute endocarditis, preoperative critical state, emergency surgery, or cardiac transplantation). RESULTS In our cohort, 7469 (91%) received cephalosporins and 729 (9%) received VGA. The overall AKI incidence was 16%. AKI occurred more frequently in the VGA group (29% vs. 15%, P < 0.001). After multivariable adjustment, VGA remained independently associated with AKI [odds ratio (OR) 1.29, 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.03 to 1.62, P = 0.024], confirmed by propensity score analysis (OR 1.32, 95% CI 1.09 to 1.60, P = 0.005). In subgroup analyses, VGA was significantly associated with AKI in high-risk patients (OR 1.53, 95% CI 1.14 to 2.04, P = 0.004), but not in low-risk patients (OR 1.19, 95% CI 0.87 to 1.64, P = 0.285). CONCLUSION In this large retrospective cohort, VGA antibiotic prophylaxis was independently associated with increased AKI risk following cardiac surgery with CPB. This association was driven primarily by patients with preoperative risk factors for AKI. Alternative prophylactic regimens should be considered in high-risk patients when possible.

items.title: Frailty patterns in European surgical patients
items.abstract: BACKGROUND Frailty represents a multidimensional decline in physiological reserve that increases vulnerability to surgical stress. Its perioperative dynamics and association with outcomes across diverse surgical populations remain insufficiently characterised. OBJECTIVE This study aimed to describe the prevalence of frailty before and after surgery and to evaluate its association with postoperative complications, mortality, and hospital length of stay. METHODS We conducted a prospective, multicentre European cohort study including adults undergoing elective or emergency surgery under general or regional anaesthesia across 64 participating centres in 10 countries. Each centre contributed data from one to three predefined recruitment days between April 2021 and December 2022. Frailty was assessed preoperatively and at 30 days using the Rockwood Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS), the FRAIL questionnaire, and the Barthel Index. The primary outcome was the association between preoperative frailty and 30-day postoperative complications (Clavien–Dindo ≥ II); secondary outcomes included 30-day mortality, postoperative cognitive impairment, and new-onset frailty. RESULTS Among 1472 patients (mean age 60.9 years; 52.9% male), preoperative frailty prevalence was 14.6% (FRAIL), 10.4% (CFS), and 10.4% (Barthel). Within 30 days, 11.9% of nonfrail patients became frail, increasing overall frailty prevalence to 21.2%. Postoperative complications occurred in 19.2% and mortality in 1.7%. Preoperative frailty was independently associated with complications: adjusted odds ratio (OR) 2.35 [95% confidence interval (CI) 1.53 to 3.60], P < 0.001); 30-day mortality OR 10.9 (95% CI 1.28 to 93.0), P = 0.029). Frailty was also associated with postoperative cognitive impairment: OR 3.47 (95% CI 1.98 to 6.08), P < 0.001). CONCLUSIONS Frailty is common among surgical patients, increases after surgery, and independently predicts postoperative complications and mortality. These findings highlight frailty as a dynamic and potentially modifiable marker of surgical vulnerability that should be routinely assessed and integrated into perioperative care. TRIAL REGISTRATION ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT04140370

items.title: Association of preoperative hemoglobin levels with intraoperative hypotension: a retrospective cohort study
items.containerTitle: Canadian Journal of Anesthesia/Journal canadien d'anesthésie
items.abstract: Purpose Intraoperative hypotension (IOH) has been increasingly linked to postoperative complications and adverse outcomes. Nevertheless, the association between preoperative hemoglobin levels and the risk of IOH has not been investigated. Methods We conducted a retrospective cohort study of 2,060 patients aged ≥ 18 yr who underwent general anesthesia between 2019 and 2023. We defined intraoperative hypotension as any mean blood pressure (MBP) Results We found no significant association between preoperative hemoglobin levels and IOH risk at MBP Conclusions Lower preoperative hemoglobin levels were significantly associated with an increased risk of IOH and longer postoperative length of hospital stay. These findings highlight the potential value of incorporating hemoglobin level assessments into IOH risk stratification and may help improve patient outcomes.

items.title: Pneumothorax rates following cardiac surgery with versus without continuous serratus anterior plane catheters: a secondary analysis of trial data with propensity score matching to a historic cohort
items.containerTitle: Canadian Journal of Anesthesia/Journal canadien d'anesthésie
items.abstract: Purpose Moderate to severe pain is common after cardiac surgery, especially in the first two postoperative days. Inadequate pain control may prolong intensive care unit (ICU) stay, may increase cost, and contributes to chronic pain. Enhanced Recovery After Cardiac Surgery (ERACS) protocols prioritize multimodal analgesia, including regional anesthesia techniques. In a recent randomized trial with continuous serratus anterior plane (SAP) catheters, we found unexpectedly high pneumothorax rates. To address this, we aimed to design a propensity-score-matched comparison using patients from the same institution to control for institutional practice patterns, surgical techniques, and patient demographics that could confound comparisons with published literature rates from other centres. Methods We conducted a secondary analysis of RCT data with propensity score matching to a historic cohort. We compared the pneumothorax rates in patients receiving continuous SAP catheters in our previous Cardiac-Serratus Anterior Plane (Cardiac-SAP) trial with those in a retrospective institutional database cohort of patients receiving standard care undergoing cardiac surgery via sternotomy. The two groups were propensity score matched in a 1:20 ratio based on age, sex, smoking status, surgery type, and pre-existing respiratory disease. We analyzed univariate comparisons using Fisher's exact test or the percentile bootstrapping method. Results We matched 50 patients from the Cardiac-SAP trial to 989 retrospective cohort patients. After matching, the SAP catheter group was associated with a significantly higher risk of pneumothorax (12% vs 3%; odds ratio, 5.3; 95% confidence interval, 2.1 to 13.6; P Conclusions Our data suggest that SAP catheter use as a part of a randomized trial for cardiac surgery was associated with a higher rate of pneumothorax in trial participants than in a historic cohort of a similar population, though causality is unclear. Differences in monitoring within the trial and the inherent risks in this population may have contributed.

items.title: Comparison of upper limb muscle activity and workload during intubation with the Macintosh direct laryngoscope versus C-MAC® and King Vision® videolaryngoscopes in simulated difficult airway scenarios: a randomized crossover trial
items.containerTitle: Canadian Journal of Anesthesia/Journal canadien d'anesthésie
items.abstract: Purpose Tracheal intubation is a physically and mentally demanding for anesthesiologists because it requires fine motor control, technical precision, rapid decision-making, situational awareness, and error avoidance. While videolaryngoscopes reduce muscle strain in normal airways, their ergonomic impact during difficult airway management remains poorly established. We aimed to compare upper limb muscle activity using dynamic surface electromyography during intubation via direct laryngoscopy (DL) vs videolaryngoscopy (VL) in simulated difficult airway scenarios. Methods We conducted a randomized crossover trial involving 35 experienced anesthesiologists who performed tracheal intubation on a high-fidelity manikin with a normal airway, locked jaw, and rigid neck, respectively, using a Macintosh direct laryngoscope, a C-MAC® videolaryngoscope (C blade), and a King Vision® channeled videolaryngoscope. The primary outcome was upper limb muscle activity, measured by surface electromyography. Secondary outcomes included intubation time, force on upper incisors, first-attempt success rate, and perceived workload (National Aeronautics and Space Administration Task Load Index [NASA-TLX] score). Results Direct laryngoscopy produced significantly higher brachioradialis muscle activity than C-MAC VL in the simulated normal airway (16 vs 13 µV; median difference [MD], 3 µV; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0 to 5; P = 0.04), locked jaw (18 vs 12 µV; MD, 6 µV; 95% CI, 1 to 11; P = 0.02), and rigid neck (16 vs 13 µV; MD, 4 µV; 95% CI, 0 to 9; P = 0.03) scenarios. Direct laryngoscopy was the fastest method but exerted the highest force on the incisors (P Conclusion In simulated difficult airways, VL reduced upper limb muscle activity compared with DL. Nevertheless, perceived workload was higher with King Vision VL than with DL, whereas it was lower with C-MAC VL. Among the devices tested, C-MAC VL provided the most favorable ergonomic balance, combining reduced muscle strain, lower perceived workload, and highest first-attempt success rate across all airway scenarios. Study registration Clinical Trials Registry of India (CTRI/2021/11/038305); first submitted on 26 November 2021.

items.title: Environmental scan of Indigenous resources and culturally specific tools across intensive care units in Alberta, Canada
items.containerTitle: Canadian Journal of Anesthesia/Journal canadien d'anesthésie
items.abstract: Purpose Indigenous Peoples in Canada are disproportionately burdened with a spectrum of health issues and consistently report lower satisfaction with their health care; nevertheless, little is known about their experiences with critical care and the support received during critical illness. We aimed to describe the current scope of critical-care-specific resources available to Indigenous patients and their families across Alberta to identify gaps and opportunities to implement actionable change to realize more equitable and culturally safe care. Source We conducted a two-phase environmental scan. Phase 1 entailed searching websites for information to support Indigenous patients, their families, and health care workers. Phase 2 facilitated 21 interviews with intensive care unit (ICU) stakeholders from across Alberta to further describe site-specific resources, services, tools, or initiatives to support Indigenous Peoples. Indigenous partners were engaged through all aspects of the project. Principal findings Our environmental scan identified a paucity of ICU-specific resources, programs, or policies to support Indigenous patients and families' navigation with critical care. We identified two national resources aimed at clinicians, rather than patients or families. Interviews with ICU stakeholders confirmed the paucity of Indigenous-specific resources. Stakeholders cited numerous barriers, including inadequate culture training, staff time constraints and burnout, physical space limits, and insufficient personnel, such as Indigenous liaisons and social workers. Conclusions Multiple gaps exist in the availability of critical-care-focused resources and supports for Indigenous Peoples experiencing critical illness in Alberta, Canada. Addressing these care gaps may improve health equity, access, and the experience for Indigenous patients and families during critical illness and further build trust and strengthen relationships with health care workers.

items.title: External oblique intercostal plane block improves early postoperative analgesia after open liver surgery: A randomized, double-blind, controlled trial
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: The external oblique intercostal (EOI) plane block is a fascial plane block that targets the unilateral cutaneous branches of intercostal nerves, and spares the sympathetic trunk. We hypothesized that the ultrasound-guided EOI plane block might provide superior analgesia compared to systemic analgesia alone for patients after open liver surgery. METHODS: In this double-blind, randomized controlled trial, 74 patients scheduled for open liver surgery were assigned to receive either EOI plane block with 30 mL of 0.375% ropivacaine (n = 37) or no EOI plane block (n = 37). All patients received postoperative standard patient-controlled intravenous analgesia. Primary outcome was the resting numerical rating scale (NRS) pain score at 3 h postoperatively. The key secondary outcomes included opioid consumption, and the total number of analgesia interventions at 3 h, 6 h, 24 h, 48 h, and 72 h postoperatively; opioid-related side effects and block-related complications; postoperative functional recovery outcomes; total ropivacaine plasma concentrations at 5, 10, 30, 60, 120, and 180 min post-block. RESULTS: The primary outcome, the resting NRS pain score at 3 h postoperatively, was significantly lower in the block group than in the control group. The block group showed a shorter length of hospital stay. There were no significant differences in cumulative opioid consumption, frequency of analgesia, or opioid-related side effects. No block-related complications were observed, and total ropivacaine plasma concentrations remained below the toxicity threshold. CONCLUSIONS: Ultrasound-guided EOI plane block reduces early postoperative pain. This technique should be regarded as a safe and effective component within a comprehensive postoperative multimodal analgesia regimen.

items.title: Arterial-to-end-tidal carbon dioxide gradient as a risk marker for recorded 90-day mortality in intracranial neurosurgery: a retrospective INSPIRE cohort study of patients with early blood gas monitoring
items.abstract: STUDY OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the first-hour arterial-to-end-tidal carbon dioxide gradient as a marker of recorded 90-day mortality, distinguishing association, component interpretation and incremental prediction. DESIGN: Retrospective cohort study. SETTING: INSPIRE v1.4.2, covering surgery from 2011 to 2020. PATIENTS: Adults undergoing their first eligible intracranial operation with arterial carbon dioxide tension (PaCO₂) recorded within 60 min of anesthesia start. End-tidal carbon dioxide (ETCO₂) was paired within ±5 min. MEASUREMENTS: The outcome was database-recorded all-cause death within 90 days. Firth regression evaluated the gradient without conditioning on either component. The revised principal association model included clinical covariates and contemporaneous mean arterial pressure, heart rate and minute ventilation. Component and internally validated prediction models were secondary. MAIN RESULTS: Among 1907 patients, 95 deaths were recorded. The clinical gradient odds ratio (OR) per 5 mmHg was 1.38 (95% confidence interval [CI], 1.09-1.73). The revised principal association model included 1830 patients and 92 events (OR, 1.34; 95% CI, 1.06-1.69). Conditional component estimates did not establish predominance of either component. Adding the gradient to clinical variables, contemporaneous physiology and ETCO₂ changed optimism-corrected area under the curve from 0.832 to 0.833, without improving the Brier score. CONCLUSIONS: A larger first-hour gradient was associated with recorded mortality in patients selected for early paired monitoring. Within the evaluated models and metrics, incremental prediction was limited. These findings do not establish a causal mechanism, treatment target or externally validated prediction tool.

items.title: Screening opens the door, but care must continue: What a large perioperative cohort reveals, and cannot yet resolve, about continuous perioperative alcohol-related care
Deep learning algorithms for predicting intraoperative hypotension: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.abstract: Background Intraoperative hypotension (IOH) is associated with myocardial injury, acute kidney injury, perioperative stroke, and 30-day mortality. Deep learning (DL) refers to a family of machine-learning methods that learn multiple levels of data representation through nonlinear transformations. In perioperative monitoring, DL models can learn patterns from time-varying physiological signals and combine them with clinical variables to estimate impending IOH risk. DL algorithms applied to continuous physiological waveforms therefore represent a rapidly expanding paradigm for early IOH prediction, but their pooled diagnostic accuracy has not been synthesised within a unified diagnostic-accuracy framework. Objective To quantify the pooled diagnostic accuracy of DL-based IOH prediction models and to identify factors that modify their performance. Methods PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library were searched through March 2026. Methodological quality was appraised with PROBAST+AI and certainty of evidence with GRADE. A bivariate random-effects model generated pooled sensitivity, specificity, and SROC-AUC; heterogeneity was quantified by τ 2 (Se), τ 2 (Sp), and ρ. Subgroup analyses (prediction window, DL architecture, modality, IOH reference, analysis unit) and random-effects meta-regression were performed. Results Twelve studies were included; nine contributed 22 validation datasets. Pooled sensitivity was 0.78 (95% CI 0.73-0.81), specificity 0.88 (0.82-0.92), and SROC-AUC 0.87 (0.83-0.90); diagnostic odds ratio 24.7 (16.1-37.9), positive likelihood ratio 6.31, negative likelihood ratio 0.26. Heterogeneity was τ 2 (Se) = 0.25, τ 2 (Sp) = 1.04, ρ = -0.28. The 5-min window achieved the highest performance (sensitivity 0.81; specificity 0.91). Meta-regression identified DL architecture as the only significant moderator of specificity (P = 0.02), with hybrid CNN-RNN exceeding pure CNN (β = 1.77, 95% CI 0.45-3.09). Deeks' test was non-significant (P = 0.06). GRADE certainty was Low. Conclusions DL models for IOH prediction achieve moderate diagnostic accuracy, with hybrid CNN-RNN architectures and 5-min prediction windows showing the most favourable performance. Universal absence of formal calibration assessment, scarce external validation, and geographic concentration constrain immediate clinical translation. Systematic review registration PROSPERO CRD420261377604 Reporting guideline: PRISMA-DTA.

items.title: Preoperative cognitive training for preventing perioperative neurocognitive disorders: A systematic review and meta-analysis with trial sequential analysis and meta-regression of randomised controlled trials
items.abstract: Study objective Although nonpharmacological interventions are recommended for preventing perioperative neurocognitive disorders (PND), cognitive training has not been explicitly advocated. Therefore, this systematic review and meta-analysis with trial sequential analysis (TSA) and meta-regression tested the hypothesis that preoperative cognitive training, compared with usual care, reduces the incidence of PND. Methods Eight databases and two clinical trial registries were searched for RCTs comparing preoperative cognitive training with usual care. Primary outcomes were postoperative delirium (POD), delayed neurocognitive recovery (DNR), and postoperative neurocognitive disorder. Results Thirteen RCTs with 1446 patients were identified. Preoperative cognitive training was associated with a lower risk of POD (RR 0.53; 95% CI 0.36-0.77; P = 0.001; low certainty). Subgroup analysis (P for interaction = 0.01) and meta-regression (β1 1.072, 95% CI 0.006-2.138, P = 0.049) suggested an association between training format and treatment effect on POD, with a potentially greater benefit for traditional training. For DNR, the incidence was lower in the training group than in the usual care group (RR 0.66; 95% CI 0.46-0.96; P = 0.03; very low certainty), but this finding was not supported by several sensitivity analyses. No significant differences were detected between subgroups for training format, total duration, or surgery type (P for interaction = 0.06, 0.37, and 0.34, respectively), and meta-regression suggested that overall risk of bias was a potential moderator for DNR (P = 0.045). TSA suggested a potential for false-positive findings, as the cumulative Z-curves did not cross the TSA boundaries, and the required information sizes were not reached for either outcome. Conclusions Preoperative cognitive training may reduce the incidence of POD, with traditional training showing a potentially greater benefit than digital training. For DNR, the current evidence is insufficient to support a preventive effect of preoperative cognitive training, although a trend toward benefit was observed. These findings are limited by high risk of bias in several included trials and failure to reach the required information sizes in TSA, particularly for DNR, which need to be confirmed in future large-scale RCTs. Systematic review protocol PROSPERO (CRD420261293607).

items.title: Beyond objective demographics: The roles of subjective perception, state of consciousness, and language concordance in patient satisfaction
Intraoperative hypotension and postoperative acute kidney injury: Evidence and controversies
items.abstract: Acute kidney injury (AKI) remains one of the most common serious complications after noncardiac surgery, and intraoperative hypotension (IOH) is consistently identified as a modifiable risk factor. Observational studies show a consistent, roughly dose-response association between IOH, particularly at mean arterial pressures below 60-65 mmHg, and postoperative AKI, with stronger associations in patients with limited renal reserve. Definitions of IOH vary widely, which complicates the comparison of studies and the translation of thresholds into clinical targets. Randomized trials of individualized or higher blood pressure targets have generally not confirmed a kidney-protective benefit, and pooled analyses with trial sequential analysis have not demonstrated that higher targets reduce AKI. This narrative review examines how IOH definitions evolved, summarizes the conflicting intervention evidence, and assesses the controversies that shape current practice. The review concludes that avoiding severe and sustained hypotension remains reasonable, whereas current randomized trial evidence does not support a general kidney-protective benefit of higher or individualized blood pressure targets. This conclusion is provisional and is tempered by the methodologic and causal uncertainties.

items.title: Observational study for perioperative intensive care unit (OPICU): Planned and unplanned ICU admissions, follow-up, discharge, and outcomes
items.abstract: Introduction Due to limited resources, identifying high-risk surgical patients who derive clinical benefit from Intensive Care Unit (ICU) admission is essential. Our primary aim was to characterize resource allocation and evaluate the true clinical benefit of ICU admissions using modified Wang criteria. Secondary aim is to identify independent risk factors for ICU admission; validate clinical scoring systems; and compare inter-group outcomes, including Clavien-Dindo complication rates, lengths of stay, and mortality. Materials and methods This multicenter, prospective, observational study was conducted across 75 ICUs. Adult inpatient surgery cases were categorized into four groups: planned admission (PAG), unplanned admission (UPAG), planned but not admitted (PBNAG), and emergent admission (EAG). Data included preoperative/intraoperative/postoperative(ICU) variables, modified Wang criteria, and mortality rates (ICU, hospital, 30/90-day). Results Of 55,963 preoperatively evaluated patients, 2764 (4.9%) were planned for ICU admission; 804/2764 patients could not be admitted because of limited ICU beds, remaining of 1960 patients with a planned ICU admission, 411/1960 did not require postoperative ICU care forming the PBNAG (14.8% of 2764). Overall, 1980 patients (3.09% of all cases) were admitted to the ICU (78.2% PAG, 12.5% EAG, 9.1% UPAG). POSSUM scores effectively differentiated PBNAG (lower) and EAG (higher) from PAG. ICU benefit indicators (e.g., vasopressor need, prolonged ventilation >12 h, arrest events) were significantly higher in UPAG and EAG versus PAG (p 2 (OR 2.7) independently increased UPAG risk, whereas minimally invasive surgery and regional anesthesia reduced ICU admissions. Overall ICU and 90-day mortality rates were 5.9% and 7.5%, respectively, peaking in the EAG group (18.1% and 18.9%). Conclusion Integrating modified Wang criteria, POSSUM scores, intraoperative complications, emergency status, and ASA class >2 is effective in predicting the necessity of ICU admission.

items.title: Infraorbital versus sphenopalatine ganglion block for patient-reported recovery after septorhinoplasty: A randomized controlled trial
items.abstract: Study objective To compare ultrasound-guided infraorbital nerve block with transnasal sphenopalatine ganglion block on recovery quality 24 h after septorhinoplasty. Design Prospective, randomized, patient- and assessor-blinded, parallel-group trial. Setting Tertiary training hospital; operating room and postoperative ward. Patients Ninety adults aged 18 to 65 years, ASA physical status I or II, undergoing elective septorhinoplasty; 89 were analyzed. Interventions After induction of general anesthesia, patients received bilateral transnasal sphenopalatine ganglion block (SPG group) or bilateral ultrasound-guided infraorbital nerve block (IO group), 2 mL of 0.5% bupivacaine per side. Surgical infiltration and multimodal analgesia were identical in both groups. Measurements The primary outcome was the total Quality of Recovery-15 (QoR-15) score at 24 h. Secondary outcomes were QoR-15 domains, visual analog scale pain scores, rescue morphine, nausea and vomiting, anesthetic consumption, emergence agitation, edema, ecchymosis and recovery room stay. Main results Total QoR-15 at 24 h was higher in the IO group (129.1 ± 9.4 versus 116.6 ± 11.7; mean difference 12.5 points, 95% CI 8.01 to 17.01; P = 0.001), above the prespecified minimal clinically important difference of 8. More IO patients crossed the acceptable symptom state threshold of 118 (86.4% versus 35.6%; P Conclusions Infraorbital nerve block gave better 24 h patient-reported recovery than sphenopalatine ganglion block after septorhinoplasty. Secondary findings are hypothesis-generating. Trial registration ClinicalTrials.govNCT06929429.

items.title: From cognitive decline to cognitive resilience: Interpreting perioperative cognitive trajectories
Remembering Simon Gelman, MD, PhD, FANZCA: A legacy of academic excellence, innovation, and mentorship
Short-term peripheral nerve stimulation for pain relief in adults: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
items.abstract: Background Short-term peripheral nerve stimulation serves as a neuromodulation therapy that modulates neural activity to provide therapeutic benefit, particularly pain relief. This study investigated the effectiveness of short-term peripheral nerve stimulation as a minimally invasive approach for achieving pain relief. Methods We systematically searched PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Scopus, MEDLINE, Cochrane Library, and Google Scholar from database inception till September 10, 2026, for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) in adults comparing short-term peripheral nerve stimulation with sham stimulation or usual care. The primary outcome was the change in average pain intensity during the implantation period. Results Eight RCTs (543 participants) were included. Compared with the control group, the intervention group showed significant reductions in average pain intensity during the implantation period at 1-4 weeks (SMD = -0.48, 95% CI = -0.71 to -0.26, P Conclusion This meta-analysis provided preliminary evidence that short-term peripheral nerve stimulation may relieve pain during the implantation period, but not all outcomes suggest sustained improvements after electrode removal. Registration prospero CRD420251243978.

items.title: Peripheral nerve block injection pressure monitoring: A systematic review
items.abstract: Study objective To determine whether injection pressure and pressure-time characteristics can discriminate potentially hazardous needle-tip locations during peripheral nerve injection. Design Systematic review of experimental preclinical studies with narrative synthesis. Setting Animal, ex vivo biological nerve, and human cadaver models of peripheral nerve injection. Interventions Needle placement and injection at intraneural, intrafascicular, perineural, or extraneural locations. Measurements CENTRAL, PubMed, Embase, and Web of Science were searched from inception to April 28, 2026 and updated on September 19, 2026. Studies reporting opening, peak, or plateau pressure or pressure-time characteristics in relation to anatomically defined needle-tip location were eligible. Human clinical studies and non-biological bench models were excluded. Risk of bias was evaluated using SYRCLE for animal studies and a domain-based framework for cadaveric studies. Because of substantial heterogeneity in experimental models, injection techniques, and pressure definitions, meta-analysis was not considered appropriate. Main results Twenty-eight studies met the inclusion criteria: 12 animal or animal ex vivo studies and 16 human cadaver studies. Intraneural injection was generally associated with higher peak and plateau pressures than perineural injection, but substantial overlap occurred across needle locations. Importantly, low pressure did not reliably rule out intraneural injection, while elevated pressure was also observed during needle-nerve contact and fascial injection. Consequently, the commonly proposed 15-psi threshold showed inconsistent sensitivity across experimental settings. Lower thresholds, including 12 psi, appeared more sensitive in some models but have not been clinically validated. Beyond absolute pressure values, the rate of pressure rise and pressure-time curve morphology showed potential for differentiating needle-tip locations. Conclusions Injection pressure monitoring may provide a nonspecific warning of needle placement within or against a poorly compliant structure. However, preclinical evidence alone cannot establish whether it should be used routinely or whether it reduces nerve injury. No universal pressure threshold or clinically recommended injection rate can currently be defined.

items.title: Processed electroencephalogram-guided anesthesia and its impact on postoperative delirium and perioperative efficiency: A systematic review and meta-analysis
Anterior inferior psoas epimysial injection: a cadaveric feasibility study of an anterior pathway to the lumbar plexus
Guidelines for Decisions to Withhold or Withdraw Life-Sustaining Treatments (LST) in Adult ICU
items.abstract: OBJECTIVE: The French Society of Anaesthesia and Intensive Care Medicine (Société française d'anesthésie et de réanimation, SFAR) and the French Society of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation (Société Française de Médecine Physique et de Réadaptation (SOFMER)) aimed at providing guidelines for decisions to withhold or withdraw life-sustaining treatments (LST) in adult ICU. DESIGN: A consensus committee of 20 experts from the SFAR and the SOFMER was convened. A formal conﬂict-of-interest (COI) policy was developed at the beginning of the process and enforced throughout. The entire guideline construction process was conducted independently of any industrial funding (i.e., pharmaceutical, medical devices). The authors were required to follow the rules of the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) system to guide the assessment of the quality of evidence. The potential drawbacks of making strong recommendations in the presence of low-quality evidence were emphasized. METHODS: 3 fields were defined: (1) modalities of the LST decision-making process; (2) modalities for implementing an LST decision; (3) Relationships with family members, communication, disagreements, and conflicts. For each field, the objective of the recommendations was to answer a number of questions formulated according to the PICO model (population, intervention, comparison, and outcomes). Based on these questions, an extensive bibliographic search was carried out using predefined keywords according to PRISMA guidelines and analyzed using the GRADE® methodology. The recommendations were formulated according to the GRADE® methodology and then voted on by all the experts according to the GRADE® grid method. RESULTS: The experts' work on synthesis and application of the GRADE® method resulted in 9 recommendations. Among the formalized recommendations, 1 was found to have a high level of evidence (GRADE 1), and 2 had low levels of evidence (GRADE 2). For 6 recommendations, the GRADE® methodology could not be fully applied, resulting in an expert's opinion. 2 questions could not be answered due to a lack of literature. After 1 round of rating, strong agreement was reached for all the recommendations. CONCLUSIONS: There was strong agreement among experts to provide recommendations to improve practices for decisions to withhold or withdraw LST in the adult ICU.

items.title: Intraoperative ventilatory settings during abdominal surgery among 1,091 anesthesia providers
items.abstract: Background Data are lacking regarding current ventilatory settings during abdominal surgery. Expert recommendations emphasize the need for protective ventilation, and several tools are now available to individualize positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP). Methods We conducted a nationwide cross-sectional survey among French anesthesiologists and nurse anesthetists in November 2025 to assess ventilatory settings during abdominal surgery, both for laparotomy and laparoscopy. Protective ventilation was defined as the combination of low tidal volume (6-8 mL/kg predicted body weight), low-to-moderate PEEP (5-8 cm H 2 O), and recruitment maneuvers. Individualization of PEEP was defined as the use of driving pressure, mechanical power, or compliance to titrate PEEP. Results Among 1091 anesthesiologists and nurse anesthetists, female responders accounted for 46% (497/1084), the median age of anesthesia providers was 39 (33-47) years, and most responders (77%, 839/1090) had an adult-based main field of activity. Main ventilatory settings used during laparotomy were 6 to 8 ml/kg of predicted body weight (93%, 1013/1084), a respiratory rate set according to EtCO 2 in 53% of responders (579/1084), and a PEEP set between 5 and 8 cmH 2 0 for 87% of responders (950/1091). Most participants performed recruitment maneuvers (98%, 1065/1091). Overall, protective ventilation was used in 70% (763/1090), and individualization of PEEP in 45% (479/1054). Similar ventilatory settings were reported for laparoscopy. Conclusions In this nationwide survey, expert consensus-based recommendations for protective ventilation during abdominal surgery appeared widely implemented in France. In contrast, individualized PEEP strategies were reported in fewer than half of cases, reflecting ongoing uncertainty and variability regarding PEEP titration in routine perioperative practice.

items.title: It’s time for a personalized approach to vasopressin
Establishing expert consensus on essential perioperative management components for hip fracture patients aged over 75: a national modified Delphi study
items.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Anesthesiologists play a central role in optimizing perioperative care and improving outcomes for patients with hip fractures (HF). Standardized care bundles are essential to guide clinicians, enhance expertise, and improve overall quality of care. We conducted a nationwide modified Delphi study to establish French expert consensus on key components of a standardized care bundle for patients over 75 years old with HF. METHODS: A two-round modified Delphi process was conducted with 30 multidisciplinary experts representative of major French academic societies to assess consensus on perioperative care practices for HF in patients over 75. Experts rated 34 clinically relevant items using a 9-point Likert scale, with consensus defined as ≥70% rating ranging from 7 to 9 for agreement or 1 to 3 for disagreement. The process was conducted via the REDCap platform and adhered to ethical and data protection standards. RESULTS: The expert panel included 11 (36.7%) anesthesiologists, 9 (30%) geriatricians, 6 (20%) orthopedic surgeons, and 4 (13.3%) hospital pharmacists. Agreement consensus was reached for 29 out of 34 proposed items. A shortlist of 12 items that achieved over 90% consensus was identified, comprising 2 organizational, 7 perioperative, and 3 surgical items. DISCUSSION: The bundle of care for HF elaborated in this study provides perioperative teams with clear, actionable objectives to improve care quality and equity. Its impact on patient outcomes warrants further evaluation.

items.title: Sex Differences in Vasopressor De-escalation With Arginine Vasopressin in Mixed Cardiogenic-Vasodilatory Shock Under VA-ECMO
items.abstract: BACKGROUNDS: Women with cardiogenic shock (CS) under VA-ECMO face excess mortality, yet the pharmacological basis of this disparity remains poorly understood. Arginine vasopressin (AVP) is increasingly used as a non-adrenergic vasopressor in this setting, but whether sex modifies the hemodynamic response to AVP is unknown. METHODS: In this multicenter retrospective cohort of VA-ECMO-supported CS patients, we assessed whether sex was independently associated with successful vasopressor de-escalation at 48 hours (norepinephrine equivalent dose [NEE] <0.25 µg/kg/min) after AVP initiation. Multivariable logistic regression and linear mixed-effects models were used to evaluate sex differences in treatment response and NEE trajectories over time. RESULTS: Among 193 eligible patients, 32% of women achieved successful de-escalation versus 49% of men (p = 0.023). Male sex was independently associated with treatment success (aOR 2.08, 95% CI 1.07-4.15, p = 0.033). A significant sex-by-time interaction was observed in NEE trajectories (p = 0.041), with divergence emerging at 48 hours (NEE 0.24 vs. 0.01 µg/kg/min, p = 0.008). The excess failure risk was confined to postmenopausal women aged ≥55 years (aOR 2.75, 95% CI 1.32-5.93, p = 0.008). CONCLUSION: Female sex, particularly in a postmenopausal context, was independently associated with impaired vasopressor de-escalation following AVP in CS on VA-ECMO. These hypothesis-generating findings suggest that hormonal status may modulate vascular responsiveness to AVP and support the need for prospective studies incorporating hormonal profiling.

items.title: Systemic hypotension in anaesthetised neonates, infants and children: beyond blood pressure thresholds—practical considerations
items.abstract: This technical note is meant to be complementary to the recently published Professional Practice Guidelines of the SFAR-ADARPEF. The limits of using blood pressure as a surrogate for changes in cardiac output and the variable accuracy of its non-invasive measurement are reminded. As clearcut population-based threshold values based on measurements obtained in awake or anaesthetised children cannot be provided, an adaptation based on the child's baseline blood pressure, comorbidity and surgical context is necessary to prevent unnecessary treatment of an acceptable low blood pressure or tolerating a too low blood pressure. The measurement of a baseline awake blood pressure, although often difficult to achieve in children, is therefore very helpful. If a low intraoperative MAP is measured, the presence of hypotension should be confirmed by repeat measurement and the simultaneous evaluation of clinical and paraclinical signs, and the observation of the surgical field. The treatment should then be adapted to the cause: anaesthetic overdose, hypovolaemia, positioning, surgical action, anaphylaxis, etc.

items.title: High-flow oxygen for apnea testing in brain death determination
items.abstract: Background Apnea testing is mandatory for brain death determination but may induce hypoxemia despite standard preoxygenation procedures. High-flow oxygen (HFO) systems may improve apneic oxygenation during the procedure, although clinical data remain limited. Methods We conducted a retrospective single-center cohort study including consecutive adult patients undergoing apnea testing for brain death determination between January 2023 and May 2026. Standard oxygen insufflation (6-15 L/min) was compared with HFO delivered through the Opt970® interface (Fisher & Paykel) at 50 L/min and FiO 2 1.0. The primary outcome was longitudinal pulse oximetry saturation (SpO 2 ) evolution during apnea testing. Secondary outcomes included desaturation events and arterial blood gas parameters. Repeated SpO 2 measurements were analyzed using a linear mixed-effects model. Results A total of 144 apnea tests were analyzed, including 78 using standard oxygen insufflation and 66 using HFO. Baseline characteristics and ventilatory parameters were comparable between groups. Lowest SpO 2 during apnea testing was significantly higher with HFO (100 [98-100] vs. 99 [95-99]; p = 0.003), while desaturation below 94% occurred less frequently (9.1% vs. 21.8%; p = 0.04). Post-test PaCO 2 was slightly higher in the HFO group (73 [67-81] vs. 70 [62-77] mmHg; p = 0.04). Longitudinal mixed-effects analysis demonstrated a significant decrease in SpO 2 over time in both groups (p 2 values throughout the procedure (β=+1.38; standard error 0.69; p = 0.047), without significant group-by-time interaction (p = 0.578). Conclusion HFO delivered through the Opt970® device was associated with modestly higher oxygen saturation during apnea testing compared with standard oxygen insufflation. Further prospective studies are required to confirm these findings.

items.title: The Carbon Footprint of Clinical Artificial Intelligence in Anaesthesiology: An Order-of-Magnitude Comparison with Current Clinical Practice
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly reshaping anaesthesiology and critical care, enhancing physiological monitoring, perioperative risk prediction, and clinical decision-making. As its adoption accelerates, attention has increasingly turned to the environmental consequences of digital healthcare, raising important questions regarding the energy consumption and carbon footprint associated with clinical AI. This study examines the environmental implications of AI in anaesthesiology and critical care by placing computational emissions within the broader context of healthcare sustainability. Current evidence indicates that, although AI systems generate measurable greenhouse gas emissions, their operational carbon footprint remains several orders of magnitude lower than that of established sources of emissions, including volatile anaesthetic agents, intensive care, and surgical care. Quantitative comparisons, complemented by an illustrative environmental break-even analysis, suggest that even modest improvements in healthcare efficiency may be sufficient to offset the operational emissions of current clinical AI applications. These findings indicate that the sustainability of clinical AI should not be judged solely by its computational footprint, but by its overall environmental value. The relevant question is not simply how much AI emits, but whether its implementation reduces resource utilisation, avoids unnecessary healthcare activities, and generates environmental savings that outweigh its own operational costs. Achieving this objective will require computationally efficient model design, low-carbon digital infrastructures, lifecycle assessment, and the routine integration of environmental metrics into AI evaluation. Rather than representing a major new source of healthcare emissions, clinical AI should be viewed as an opportunity to advance both digital innovation and environmental stewardship. By integrating sustainability alongside clinical effectiveness, anaesthesiologists are uniquely positioned to guide the responsible development and implementation of AI technologies that benefit both patients and the healthcare systems in which they are delivered.

items.title: Confounding by indication beyond exposure misclassification in cesarean anesthesia and postpartum depression
VentiProtect ARDS, vibe coding lung protection: a five-minute clinician-built ventilator tool as proof-of-concept for physician prompt engineering
items.abstract: Lung-protective ventilation in acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) remains under-applied at the bedside, partly due to the absence of integrated, context-aware decision-support tools. Large language models (LLMs) with advanced code generation capabilities have created a new possibility: physicians can now build the bedside tools they need without depending on software vendors or programming expertise. This practice, broadly termed "vibe coding", has entered medical discourse but has not been formally evaluated as a clinical competency. We report the development of VentiProtect ARDS, a real-time ventilator titration assistant built by a single physician in a single session of 4 minutes 25 seconds, as a proof-of-concept for physician prompt engineering: the structured translation of clinical knowledge into a natural-language specification that constrains LLM code generation. A structured eight-block prompt was developed through an iterative pre-prompt reasoning process and submitted to Claude Opus 4.6 via the Antigravity agentic development environment. The generated application computes predicted body weight, tidal volume, driving pressure, respiratory system compliance, mechanical power, and oxygenation index, with real-time colour-coded alerts and an active suggestion engine that calculates exact corrective ventilator settings. Formula accuracy was verified using an independent automated test suite of 100 scenarios (1,400 individual checks) with no computational errors identified. The tool runs locally with no installation, network dependency, or patient data transmission. This proof-of-concept suggests that physician prompt engineering may represent a potential clinical competency that does not require programming experience, although a single self-performed case cannot establish it across physicians. The LLM generates syntax. The physician generates medicine.

items.title: Assessing the ecotoxicological impact of drugs used in anesthesia and intensive care: do we have enough data and tools?
ECMO Weaning Blood Processing: A Scoping Review
items.abstract: Background Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) has been widely used for life support in severe refractory cardiac and respiratory failure. During ECMO weaning, the circuit usually retains 500-800 mL of residual blood. Direct discarding leads to blood loss, increased anemia, and higher allogeneic transfusion requirements, while appropriate autologous blood reinfusion can reduce transfusion risks and medical costs. However, evidence on blood processing strategies during ECMO weaning remains scattered, and no unified clinical guidelines exist. Methods This scoping review strictly followed the PRISMA‑ScR 2018 checklist and JBI methodology. We systematically searched PubMed, Embase, Web of Science Core Collection, Cochrane Library, CNKI, and Wanfang from inception to March 28, 2026. Two reviewers independently screened literature, extracted data, and assessed quality. Descriptive synthesis and qualitative analysis were performed due to high heterogeneity and lack of randomized controlled trials (RCTs). Results A total of 68 articles were retrieved, and 9 studies were finally included. The identified blood processing strategies were classified into four categories: blood cell salvage system (BCS) autologous reinfusion, pump-controlled blood reinfusion, modified CPD blood bag storage reinfusion, and direct discard. Conclusion Based on current observational evidence, autologous blood reinfusion during ECMO weaning appears feasible and is associated with favorable surrogate hematological outcomes compared with direct discard. Identified strategies differ in indications, operation, and costs, and may be selected individually according to ECMO mode, hemodynamic status, and institutional conditions. Given the limited number, low quality, and high heterogeneity of included studies, no conclusions regarding hard clinical outcomes can be drawn. This review highlights the urgency of high‑quality studies with long‑term clinical endpoints to further verify efficacy and safety.

items.title: Hemoadsorption to prevent acute kidney injury in elective cardiac surgery: a systematic review of randomized controlled trials with meta-analysis and trial sequential analysis
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: This meta-analysis aimed to evaluate whether intraoperative hemoadsorption during cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) improves postoperative outcomes compared with the standard of care. METHODS: We systematically searched EMBASE, PubMed, and the Cochrane Library for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing hemoadsorption versus standard care in patients undergoing cardiac surgery with CPB. Data were analyzed using a frequentist approach and trial sequential analysis (TSA). The primary outcome was the incidence of cardiac surgery-associated acute kidney injury (CSA-AKI) within 7 days after surgery. The protocol was prospectively registered in PROSPERO (CRD42025634991). RESULTS: A total of six RCTs comprising 798 patients were included. Four RCTs (n = 723; 355 hemoadsorption, 368 control) reported CSA-AKI incidence, which did not significantly differ between groups (RR = 0.93 [95% CI: 0.71-1.21], p = 0.57; I² = 42.0%). Hemoadsorption was not associated with significant differences in secondary outcomes: interleukin-6, tumor necrosis factor, 28-day mortality, SOFA score, and ICU length of stay. CONCLUSION: Hemoadsorption during CPB was not associated with a reduction in CSA-AKI or with improvement in secondary clinical outcomes in elective patients undergoing cardiac surgery. However, the accrued sample represented only 48% of the heterogeneity-adjusted required information size (1,491 patients), and the cumulative Z-curve crossed neither the monitoring nor the futility boundary. REGISTRATION: PROSPERO International Register of Systematic Reviews (CRD42025634991; January 31, 2025).

items.title: I-gelTM Plus implements higher oropharyngeal leak pressure in the lateral decubitus position than original i-gelTM: a prospective randomized controlled trial
items.abstract: Background The supraglottic airway device i-gel TM Plus (Intersurgical Ltd., Berkshire, UK) may provide more secure ventilation than the original i-gel TM (Intersurgical Ltd., Berkshire, UK). This prospective randomized trial was conducted to evaluate the performance of i-gel TM Plus compared with the original i-gel TM in patients in the lateral decubitus position under general anesthesia with a neuromuscular blocking drug. Methods We inserted two types of i-gel TM in the supine position in adult patients undergoing general anesthesia with 0.6 mg/kg IV rocuronium. The primary outcome was oropharyngeal leak pressure in the lateral position. Secondary outcomes included expiratory tidal volume and glottic view in that position. Results We analyzed 84 surgical patients in the i-gel TM Plus [n = 42] and original i-gel TM [n = 42] groups. The oropharyngeal leak pressure and expiratory tidal volume at the oropharyngeal leak pressure in the supine position were similar between the two groups. The lateral decubitus position demonstrated higher oropharyngeal leak pressure (P TM Plus group (median [interquartile range], 22 [20-25] cmH 2 O and 694 [602-750] ml, respectively) than in the original i-gel TM group (15 [14-18] cmH 2 O and 470 [420-634] ml, respectively). However, fiberoptic glottis view grade scores did not differ between the two groups. Conclusion The i-gel TM Plus implements higher oropharyngeal leak pressure in the lateral decubitus position than the original i-gel TM . Our results indicate that the i-gel TM Plus may be a better choice as a supraglottic airway device in the lateral decubitus position than the original i-gel TM in paralyzed patients. Registration University Hospital Medical Information Network (UMIN000061937).

items.title: Withholding Pre-emptive Antibiotics After Pancreaticoduodenectomy in Patients with Biliary Colonization: A Multicenter Propensity Score-Matched Cohort Study
items.abstract: Background Pre-emptive antibiotic therapy is frequently prescribed after pancreaticoduodenectomy when intraoperative bile cultures are positive, despite the absence of clinical infection. Evidence supporting this practice remains limited. We assessed the association between withholding pre-emptive antibiotics and postoperative outcomes in patients with biliary colonization. Methods This multicenter retrospective cohort study included 301 consecutive adults undergoing pancreaticoduodenectomy with positive intraoperative bile cultures in four French tertiary centers between January 2014 and December 2024. Overall, 89 patients received PE-ATB, and 212 did not. Propensity score matching at a 1:2 ratio yielded 138 patients, including 46 treated patients and 92 controls. The primary outcome was 5-year overall survival. Secondary postoperative outcomes were examined using prespecified exploratory non-inferiority margins. Results Preoperative biliary stenting independently predicted PE-ATB use (odds ratio, 4.11; 95% confidence interval, 1.26-13.40;P = 0.019). In the matched cohort, withholding PE-ATB was compatible with the non-inferiority margin for intra-abdominal abscess, pancreatic fistula, transfusion requirements, and antibiotic duration. Overall postoperative infection did not differ significantly between groups (odds ratio, 1.42; 95% confidence interval, 0.66-3.07; P = 0.376). Five-year mortality was higher in the group without PE-ATB in the matched cohort (hazard ratio, 2.02; 95% confidence interval, 1.01-4.04; P = 0.048), whereas no survival difference was observed in the overall unmatched cohort. Conclusions Withholding PE-ATB was not associated with worse early postoperative outcomes and was associated with reduced antibiotic exposure. The survival difference observed only after matching should be considered cautiously and may reflect residual confounding. Prospective randomized trials are needed.

items.title: From Microbial burden to host response dysregulation: toward host-centered precision medicine in severe pneumonia and pneumonia-associated sepsis
Which spontaneous breathing trial should be used to reproduce post-extubation respiratory effort in COVID-19-related ARDS? A multicenter randomized crossover study
items.abstract: Background Spontaneous breathing trials (SBT) guide extubation decisions in intensive care unit (ICU), predicting the respiratory effort required by the patient after extubation. Different SBTs exist and should be adapted to critical illness. Viral pneumonias such as COVID-19 combine lung injury, sepsis-induced systemic inflammation, and encephalopathy, making classification challenging. The objective was to assess which SBT could be used to reproduce postextubation respiratory effort in COVID-19-related acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) patients. Methods In this multicenter randomized crossover study, COVID-19-related ARDS patients mechanically ventilated at least 24 hours and ready for extubation underwent 3 different 15-minute SBT at random order: pressure support ventilation of 7-cmH2O with positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) of 0-cmH2O (PSV7PEEP0), PSV 0-cmH2O with PEEP 0-cmH2O (PSV0PEEP0) and T-piece trial. At baseline, end of each SBT, and 20 minutes after extubation, surrogates of respiratory effort were measured: esophageal pressure-time-product (PTPes), PTPes per minute (PTPes.min), swing esophageal pressure (SwingPes), and SwingPes per minute (SwingPes.min). Results Sixty measurements of respiratory effort from 12 patients were analyzed. Median PTPes.min increased from 193.8 [170.8-227.2] cmH2O.s/min at baseline to 236.6 [192.1-313.6] after extubation, with no significant differences between SBTs and postextubation. SwingPes and SwingPes.min were lower during PSV7-PEEP0 than after extubation, with median paired differences of 4.7 (95% CI 0.6-9.8) and 115.3 (95% CI 4.8-297.8), but these differences did not remain significant after correction for multiple comparisons. Conclusion No SBT modality differed significantly from post-extubation respiratory effort, suggesting that none could be excluded in COVID-19-related ARDS patients.

items.title: Anticholinergic Drug Burden and Postoperative Delirium: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.abstract: Introduction Postoperative delirium (POD) is an important postoperative neurocognitive complication, and cumulative anticholinergic drug burden (ADB) may increase its risk by impairing central cholinergic neurotransmission. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to clarify the overall association between ADB scores and POD risk in adult surgical patients. Methods We searched major databases and trial registries through February 2026 for studies that assessed ADB using validated scales and reported POD outcomes in adult surgical patients. Random-effects models pooled SMDs and ORs. Prespecified subgroup and sensitivity analyses explored heterogeneity and robustness. Risk of bias was assessed using NOS, and evidence certainty was rated using GRADE. Results Ten reports from nine independent cohorts comprising 10,457 participants were included. Patients with POD had higher ADB scores than those without POD (SMD = 0.31, 95% CI: 0.20-0.43). Each one-point increase in continuous ADB was associated with 22% higher odds of POD (OR = 1.22, 95% CI: 1.09-1.37). Both low-to-moderate and high burden were associated with increased POD risk. In scale-specific analyses, the association was significant for ACB. The association was attenuated in studies that excluded patients with cognitive impairment. Methodological quality ranged from moderate to high, and certainty of evidence was low. Conclusions Higher ADB is significantly associated with higher odds of POD, with a graded increase in risk across burden levels. Baseline cognitive impairment appears to amplify this association. These findings support preoperative ADB assessment and medication optimization in vulnerable surgical patients, while highlighting the need for prospective head-to-head comparisons of anticholinergic burden scales. Registration PROSPERO (CRD420261294941).

items.title: Impact of additional tailored Information and music to reduce preoperative anxiety in surgical outpatients: a prospective before-after study
items.abstract: Introduction Non-pharmacological techniques have recently been developed to decrease preoperative anxiety, and music or video may be combined, as in children. This study aims to compare two additional preoperative strategies in adult outpatients. Patients and method This before-after trial was approved by the ethics committee and included adults undergoing ambulatory procedures under general anaesthesia. It compared usual care before surgery and another period with a video of the expected local journey combined with a relaxing music session. After consent, the level of anxiety was measured via the APAIS score, a repeated visual analogue scale for anxiety, and investigators collected preoperative fears. The main objective was to reduce the number of patients with significant preoperative anxiety. Secondary outcomes compared anxiety during the journey, pain, and quality of recovery after surgery. A P-value Results 99 patients were included in each period, and 194 completed the study. The intervention group showed a significant reduction in the rate of patients with significant anxiety at admission in the operating room: 23/95 (24.2%, 95%CI [16.7-33.7]) vs. 43/99 (43.4%, 95%CI [34.1-53.3]) with P = 0.005. Secondary outcomes showed no difference in anxiety after surgery, neither in length of stay nor incidence of PONV. The postoperative level of pain was also statistically reduced (P = 0.033). Conclusion The study suggests that a combined video and music strategy decreases the rate of significant anxiety in patients undergoing outpatient procedures. This low-cost strategy showed a high level of satisfaction and should be encouraged in adults. Trial registration Clinicaltrials.gov: NCT06461052.

items.title: Effect of a Tailored Educational Programme on Adequacy of Anaesthesia and Major Postoperative Complications: A Before–After Quality-Improvement Study in Intermediate- and High-Risk Surgery
