items.abstract: Background State Entropy (SE) and Surgical Pleth Index (SPI) parameters aim to optimise anaesthetic depth and intraoperative opioid administration, but their impact on postoperative complications remains unclear. Insufficient training and limited decision support may contribute to inconsistent findings. Thus, we evaluated whether tailored training to improve SE and SPI compliance reduced major postoperative complications. Methods Adult inpatients undergoing intermediate- to high-risk noncardiac surgery were included in this prospective single-centre before-after study in France. The educational intervention and outcomes were based on the Kirkpatrick framework. All anaesthesia providers were invited to participate voluntarily in lectures and bedside training on SE and SPI monitoring. Training impact was assessed using a composite of major postoperative complications within 28 days as the primary outcome. Secondary outcomes included changes in monitoring practices. Results Among 1,623 eligible patients, 1,025 were included over a 13-month period (517 before and 508 after training). Of 202 eligible providers, 91 participated in the one-month training programme (45%). After training, simultaneous SE and SPI sensor use increased from 26% to 42% (P Conclusion This training did not reduce the incidence of major postoperative complications, despite improvements in intraoperative monitoring practices. Future educational strategies should strengthen provider engagement and reinforcement to translate improved monitoring practices into clinical benefit. Registration ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT06111248.

items.title: Procedure-specific bleeding risk assessment: a multidisciplinary expert consensus companion to the 2026 periprocedural anticoagulant management guidelines
items.abstract: Background Periprocedural anticoagulant management requires balancing thrombotic risk against procedure-specific bleeding risk. Existing procedure bleeding risk classifications are fragmented across specialties, inconsistent in methodology, and rarely extend beyond a few procedural domains, limiting their clinical applicability. Objective To develop a comprehensive, standardized, procedure-specific bleeding risk classification to accompany the 2026 GIHP-SFAR periprocedural anticoagulant management guidelines. Methods A formal multidisciplinary consensus was conducted under the auspices of GIHP and SFAR, in collaboration with 24 surgical and interventional specialty societies. For each procedural domain, a working group performed a systematic literature review. Procedures were classified into four tiers: no bleeding risk, low bleeding risk, high bleeding risk, and very high bleeding risk. A specific category was created for procedures carrying particular contextual risk (e.g., anatomical site, patient factors, or need for reversible anticoagulation). Consensus was reached by the full expert panel. Results Twenty-four procedural domains were classified, ranging from regional anaesthesia and digestive endoscopy to cardiac surgery, neurosurgery, and ophthalmology. Each domain provides a procedure-specific bleeding risk table, with narrative supporting evidence. Procedures warranting delayed resumption of anticoagulation (≥72 hours) or use of short-acting/reversible anticoagulants are identified. The classification covers common and complex surgical scenarios, including those with limited published evidence where structured expert opinion was applied. Conclusion This companion document provides clinicians with a standardized, evidence-based, procedure-specific bleeding risk framework across 24 domains to support individualized periprocedural anticoagulant decisions in daily practice.

items.title: Dysnatremia in critically ill burn patients: incidence, timing and association with kidney outcomes
items.abstract: Background Dysnatremia is common in critically ill patients and has been linked to poor outcomes and renal prognosis. Burn patients are particularly vulnerable, but the prognostic significance of dysnatremia in this population remains unclear. Methods We conducted a single-center retrospective cohort study of 1,758 burn patients admitted to a French burn center between 2011 and 2023. Dysnatremia was defined as at least one episode of hyponatremia ( 145 mmol/L) during intensive care unit (ICU) stay. The primary endpoint was the incidence of dysnatremia; secondary endpoints included major adverse kidney events (MAKE) at ICU discharge and acute kidney injury (AKI) occurrence and severity. Results Dysnatremia occurred in 56.3% of patients (n = 990), with hyponatremia in 50.5% (n = 888) and hypernatremia in 23.8% (n = 418). MAKE at ICU discharge did not differ between hyponatremic and normonatremic patients (12.6% vs. 10.9%, p = 0.304) but was sixfold higher with hypernatremia (32.3% vs. 5.4%, p Conclusion Dysnatremia affects over half of burn patients. Sodium disturbances should be viewed as markers of systemic severity, warranting close monitoring and preventive strategies.

items.title: Getting the Question Right Before Seeking the Answer! Lessons from the BUFFALO pilot trial for designing definitive paediatric airway studies
Inter‐Rater Reliability in Pre‐Anaesthetic Airway Assessment: A Protocol for a Systematic Review
items.abstract: Background Pre‐anaesthetic airway assessment relies on subjective clinical judgement, whether performed through direct physical examination, such as Mallampati classification or thyromental distance, or through composite scoring systems that combine several such components, including the Simplified Airway Risk Index, the El‐Ganzouri Risk Index and the Wilson score. The clinical value of these assessments depends not only on their predictive accuracy but also on whether they can be applied consistently across assessors. However, evidence on the inter‐rater reliability, agreement or variability of these composite tools and their individual components remains scattered across the literature and has not previously been systematically synthesised. This systematic review therefore aims to identify, assess and synthesise the available literature on inter‐rater reliability, agreement or variability in composite airway assessment tools and individual airway assessment components in the context of pre‐anaesthetic or preoperative assessment. Based on previous inter‐observer studies of individual airway assessment components, we hypothesise that inter‐rater reliability of these tools and components will predominantly range from moderate to excellent. Methods This systematic review protocol has been developed in accordance with Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Review and Meta‐Analysis Protocols (PRISMA‐P) and informed by the PRISMA 2020 statement and the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews. A systematic search will be conducted in MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL and CENTRAL, supplemented by reference list screening and forward citation tracking of foundational articles. Studies involving adult patients or healthy volunteers, in which two or more assessors independently evaluated a composite airway assessment tool or individual airway assessment component through physical assessment of a real participant, will be eligible for inclusion. Two reviewers will independently screen studies and extract data using a standardised, piloted form. Methodological quality will be assessed using a checklist adapted from the Guidelines for Reporting Reliability and Agreement Studies. Findings will be synthesised primarily narratively; quantitative synthesis may be considered where studies are judged sufficiently homogeneous. Conclusion This systematic review will synthesise the available literature on inter‐rater reliability, agreement or variability in composite airway assessment tools and individual airway assessment components and may help clarify the consistency of these routinely used pre‐anaesthetic assessments across both clinical and research populations.

items.title: Postoperative Vasoactive Exposure Patterns and Outcomes After Non‐Cardiac Surgery: A Prespecified Analysis of the SQUEEZE Cohort
items.abstract: Background Postoperative vasoactive therapy is usually summarised by its presence or duration, although haemodynamic support evolves over time. We investigated whether reproducible postoperative vasoactive exposure patterns provide prognostic information beyond the duration of postoperative vasoactive therapy. Methods We performed a prespecified substudy of the international SQUEEZE cohort. Adults receiving postoperative vasoactive infusion within seven postoperative days after non‐cardiac surgery were included. Unsupervised k‐means clustering identified exposure patterns using duration of postoperative vasoactive infusion, cumulative vasoactive agent‐days, and peak number of concurrent agents. Associations with 30‐day mortality, acute kidney injury (AKI), and hospital length of stay were assessed using multivariable regression. A prespecified landmark analysis evaluated early postoperative vasoactive exposure burden during postoperative days 0–1. Results Among 25,672 patients, 6676 (26.0%) received postoperative vasoactive infusion. Four reproducible exposure patterns were identified. Adjusted 30‐day mortality ranged from 9.7% in the low‐burden pattern to 35.3% in the high‐burden pattern but was not strictly monotonic, whereas adjusted AKI risk increased from 28.0% to 56.0% across patterns. In covariate‐adjusted models fitted to the same complete‐case cohort, discrimination was higher when exposure pattern rather than duration was included (AUC 0.818 vs. 0.795), while adding duration to pattern classification resulted in little additional discrimination (AUC 0.819). Findings were consistent in the early postoperative landmark analysis. Conclusions Postoperative vasoactive exposure follows reproducible patterns characterised by persistence and overall treatment burden rather than binary classification alone. These patterns were associated with mortality, AKI, and hospital length of stay, and provided prognostic information beyond duration alone. Editorial Comment This substudy and analysis of the SQUEEZE cohort, which represents a large sample of cases with focus on post‐operative vasopressor treatments, shows that more intensive vasopressor therapy was associated with worse postoperative outcomes, including for mortality and 30 days and postoperative acute kidney injury occurrence. Trial Registration: ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT03805230

items.title: Authors' Reply to Letter to the Editor: “Impact of Rehabilitation in the Neurointensive Care Unit on Long‐Term Survival in Patients With Traumatic Brain Injury”
Authors´ Response to “Estimating Plasma Volume Changes”
Female Representation and Quality Indicators in Anesthesiology and Critical Care Podcasts
items.abstract: Background Podcasts have emerged as prominent tools for asynchronous medical education, widely adopted across training levels and specialties. Diverse representation strengthens medical discourse, making an evaluation of speaker demographics essential for understanding equity and quality in digital knowledge dissemination. This study systematically evaluates female representation and quality assurance indicators in anesthesiology and critical care podcasts, including longitudinal publication trends. Methods We systematically searched Apple Podcasts and Spotify using specialty‐specific terms and manually reviewed the top twenty journals in the field for affiliated podcasts. Included were active, English‐language, physician‐hosted podcasts. Results Eighty‐five podcasts (53.0% US‐based) comprising 10,190 episodes were analyzed. Of 12,522 hosts, 31.5% ( n = 3945) were female; of 10,822 guests, 35.9% ( n = 3882) were female. Notably, among US‐based podcasts, female guest representation exceeded the 26.5% female workforce proportion among US anesthesiologists. Episodes with exclusively male hosts had 2.13 times the odds of featuring only male guests (95% CI 1.88–2.41). A positive trend of increasing female participation was observed from 2010 to 2024. Content support was variable: using broad, inclusive definitions, 42.0% of episodes had show notes and 48.4% provided supplemental material. Analysis of quality‐related structures showed that 40.0% ( n = 34) of podcasts produced episodes linked to a publication, 50.6% featured some episodes with three or more speakers, 21.2% of podcasts were journal‐affiliated, and 20.0% were university‐affiliated. Conclusion While a sex imbalance persists in anesthesiology and critical care podcasting, female participation among US‐based podcasts exceeds local workforce demographic benchmarks, with a clear positive trend from 2010 to 2024. However, persistent sex similarity in speaker selection suggests ongoing biases. Quality assurance mechanisms remain highly variable, highlighting opportunities for incremental improvement. Future efforts could focus on structured guest selection and transparent quality indicators to accelerate progress toward equitable representation and educational quality in this influential medium. Editorial Comment In modern times, many clinicians look for, and listen to, podcasts aimed at education in clinical specialties. This sampling of podcasts related to our specialty looked at how females and males contributed to podcast content generation and dissemination, as a marker for male versus female representation in speakership for continuing specialty education.
items.limitations: Several limitations are noted. First, data extraction was performed by multiple reviewers to manage the scale of the task, a necessary approach given the project's scope. This may introduce inter‐rater variability, despite team meetings held to synchronize procedures. Second, our analysis categorizes speaker sex as a binary variable (male/female) using proxies such as names, voice, and pronouns. We recognize that pronouns denote gender identity rather than biological sex, and that our binary classification does not capture intersex, non‐binary, or self‐determined gender identities, a conceptual limitation that risks perpetuating homogenizing norms. Sixth, our analysis focused exclusively on sex representation, and we acknowledge the absence of data on racial and ethnic diversity as a limitation. However, reliably categorizing speaker race or ethnicity from audio, names, or show notes is fraught with methodological challenges. Finally, the geographic distribution of our sample, predominantly US‐based, limits the direct generalizability of our findings to regions with different workforce demographics. While workforce data are available for other countries, the number of podcasts originating from each individual country in our sample was too small, with the exceptions of Australia/New Zealand and Great Britain, to support meaningful country‐specific comparisons. Relatedly, our findings must be interpreted alongside evidence that male sex is predictive of podcast use among anesthesiologists.

items.title: Investigating Fibrinolysis Resistance in Sepsis Using High‐Multiplex Plasma Proteomics: A Statistical Analysis Plan
items.abstract: Background Sepsis‐induced coagulopathy is characterised by consumptive coagulation abnormalities and resistance to fibrinolysis, which is increasingly recognised as a driver of microvascular thrombosis, organ dysfunction and mortality. The molecular determinants of the fibrinolysis‐resistant phenotype remain incompletely defined. Objective To present a pre‐specified statistical analysis plan for a plasma proteomic investigation of fibrinolysis resistance in 89 samples collected serially from 32 critically ill patients with sepsis, using the Olink Explore HT platform (approximately 5400 proteins). The plan is designed to characterise protein associations with a validated bedside measure of fibrinolysis resistance, the ratio of tissue plasminogen activator‐induced lysis time to fibrin clot amplitude (TPA‐LT/FIBA10). The associations will be examined across the fibrinolysis resistance severity continuum and between three ordinal severity grades, and over time within individual patients. Methods The analytic framework combines five complementary approaches: (i) limit‐of‐detection‐based data filtering, (ii) continuous‐variable modelling of protein abundance against TPA‐LT/FIBA10 using limma‐trend regression, (iii) categorical comparison across severity grades using empirical Bayes moderated statistics, (iv) linear mixed‐effects modelling of longitudinal intra‐patient trajectories and (v) pathway‐level enrichment analysis to translate statistical associations into mechanistic hypotheses. A semi‐supervised pathway clustering analysis will describe how proteins change by fibrinolysis resistance in eight a priori defined domains. Discussion This multi‐model design is intended to define genuine biological signals in a high‐dimensional dataset while remaining transparent about the exploratory nature of several components. The statistical reasoning behind each method is discussed alongside anticipated limitations. Trial Registration ClinicalTrials.gov : NCT06680180

items.title: Leadership Education for Doctors—A Scoping Review
items.abstract: Introduction Clinical leadership is essential for patient safety and effective healthcare delivery. While leadership training is increasingly integrated into medical education, there is no consensus on how to define, teach, or evaluate these skills. This scoping review aimed to map the existing literature on medical clinical leadership training and identify gaps. Methods Following PRISMA‐ScR guidelines, a comprehensive search was conducted across five major databases. Eligible studies were original studies involving any interventions with the purpose of improving leadership skills of participants, where most participants were doctors or medical students. Studies were screened and selected by multiple reviewers, and data were charted using a tool constructed for this study. Synthesis and thematic analysis were conducted with support from Datalab at the Library of Copenhagen University. Results Sixty‐two studies met the inclusion criteria. Out of these, 47 employed descriptive pre/post designs. Clinical leadership was defined explicitly by 15 studies, though a thematic analysis identified nine shared elements, including communication, emotional intelligence, and patient safety. Teaching methods varied, with simulations and lectures being most common. Out of 62 studies, 36 relied on self‐assessment for evaluation and satisfaction surveys, with limited long‐term or objective outcome measures. Evaluation methods of 56 studies fell within Kirkpatrick's levels 1 and 2, focusing on reaction and learning, rather than behavior‐ or long‐term changes. Conclusion Clinical leadership education is a growing but fragmented field. A clearer definition of clinical leadership, teaching methods, and evaluation tools are needed to improve future training programs and assess their effectiveness. Editorial Comment This scoping review summarizes the current literature regarding education on clinical leadership skills. More specifically the authors identified nine themes of clinical leadership by using a thematic analysis method, and also reported on different teaching and assessment methods. By assessing altogether 62 studies, concerning mainly doctors and medical students as learners, they identified a need for defining clinical leadership, and the teaching and evaluation methods more clearly.

items.title: The Impact of Anaesthesia Method on the Use of Anaesthesia Department Resources in Total Knee Arthroplasty
items.abstract: Background Spinal and general anaesthesia seem to lead to similar health‐related outcomes in total knee arthroplasty. However, to produce economically and environmentally sustainable health care, we should also consider other factors. Current guidelines recommend preferring regional anaesthesia and total intravenous anaesthesia to reduce environmental impact. In this study, we analysed time, costs, and disposable materials associated with spinal anaesthesia and total intravenous anaesthesia during total knee arthroplasty. Methods A total of 395 patients undergoing total knee arthroplasty were randomised to spinal or general anaesthesia. Outcomes were total operating room time, non‐operative operating room time, post‐anaesthesia care unit time, use of drugs affecting haemodynamics, and the need for arterial cannulation and urinary catheterisation. In addition, we evaluated the financial costs and waste produced by single‐use equipment and medicines in both anaesthesia methods. Results Anaesthesia method did not affect operating room time (median 152 min [interquartile range 136–168 min] vs. 150 min [137–165 min], Hodges–Lehmann estimate 2 min [95% CI –3 to 6 min], p = 0.49). However, after spinal anaesthesia, patients appeared to spend more time in the postanaesthesia care unit than after general anaesthesia (median 104 min [71–148 min] vs. 73 min [49–98 min], Hodges–Lehmann estimate 32 min [95% CI 23–42 min], p < 0.001). Medication for hypotension was more common in the general anaesthesia group, whereas medication for hypertension was more common in the spinal anaesthesia group. General anaesthesia generated more disposable material (1252 vs. 611 g), and both medicine and equipment expenses were higher (total costs €83 vs. €36). Conclusion With this anaesthesia regimen, knee arthroplasty patients occupied the operating room for a similar duration regardless of anaesthesia method, but patients required longer recovery in the postanaesthesia care unit after spinal anaesthesia. Regarding disposable material and medicine use, spinal anaesthesia appeared to be more economical and material‐sparing than total intravenous anaesthesia. Furthermore, spinal anaesthesia appeared to cause less hypotension requiring haemodynamic interventions than general anaesthesia. Editorial Comment This health‐economic analysis estimates for how different aspects of general or spinal anaesthesia care contribute to process flow and item costs. Findings suggest that there may be measurably more costs associated with one of the anaesthesia type choices compared with the other, though this will depend on choices for materials and more. Trial Registration EudraCT (2016‐002035‐15)

items.title: Acute Profound Hypotension Following Intraoperative Plasma Transfusion—A Case Series
items.abstract: Background Blood transfusions can be lifesaving but carry risks of serious adverse reactions, including the less recognized hypotensive transfusion reaction, characterized by hypotension that may be difficult to distinguish from other transfusion reactions or haemorrhage‐related shock. At the Karolinska University Hospital, an increased incidence of perioperative hypotensive transfusion reactions without typical allergic features has been observed during recent years. The aim of this study was to identify and describe common clinical characteristics among patients who experienced perioperative transfusion reactions. Methods This case series utilized data from a local quality registry at the Karolinska University Hospital, Sweden, covering the period from June 2024 to June 2025. Data collected included patient demographics, relevant clinical parameters and summaries of each reaction. Descriptive statistics were applied to identify potential common traits. Results Seventeen patients with perioperative transfusion reactions were included. All but one developed hypotension and in 11 cases hypotension was the sole manifestation. None of these 11 showed elevated serum tryptase levels. All patients except one received plasma via a Belmont Rapid Infuser RI‐2 and seven patients also received packed red blood cells. In 11 cases, the blood pressure drop occurred immediately after plasma infusion. During this period, the Belmont Rapid Infuser was withdrawn after 7 months. No reactions were reported in the 4 months following withdrawal. However, reactions recurred following subsequent device use. Conclusion Most transfusion reactions were characterized by profound and immediate hypotension following plasma transfusion, often presenting as isolated hypotension without biochemical or clinical evidence consistent with IgE‐mediated anaphylaxis. A temporal association with the use of the Belmont Rapid Infuser RI‐2 was observed. These findings should be regarded as hypothesis‐generating, warranting further prospective mechanistic and safety studies. Editorial Comment Hypotensive transfusion reactions are uncommon but clinically important, and may be mistaken for bleeding or anaphylaxis. This case series describes 17 perioperative cases, mainly presenting as abrupt isolated hypotension after plasma administration. The absence of device‐use denominators, signs of anaphylaxis in most patients and the incomplete, delayed calcium measurements mean that other mechanisms cannot be separated from a device‐related effect. The main message for practice is therefore active vigilance when using a rapid plasma infusion device.
items.limitations: This study has several limitations. The case reporting form was intentionally concise to encourage reporting compliance, which restricted data granularity. Detailed changes in vasoactive drug infusion rates and haemodynamic recovery could not be retrospectively reconstructed. In addition, the frequency of use of each blood warming device was not recorded, limiting the ability to quantify relative risk. The absence of denominators for device‐specific plasma transfusion rates prevents estimation of the true incidence or relative risk attributable to the Belmont device.

items.title: Swedish Consensus Recommendation for Follow‐Up After ICU Stay
items.abstract: Background A substantial proportion of intensive care unit (ICU) survivors experience long‐term physical, psychological and cognitive impairments after critical illness. However, methods for identifying patients in need of post‐ICU support vary widely. As a result, many patients are left without access to established rehabilitation pathways. This consensus recommendation provides a framework for the organisation and content of follow‐up for adult ICU survivors in Sweden, informed by available evidence, stakeholder perspectives and expert consensus. Methods The National System for Knowledge‐Driven Healthcare Management (NPO) in Sweden commissioned the development of a practice recommendation for the follow‐up of critically ill adults. Multidisciplinary experts in ICU survivorship formed a task force group. A systematic literature search in four databases was conducted in 2024 to identify pre‐existing systematic reviews on the topic. The literature was reviewed, assessed for quality and recommendations were developed based on the literature evidence. The draft was discussed among multiprofessional groups involved in follow‐up, in workshops with critical care nurses ( n = 30) and professionals responsible for follow‐up clinics ( n = 74) and among patient representatives ( n = 4). The final draft underwent external peer review by representatives from relevant professional organisations, the national registry for intensive care and governmental agencies in Sweden. Results The consensus recommendation suggests that all adult patients with an ICU length of stay ≥ 48 h are recommended for follow‐up, with an initial contact within 1 week of ICU discharge to assess clinical status, identify early problems and ensure continuity of care. Patients and their families are recommended to be offered an outpatient follow‐up visit at 2–3 months after discharge, led by ICU clinicians and, when possible, delivered by a multidisciplinary team. Validated screening tools and objective tests are recommended to assess relevant outcomes, including post‐traumatic stress, anxiety, depression, cognitive impairment, physical function and Health‐Related Quality of Life (HRQoL) as appropriate. Patients with identified problems should be referred to appropriate healthcare providers or specialist services for further management. Conclusion This consensus recommendation provides a framework for patient selection, timing and assessment to support a more structured and equitable management of post‐intensive care syndrome. Editorial Comment Systematic follow up of ICU survivors after hospital discharge is needed in order to assess long‐term patient‐centred outcomes. This is a consensus set of recommendations and not a GRADE‐based clinical practice guideline for doing this, which can be considered by relevant ICUs.
items.limitations: The consensus recommendation adopts a pragmatic approach to enhance feasibility, using ICU length of stay as a simple and applicable criterion for identifying patients at risk, despite its limitations as a predictor of long‐term outcomes. While more complex risk stratification models may offer greater precision, their routine use is currently limited by feasibility, validation and clinical usability. ICU length of stay was therefore selected as a pragmatic compromise, enabling consistent identification of at‐risk patients in everyday practice, and should be interpreted alongside clinical judgement and individual patient factors. To support implementation, follow‐up may be integrated into existing care pathways, with emphasis on protected time for assessments and effective coordination across ICU, ward and community services. Robust documentation and communication systems are needed to maintain continuity of care and ensure consistent application of rehabilitation plans throughout the patient's journey. However, some limitations should be acknowledged. First, the evidence base underpinning follow‐up interventions after critical illness remains heterogeneous and, in some areas, limited, particularly regarding patient selection, optimal timing and long‐term impact of follow‐up services. As a result, some recommendations are necessarily based on expert consensus in addition to the available literature. Second, while the recommendation aims to be pragmatic, its implementation may be challenging in routine clinical practice. In particular, the establishment of structured follow‐up services requires sufficient staffing, time and organisational resources, which may not be readily available in all settings. A further limitation relates to the literature base underpinning the recommendation. The evidence synthesis primarily relied on existing systematic reviews rather than conducting new independent searches for individual studies. An integrative review was included because it provided a broader understanding of patients' symptoms, needs and experiences following critical illness across different study designs. This review was used primarily to inform the identification of relevant follow‐up domains and patient needs, rather than as evidence of intervention efficacy. Also, the total number of participants reported across systematic reviews should be interpreted with caution, as not all participants contributed to each review question. While this approach allows for an efficient and comprehensive overview of the available evidence, it also means that the recommendation reflects the heterogeneity and methodological limitations present in the underlying reviews, including variation in intervention components, patient populations and outcomes. In addition, more recent primary studies not yet included in published reviews may have been missed. This approach may limit both the level of detail and the timeliness of the evidence informing the recommendations. Fina

items.title: Issue Information

Haemodynamic and Respiratory Effects of Dexmedetomidine as an Adjuvant to Oxycodone Patient‐Controlled Analgesia After Lumbar Spinal Fusion: A Post Hoc Analysis of the DoseRespDex Randomised Controlled Trial
items.abstract: Purpose Dexmedetomidine has been studied as an adjunct to opioid patient‐controlled analgesia (PCA) because of its opioid‐sparing properties and limited respiratory depression. However, potential dose‐dependent haemodynamic effects should be considered, and data on dexmedetomidine administered via PCA remain limited. Methods In this post hoc analysis of a randomised, double‐blind, placebo‐controlled trial, 98 adults undergoing lumbar spinal fusion were randomised 1:1:1:1 to 24‐h PCA with oxycodone 1 mg/mL alone (D0; placebo referring to normal saline replacing dexmedetomidine in the PCA syringe) or combined with dexmedetomidine 2.5 μg/mL (D2), 5 μg/mL (D5) or 10 μg/mL (D10). Outcomes of interest for the present analysis included mean arterial pressure (MAP), heart rate (HR), respiratory parameters and adverse events. Plasma dexmedetomidine concentrations were analysed as a pre‐planned pharmacokinetic sub‐analysis. Results Mean changes over time differed significantly between groups for MAP ( p = 0.005) and HR ( p < 0.001). Plasma dexmedetomidine concentrations increased across the D2, D5 and D10 groups, with observed median peak concentrations of 0.15, 0.31 and 0.55 ng/mL in D2, D5 and D10. Over 72 h, MAP was lower in D5 versus D0 (−11.2 mmHg, 95% confidence interval [CI] −19.9 to −2.5, p = 0.004) and D10 versus D0 (−9.1 mmHg, 95% CI −17.4 to −0.8, p = 0.032). All dexmedetomidine doses reduced HR versus D0 (D2: −10.2; D5: −9.9; D10: −11.9 bpm; all p < 0.01), without differing from each other. Haemodynamic changes resolved by 48 h. No bradycardia occurred, and no between‐group differences were detected in the measured respiratory variables. Conclusion Dexmedetomidine as an adjunct to oxycodone PCA produced transient haemodynamic effects without differences in bradycardia or in the measured respiratory variables. Although higher doses resulted in higher plasma concentrations, the magnitude of haemodynamic effects did not follow a clear dose–response pattern in the range studied. Dexmedetomidine 5 μg/mL combined with oxycodone 1 mg/mL may represent a reasonable candidate dose for further investigation. Editorial Comment In this post hoc analysis of patients undergoing posterolateral spinal fusion, adjunctive dexamethasone (2.5, 5 or 10 mg/mL), administered alongside oxycodone PCA (1 mg/mL), resulted in a transient, minor decrease in mean arterial blood pressure and in heart rate at the highest doses, with no effect on respiratory parameters and with no adverse events. No correlation between plasma concentrations of dexmedetomidine and haemodynamic parameters was demonstrated. Trial Registration NCT02454881, EudraCT 2014‐003252‐31
items.limitations: Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the parent trial was powered for the primary efficacy outcome (a 25% reduction in cumulative 24‐h oxycodone consumption) and not for the haemodynamic or respiratory outcomes examined here; statistical inferences should therefore be regarded as exploratory. Second, respiratory monitoring relied on intermittent SpO2, RR and supplemental oxygen use, without continuous capnography or arterial blood gases, and all patients received supplemental oxygen during 0–24 h. Perioperative fluid data were unavailable, although the standardised protocol and randomised design likely minimised between‐group differences. Finally, the modest per‐group sample size (n = 24–25) limits generalisability. Within the limitations of this post hoc analysis, dexmedetomidine 5 μg/mL combined with oxycodone 1 mg/mL may warrant evaluation in future confirmatory studies. No between‐group differences were detected in the measured respiratory variables, although this should not be interpreted as established respiratory safety.

items.title: Correction to “Temperature Dysregulation Following Intrathecal Morphine for Cesarean Delivery Patients—A Scoping Review”
items.abstract: C. Draegert, P. Pape, H. Kruse, H. K. Nedergaard, and A. J. Wikkelsø, “ Temperature Dysregulation Following Intrathecal Morphine for Cesarean Delivery Patients—A Scoping Review,” Acta Anaesthesiologica Scandinavica 70, no. 10 (2026): e70350, https://doi.org/10.1111/aas.70350. In the Author Contributions section, one of the author's contributions was inadvertently omitted. The Author Contributions section should have included all five authors and should have read as follows: “Christina Draegert: study conception, article screening, data extraction, writing of the draft, draft revision. Helene K. Nedergaard: study conception. Anne J. Wikkelsø: study conception. Pernille Pape: article screening, data extraction. Heidi Kruse: article screening. All five authors have assisted in revising and subsequently approving the final manuscript.” We apologize for this error.

items.title: From Cohort to Outcome: Clarifying Patient Flow and Mortality After Prehospital Transfusion
Answer to Gricourt et al.
Discussing Future Treatment and Care in the ICU : Perspectives From Patients
items.abstract: Introduction Treatment in the intensive care unit (ICU) is usually predicated on curative treatment, but continuing all available treatment options may not always be beneficial for the patient or in line with their wishes. However, patients admitted to the ICU are often assessed as incapable of making decisions regarding their care; hence conversations about wishes for treatment are postponed. This study aimed to investigate the experiences of patients who participated in a conversation concerning treatment and care following ICU discharge based on the Danish version of the Recommended Summary Plan for Emergency Care and Treatment (ReSPECT) form. Method Semi‐structured telephone interviews were conducted with patients who had a conversation about future treatment and care with an intensivist using the ReSPECT form during an ICU admission between November 2024 and July 2025. Relatives who participated in the conversation and were present during the interviews were asked to elaborate on their experiences of the conversation's timing and how they felt about participating in the conversation. Data was analysed using content analysis. Results Nineteen patients were included in the study, of whom 15 patients (83%) participated in a telephone interview. Two themes were identified: Timing of the conversation and Clarifying goals of care and options . Based on these, four sub‐themes were identified, two for each theme: Too soon, but not much later ; Wishes in accordance ; Hard, but necessary and Communicating in an understandable manner . Most patients were satisfied with having had a conversation about future treatment and care. Patients found the conversation relevant and necessary. The intensivists were praised for their communication skills and their ability to know and explain recommendations for future treatment and care. However, most patients believed that the conversation was conducted too soon after recovering from intensive care. They would have preferred to have had the conversation later during their admission. Conclusions Most participating ICU patients found a conversation about future treatment and care relevant but preferred it to be held after ICU discharge. Future research should investigate the benefits of incorporating intensivists in these conversations in general wards. Editorial Comment In this prospective study, former ICU patients were interviewed and asked about their experiences and opinions regarding a structured ReSPECT discussion that had been conducted in the end of their ICU stay. The goal of that interview was advance care planning, involving the patients and their family members. This study reports a qualitative analysis of interviews conducted at least 4 weeks later. Two main themes and four subthemes were identified. Almost all patients remembered having had the discussion, but the content was less clearly remembered. ICU physicians’ communication skills were appreciated. The study assesses a function of our daily work from patient and family perspective, and discusses important issues such as optimal timing of the advance care planning.
items.limitations: However, the difficulty in finding suitable patients is a limitation. And as described in the introduction, patients are often assessed as incapable of informed decision‐making due to reduced or altered consciousness. This assumption was also supported by the fact that most project sites had trouble finding eligible patients for this study. Therefore, the participants cannot be assessed as representatives of the ICU patients most in need of ACP. Furthermore, the physicians themselves defined ‘severe comorbidities’ with no explicit definition making room for a substantial subjective interpretation of the term ‘severe comorbidities’ and assessing patients eligible for participation. Also, not having former ICU patients and relatives included in the research process is a limitation. Considering the research question, their views and input would have been valuable when designing the study and would have strengthened the study's ability to capture relevant and meaningful data. In future studies, this would be recommendable. Most of the patients in this study were content to have had a conversation about future treatment and care and found it relevant and necessary. The intensivists were praised for their communication skills and their ability to explain recommendations for future treatment and care.

items.title: Attitudes Towards Clinical Research in Acute Illness—A Population‐Based Survey in Sweden
items.abstract: Background To investigate the attitudes of the Swedish population towards participation in research and preferences regarding legally authorized representative when a participant is unable to give informed consent. Methods A national survey conducted by a Swedish analysis and research company on a representative sample of the Swedish population on two occasions (2020 and 2023). The questions were based on the prerequisite that the respondents could not provide informed consent on their own. The questionnaire included two scenarios: one allowing time to consult a legal representative (non‐emergency) and one where research had to start immediately, before consulting a legal representative (emergency). Results In total, 2086 respondents were included in the analysis. A majority were positive to participate in both non‐emergency (81% [1690/2086]) and emergency research (82% [1714/2086]) in situations where they would be unable to provide informed consent. Next of kin was preferred as a surrogate decision maker in 81% (1686/2086) of respondents and less than 1% (11/2086) preferred an unrelated legal representative such as an attorney. Conclusion This study shows that in a representative sample of the Swedish population there is a positive attitude towards research in the acute setting and in critical illness, even in situations when a potential participant cannot receive information and provide informed consent and that a next of kin is the preferred legally authorized representative. Editorial Comment This article reports results of a national survey from Sweden, where it shows that, among Swedish citizens, there appears to be broad acceptance of allowing family members to act as surrogate decision‐makers in informed consent decisions for study participation among acutely critically ill patients who cannot perform consent themselves. At this point in time, Swedish law does not allow this.
items.limitations: Our study has several limitations worth commenting. First, the respondents were presented with hypothetical scenarios and questions, although based on real world scenarios, and it is not certain that the responders would have the same view when being exposed to an authentic situation, as it might be difficult to imagine oneself and a relative in such a situation. However, a high rate of consent to continue in the research projects among survivors in recent critical care randomized clinical trials, performed in Sweden, where a deferred consent approach was used suggests that the results are valid also in authentic situations. The questions in our survey might also be biased towards certain answers even though the questions were formulated to be as neutral as possible and reviewed by several persons outside the study. We performed two surveys, 2 years apart and the fact that the first survey was distributed in the middle of the Covid‐19 pandemic when the public debate encompassed critical illness and clinical research may have affected the results. Another limitation is that we have not corrected analyses for multiplicity. In conclusion, this study shows that in a representative sample of the Swedish population there is a positive attitude towards research in the acute setting and in critical illness, even in a situation when a potential research participant cannot receive information and provide an informed consent. The study indicates that the preferred legally authorized representative is a close relative.

items.title: Characteristics and Outcomes After General Anaesthesia in Elderly Patients: A Nationwide Cohort Study
items.abstract: Background Elderly patients are more frail and have a higher burden of comorbidity, which could influence the risk of complications after anaesthesia. The aim of this study was to describe the elderly patient population undergoing general anaesthesia in Denmark. Methods This was a national registry‐based observational cohort study of adult patients (≥ 18 years) undergoing general anaesthesia in Denmark in 2020 and 2021, with a primary focus on patients 80 years and above. Patient and procedure characteristics of interest were age, sex, BMI, ASA classification, Elixhauser Comorbidity Index, comorbidities, type of procedure, and class of priority. The primary outcome of interest was 30‐day mortality. Secondary outcomes included acute kidney injury within 7 days, length of hospital stay, and number of days in the ICU. Results A total of 453,133 cases of general anaesthesia in 328,951 unique patients in Denmark during 2020 and 2021 were included in this study. Of these, 25,955 (8%) patients were 80 years of age and above. Elderly patients undergoing general anaesthesia were of higher ASA classification, suffered from a higher degree of comorbidity measured by Elixhauser Comorbidity Index, had a lower proportion of elective procedures and a higher proportion of expedited and urgent procedures. Mortality for all patients at 30 days was 1.5% ( n = 4814). While mortality was low for cases aged between 18 and 65 years, 30‐day mortality increased for each year after 65 years of age even after adjusting for covariates. Mortality was especially high for patients with high Elixhauser Comorbidity Index, high ASA classification, and for non‐elective procedures. Conclusion In this nationwide registry‐based cohort study, we described the elderly patient population undergoing general anaesthesia in Denmark. We found that 30‐day mortality increased for each year after 65 years of age even after adjusting for covariates. Editorial Comment This large cohort study from Denmark assesses perioperative case factors including age, comorbidity and more, then describing different risk levels for 30 day mortality, particularly with advanced age.
items.limitations: The findings of our study need to be interpreted in the context of some limitations. First, not all hospitals reported all cases of general anaesthesia to the database in 2020 and 2021, and our data were collected during the COVID‐19 pandemic. The generalizability of our results may be affected by these factors. However, as discussed in our related works, data completeness is estimated to be high and did not vary substantially between 2020 and 2021. In addition, COVID‐19 related mortality and capacity strain was low in Denmark compared to other countries.

items.title: Serious Adverse Events in Adult ICU Patients: A Substudy of the PATIENCE Cohort
items.abstract: Introduction Prokinetic agents are used to enhance upper gastrointestinal motility, but adverse events related to these agents are poorly described. We aimed to provide detailed epidemiological data on predefined serious adverse events ( SAEs ) in a cohort of adult intensive care unit ( ICU ) patients with and without prokinetic treatment. We hypothesised that all predefined SAEs would occur in both patients treated and those not treated with prokinetic agents, and that a higher number of SAEs would occur among patients treated with prokinetic agents for more than three consecutive days. Methods This substudy of the inception cohort study “Prokinetic agents in adult intensive care unit patients” included acutely admitted adult ICU patients. The prokinetic agents assessed (exposures) were erythromycin, metoclopramide, domperidone, and prucalopride. The primary outcome was the proportion of patients experiencing at least one episode of five pre‐specified SAEs during ICU stay (cardiac arrhythmias, cardiac arrest, vomiting with aspiration, diarrhoea, extrapyramidal symptoms). Secondary outcomes were (1) proportion of patients experiencing each SAE , (2) the proportion of patients experiencing any of the SAEs after prokinetic treatment stratified by longest consecutive treatment duration, (3) time from index ICU admission to first SAE and (4) time from prokinetic initiation to first SAE . All analyses were descriptive, summarising SAE proportions and timing overall and according to prokinetic exposure. Results Among 1440 adult ICU patients, 710 SAEs occurred in 354 patients (24.6%), most commonly cardiac arrhythmias (199/1440, 13.8%). Across the exposure groups, the proportion of patients experiencing one or more SAEs ranged from 23.0% to 42.5%. Among patients treated with prokinetic agents for > 3 consecutive days, 14/59 (23.7%) experienced a SAE , which was similar to the proportion observed among patients not receiving prokinetic agents (291/1.253, 23.2%). Most SAEs occurred on median Day 2 after ICU admission and on median Day 3 after prokinetic initiation. Conclusion One in four adult ICU patients experienced at least one SAE , with cardiac arrhythmias being the most frequent. Among patients receiving prokinetic agents, the proportion experiencing one or more SAEs ranged from 23.0% to 42.5% across treatment groups. The findings from this study may help inform the design of a future clinical trial. Editorial Comment This analysis presents reported serious adverse event observed in an ICU trial cohort assessing gastrointestinal prokinetic drug effects. Serious adverse events were reported frequently in both the drug treatment groups and the comparison (no prokinetic drug) group. Types of serious adverse events reported are presented.

items.title: Combined intrathecal and epidural morphine for major abdominal surgery: A two-centre feasibility randomised controlled trial
items.abstract: Epidural analgesia using continuous local anaesthetic infusions has declined in popularity, while single-shot intrathecal hydrophilic opioids are increasingly utilised. However, intrathecal opioids have a finite duration of action, which may be insufficient to provide adequate analgesia following major open abdominal surgery. This two-centre randomised controlled trial aimed to determine the feasibility of a strategy combining a single preoperative intrathecal morphine (ITM) injection with postoperative epidural morphine boluses (intervention), compared to ITM alone (control), in terms of recruitment and protocol adherence. Feasibility criteria were met for both recruitment (68%) and protocol adherence (80%). However, the scalability of this study is limited by its resource requirements. Marginal mean pain scores at rest and with movement (dynamic) were similar between groups at all timepoints. Total opioid consumption was comparable between groups, except on postoperative day 1, when consumption was lower in the intervention group (20 mg (IQR 4–36; range 0–220)) compared with the control group (48 mg (IQR 6–94; range 0–212); P =0.04). The number of pruritus events was similar across groups ( n = 46), although a greater proportion of patients in the epidural group required treatment with naloxone (14 vs. 5). One patient in the control group received naloxone for sedation; no patients required naloxone for respiratory depression. Further research is required to improve postoperative analgesia and enhance quality of recovery following major abdominal surgery.

items.title: Sustainable healthcare: The action that the evidence demands
Anaesthetic implications and occupational safety considerations of pressurised intraperitoneal aerosol chemotherapy procedures: An Australian 5-year single-centre experience
items.abstract: Pressurised intraperitoneal aerosol chemotherapy is an emerging treatment for peritoneal carcinomatosis, combining aerosolised chemotherapy delivery with minimally invasive surgical techniques. This study describes anaesthetic practice, perioperative outcomes, and occupational safety considerations associated with the delivery of pressurised intraperitoneal aerosol chemotherapy, based on a 5-year, single-centre experience. A retrospective review was conducted on patients who underwent pressurised intraperitoneal aerosol chemotherapy between December 2019 and April 2025. Data included demographic information, anaesthetic techniques, perioperative complications, and occupational safety measures implemented to protect healthcare staff. The study included 38 patients who underwent a total of 66 pressurised intraperitoneal aerosol chemotherapy procedures. The median age of the patients was 51 years (range 18–88 years). The median anaesthesia duration was 132 min (range 92–235 min). Common anaesthetic techniques utilised included sevoflurane for maintenance, rocuronium for neuromuscular blockade, and sugammadex for reversal of neuromuscular blockade, along with specific monitoring protocols. No notable intraoperative complications related to anaesthesia were observed. The median hospital stay was 1 day (range 0–7 days); prolonged admissions were associated with nausea and vomiting, pain, atelectasis, hypokalaemia, and fever. Occupational safety measures, including the use of personal protective equipment and aerosol containment strategies, were implemented to reduce exposure risks during the procedure, with no reported incidents of chemotherapy exposure among healthcare personnel. Pressurised intraperitoneal aerosol chemotherapy represents a viable treatment option with manageable anaesthetic challenges and significant occupational safety considerations. Ongoing education and adherence to safety protocols, along with collaboration among multiple teams, are crucial in minimising risks to both patients and healthcare workers.

items.title: Harm reduction opportunities following ICU admission for prescription opioid overdose: An 8-year comparative audit at the Royal Melbourne Hospital
items.abstract: Intensive care unit (ICU) admission following prescription opioid overdose represents an important opportunity for multidisciplinary intervention and harm reduction, yet Australian data describing inpatient management are limited. A retrospective audit was conducted of 70 adults admitted to the ICU at the Royal Melbourne Hospital with prescription opioid overdose between 2021 and 2024. The primary outcome was provision of take-home naloxone (THN) before discharge among patients meeting institutional eligibility criteria. Secondary outcomes included opioid education, multidisciplinary involvement and discharge opioid management, with comparison with the previous institutional audit where comparable data were available. Only five patients (7.5%, 95% confidence interval 3.2–16.3) were supplied with THN despite all meeting institutional eligibility criteria. Polypharmacy overdose was common (77%). Most patients received at least one specialist referral (83%), although 15% received no inpatient specialist referral. Opioid education was documented in 58 patients (87%) compared with 17% previously ( P <0.001), although content and documentation were inconsistent. These findings demonstrate persistent gaps in THN provision, structured opioid education and coordinated discharge planning, highlighting ICU admission as an important opportunity for prescription opioid harm reduction. Strengthening guideline-based multidisciplinary interventions during admission may improve patient outcomes and inform harm reduction strategies nationally.

items.title: Paediatric anaesthesia research in Australia and New Zealand
Navigating the translational chasm: a scoping review of large language models and hybrid architectures in intensive care
items.abstract: Foundation models, particularly large language models, can process the unstructured data central to the intensive care record, yet their clinical readiness remains poorly defined. This study aimed to map foundation-model and large language model applications in adult intensive care, characterise their architectural paradigms, and chart their validation and deployment features. Empirical studies applying a large language model or other foundation model to adult intensive care tasks were eligible for inclusion. Traditional machine-learning-only, non-intensive care, and paediatric studies were excluded. PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus were searched (January 2022–February 2026). A supplementary preprint and conference search through mid-2026 was analysed separately. Data were extracted in duplicate using an operationalised taxonomy (generative large language models, clinical language models, retrieval-augmented generation, and hybrid pipelines). Evidence-maturity mapping was performed without formal risk-of-bias appraisal. Sixty-four studies addressed decision support (51.6%), clinical NLP (23.4%), predictive analytics (20.3%), and ICU operations (4.7%). Standalone configurations predominated (79.7%); retrieval-augmented generation (6.3%) and hybrid (14.1%) architectures concentrated in higher-stakes tasks. Maturity was limited: 46.9% relied solely on retrospective MIMIC data, 6.3% reported external validation, 90.6% remained internally retrospective, and only 3.1% achieved prospective evaluation. Hybrid and retrieval-augmented architectures appear better aligned with high-risk ICU tasks, though no comparative synthesis was performed. Prospective validation and a risk-stratified ‘clinical co-pilot’ framework are needed.

items.title: How well can you climb a flight of stairs: evaluating the relationship between self-reported and objective measurement
items.abstract: Subjective assessment of functional capacity is known to be variable. We investigated the association between patients’ self-reported ability to climb a flight of stairs (FOS) using a graded index and their actual performance in doing so. We compared this with data on their Duke Activity Status Index (DASI) score, usual walking speed and physiological measures of both systemic and peripheral microvascular cardiovascular function. Fifty-eight patients undertook the study before a range of elective surgeries. Patient self-reported ability was strongly associated with their actual time to climb a FOS. Those reporting that this would be easy had a mean climb time of 17.4 s, which was significantly different to those reporting that it would be moderately hard (26.0 s, p = 0.001). Similar results were seen when the data were analysed according to usual walking speed of less than or greater than 1 m −s . The median DASI scores were significantly different between the groups even after adjustment for age (easy vs moderately hard: adjusted mean difference of 16 points, p = 0.002, and moderately easy vs moderately hard 14 points, p = 0.004). Most systemic and peripheral measures of cardiovascular function were not different between groups. We conclude that patients’ self-reported stair climb ability using a graded scale was associated with objectively measured performance. A graded index gives more information about functional capacity than a binary response. A DASI score, a 20 m walk test and a timed stair climb test were all closely correlated with each other.

items.title: Anaphylaxis: Early history and when did anaesthesia get involved?
Building sustainable resilient health systems: The Australian and New Zealand College of Anaesthetists statement on desflurane
items.abstract: Climate change is recognised as a public health emergency requiring urgent and decisive action. The adverse effects on the environment from delivering healthcare are well established, and identifying areas for positive change that are under our direct control as anaesthetists is imperative. Desflurane, a volatile anaesthetic gas, has significantly greater negative environmental and financial impacts, with little benefit to patient safety or quality of care, compared with clinically equivalent alternatives. In this context, the Australian and New Zealand College of Anaesthetists released a statement on desflurane in 2024 to provide balanced guidance for reducing desflurane consumption based on current evidence and expert consensus opinion. This article summarises the background for the statement and presents the ‘ANZCA Statement on Desflurane’ verbatim.
