The DayCOR clinical quality registry: Recording patient-reported measures in day care anaesthesia
items.abstract: Day case surgery is changing, with older and sicker patients presenting, new procedures occurring and many previously inpatient procedures converted to day-stay. The impact of these changes and additions, especially the management of elderly patients, was assessed using a digital survey of patient-reported measures commencing in March 2018. Running initially in two hospitals, spreading to include a large group of Private Hospitals in Melbourne, the survey was offered to all patients attending the facilities, following an introduction of the survey process in patient admission papers with consent obtained on the day of surgery. A 15-question digital questionnaire was sent to each consenting patient by text and email 24 h post-discharge. The patient could opt out at that stage by not opening the message; 242,025 adult patients responded (response rate of 84%), with 4.5% opting out and 9% failing to complete the survey. An ‘Alert,’ generated digitally for any problem identified in the response, was emailed to the treating anaesthetist and to an oversight group comprised of an anaesthetist, a nurse and an administrator to facilitate appropriate action and early resolution. This digital survey saves the staff costs associated with initiating individual patient contact and fully satisfied the requirements for patient-reported outcome measures and experience measures. As well as early indication of the patient’s postoperative course, confirmation of the ability to manage the elderly patient and the reliability of transferring inpatient procedures to day case management were indicated.

items.title: Safety and efficacy of volatile sedatives in critically ill patients receiving mechanical ventilation: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.abstract: Volatile sedatives are increasingly utilised for sedation in critically ill patients receiving invasive mechanical ventilation. Despite numerous randomised controlled trials and observational studies comparing volatile sedation to intravenous sedation, questions regarding its safety and efficacy persist. A systematic search was performed in PubMed, EMBASE, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, and Web of Science databases for studies published up to July 2025. The analysis included randomised controlled trials and observational studies that compared the use of volatile sedation with intravenous sedation in patients admitted to the intensive care unit for mechanical ventilation. Eligible studies involved adults aged ⩾18 years, requiring mechanical ventilation, and utilising either volatile or intravenous sedatives. They also needed to report at least one outcome of interest: incidence of delirium, mortality, intensive care unit length of stay, or duration of mechanical ventilation. From 3182 identified publications, fifteen studies were included in the systematic review. Volatile sedation was not associated with a significant difference in the incidence of delirium compared to intravenous sedation (risk ratio 0.72; 95% confidence interval 0.38–1.34), mortality (risk ratio 0.97; 95% confidence interval 0.80–1.17), intensive care unit length of stay (mean difference 0.28 days; 95% confidence interval −1.74 to 2.30), or duration of mechanical ventilation (mean difference −37.20 h; 95% confidence interval −78.60 to 4.20). Volatile sedation was not associated with significant differences in mechanical ventilation duration, delirium incidence, intensive care unit length of stay, or mortality compared to intravenous sedation. Further large-scale, high-quality randomised trials are needed to clarify its clinical benefit in critical care settings.

items.title: Prognostic significance of nucleated red blood cells in trauma patients
items.abstract: Nucleated red blood cells are early erythroid precursors typically confined to the bone marrow. Their appearance in peripheral blood reflects stress erythropoiesis and has been linked to hypoxia and systemic inflammation. While nucleated red blood cells have prognostic value in sepsis and critical illness, their significance in trauma remains poorly understood. This study aimed to evaluate the prognostic value of nucleated red blood cells during the first 10 days in the intensive care unit following severe trauma, and their association with 30-day mortality. We conducted a retrospective observational cohort study including 1636 adult trauma patients admitted to the Reims Level-1 Trauma Center between January 2019 and March 2025, recorded in the TraumaBase © registry. Nucleated red blood cell counts were measured daily for the first 10 intensive care unit days. K-means clustering identified four nucleated red blood cell phenotypes based on temporal patterns. Outcomes included 10- and 30-day mortality, incidence of acute respiratory distress syndrome, septic shock, mechanical ventilation, and length of stay. Survival analyses used Cox proportional hazards models adjusted for age, Injury Severity Score, Simplified Acute Physiology Score II, and the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment, and propensity-weighted regression assessed dichotomised nucleated red blood cell status. Nucleated red blood cells were detected in 221 patients (13.5%). Phenotype classification revealed: transient early nucleated red blood cells (phenotype 1), single peak (phenotype 2), multiple intermittent peaks (phenotype 3), and persistent elevation (phenotype 4). Phenotype 2 was associated with reduced 10-day mortality (adjusted hazard ratio 0.06, 95% confidence intervals 0.01–0.46), while phenotype 4 exhibited markedly increased mortality (adjusted hazard ratio 9.6, 95% confidence intervals 2.23–41.4, P < 0.001). Nucleated red blood cell+ patients had higher risks of acute respiratory distress syndrome, septic shock, mechanical ventilation, and 30-day mortality. Kaplan–Meier curves confirmed significant differences in survival across phenotypes (log-rank P < 0.001). Nucleated red blood cell presence, particularly persistent elevation, identifies trauma patients at higher risk of adverse outcomes. Routine, daily nucleated red blood cell monitoring may serve as a simple, low-cost prognostic tool in intensive care unit trauma care. Prospective studies are needed to validate these findings and integrate nucleated red blood cell dynamics into risk stratification.

items.title: Methadone to manage pain in pregnancy at Te Toka Tumai Auckland City Hospital: A retrospective observational analysis
items.abstract: Pain during pregnancy is common, yet evidence-based management remains limited. While non-pharmacological treatments are first-line, severe pain may necessitate pharmacological intervention. Methadone is well studied for opioid use disorder, but its role in acute pain management during pregnancy is less defined. This retrospective observational study examined pregnant patients prescribed low-dose methadone for pain management between January 2022 and December 2023 at a tertiary multidisciplinary pain service. Patients receiving opioid substitution therapy were excluded. Data on methadone dosing, pain scores, maternal side effects, and neonatal outcomes were analysed. Twenty-three patients were identified, with 22 included in the analysis. The mean gestation at methadone initiation was 29.7 weeks (standard deviation 5.1), and the median starting dose was 5 mg per day (interquartile range 2.5 to 5). Pain severity decreased significantly: the proportion reporting severe pain at rest fell from 82% to 14% at 48 hours (absolute risk reduction (ARR) 68%, number needed to treat (NNT) 2), and the proportion reporting severe pain with movement fell from 95% to 32% (ARR 64%, NNT 2), with sustained improvement at 4 weeks. Side-effects included sedation (14%) and nausea (23%) and were generally well tolerated. Among 19 neonates, no cases of neonatal abstinence syndrome were observed. Six required neonatal intensive care unit admission, but none for opioid withdrawal. These findings suggest that low-dose methadone, when used within a closely monitored multidisciplinary setting, may provide effective pain relief in the pregnant patient without significant neonatal harm. However, this high level of oversight may limit generalisability to other care settings. Further research is warranted to guide safe implementation and optimise dosing.

items.title: Anaesthesia, anthropology, and colonialism in the Pacific – An unusual case report
items.abstract: Nikolai Miklouho-Maclay was a renowned Russian ethnologist who spent most of his life in the Pacific and was one of the first Europeans to live among and study the Melanesian people of Papua New Guinea. He is regarded as one of the first scientific anti-racists. New Guinea at this time was one of the remotest places on earth and had little contact with Europeans, mainly occasional missionaries and explorers. In September 1871, Maclay landed at Garagassi Point, Astrolabe Bay, on the north coast of New Guinea. Travelling with him were two assistants: Ohlsen – a Swede, and Boy – a young Samoan. Boy then proceeded to become very ill and his constant groaning was silenced only when Maclay administered morphia. Maclay was threatened by the local indigenous tribal people who wanted his belongings. They knew his two companions were possibly dying and Maclay tried to appear normal despite being ill with malaria. On the night of 13 December, Maclay poured chloroform onto cotton wool and held it over Boy’s airway – he died soon after. Maclay, as an anthropologist, wanted a Polynesian brain for study. Despite Ohlsen’s protests, Maclay removed part of Boy’s forehead and scalp but then abandoned this as he did not have a container to hold a brain. Maclay had promised Prof Karl Gegenbaur of Germany that he would obtain a ‘dark man’s’ larynx, tongue and related muscles, which he resected. Maclay came to Australia in 1878, becoming a prominent member of the Australian scientific community.

items.title: Impact of direct transfer to critical care on mortality for patients who undergo emergency colorectal cancer resection: a national population-based cohort study in England
items.abstract: Background: It is recommended that patients receiving emergency surgery and with 'high-risk' of morbidity and mortality should be transferred directly from theatre to critical care. Using a national, population-based cohort study, we estimated the effect of direct transfer to critical care on 90-day mortality after emergency colorectal cancer resection, and the variation amongst English NHS hospitals. Methods: Patients who underwent emergency colorectal cancer resection between December 2016 and November 2019 according to Hospital Episodes Statistics, National Bowel Cancer Audit or National Emergency Laparotomy Audit were included. Patients were identified as having a direct transfer to critical care through linkage with the Intensive Care National Audit and Research Centre Case Mix Programme. Multivariable logistic regression and propensity score methods were used to measure the effect of direct transfer to critical care on 90-day mortality. Results: In total, 10,441 patients underwent an emergency colorectal cancer resection. Unadjusted 90-day mortality was higher in the direct transfer to critical care cohort (10.9%) than in patients without direct transfer to critical care (3.7%) (odds ratio [OR]: 3.16, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 2.65-3.77). There was no evidence of an association after risk adjustment (adjusted OR: 1.16, 95% CI: 0.94-1.43) or after propensity score analysis (weighted OR: 0.94, 95% CI: 0.69-1.27). For patients at high risk with a predicted mortality ≥5%, the proportion of patients with a direct transfer to critical care varied widely amongst hospitals (interquartile range 68%-92%; median 83%). Conclusions: Our findings suggest that apparent higher postoperative mortality in patients having direct transfer to critical care can be mostly explained by characteristics of patients, tumours, physiology and surgery. However, the extent to which direct transfer to critical care is used varies widely amongst hospitals. Further work to understand this variation has the potential to improve patient outcomes after emergency colorectal cancer resection.

items.title: Patient preference for intraoperative opioid strategy and early postoperative recovery after noncardiac surgery: a prospective partially randomised patient-preference trial (the PERFECT trial)
items.abstract: Background Patient-centred care increasingly encourages patients to participate in decisions regarding their anaesthetic management. However, whether expressing a preference regarding their anaesthetic management is associated with improved postoperative recovery remains unknown. We evaluated the association between preference expression and quality of recovery after noncardiac surgery. Methods In this prospective partially randomised patient-preference study conducted at two academic hospitals, adults undergoing minimally invasive abdominal, urologic, or gynaecologic surgery received standardised information on opioid-based and opioid-free anaesthesia, co-developed with patient partners. Participants expressing a preference received their preferred strategy, whereas those without a preference were randomised 1:1 to either strategy. The primary outcome was the Quality of Recovery-15 (QoR-15) score on postoperative day (POD) 1. Results Among 220 analysed participants, 177 (80.5%) expressed a preference, and 43 (19.5%) underwent random allocation. Mean [standard deviation] QoR-15 scores on POD 1 were higher among participants expressing a preference than among randomised participants (108.8 [18.2] vs 100.8 [23.5]), with an unadjusted mean difference of 7.9 points (95% confidence interval [CI] 1.5–14.4; P =0.017). The adjusted marginal mean difference was 7.1 points (95% CI 0.3–13.9; P =0.042). Scores on the QoR-15 also remained higher on POD 2. Sensitivity analyses showed consistent effect estimates but attenuated statistical significance. Secondary outcomes, including postoperative nausea and vomiting and bradycardia, were similar between groups. Conclusions Expression of a preference regarding intraoperative opioid management was associated with better reported early postoperative patient-reported recovery. Given the non-randomised comparison and limited precision, -generating and support further investigation into the role of patient-preference expression in perioperative recovery. Trial registration The full, long-term study is pre-registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (identifier, NCT06855641; first posted, 3 March 2025; Alexandre Joosten). https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06855641.

items.title: Association of Intraoperative Trigeminal Cardiac Reflex With Postoperative Myocardial Injury in Patients Undergoing Skull Base Tumor Surgery: A Prospective Cohort Study
items.abstract: Background: The association between intraoperative trigemino-cardiac reflex (TCR) and postoperative myocardial injury in patients undergoing skull base tumor resection remains unclear. Methods: This single-center prospective observational study enrolled patients undergoing elective skull base tumor resection between April 2023 and September 2024. The primary outcome was postoperative myocardial injury, defined as a cardiac troponin I level >16 ng/L within 24 hours after surgery. Patients were categorized into TCR and non-TCR groups. Logistic regression analyses were performed to explore factors associated with intraoperative TCR and postoperative myocardial injury. Results: Among 476 included patients, intraoperative TCR occurred in 27.9%, and postoperative myocardial injury occurred in 4.83%. Patients experiencing TCR had a higher rate of myocardial injury (8.3% vs. 3.5%, P =0.029). Multivariable analysis suggested that brainstem compression (adjusted OR=1.86; 95% CI: 1.19-2.91; P =0.007) and larger tumor diameter (adjusted OR=1.04; 95% CI: 1.02-1.07; P <0.001) independently associated with intraoperative TCR. TCR (adjusted OR=2.70; 95% CI: 1.12-6.53; P =0.028), older age (adjusted OR=1.06; 95% CI: 1.02-1.10; P =0.003), lower BMI (adjusted OR=0.80; 95% CI: 0.70-0.93; P =0.003), and tumor recurrence (adjusted OR=4.07; 95% CI: 1.43-11.57; P =0.009) were associated with postoperative myocardial injury after adjusting for selected confounders. Conclusion: Postoperative myocardial injury occurred in 4.83% of skull base tumor surgery patients. Intraoperative TCR increased the risk of this injury, though the link may relate to surgical complexity and patient characteristics. TCR may therefore serve as a potential clinical marker of patients at elevated perioperative cardiovascular risk rather than a direct causal mechanism.

items.title: Global Neurointensive Care: A Field Yet to Be Born
items.abstract: Neurological conditions represent the leading cause of disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs) and the second leading cause of death globally, with more than 11 million deaths annually, 87% of which occur in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). While global neurosurgery has emerged as a recognized field with dedicated frameworks for advocacy and action, the critical care continuum of neurological disease has been persistently overlooked. Global neurointensive care (GNIC) does not yet exist as a formally defined discipline, yet its need is urgent and measurable: ICU bed density in LMICs ranges from 0.1 to 2.5 per 100,000 inhabitants compared with 5 to 30 per 100,000 in high-income countries (HICs); a cross-sectional survey of 408 providers from 42 LMICs found that only 36.8% had access to a dedicated neurointensive care unit; and traumatic brain injury (TBI) mortality at 6 months exceeds 37% in Latin American LMICs. This viewpoint defines GNIC, characterizes the epidemiological and structural dimensions of the unmet need with granular supporting evidence, reviews existing initiatives and their limitations, and proposes a 6-domain strategic agenda for its development. GNIC must be established as a field parallel and complementary to global neurosurgery, ensuring the critical care continuum of neurological disease is not abandoned in the global effort towards universal health coverage.

items.title: Immediate Perioperative Hypersensitivity and Anaphylaxis in Neuroanesthesia Practice: A Focused Review
items.abstract: Perioperative hypersensitivity reactions are uncommon but potentially catastrophic. Neurosurgical and spine patients are especially vulnerable, as the injured brain and spinal cord tolerate anaphylaxis-induced hypotension poorly, cerebral and spinal perfusion may fall precipitously, and draping of the head and torso may obscure cutaneous signs. These procedures also rely heavily on topical hemostatic agents. National audits estimate the incidence of perioperative anaphylaxis at roughly 1 in 5000 to 10,000 anesthetics, but estimates vary geographically. No study has reported a denominator-based incidence confined to neurosurgery, leaving the true burden uncharacterized for this surgical specialty. This focused review summarizes the agents, mechanisms, and perioperative implications of immediate hypersensitivity and anaphylaxis relevant to neuroanesthesia. Immediate reactions are immunologic (IgE-mediated, or IgG- and complement-mediated) or nonimmunologic (direct mast-cell activation) but converge on mast-cell and basophil mediator release, which renders their presentations largely indistinguishable. We examine agents of relevance to neurosurgery, including neuromuscular blocking agents, cefazolin and other β-lactams, chlorhexidine, sugammadex, gelatin-based and other hemostatic agents, protamine, tranexamic acid, fluorescent and dye agents, and iodinated contrast media—alongside their mechanisms and safer alternatives. Management follows international consensus recommendations centered on prompt epinephrine administration and fluid resuscitation titrated to severity. Antihistamines and corticosteroids are useful adjuncts but should not delay resuscitation. Improved outcomes depend on greater awareness, careful allergy assessment and appropriate de-labeling, surgical-anesthesia communication, and wider access to testing and dedicated surveillance.

items.title: Association of Perioperative Hematocrit With Postoperative Neurological Complications in Adults Undergoing Revascularization Surgery for Moyamoya Disease: A Retrospective Cohort Study
items.abstract: Objective: Hematocrit influences blood viscosity and cerebral oxygen delivery, but its perioperative significance in adults with moyamoya disease (MMD) remains unclear. This study evaluated the associations of preoperative hematocrit, postoperative hematocrit, and delta hematocrit, defined as preoperative minus postoperative hematocrit, with postoperative neurological complications following revascularization surgery. Methods: This retrospective cohort study included 220 adults who underwent revascularization for MMD at a tertiary center in South Korea between 2012 and 2020. The primary analysis assessed the association between preoperative hematocrit and postoperative neurological complications. Secondary analyses examined postoperative hematocrit and delta hematocrit. Multivariable associations were estimated using Firth penalized logistic regression. Restricted cubic spline analyses were performed to assess potential nonlinear associations. Results: Postoperative neurological complications occurred in 47 patients (21.4%). Higher preoperative hematocrit (odds ratio [OR]=1.17, 95% CI: 1.04-1.33; P =0.008) and postoperative hematocrit (OR=1.15, 95% CI: 1.04-1.29; P =0.005) were associated with complications after multivariable adjustment. Delta hematocrit was not associated with complications in linear analysis (OR=0.91, 95% CI: 0.80-1.01; P =0.081). An exploratory restricted cubic spline analysis did not identify a significant association between delta hematocrit and postoperative neurological complications (overall P =0.060). Conclusions: Higher preoperative and postoperative hematocrit levels were associated with postoperative neurological complications after multivariable adjustment; however, because the timing of the postoperative measurement relative to the onset of complications was uncertain, postoperative hematocrit should not be interpreted as a predictive variable. Perioperative change in hematocrit showed a more complex exploratory pattern after accounting for baseline hematocrit, but this finding requires confirmation in larger cohorts.

items.title: In Response: Hormonal Status as an Uncontrolled Variable in the Assessment of Aprepitant Efficacy for PONV Following Acoustic Neuroma Surgery
The Association Between Intraoperative Cell Salvage and Tumor Recurrence in Patients Undergoing Meningioma Resection: An Observational Study
items.abstract: Background: The oncologic safety of intraoperative cell salvage (ICS) during meningioma surgery remains controversial due to concerns about hematogenous tumor dissemination. We investigated the association between ICS use and postoperative tumor recurrence in patients undergoing meningioma resection. Methods: This study retrospectively included adult patients who underwent meningioma resection with intraoperative blood loss >1000 mL at Beijing Tiantan Hospital between August 2015 and November 2022. The primary outcome was postoperative tumor recurrence. Propensity scores were estimated using clinically relevant baseline variables, and inverse probability of treatment weighting with stabilized weights was applied to reduce confounding. Results: Among 988 patients, 89 (9.0%) developed recurrence during a mean follow-up of 60 months. Recurrence was less frequent in patients receiving ICS than in those without ICS (7.9% vs. 14.9%, P =0.004). After inverse probability of treatment weighting adjustment, baseline characteristics were well balanced between groups. In the weighted Cox model, ICS use was not associated with increased recurrence risk ( HR =0.62, 95% CI: 0.39-0.99, P =0.043). Higher WHO grade was independently associated with increased recurrence risk, whereas gross total resection was associated with reduced risk. Sensitivity analyses yielded consistent results. Conclusion: In patients undergoing meningioma surgery with substantial intraoperative blood loss, intraoperative cell salvage was not associated with an increased risk of tumor recurrence.

Propofol injection discomfort recall after monitored anesthesia care or general anesthesia: a prospective observational cohort study
items.abstract: Purpose Pain during propofol injection is common, yet little is known about how often patients remember this experience after anesthesia or which perioperative factors influence memory formation during induction. Methods In this prospective single-center observational cohort study, English-speaking adults (≥ 18 years) receiving propofol under general anesthesia (GA) or monitored anesthesia care (MAC) were enrolled. Perioperative characteristics, intravenous access details, anesthetic medications and clinician-observed injection pain were recorded. On postoperative day 1, patients were interviewed using a standardized questionnaire assessing recall of discomfort during induction. Univariate and multivariate logistic regression analyses calculated adjusted odds ratios (aOR) and identified factors associated with recall. Results Of the 1,699 enrolled patients, 1,319 completed the postoperative day 1 assessment; 8.1% reported recall of injection discomfort. Multivariate analysis indicated that younger age (aOR = 1.03; 95% CI = 1.01-1.04; p Conclusion Approximately one in twelve patients recalled discomfort during propofol injection. Patient characteristics and modifiable anesthetic practices, particularly premedication and intravenous access site, were associated with memory of propofol injection discomfort. These findings highlight that memory formation during induction represents a distinct and clinically relevant patient-centered outcome.

Needle tip position influences bupivacaine concentration within the pterygopalatine fossa during suprazygomatic maxillary nerve block: a cadaveric study
items.abstract: Purpose The primary objective was to evaluate the influence of needle tip positioning during suprazygomatic maxillary nerve block on bupivacaine concentration within the pterygopalatine fossa (PPF). The secondary objective was to correlate early injectate spread on computed tomography (CT) with PPF bupivacaine concentrations. Methods Suprazygomatic maxillary nerve block attempts ( n =34) were performed on 17 human cadaveric heads with different needle tip positions. Each attempt involved injection of 5 mL containing 0.4% bupivacaine, iohexol, and methylene blue. Computed tomography was used to determine needle tip location and early injectate spread. PPF samples were harvested via a transmaxillary approach for bupivacaine quantification by liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry. Results The highest median [Q1–Q3] bupivacaine concentrations were observed when needle tip was positioned within pterygomaxillary fissure or PPF, with 829.3 [728.1–1015.7] µg/g, and when positioned directly against maxillary tuberosity, with 535.3 [355.7–820.7] µg/g. Concentrations were highly variable with off-bone infratemporal placements (range, 0.1–335.8 µg/g). Lateral needle displacement was associated with lower bupivacaine concentrations ( β =−0.193, 95% CI −0.301 to −0.086; P <0.001), whereas anterior ( β =0.107, 95% CI 0.018–0.196; P =0.020) and cranial displacement ( β =0.079, 95% CI 0.017–0.141; P =0.014) were associated with higher concentrations. CT contrast spread between temporalis and lateral pterygoid muscles was not associated with higher PPF bupivacaine concentrations ( P =0.117). Conclusion Needle tip position influenced bupivacaine concentration within PPF, with concentrations generally increasing as the needle approached PPF and with more anterior positioning, including placement at the maxillary tuberosity. More superficial or posterior infratemporal placements yielded lower and more variable concentrations. Moreover, infratemporal contrast spread on early CT imaging was not associated with higher PPF bupivacaine concentrations.

Stress hyperglycemia ratio as a marker of major postoperative complications after cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass
items.abstract: Purpose This study examined whether the stress hyperglycemia ratio (SHR) at intensive care unit (ICU) admission is associated with major postoperative complications after cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass and whether this association differs from that of absolute ICU admission glucose. Methods This single-center retrospective study included 731 surgical episodes from 709 adults who underwent cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass. SHR was calculated as the first ICU glucose divided by HbA1c-derived estimated average glucose. The primary outcome was an unweighted composite of 30-day mortality, stroke, Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes stage 3 acute kidney injury, reoperation for bleeding, prolonged mechanical ventilation, and deep sternal wound infection. Multivariable logistic regression adjusted for clinically relevant covariates. Results The composite outcome occurred in 90 surgical episodes (12.3%). SHR was associated with the composite outcome after adjustment (odds ratio [OR], 1.103 per 0.1 increase; 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.008-1.208; P = 0.033), whereas ICU admission glucose was not significantly associated (OR, 1.019 per 10 mg/dL increase; 95% CI 0.946-1.096; P = 0.626). Conclusion SHR at ICU admission was associated with major postoperative complications in the primary analysis, whereas absolute ICU admission glucose was not significantly associated after multivariable adjustment. Confidence intervals for SHR included 1.0 in several sensitivity analyses. SHR warrants prospective evaluation as an early postoperative risk marker after cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass.

items.title: Development and external validation of a LASSO-based nomogram to predict epidural-associated postpartum urinary retention
items.abstract: Purpose To develop and validate a risk prediction model for postpartum urinary retention (PUR) among parturients receiving epidural analgesia (EA) during vaginal delivery, to support individualized bladder management. Methods This dual-center retrospective cohort study analyzed electronic medical records from two hospitals (2022-2024). Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression was used to select independent predictors from demographic, labor, and analgesia-related variables. A clinical nomogram was developed. The model underwent internal and external validation; performance was assessed using calibration, discrimination (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUC]), and decision curve analysis (DCA). Results Among 1019 parturients receiving EA (PUR incidence 16.09%), prolonged analgesia duration and prolonged second-stage labor were independently associated with PUR, whereas higher intermittent catheterization frequency (ICF) was associated with a lower rate of recorded PUR. The model demonstrated excellent discrimination, satisfactory calibration, and clinical net benefit across validation cohorts. Conclusion The validated nomogram provides real-time, individualized estimates of PUR risk during late labor. By identifying parturients at elevated risk, it offers an evidence-based basis for risk-adaptive bladder monitoring and individualized care; however, whether such model-guided management ultimately reduces PUR incidence remains to be established in prospective interventional studies.

Intravenous dexmedetomidine during cesarean delivery under neuraxial anesthesia: a triple-blind, placebo-controlled randomized trial
items.abstract: Purpose Some parturients experience discomfort, pain, and nausea/vomiting during cesarean delivery under neuraxial anesthesia. We evaluated whether intravenous dexmedetomidine administered after fetal delivery and cord clamping improved maternal intraoperative experience. Methods In this prospective, triple-blind, placebo-controlled trial, women aged 20-45 years undergoing elective cesarean delivery under combined spinal-epidural anesthesia were randomized 1:1 to dexmedetomidine or saline. Dexmedetomidine was administered after cord clamping as a loading dose of 1 μg/kg over 10 min, followed by 0.4 μg/kg / hr until peritoneal closure; controls received equivalent-volume saline. The primary outcome was satisfaction with intraoperative sedation/analgesia, assessed on postoperative day 1 using a 7-point verbal rating scale. Secondary outcomes were Quality of Recovery-40 score, maximum intraoperative pain score, intraoperative nausea/vomiting, and motor recovery time. Results Eighty-three participants were randomized; 81 contributed to the available-case analysis. Satisfaction scores were higher with dexmedetomidine than saline (Hodges-Lehmann location shift, 1.0 point; 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.0 to 2.0; P Conclusion Post-delivery intravenous dexmedetomidine improved patient-reported satisfaction with intraoperative sedation and analgesia. Exploratory findings suggested reduced pain and nausea/vomiting without improved 24-h recovery. These findings support further evaluation of dexmedetomidine as a selective adjunct rather than for routine sedation. Trial registration UMIN000025489 ( https://center6.umin.ac.jp/cgi-open-bin/ctr_e/ctr_view.cgi?recptno=R000029334 ).

The impact of dexmedetomidine on postoperative delirium and early postoperative cognitive impairment in elderly patients undergoing general surgery: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.abstract: Anesthetic management in general surgery poses substantial risks in elderly patients because age-related physiologic decline and preexisting comorbidities increase vulnerability to peri-operative complications. Older adults have reduced physiological reserve, impaired organ function, and slower recovery from surgical and anesthetic stress, placing them at increased risk for postoperative delirium and early postoperative cognitive impairment. Dexmedetomidine, a selective α2-adrenergic receptor agonist, has sedative, anti-inflammatory, and opioid-sparing properties that may influence early postoperative cognitive outcomes without significant respiratory depression. This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the association between dexmedetomidine and 24-h postoperative delirium/early postoperative cognitive impairment in elderly patients undergoing general surgery. Four studies involving 479 patients met the inclusion criteria. Across the included studies, dexmedetomidine was generally administered as a 1 µg/kg loading dose followed by continuous intraoperative maintenance infusion of 0.2-0.7 µg/kg/h. Pooled analysis showed that dexmedetomidine was associated with significantly lower odds of 24-h postoperative delirium/early postoperative cognitive impairment compared with control treatment (pooled OR 0.38, 95% CI 0.24-0.61; p < 0.001). These findings suggest that dexmedetomidine is associated with lower odds of early postoperative cognitive outcomes in elderly surgical patients compared with control treatment. Larger, long-term studies are needed to confirm these findings and establish standardized dosing protocols.

items.abstract: The evolution of Capillary refill time (CRT) use in clinical medicine is interesting, transforming a simple bedside observation into a reliable tool for assessing tissue perfusion in critically ill patients. When Henry Beecher and colleagues first systematized CRT measurement in 1947, they recognized its potential as a rapid method to evaluate circulatory status in trauma casualties, establishing a foundational framework that would influence intensive care practice for decades to come. However, clinicians soon discovered that relying on visual inspection alone introduced troubling variability between observers and even within the same observer's assessments, with expertise and training significantly influencing measurement accuracy. This recognition of CRT's limitations sparked a concerted effort to transform the measurement from a purely subjective exercise into a standardized, objective clinical tool. Researchers systematically refined protocols by establishing consistent pressure application techniques, standardized measurement sites, and defined normal thresholds (approximately 3 s for healthy adults). These methodological advances set the stage for rigorous clinical validation. Subsequent research revealed that CRT correlated powerfully with microvascular blood flow and independently predicted mortality and organ dysfunction in septic patients. Meta-analyses encompassing over 60,000 patients confirmed that abnormal CRT carried substantially elevated mortality risk, particularly when measured using standardized techniques. More recently, the ANDROMEDA-SHOCK trials demonstrated that CRT could serve not merely as a prognostic marker but as an actionable resuscitation target. CRT is nowadays considered an adjunct bedside marker to guide fluid and vasopressor resuscitation in adults with sepsis and septic shock, supporting individualized hemodynamic strategies while reducing over-resuscitation risks.

items.title: Clinical validation of an intra-abdominal pressure monitoring system by comparison with pneumoperitoneum pressure
items.journal: Journal of Clinical Monitoring and Computing
items.containerTitle: Journal of Clinical Monitoring and Computing
items.abstract: In critically ill patients, intra-abdominal hypertension (IAH) is associated with organ dysfunction and increased mortality. Acute kidney injury may occur early, since the kidney is particularly vulnerable to elevated intra-abdominal pressure (IAP). Accurate and timely measurement of IAP is essential for early detection of IAH and the initiation of appropriate therapeutic interventions. Therefore, the aim of this study was to assess the accuracy of an IAP monitoring system compared to a reference standard, the CO2 insufflator, during laparoscopy. The second aim was to assess the changes in renal biomarker levels during and after increases in IAP through pneumoperitoneum. A prospective cohort study in patients undergoing laparoscopy at the University Medical Center Groningen. IAP measurements were performed with a urinary catheter using an IAP monitoring system (Accuryn® Monitoring System, Accuryn Medical) and compared to the pressure set at the CO2-insufflator system. Bland-Altman analysis was performed with accounting for repeated measures. Urine samples were collected at several time-points and Kidney Injury Molecule 1 (KIM-1), Tissue Inhibitor of Metalloproteinase 2 (TIMP-2), urinary Neutrophil Gelatinase-Associated Lipocalin (NGAL), Liver-type Fatty Acid-Binding Protein (L-FABP), and albumin-creatinine ratio were measured. Between March 2025 and January 2026, 99 measurements were performed in 29 patients. One patient (3%) underwent hemicolectomy, and 28 patients underwent endometriosis surgery (97%). Analysis showed a bias of -1.4 mmHg (95% CI (-1.96 - (-0.82)) and limits of agreement of − 5.96 mmHg and 3.2 mmHg (95% CI -6.8–3.99) between the IAP monitoring system and the CO2-insufflators. The precision was 2.3 mmHg. The levels of renal biomarkers KIM-1, TIMP-2 and albumin/Cr ratio increased during laparoscopy compared to baseline, suggesting that relatively small IAP increases during laparoscopy have a subclinical effect on the kidney. The IAP monitoring system underestimated the IAP set by the CO2-insufflator by approximately 1 mmHg. The wide limits of agreement warrant cautious interpretation. Overall, the IAP monitoring system showed reasonable accuracy and precision. The increase of several renal biomarkers during laparoscopy compared to baseline may reflect a direct effect of elevated IAP on the kidney.

items.title: Clinical implications of intraoperative premature ventricular contractions for 30-day cardiovascular outcomes after liver transplantation
items.journal: Journal of Clinical Monitoring and Computing
items.containerTitle: Journal of Clinical Monitoring and Computing
items.abstract: To examine the association between intraoperative premature ventricular contraction (PVC) burden and 30-day major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) in liver transplantation (LT) recipients, and to determine whether complex ventricular ectopy carries prognostic significance distinct from isolated PVCs. In this retrospective cohort study, continuous intraoperative ECG recordings from 2,290 consecutive LT recipients were analyzed using a validated AI-based detection pipeline. PVCs were classified as isolated or complex (couplet, NSVT, bigeminy, trigeminy), with total complex PVC burden as the primary exposure. Associations with 30-day MACE were estimated by multivariable logistic regression across burden tertiles. Sensitivity analyses used a hard MACE endpoint excluding arrhythmic components and with additional adjustment for isolated PVC burden. MACE occurred in 515 patients (22.5%). PVCs were detected in 98.2% of patients; isolated PVC prevalence did not differ between those with and without MACE (98.4% vs. 98.0%, P = 0.666), whereas complex PVC prevalence was significantly higher in the MACE group (93.2% vs. 85.8%, P < 0.001). Total complex PVC burden showed a graded association with MACE across tertiles (T1 aOR 1.71, 95% CI 1.11-2.65; T2 aOR 2.26, 95% CI 1.47-3.47; T3 aOR 2.79, 95% CI 1.83-4.27), whereas isolated PVC burden was not associated with MACE in any tertile. The association persisted in both sensitivity analyses. Complex intraoperative ventricular ectopy, but not isolated PVCs, was independently associated with 30-day MACE in LT recipients. AI-enabled PVC quantification may identify an intraoperative signal associated with postoperative cardiovascular risk, although prospective and external validation is required before clinical application.

items.title: Alteration of sublingual microcirculation in anemic patients during gastric cancer surgery under goal-directed fluid therapy: a prospective cohort study
items.journal: Journal of Clinical Monitoring and Computing
items.containerTitle: Journal of Clinical Monitoring and Computing
items.abstract: Goal-directed fluid therapy (GDFT) relies primarily on macrocirculatory hemodynamic variables for optimizing fluid therapy. Patients undergoing gastric cancer surgery often present with anemia, which may impair microvascular endothelial function and tissue oxygenation. How preoperative anemia influences intraoperative sublingual microcirculation and macro- and micro-circulatory coherence under GDFT is not known. Patients undergoing open radical gastrectomy were divided into anemic and non‑anemic groups according to their hemoglobin (Hb) levels. All patients received GDFT guided by pulse pressure variation. Sublingual microcirculatory (microvascular flow index [MFI], proportion of perfused vessels [PPV], total and perfused vessel density) and macrocirculatory (cardiac index [CI] and mean arterial pressure [MAP]) variables were measured before (T0) and immediately after induction of general anesthesia (T1), after tumor resection (T2) and at the end of surgery (T3). Mixed linear models were used to compare intergroup differences in sublingual microcirculation over time, and to analyze the correlations between macro- and micro-circulatory variables. Correlations between preoperative Hb and changes in MFI from each intraoperative time point to T0 were additionally assessed. A total of 49 patients were analyzed in present study. MFI showed a significant group‑by‑time interaction between the two groups (P = 0.030). In anemic patients (n = 22), MFI was significantly lower than that in non‑anemic patients (n = 27) at T1 (P = 0.013), and between-group differences were no longer evident at T3 (P = 0.461) under GDFT, although MFI remained below baseline in both groups. PPV was lower in anemic patients at T2 (P = 0.010). Correlation analyses demonstrated that lower preoperative Hb levels were associated with greater reductions in ΔMFI from T1 to T0 (Pearson's r = 0.343, P = 0.016) and T2 to T0 (Spearman's ρ = 0.369, P = 0.009). No significant associations were found between macro- and micro-circulatory variables in either group. Under GDFT, anemic patients exhibited greater perioperative alterations in sublingual microcirculation, particularly after anesthesia induction and tumor resection. Lower preoperative Hb concentrations were associated with greater reductions in MFI. Further, the lack of detectable associations between macrocirculatory and sublingual microcirculatory variables suggests that conventional hemodynamic targets may not fully reflect sublingual microvascular perfusion in this vulnerable population.Trial registration number: NCT07583927.

items.title: A tablet-based augmented reality system to reduce preoperative anxiety in pediatric patients: a quasi-experimental pilot study
items.journal: Journal of Clinical Monitoring and Computing
items.containerTitle: Journal of Clinical Monitoring and Computing
items.abstract: Preoperative anxiety in pediatric patients remains a significant clinical challenge, yet existing interventions are limited by resource requirements and inconsistent effectiveness. The aim of this pilot study was to evaluate the feasibility and preliminary effects of a tablet-based augmented reality (AR) system integrated into routine perioperative patient transfer on preoperative anxiety in pediatric patients. In this single-center, quasi-experimental pilot study, 27 pediatric patients aged 3–10 years were assigned to an AR ( n = 13) or control ( n = 14) group based on surgery month. The AR system, implemented on a standard tablet device, overlaid virtual characters onto real-world surroundings to guide patients from the surgical center entrance to the operating room. The primary outcome was preoperative anxiety assessed using the modified Yale Preoperative Anxiety Scale (mYPAS) at operating room entry. Secondary outcomes included guardian-rated comfort visual analog scale scores and postoperative agitation. The AR group was younger than the control group. Median mYPAS scores at operating room entry were lower in the AR group than in the control group (28.3 [23.3–36.7] vs. 40.0 [36.7–52.9]; median difference − 11.7; 95% CI, − 18.4 to − 1.60; p = 0.01). No significant differences were observed in secondary outcomes. This pilot study demonstrates the feasibility of integrating a tablet-based AR system into perioperative workflows. Preliminary findings also indicate that this approach may help reduce preoperative anxiety in this population. Given the pilot nature of the study, non-randomized allocation, and baseline imbalances between groups, validation in larger, well-controlled, randomized trials is required.

items.title: Quantitative neuromuscular monitoring during general anesthesia: a prospective clinical audit of adherence to international guidelines
items.journal: Journal of Clinical Monitoring and Computing
items.containerTitle: Journal of Clinical Monitoring and Computing
items.abstract: Quantitative neuromuscular (qNM) monitoring is recommended whenever neuromuscular blocking agents (NMBAs) are administered, but adherence in routine clinical practice remains inconsistent. This audit evaluated adherence to recommended qNM monitoring standards in adult patients undergoing general anesthesia at a Portuguese tertiary hospital. This prospective clinical audit evaluated adherence to recommended qNM monitoring standards in adult patients undergoing general anesthesia at a major Portuguese tertiary hospital. Over five predefined weekdays between March and May 2025, all adult patients receiving general anesthesia across six operating or procedural areas were assessed. Of 329 patients included, 308 (93.6%) received NMBAs. Quantitative neuromuscular monitoring was omitted in 13.0% despite universal device availability. Utilization was lower in ambulatory and obstetrical settings and in procedures lasting less than one hour. Increasing anesthesia duration was associated with greater monitoring use in univariable analysis, but this association was not independent of clinical location. Equipment-related limitations accounted for a small proportion of omissions. This audit demonstrates high but incomplete adherence to qNM monitoring standards. Non-adherence is clustered primarily in procedures lasting less than one hour and in ambulatory and obstetrical settings. Although equipment was universally available, factors beyond equipment availability appear to contribute to incomplete implementation. Additional research is required to better understand the reasons underlying monitoring omission. In the meantime, targeted educational strategies and reinforcement of evidence-based neuromuscular monitoring practices may further enhance perioperative patient safety.

items.title: A narrative review of methods for estimating blood pressure waveforms from photoplethysmography
items.journal: Journal of Clinical Monitoring and Computing
items.containerTitle: Journal of Clinical Monitoring and Computing
items.abstract: Accurate, continuous blood pressure (BP) monitoring is important for preventing, diagnosing, and managing cardiovascular disease. Estimating the full arterial BP waveform can provide more clinical information than cuff-based measurements that report only systolic and diastolic BP. This review summarizes recent progress in predicting arterial BP waveforms from photoplethysmography (PPG) and identifies the main methodological gaps that limit clinical translation. We reviewed research published since 2021 on PPG-based BP waveform estimation. We organized the literature around core pipeline elements, including open-source datasets, preprocessing and quality control, model architectures, and validation practices. We also surveyed commercially available technologies that measure BP waveform. Data cleaning approaches can be grouped into three main categories: (1) template-based pulsation comparison, (2) feature extraction paired with classical machine learning, and (3) neural network–based quality assessment. For waveform prediction, recent work is dominated by deep learning, particularly U-Net–based architectures, autoencoder families, and attention-based models. Progress in PPG-based BP waveform prediction is rapid, but comparability and reproducibility remain major barriers. Benchmark datasets with consistent acquisition protocols, transparent preprocessing, and standardized validation criteria are needed to support fair comparison.

items.title: Impact of burst suppression duration on delirium and its diagnostic value in mechanically ventilated ICU patients
items.journal: Journal of Clinical Monitoring and Computing
items.containerTitle: Journal of Clinical Monitoring and Computing
items.abstract: Intensive care unit (ICU) delirium affects up to 50% of mechanically ventilated patients. This condition is associated with increased morbidity and mortality. Although bispectral index (BIS) monitoring is widely used for sedation assessment, its predictive value for delirium remains limited. Burst suppression (BS) is an electroencephalographic pattern reflecting profound cerebral dysfunction. BS has been proposed as a predictor of delirium. However, the quantitative role of burst suppression duration (BSD) in delirium risk stratification has not been established. This prospective observational study enrolled 300 mechanically ventilated adult ICU patients between April 2021 and October 2024 at Harrison International Peace Hospital. Continuous video-electroencephalogram (vEEG) monitoring was performed. BSD was quantified from the vEEG recordings. Delirium was assessed using the Confusion Assessment Method for the ICU (CAM-ICU). Multivariate logistic regression was used to identify independent risk factors. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis was performed to evaluate the diagnostic performance of BSD. Among 300 patients, 130 (43.3%) developed delirium. The delirium group had significantly longer BSD than the control group (median 81.1 s, IQR 41.5–148.5 vs. 17.2 s, IQR 5.8–32.9; P < 0.001). Multivariate analysis identified BSD (adjusted OR = 1.018, 95% CI 1.012–1.023; P < 0.001), BIS (adjusted OR = 0.964, 95% CI 0.946–0.982; P < 0.001), age (adjusted OR = 1.024, 95% CI 1.002–1.047; P = 0.031), and hypertension (adjusted OR = 1.748, 95% CI 1.002–3.051; P = 0.049) as independent risk factors. ROC analysis demonstrated that BSD achieved an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.871 (95% CI 0.829–0.913). The optimal cutoff of 41.5 s yielded a sensitivity of 80.8% and a specificity of 78.2%. The combination of BSD and BIS improved the AUC to 0.914 (95% CI 0.882–0.946). BSD is an independent risk factor for delirium in mechanically ventilated ICU patients. It demonstrates high diagnostic accuracy as a quantitative biomarker. The combination of BSD and BIS provides superior predictive performance. This combined approach offers a practical quantitative tool for early delirium risk stratification.

items.title: Peripheral intravenous waveform analysis – a novel tool to confirm intravascular catheter placement
items.journal: Journal of Clinical Monitoring and Computing
items.containerTitle: Journal of Clinical Monitoring and Computing
items.abstract: Peripheral intravenous (IV) catheter infiltration is a common complication which can cause harmful extravasation of fluid and medications. Significant injury can occur before standard infusion pumps detect a threshold pressure. Peripheral IV waveform analysis (PIVA) uses fast Fourier transform (FFT) to measure the amplitude of the venous waveform. This study aims to evaluate if PIVA can differentiate between IV catheter positions, primarily intravenous versus subcutaneous, in a rat model. Surgical cutdown was performed on the right proximal saphenous vein. Pressure and waveforms were recorded from a 22G IV catheter open-to-air, in the vein, and in the adjacent subcutaneous (SC) tissue. Measurements were performed at baseline and after injection of 1 mL Plasmalyte and are reported as median (interquartile range). The peak amplitude corresponding to the heart rate frequency labeled as f1. Pre-flush intravascular f1, 0.0824 mmHg (IQR 0.0256, 0.1480), differed significantly from both SC, 0.0001 mmHg (0.0000, 0.0004), and open-to-air, 0.0001 mmHg (0.0000, 0.0008), conditions, ANOVA p = 0.03, pairwise p = 0.049 and 0.049, respectively. These significant differences remained after flush. Post-flush pressures between IV, 7.9 mmHg (6.6, 8.9) and SC, 20.5 mmHg (11.3, 28.8) were significantly different, p = 0.0001. There was no significant difference in pre-flush and post-flush pressure within IV, SC, and open-air groups, p = 0.687, p = 0.110 and p = 0.219, respectively. PIVA was superior to absolute pressure measurement for detecting intravascular versus extravascular placement of an IV catheter. This study demonstrates utility of PIVA as a novel method for confirming proper IV placement.

Can painkillers quiet the bladder? Acetaminophen/ibuprofen and catheter-related bladder discomfort
Large congenital cervical teratoma in a neonate: EXIT procedure under spinal anesthesia and early surgical excision -A case report-
items.abstract: Background: Cervical teratomas are rare congenital tumors in neonates associated with high morbidity and mortality due to the potential for severe airway obstruction at birth. Here, we present a case of successful airway management using an ex utero intrapartum treatment (EXIT) procedure under spinal anesthesia for a prenatally detected cervical mass, with definitive treatment achieved by postnatal surgical excision. Case: The infant was born via emergency cesarean section after exhibiting fetal distress due to a cervical mass and underwent an EXIT procedure under spinal anesthesia. A surgical tracheostomy was performed as the newborn could not be intubated. On postnatal day 6, a 439-g cervical teratoma was successfully removed, and the patient was discharged on postnatal day 48. Conclusions: This case suggests that spinal anesthesia may represent a viable anesthetic option for EXIT procedures in neonates with cervical teratoma in selected emergency settings while maintaining uteroplacental circulation and enabling rapid airway control.

items.title: Clinical Factors Associated with Intraoperative Increase in Cardiac Troponin and Its Prognostic Value During Liver Transplantation
items.abstract: Background: Perioperative elevations of high-sensitivity cardiac troponin I (hs-cTnI) are common during liver transplantation (LT); however, the clinical significance of new-onset intraoperative elevations remains unclear. We evaluated the frequency, magnitude, associated factors, and prognostic implications of intraoperative hs-cTnI elevations, distinguishing new-onset from pre-existing elevations. Methods: We retrospectively analyzed 4151 consecutive LT recipients (2008-2021). The primary endpoint was 90-day mortality. Elevated hs-cTnI was defined as > 40 pg/mL (1× upper reference limit [URL]). The relative importance of 19 variables for new-onset intraoperative hs-cTnI > 400 pg/mL (10× URL) was ranked using an exploratory shapley additive explanations (SHAP) analysis. Results: Intraoperative hs-cTnI > 1× URL occurred in 66.1% (2745/4151) of patients, including new-onset elevation in 62.5% (2304/3685) of patients with normal baselines (~90% had an increase of > 20%). In pre-existing elevation, an exploratory threshold > 22× URL was associated with mortality (adjusted HR 5.91, 95% CI 3.11-11.22; P < 0.001), whereas new-onset elevation was not (P = 0.74). Per doubling of intraoperative hs-cTnI, 90-day mortality increased overall (adjusted HR 1.21, 95% CI 1.11-1.32) and in pre-existing elevation (adjusted HR 1.29, 95% CI 1.13-1.46; both P < 0.001). Low intraoperative hematocrit, anemia, factor VIII, von Willebrand factor, and neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio showed the highest SHAP importance for new-onset >10× URL. Conclusions: New-onset intraoperative hs-cTnI elevations were common during LT and linked to anemia, hypercoagulability, and inflammation. However, they did not predict 90-day mortality in patients with normal baselines; risk increased only in pre-existing elevations. Intraoperative hs-cTnI elevations should be interpreted in the context of preoperative levels.

items.title: K-MIMIC and the next stage of multimodal critical care data
Macroscopic dye distribution after classical versus extrafascial interscalene block: an exploratory comparative cadaveric pilot study
items.abstract: Background Extrafascial injection has been proposed as a phrenic nerve-sparing alternative for interscalene brachial plexus block (ISB), but the anatomical basis for the reported reduction in phrenic nerve involvement remains incompletely characterized. We compared macroscopic dye distribution patterns between classical ISB and extrafascial injection in paired cadaveric specimens. Methods In five formalin-fixed cadavers, bilateral ultrasound-guided injections with indigo carmine (20 ml per side) were performed. A classical ISB and extrafascial injection were applied to contralateral sides. Three blinded anatomists independently assessed staining intensity (deep, light, none) in real time during dissection. Results Both techniques produced deep staining of C5-6 roots, upper trunk, and suprascapular nerve in 5/5 specimens. The phrenic nerve was stained in all 10 specimens (5/5 in each group); deep staining occurred in 4/5 (80%) classical ISB specimens and 0/5 extrafascial specimens, though all 5 extrafascial specimens showed only light staining. Spread to infraclavicular cords was limited with both techniques. Conclusions Dye reached the C5-6 roots, upper trunk, suprascapular nerve, and phrenic nerve in all 5 specimens of both groups. Phrenic nerve staining intensity was lower with the extrafascial technique than with classical ISB in 4 of 5 paired cadavers, identical in 1 of 5, and never higher. The functional and clinical implications of this intensity difference cannot be determined from the present anatomical model and require prospective validation.

items.title: Individualized intraoperative BIS targeting based on preoperative BIS values in the awake state: a review and strategy prospect for preventing postoperative delirium in older patients
items.abstract: Postoperative delirium (POD) is a frequent and serious complication in older surgical patients and is associated with adverse short- and long-term outcomes. Bispectral Index (BIS) monitoring is widely used to guide intraoperative depth of anesthesia. However, the conventional strategy of maintaining a uniform BIS target range may not adequately account for interindividual differences in preoperative brain function, particularly in older adults with reduced neural reserve. This narrative review integrates evidence from three complementary domains: 1) clinical studies evaluating the association between preoperative resting BIS values in the awake state and the risk of POD; 2) mechanistic and clinical evidence linking excessive anesthetic depth, particularly electroencephalographic burst suppression, to POD; 3) interventional trials assessing the effect of intraoperative BIS-guided anesthesia management on delirium outcomes. Accumulating evidence indicates that a lower preoperative resting BIS value in the awake state is potentially independently associated with an increased risk of POD in older patients. Intraoperative BIS-guided anesthesia has been shown to reduce exposure to deep anesthesia and EEG burst suppression, which are consistently linked to higher delirium incidence. These findings suggest that patients with preoperatively identified brain vulnerability may benefit from higher individualized intraoperative BIS targets, rather than a fixed universal range. Integrating preoperative resting BIS assessment into perioperative anesthesia management may enable risk stratification and support individualized regulation of anesthetic depth in older adults. When incorporated into a multimodal delirium prevention framework, this individualized approach may offer a rational pathway toward improved delirium prevention and perioperative neuroprotection in older adults, warranting validation in future prospective randomized studies.

Optimal volumes of early oral fluid intake in the post-anesthesia care unit for patients not under postoperative fasting orders: a meta-analysis and trial sequential analysis of clinical recovery and safety outcomes
items.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Postoperative recovery in the post-anaesthesia care unit (PACU) is frequently complicated by thirst, oropharyngeal dryness, and postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV). Early oral fluid intake has been proposed to alleviate these discomforts. However, its optimal timing and volume remain uncertain. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis with trial sequential analysis (TSA) to evaluate the safety and clinical outcomes of PACU-initiated early oral fluid intake in adults after general anaesthesia, focusing on administered fluid volume. METHODS: We systematically searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, CENTRAL, Ovid, Web of Science, and Wanfang Database for studies published from January 2014 to December 2024. Eligible studies enrolled adults (≥18 years) recovering in the PACU after general anaesthesia who received early oral fluid intake versus delayed intake or standard fasting. Primary outcome was PONV incidence. Secondary outcomes included thirst alleviation, oropharyngeal discomfort, patient satisfaction, time to PACU discharge, and gastrointestinal recovery. Subgroup analyses by fluid volume and timing were considered exploratory. Two reviewers independently screened studies, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias. Random-effects models were used. TSA and GRADE were applied to the primary outcome. RESULTS: Thirteen studies (11 randomised controlled trials, 2 non-randomised studies) involving 4,528 adults were included. Early oral fluid intake significantly reduced PONV incidence (RR 0.60, 95% CI 0.50 to 0.73; moderate certainty). TSA indicated that the cumulative evidence crossed the trial sequential monitoring boundary, supporting the robustness of this finding. Exploratory subgroup analyses suggested that volumes of 20-49 mL and 100-199 mL were associated with lower PONV. Early oral intake also shortened time to first flatus (MD -3.27 hours; low certainty). Evidence for thirst alleviation, patient satisfaction, oropharyngeal discomfort, and PACU discharge time was of very low certainty owing to substantial heterogeneity and imprecision. No aspiration events were observed, although trials were not powered to exclude rare adverse events. CONCLUSIONS: PACU-initiated early oral fluid intake appears feasible and was associated with reduced PONV in appropriately selected adults after general anaesthesia. Evidence for secondary outcomes remains limited by heterogeneity and risk of bias. Larger, standardized trials are needed to define optimal timing and volume and to strengthen evidence for patient-reported and recovery outcomes.

Depression and anxiety among older surgical patients with cognitive impairment: a multicenter longitudinal cohort study
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Cognitive impairment (CI), depression, and anxiety are underrecognized yet frequently co-existing conditions linked to poor surgical outcomes in older patients. We examined: 1) the prevalence and perioperative trajectory of depression/anxiety in patients with and without CI; 2) preoperative patient-reported outcome measures; and 3) postoperative outcomes associated with depression/anxiety. METHODS: This study included 369 surgical patients (≥65 years) from two academic tertiary care hospitals. CI was assessed with the Ascertain Dementia Eight preoperatively, while depression/anxiety was measured using the Patient Health Questionnaire-4 preoperatively, at 30-, and 90 days postoperatively. The trajectory of depression/anxiety in CI versus no-CI patients was analyzed with linear mixed-effects models. RESULTS: Preoperatively, 28% of patients had depression/anxiety, 13% had CI, and 8% had co-existing depression/anxiety and CI. Those with depression/anxiety were more likely to have co-existing CI than those without depression/anxiety (29% vs. 6%; P<0.001). Patients that screened positive for preoperative CI experienced significantly worse psychological symptoms at all times compared to those without CI. Among those with preoperative CI, mean psychological symptoms remained above screening thresholds for depression/anxiety at all time points and significantly worsened at 90 days post-surgery compared to baseline levels. Patients with depression/anxiety reported significantly worse preoperative health, including greater pain and functional disability, as well as worse quality of life and sleep. CONCLUSIONS: Given greater psychological burden in those with CI, screening for both conditions may enable early identification of patients at higher risk for poor outcomes. This approach may ultimately enhance risk stratification and optimization of perioperative care in older adults.
