items.title: Sex differences in cardiovascular disease burden, risk factors, and disease spectrum in Europe: a global burden of disease 2023 analysis within the ESC Atlas framework
items.abstract: Despite growing recognition of sex disparities in cardiovascular disease (CVD), contemporary, harmonized analyses of sex-specific burden in the European region that could inform targeted prevention strategies, remain limited. Sex-specific patterns in CVD burden and risk factor exposure across 55 European Society of Cardiology (ESC) member countries were examined using data from the 2023 Global Burden of Disease study. Risk factor exposure was quantified using age–sex-standardized summary exposure values for 10 established cardiovascular risk factors. Disease incidence and mortality for major CVD categories, including maternal hypertensive disorders, were estimated by calculating age–sex-standardized rates per 100 000 person-years using the 2013 European Standard Population. Analyses were performed by sex at country, regional, and ESC-wide levels and over time (1990–2023). In 2023, in the ESC region, the overall CVD burden was broadly similar in men and women, with women accounting for 55% (6.0 million) of cases and 50% of deaths (1.5 million). This apparent parity, however, concealed marked sex differences in disease composition, risk exposure, and geographic disparities. Compared with men, women had a lower proportion of CVD due to ischaemic heart disease (21% vs 38%) and a higher contribution from peripheral arterial disease (23% vs 19%). Major differences were also apparent in risk profiles, particularly for behavioural risk factors—with summary exposure values of tobacco and alcohol being 10%–20% points higher in men than women; contrasting with cardiometabolic factors, such as high body mass index and low physical activity, that were often 5%–15% points higher in women than men, and more modest differences in environmental and biological risks, including air pollution, fasting glucose, or cholesterol. Cardiovascular disease burden further varied widely across countries and disparities affected women more strongly than men, with an approximately three-fold difference between the lowest- and highest-incidence countries in women, compared with a two-fold difference in men, and even larger disparities in mortality and premature mortality (up to 25-fold in women). Maternal hypertensive disorders substantially shaped both the scale and composition of CVD burden in women, accounting for 25% of incident CVD in women and exhibiting substantial geographic variation, with up to 18-fold differences in incidence across countries. These findings challenge conventional approaches that treat CVD as a homogeneous condition. In particular, the substantial contribution of non-ischaemic conditions and maternal hypertensive disorders to the burden in women, alongside distinct patterns of risk exposure and wider geographic disparities, underscore the importance of adopting a life-course and sex- and gender-informed approach to cardiovascular prevention and policy.

items.title: A decade-long device–valve interaction: severe aortic regurgitation after residual ventricular septal defect closure
items.abstract: A NTI1008"49-year-old woman underwent tetralogy of Fallot repair at age 16, including closure of a 25 mm intracristal ventricular septal defect (VSD) and right ventricular outflow tract reconstruction. Sixteen years later, a postoperative residual VSD was closed transcatheterly. Eleven years after device implantation, echocardiography showed mild-to-moderate aortic regurgitation (AR), which progressed to severe over 2 years, while the ascending aortic diameter increased from 38 to 45 mm despite 6-month surveillance. At the current admission, three-dimensional transoesophageal echocardiography showed the occluder impinging on the non-coronary and right coronary cusps at the commissure, restricting cusp motion and producing severe AR on colour Doppler (Panel A). Computed tomography confirmed protrusion into the aortic valve complex (Panel B). At surgery, both cusps were markedly thickened and firmly adherent to the occluder at the commissure (Panel C). The protruding portion of the device and adherent cusp tissue were excised (Panel D), followed by mechanical aortic valve replacement (Panel E). Recovery was uneventful, with normal prosthetic function at 1 month.

items.title: When platelets are under pressure: an angiotensin II-TGF-β axis in hypertensive patients leads to receptor PAR4 overexpression
items.abstract: Angiotensin II-TGF-β1-Smad2 signalling promotes PAR4 overexpression and platelet priming in hypertension. The schematic depicts the proposed mechanism by which an angiotensin II-high hypertensive phenotype drives megakaryocyte reprogramming and platelet hyperreactivity. In normosensitive individuals and in hypertensive patients without increased angiotensin II signalling, TGF-β1, Smad2 activation, and platelet PAR4 expression remain unchanged, resulting in quiescent platelets. In contrast, increased angiotensin II signalling promotes TGF-β1/Smad2 activation in megakaryocytes, leading to increased PAR4 expression in newly generated platelets. PAR4-high platelets display increased platelet activation markers and are associated with enhanced thrombotic risk. Valsartan, through angiotensin II type 1 receptor blockade, attenuates this pathway and may reduce PAR4-dependent platelet activation in this specific hypertensive phenotype.

items.title: Fifth Universal Definition of Myocardial Infarction and an update on lipoprotein(a) and inflammation
items.abstract: For the podcast associated with this article, please visit https://academic.oup.com/eurheartj/pages/Podcasts. This Issue starts with an ESC Guidelines article entitled ‘Fifth Universal Definition of Myocardial Infarction (2026): On behalf of the Joint European Society of Cardiology (ESC)/American College of Cardiology (ACC)/American Heart Association (AHA)/World Heart Federation (WHF) Task Force for the Universal Definition of Myocardial Infarction Endorsed by the European Association for Cardio-Thoracic Surgery (EACTS), and the Society of Thoracic Surgeons (STS) Affirmation of Value by the Society for Cardiovascular Angiography and Interventions (SCAI)’, by Nicholas Mills from the University of Edinburgh, UK, and colleagues. The authors of this very much-awaited Fifth Universal Definition provide an updated, pathophysiology-based classification of Myocardial Infarction that standardizes the diagnosis, improves clinical care, promotes research, and defines disease coding.1 The Issue continues with a focus on dyslipidaemias. In a State of the Art Review article entitled ‘Lipoprotein apheresis in the era of new lipid-lowering therapies’, Francesco Sbrana from Fondazione Toscana Gabriele Monasterio in Pisa, Italy, and colleagues aim to review the current role of lipoprotein apheresis (LA) in managing severe lipid disorders, particularly homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia (HoFH), and to highlight its benefits, current challenges, and potential future clinical applications.2 HoFH is a rare and severe genetic disorder characterized by extremely elevated low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) levels from birth, resulting in a very high risk of premature atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) and aortic outflow obstruction from both the aortic valve and supravalvular aortic stenosis. During the 1960s, in a pioneering way, LA was used to treat children with HoFH. Over the years, LA has evolved into increasingly selective methods, which have been used in paediatric HoFH since the 1990s. Today, LA is able to selectively remove atherogenic apoB100-containing lipoproteins from the blood: the main component of LDL-C, very LDL-cholesterol, and lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)]. LA has demonstrated protective effects in the endothelium and microcirculation, prevention of the development of new aortic and coronary lesions in HoFH, reducing the incidence of major cardiovascular events, and proving helpful in subjects who fail to reach the LDL-cholesterol target or who have elevated Lp(a) levels in secondary prevention. Although advances in pharmacological therapies (proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin Type 9 inhibitors, antisense oligonucleotides, and siRNA-based treatments) have expanded the options for lipid management, LA remains a safe therapeutic approach for patients with severe lipid disorders, including HoFH, to reduce their cardiovascular risks. Currently, to put LA into perspective, some obstacles need to be overcome, including: (i) the underdiagnosis of HoFH and high Lp(a) levels; (ii) therapeutic inertia resulting from the use of new lipid-lowering drugs with partial achievement of lipid targets; and (iii) availability of qualified LA centres and practitioners. Further prospective studies may prove useful to identify other therapeutic scenarios for LA, such as renal disease, diabetic foot ulcer, peripheral arterial disease, pre-eclampsia, macular degeneration, or sudden sensorineural hearing loss. In these clinical settings, prospective, randomized clinical trials are therefore warranted. In a State of the Art Review article entitled ‘Homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia: insights from the Global HICC Registry’, Willemijn Schonck from the University of Amsterdam in The Netherlands, and colleagues outline the rationale, structure, and objectives of the HoFH International Clinical Collaborators (HICC) and highlights the key contributions of this global initiative to date in advancing the full clinical spectrum from diagnosis to outcomes in patients living with HoFH.3 To address the global paucity of observational data, the HICC registry was established. To date, over 950 HoFH individuals from 45 countries have been included. The median age at diagnosis was 12 years, and untreated LDL-C levels were markedly elevated (median 14.7 mmol/l). At diagnosis, 9% had ASCVD or (supra)aortic valve disease, and despite the widespread use of lipid-lowering therapy (LLT), only 4% achieved guideline-recommended LDL-C goals. Early initiation of LA was associated with greater LDL-C reductions and delayed ASCVD onset. Cardiovascular burden remains substantial, with a median age at death of 37 years. No sex differences were observed in age or clinical characteristics at diagnosis, treatment patterns, or timing of ASCVD, although the usual sex gap in cardiovascular disease onset was absent. Profound global disparities persist, including limited genetic screening, restricted access to LLT, and earlier onset of major adverse cardiovascular events in non-high-income countries. Reproductive care for women remains highly variable and understudied. The HICC aims to guide global stakeholders in improving clinical outcomes for individuals with HoFH through earlier diagnosis, equitable access to advanced therapies, and broader inclusion of underserved regions. By generating evidence from routine clinical care and patient-reported data, identifying gaps in care, and fostering international collaboration, HICC seeks to advance a more equitable and effective global approach to HoFH management. There is growing interest in Lp(a).4–13 Current guidance recommends better LDL-C control in patients with elevated Lp(a), as Lp(a)-lowering therapies are unavailable. Whether risks attributable to Lp(a) are mitigated in patients with CAD who achieved LDL-C < 55 mg/dl remains unknown. In a Fast Track Congress article entitled ‘Lipoprotein(a) and residual cardiovascular risks in Japanese patients with coronary artery disease who achieve guideline-recommended low-density lipoprotein cholesterol goals’, Yu Kataoka from the National Cerebral and Cardiovascular Center in Suita, Japan, and colleagues investigate whether elevated Lp(a) levels contribute to cardiovascular outcomes in Japanese patients with coronary artery disease (CAD) and to what extent lowering LDL-C < 55 mg/dl mitigates this risk.14 A multicentre retrospective observational study analysed 1581 Japanese patients with CAD. Risk of major cardiovascular events (MACE) was compared according to Lp(a) levels (<30, ≥30 and <50 mg/dl, and ≥50 mg/dl) and amongst LDL-C strata (<55 mg/dl vs ≥55 mg/dl) 8 weeks after PCI. During the 5.1-year observation amongst patients with LDL-C ≥ 55 mg/dl (n = 1069), MACE occurred in 21% with risk of MACE increasing with Lp(a) levels (3.9, 7.9, and 11.0 events per 100 person-years for <30, ≥30 and <50 mg/dl, and ≥50 mg/dl, log-rank P < .001). Amongst those with LDL-C < 55 mg/dl (n = 512), the proportion with MACE was lower overall (4.3%, P < .001). However, elevated Lp(a) levels still identified those at higher risk of MACE (1.4, 4.7, and 7.5 events per 100 person-years in Lp(a) < 30, ≥30 and <50 mg/dl, and ≥50 mg/dl, P < .001). The standardized 5-year MACE rate was over two and five times higher in patients with Lp(a) ≥ 30 and <50 mg/dl and ≥50 mg/dl compared with Lp(a) < 30 mg/dl. The ROC analyses identified Lp(a) ≥ 28 mg/dl as the threshold for MACE (AUC = .68, P < .001). The authors conclude that whilst lower achieved LDL-C attenuates in part the risk from Lp(a), elevated Lp(a) levels still associate with worse cardiovascular outcomes. The Lp(a) threshold amongst Japanese patients with CAD at risk of recurrent events appears lower than in Caucasian populations which merits further evaluation. The manuscript is accompanied by an Editorial by Florian Kronenberg from the Medical University of Innsbruck, Austria.15 The author notes that from a clinical practice perspective, the data strongly support routine measurement of Lp(a) at least once in all adults, as recommended by recent ESC/EAS and US recommendations, and particularly in Japanese and other East-Asian patients in whom risk thresholds appear lower. In those with elevated Lp(a), clinicians should pursue long-term intensified LDL-C lowering and systematically address all modifiable risk factors, recognizing that such measures attenuate but do not abolish Lp(a)-mediated risk, as also demonstrated in the Japanese study. These recommendations are strongly supported and extended to Japanese practice by Kataoka et al.: achieving LDL-C < 55 mg/dl was associated with lower standardized 5-year MACE rates across all Lp(a) categories compared with remaining above this threshold. Even in patients with high Lp(a), lowering LDL-C into the guideline-recommended range attenuated, although it did not eliminate, risk. These observations are consistent with the concept that LDL-C and Lp(a) confer largely independent risks, and that lowering LDL-C is necessary but insufficient when Lp(a) is markedly elevated. We are now just a short time away from the results of the first outcome trial of a potent, specific Lp(a)-lowering therapy. Until now, we have only been able to speculate on the potential clinical consequences of these therapies. The first outcome studies will hopefully clarify what Lp(a) levels are required for study inclusion and whether there are heterogeneities in the results across different subgroups. This will help us design future Lp(a)-lowering programmes that are globally inclusive rather than anchored to thresholds derived from White populations alone. Inflammation plays a key role in atherothrombosis and markers of inflammation predict cardiovascular events.10,16–19 An elevated level of either interleukin-6 (IL-6) or high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hsCRP) is associated with poor cardiovascular outcomes after acute coronary syndrome (ACS). Whether the prognostic information provided by hsCRP and IL-6 is independent and complementary after ACS is unclear. In a Clinical Research article entitled ‘Interleukin-6 and C-reactive protein prognostic value following acute coronary syndrome’, Johan Wouter Jukema from Leiden University Medical Center in The Netherlands, and colleagues aim to determine whether baseline levels and changes in IL-6 and hsCRP, individually or together, independently predict MACE and death after acute coronary syndrome (ACS) in statin-treated patients.20 The ODYSSEY OUTCOMES trial compared alirocumab with placebo in post-ACS patients on optimized statin therapy. In post-hoc analyses, the relation between log-transformed hsCRP and IL-6 levels and risk of MACE and all-cause death was assessed in proportional hazards models. A total of about 11 800 patients had baseline hsCRP and IL-6 data; 1306 had a MACE primary endpoint and 458 died. Median hsCRP, IL-6, and LDL-C were 1.54 mg/l, 5 pg/ml, and 86 mg/dl, respectively. hsCRP and IL-6 had moderate correlation (r = 0.52). In models for one biomarker adjusted for the other biomarker, treatment assignment, age, sex, diabetes, LDL-C, and time since index ACS, hsCRP was a significant independent predictor of MACE (P < .0001) and IL-6 was not (P = .21); both independently predicted death (P < .0001 for hsCRP and P = .0003 for IL-6). Relationships did not depend on treatment (all Pinteraction > .25). When dichotomized at 2 mg/l (hsCRP) and 5 pg/ml (IL-6), risks of MACE and death were significantly elevated when both, but not when one marker was elevated (Figure 1). Inflammasomes are key signalling platforms that detect noxious stimuli and activate the highly pro-inflammatory cytokine, IL-1β, which stimulates elaboration of IL-6 by inflammatory cells and CRP by the liver. When dichotomized at conventional thresholds (5 pg/ml for IL-6; 2 mg/l for hsCRP), MACE and death following ACS were significantly higher only when both biomarkers were elevated. ACS, acute coronary syndrome; CI, confidence interval; CRP, C-reactive protein; hsCRP, high-sensitivity C-reactive protein; IL, interleukin; MACE, major adverse cardiovascular events; NLRP3, nucleotide-binding leucine-rich repeat-containing pyrine receptor 3.20 The authors conclude that in patients with recent ACS, hsCRP independently predicts MACE, while both hsCRP and IL-6 predict death. Together, the two markers provide complementary prognostic information. hsCRP conveys independent information on inflammatory risk beyond that provided by IL-6. The manuscript is accompanied by an Editorial by Erik Stroes and Maxim Annink from the University of Amsterdam in The Netherlands.21 The authors highlight that the study by Jukema et al. makes a strong case for rethinking how we assess inflammatory risk after ACS. The observation that combined rather than individual biomarker elevation drives MACE risk is itself an argument against relying on any single inflammatory marker. This is supported by recent work by Nurmohamed et al. showing that targeted proteomics can identify inflammatory proteins predictive of MACE even in patients with low CRP levels, pinpointing pathways that CRP misses altogether. Just as lipid risk assessment has evolved from LDL-C alone towards integrated evaluation including Lp(a) and triglyceride-rich remnants, inflammatory risk stratification should move towards multi-marker panels that capture the diversity of proatherogenic inflammatory pathways. Such panels could help select patients for emerging and probably costly anti-inflammatory therapies, aligning treatment intensity with individual pathobiology. The goal is not a single number that summarizes inflammation, but a profile that guides precision, and perhaps intensity, of the intervention. As anti-inflammatory cardiovascular therapies progress from proof-of-concept to clinical implementation, translating the optimal inflammatory signature into scalable, actionable tools will be an important next step. In a Clinical Research article entitled ‘Cholesterol-lowering therapy from childhood/adolescence and long-term outcomes in familial hypercholesterolaemia: the SAFEHEART study’, Antonio Vallejo-Vaz from the University of Seville, Spain, and colleagues assess the long-term impact of contemporary management of FH on LDL-C and cardiovascular events.22 Evidence supporting initiation of cholesterol-lowering medication (CLM) in childhood to lower this cumulative cholesterol burden and cardiovascular sequelae is sparse. SAFEHEART is an observational prospective cohort study including children/adolescents (age <18 years) with genetically confirmed heterozygous FH (FH-Ch), their non-affected children and adolescents’ relatives (non-FH-Ch), and FH parents (FH-P). Impact of CLM, LDL-C burden, and cardiovascular events were assessed. Overall, 348 FH-Ch, 165 non-FH-Ch, and 288 FH-P were included (50% female; median untreated LDL-C: 5.46, 2.63, and 7.19 mmol/l, respectively). Median follow-up was 12.4 years. At follow-up, 84% FH-Ch, 4.2% non-FH-Ch, and 95% FH-P were receiving CLM. FH-Ch started therapy at a median age of 14.5 vs 36 years in their FH-P. Latest on-treatment LDL-C was 3 mmol/l in FH-Ch and 2.44 mmol/l in FH-P; LDL-C among non-FH-Ch (not on CLM) was 2.72 mmol/l. By age 30–40 years, median LDL-C burden over life was 5909 and 10 207 mg/dl*years among FH-Ch and FH-P, respectively. By age 39 years, the rate of cardiovascular events was 0.0%, 0.3%, and 5.2% among non-FH-Ch, FH-Ch, and FH-P, respectively. The authors conclude that treatment of FH from childhood/adolescence reduces the cumulative LDL-C burden compared with later onset treatment from adulthood in affected parents and permits attainment of LDL-C levels close to non-FH individuals; this finding is associated with the observation of a reduction in the cardiovascular risk of young FH patients. These findings support FH as a paediatric condition requiring early-life detection and treatment. The manuscript is accompanied by an Editorial by Archna Bajaj and Marina Cuchel from the University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, PA, USA.23 The authors highlight that in the SAFEHEART registry there were differences reported in the treatment of young female patients compared with males. Intense lipid-lowering treatment, defined as treatment that would be expected to decrease LDL-C by at least 50%, was present in 61% of males from the HeFH children/adolescents group, but only in 50% of females, highlighting a gap that needs to be addressed, particularly as females are often undertreated over their lifetime due to required interruption of lipid-lowering treatment for periods of pregnancy and lactation. In summary, while great strides have been made in the diagnosis and treatment of HeFH patients, aided by the development of novel LDL-C-lowering therapies in recent years, there still remains a considerable gap in improving the management of such patients across real-world settings. Giant aortic aneurysm in a child with a lethal arteriopathy due to a novel mutation in the FBLN4 gene
items.abstract: A lethal inherited arteriopathy syndrome associated with a novel, homozygous mutation (D203A) of the EFEMP2 (FBLN4) gene was discovered in an ethnically unique cohort of 22 infants from Kerala, India.1 EFEMP2 encodes fibulin-4 that has been identified as a critical determinant of elastogenesis. This connective tissue disease is characterized by a severe vascular phenotype with gross dilatation, elongation, tortuosity and narrowing of elastic arteries, in addition to cutis laxa, joint hyperlaxity and typical facial features.2 Although classified under Autosomal Recessive Cutis Laxa 1B in OMIM, this particular syndrome has a far more lethal outcome than other inherited arteriopathy syndromes including Arterial Tortuosity Syndrome, Loeys-Dietz Syndrome and Marfan Syndrome. In an expanded cohort of 63 patients, the median age at death is 15 months. Our current patient, an isolated survivor, a 14-year-old girl presented with symptoms of dyspnoea on exertion. She was diagnosed with the above-mentioned mutation 5 years ago and was on follow-up for the ascending aortic aneurysm. Her current CT aortogram and 3D reconstruction revealed a dilated ascending aorta of maximum diameter of 12 cm and occupying almost the entire left hemithorax. Due to the mass effect, there was complete left bronchus compression at its origin with a fully collapsed left lung (Figure A–D). The abdominal aorta, arch vessels and intracranial arteries showed a tortuous course consistent with the disease. She underwent ascending aorta and arch replacement using a dacron graft and had an uneventful recovery and is doing well at 2 years follow-up (Figure E and F).

items.title: Clonal haematopoiesis and the cardiovascular–kidney–metabolic continuum
items.abstract: This commentary refers to ‘Clonal haematopoiesis and cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic syndrome: a cohort study’, by A. Chang et al., https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehag655 and the discussion piece ‘Defining CKM progression by a cardiovascular endpoint: a built-in circularity’, by A. Kazory and A. Koratala, https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehag857. We thank Drs Kazory and Koratala for their thoughtful response to our recent report on clonal haematopoiesis of indeterminate potential (CHIP) and cardiovascular–kidney–metabolic (CKM) syndrome.1 The authors note that development of clinical cardiovascular disease (CVD) was used to determine progression to Stage 4 CKM. However, Stage 4 was not an outcome definition created for our study; clinical CVD defines Stage 4 within the established CKM staging framework. Now codified in multi-society guidelines,2 the CKM syndrome framework conceptualizes CKM as a continuum culminating in clinical CVD at Stage 4. Accordingly, evaluating whether an exposure is associated with transition from Stages 0–3 to Stage 4 is consistent with the framework itself. We respectfully wish to clarify that this does not create ‘built-in circularity.’ Clonal haematopoiesis of indeterminate potential does not contribute to the definition of CKM stage or the Stage 4 outcome; rather, our analysis asked whether baseline CHIP was cross-sectionally associated with CKM stage and prospectively associated with transition to a prespecified CKM stage. That CHIP has previously been associated with CVD informs the interpretation of this finding, but does not make the analysis circular.

items.title: Defining cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic progression by a cardiovascular endpoint: a built-in circularity
items.abstract: This commentary refers to ‘Clonal haematopoiesis and cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic syndrome: a cohort study’, by A. Chang et al., https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehag655 and the discussion piece ‘Clonal haematopoiesis and the cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic continuum’, by A. Chang and M. C. Honigberg, https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehag858. We read with interest the study by Chang et al. examining the association of clonal haematopoiesis of indeterminate potential (CHIP) with cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) syndrome.1 The authors provide an important analysis linking CHIP, inflammatory proteomic signatures, and adverse cardiovascular outcomes. However, we question whether these longitudinal findings truly demonstrate CKM progression or largely reflect the already established association between CHIP and cardiovascular disease (CVD). The primary longitudinal outcome was progression from CKM stages 0–3 to stage 4. Yet, stage 4 is defined by the development of clinical CVD, such as coronary artery disease or heart failure. Thus, among participants without CVD at baseline, ‘progression to CKM stage 4’ essentially meant developing CVD. This is important because CHIP is already known to be tightly associated with several cardiovascular outcomes.2 Therefore, showing that CHIP predicts a composite of cardiovascular events does not necessarily mean that it predicts progression of the broader, multi-component CKM syndrome. The magnitude of the reported associations further reinforces this concern. The strongest associations were observed for specific cardiovascular outcomes: spliceosome and JAK2 CHIP were associated with heart failure with hazard ratios (HRs) of 2.62 (95% CI 2.01–3.41) and 2.79 (95% CI 1.58–4.91), respectively, and JAK2 CHIP was associated with peripheral artery disease with an HR of as high as 3.80 (95% CI 1.81–7.98). Interestingly, the signal became substantially weaker when examined within the broader CKM construct: non-DNMT3A CHIP was associated with progression to stage 4 with an HR of 1.24 (95% CI 1.17–1.31), while any CHIP had an HR of only 1.13 (95% CI 1.09–1.17); its cross-sectional association with greater CKM severity was only minimal (OR 1.04; 95% CI 1.01–1.08). This striking dilution suggests that the apparent CKM-level signal is largely inherited from its cardiovascular component rather than reflecting an independent multi-component CKM phenomenon.

items.title: Weekly Journal Scan: PREMIUM evidence that aspirin omission in STEMI patients undergoing primary percutaneous coronary intervention is unjustified and unsafe
items.abstract: Comment on ‘Aspirin Omission at the Time of Primary Percutaneous Coronary Intervention in STEMI’ which was published in The New England Journal of Medicine, https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2606997. DAPT with low-dose aspirin and a P2Y12 inhibitor remains the default treatment strategy for 12 months after an acute coronary syndrome (ACS) in patients without high bleeding risk.2 Its rationale extends beyond the prevention of stent thrombosis, as the simultaneous inhibition of thromboxane A2- and adenosine diphosphate (ADP)-dependent platelet activation reduces also recurrent atherothrombotic events arising from non-target lesions in the coronary circulation and other vascular territories.3 However, evidence from randomized trials and meta-analyses has challenged the need for a uniform DAPT strategy, suggesting that shorter DAPT regimens, particularly in appropriately selected patients at low ischaemic risk, may reduce bleeding without compromising protection against ischaemic events.4–7 The STOPDAPT-3 trial found that immediate aspirin omission with prasugrel monotherapy at the time of PCI in 6002 Japanese patients with ACS or HBR did not reduce major bleedings and was associated with an excess of early coronary events, including stent thrombosis.4 Of note, in the control group, DAPT was maintained for the first month after PCI, followed by aspirin monotherapy, thus testing aspirin withdrawal specifically during the period of highest thrombotic risk rather than a long-term aspirin-free strategy. The NEO-MINDSET trial, in which aspirin was stopped as early as 2 days after PCI for ACS, failed to demonstrate non-inferiority and showed numerically more death, MI, stroke, and a three-fold higher incidence of stent thrombosis.5

items.title: Micro- and nanoplastics in acute coronary thrombosis: exposure, enrichment, or a dual mechanism?
items.abstract: This commentary refers to ‘Micro- and nano-plastics in the coronary circulation and air pollution exposure in ischaemic heart disease presentation’, by P. Paolisso et al., https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehag447 and the discussion piece ‘Coronary micro- and nanoplastics in ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction: antecedent exposure or post-thrombotic enrichment’, by J. Qin et al., https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehag800. We thank Qin et al.1 for their thoughtful commentary on our study of micro- and nanoplastics (MNPs) in the coronary circulation across the spectrum of coronary artery disease. The authors raise two principal points: whether the proximal-to-peripheral gradient observed in ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) reflects antecedent exposure or post-thrombotic enrichment and whether smoking confounds the association between MNPs and acute coronary thrombosis. We welcome the opportunity to clarify these issues. We agree that our cross-sectional, single-timepoint sampling design cannot definitively separate focal accumulation preceding plaque rupture from secondary enrichment occurring after thrombotic occlusion. We emphasize that this local mechanism cannot alone account for our findings. Indeed, our most robust finding was not the concentration gradient itself but the markedly different rate of patients with detectable MNPs across the three groups, highest in STEMI, intermediate in chronic coronary syndromes, and lowest in controls, a binary difference in presence vs absence that local stasis or thrombus-related sequestration at a single occlusion site does not readily explain. Moreover, we deliberately used peripheral arterial blood, sampled at the vascular sheath and remote from the culprit lesion, as the reference compartment for this comparison to avoid confounding from local thrombus formation and flow disruption at the site of coronary occlusion. Peripheral arterial MNP concentrations were also significantly higher in STEMI than in chronic coronary syndromes or controls, a systemic difference that stasis or thrombus-related sequestration at the occlusion site cannot explain.2 We therefore view antecedent exposure and post-thrombotic local enrichment not as competing explanations but as plausibly coexisting phenomena: a higher systemic MNP burden predisposing to atherothrombotic events, superimposed on focal concentration once coronary flow is disrupted. The design proposed by the authors—comparing polymer burden and composition across peripheral blood, upstream and downstream coronary blood, aspirated thrombus, and plaque tissue from the same patient—is precisely the direction we are now pursuing, building on prior work demonstrating MNPs within coronary and peripheral thrombi and within atherosclerotic plaque itself.3–6

items.title: Coronary micro- and nanoplastics in ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction: antecedent exposure or post-thrombotic enrichment?
items.abstract: This commentary refers to ‘Micro- and nano-plastics in the coronary circulation and air pollution exposure in ischaemic heart disease presentation’, by P. Paolisso et al., https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehag447 and the discussion piece ‘Micro- and nanoplastics in acute coronary thrombosis: exposure, enrichment, or a dual mechanism?’, by R. Marfella et al., https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehag803. We read with interest the study by Paolisso et al., who quantified micro- and nanoplastics (MNPs) in paired peripheral and coronary blood samples from patients with ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), chronic coronary syndromes, and angiographically normal coronary arteries. The paired sampling design, rigorous contamination controls, and complementary analytical methods are important strengths. However, the spatial gradient observed in STEMI permits an alternative interpretation.1 In STEMI, MNP concentrations were highest in coronary blood sampled upstream from the culprit occlusion before lesion crossing (Tube B), followed by downstream coronary blood after lesion crossing (Tube C) and peripheral arterial blood (Tube A). This pattern may reflect focal accumulation before plaque rupture, but all samples were obtained after a TIMI 0/1 thrombotic occlusion had formed. Markedly reduced flow and stasis near the occlusion, prolonged residence of circulating particles, or incorporation into thrombotic material could also produce secondary enrichment. Plastic polymers have been detected in coronary thrombi from patients with myocardial infarction and in thrombi retrieved from coronary, cerebral, and deep venous sites. These observations establish that thrombi can contain plastic particles, but not whether the particles promoted thrombosis or became incorporated during clot formation. The proximal-to-peripheral gradient should therefore be regarded as lesion-associated enrichment rather than evidence that focal deposition necessarily preceded the acute event.1–3

items.title: Cortisol in cardio-kidney-metabolic disease
items.abstract: Despite guideline-directed therapy, many patients with cardio-kidney-metabolic (CKM) disease remain uncontrolled due to therapeutic inertia, adherence barriers, and underrecognized secondary causes. Hypercortisolism, ranging from mild autonomous cortisol secretion (MACS) to overt Cushing syndrome, is an increasingly recognized contributor. MACS is associated with a 2.5-fold higher risk of cardiovascular death and increased prevalence of hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), and kidney impairment. Cortisol excess promotes muscle insulin resistance, hepatic gluconeogenesis, β-cell dysfunction, sodium retention, and vascular remodelling, worsening glycaemia and blood pressure, leading to poor CKM outcomes. Recent prospective studies suggest that hypercortisolism is more prevalent than previously suspected in selected CKM phenotypes, including 24% in patients with difficult-to-control T2DM in CATALYST and 27% in patients with resistant hypertension in MOMENTUM. The overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test remains the diagnostic test of choice. Therapeutic strategies include adrenal steroidogenesis inhibitors, glucocorticoid receptor antagonists, and pituitary-directed therapies in selected cases, while surgery remains the first-line treatment for surgically remediable disease. This review summarizes the epidemiology and mechanisms linking cortisol excess to CKM dysfunction, and also highlights the need for clinical trials, standardized diagnostic thresholds, and assays to enable integration of cortisol-targeted therapies into management pathways to mitigate residual CKM risk. This review will serve as a practical guide for cardiologists to manage a potentially reversible contributor to poor CKM control.

items.title: Extensive type B aortic dissection with Michels type IX hepatic arterial anatomy causing acalculous gangrenous cholecystitis
items.abstract: A 36-year-old man with hypertension presented with a 3-day history of abrupt-onset back and chest pain, followed by abdominal pain. Computed tomography angiography demonstrated an acute Stanford type B aortic dissection (Panel A, arrowheads) extending from the proximal descending thoracic aorta to both common iliac arteries, with multiple re-entry tears and severe ostial compromise of the superior mesenteric artery (SMA) (Panel A, red arrow). Three-dimensional reconstruction showed a replaced common hepatic artery arising from the SMA (Michels type IX anatomy1; Panel B, blue arrows), rendering the entire hepatobiliary arterial inflow SMA-dependent. The gallbladder was markedly distended without visible calculi (Panel C, asterisk). Angiography confirmed non-opacification of the SMA origin and poor distal perfusion. Endovascular aortic repair involved three overlapping stent grafts and supra-aortic branch reconstruction. Subsequent SMA stenting restored visceral flow (see Supplementary data online, Figure S1). Persistent abdominal pain and gastrointestinal bleeding prompted immediate laparoscopy. Moderate bile-stained ascites was present. The small bowel and colon were viable, but the gallbladder was gangrenous, measuring 10 × 8 × 6 cm, with focal bile leakage (Panel D). Laparoscopic cholecystectomy was performed. The opened specimen showed haemorrhagic mucosal necrosis without gallstones (Panel E), and haematoxylin and eosin staining confirmed haemorrhagic necrosis with acute inflammation (Panel F). Michels type IX anatomy is rare, occurring in 2.96% of 5002 patients.2 Here, the variant rendered cystic arterial perfusion SMA-dependent; SMA malperfusion from the type B dissection therefore caused acalculous gangrenous cholecystitis despite viable bowel. Clinicians should consider gallbladder ischaemia in this setting.

AI algorithms and external validation: promises, pitfalls, and a practical blueprint
items.abstract: External validation involving the testing of a frozen AI model on independent data from other sites, populations, time periods, or devices provides the clearest estimate of intended-use setting performance when those external data are deployment-representative of the expected population, measurement processes, and clinical workflow. It yields realistic estimates of discrimination and calibration, exposes shortcut learning and distribution shift, quantifies clinical utility through decision-analytic measures, and reveals subgroup disparities requiring mitigation. Yet common pitfalls undermine credibility: quasi-external splits with hidden relatedness; spectrum and prevalence mismatch; site, workflow, and hardware effects; label noise and reference-standard drift; analytic flexibility and selective reporting; small, underpowered samples; reliance only on the area under the curve; unreported threshold tuning; and leakage. A practical blueprint emphasizes pre-registration; representative, multi-site cohorts spanning geography, time, and acquisition; prevention of patient and temporal overlap; comprehensive evaluation of discrimination, calibration (including calibration-in-the-large, calibration slope, and calibration plots), and net benefit with confidence intervals; pre-specified subgroup and fairness audits; transparent labelling procedures and uncertainty analyses; principled sample-size calculations; and minimal, well-documented model updating (recalibration before revision). Finally, external validation should connect to post-deployment governance via drift detection, performance triggers, and change-control plans, complemented by site-specific local evaluation to ensure safety and reliability across diverse clinical environments. When executed to these standards, external validation transforms promising prototypes into dependable clinical tools, clarifying where a model performs, where it fails, and what adaptations are necessary for safe, equitable, and sustainable use. This framework links statistical evaluation to clinical use, model updating, and post-deployment monitoring.

Interstitial lung disease with associated severe pulmonary hypertension is rarely idiopathic by clinical or pathologic measures
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Heart and Lung Transplantation
items.abstract: Background Interstitial lung disease (ILD) patients who develop severe pulmonary hypertension (PH) have rapidly progressive disease and increased mortality, but their clinical and pathologic phenotypes are poorly defined. Improved understanding and identification of these patients will expedite beneficial PH-targeted therapeutics and referral for lung transplantation. Methods We conducted a comprehensive retrospective study of a large cohort of ILD patients who underwent lung transplant at University of California, Los Angeles. Multidisciplinary Discussion (MDD) was used to establish ILD etiologies incorporating all available clinical, radiographic, and pathologic data. Severe pre-capillary PH was defined as pulmonary vascular resistance >5 Wood units on cardiac catheterization. Quantitative histopathologic analysis of explanted idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) lungs was performed using blinded whole-slide annotation by two pulmonary pathologists, comparing the pathologic features of IPF with severe PH to IPF without PH. Results Among 347 ILD patients, 13% had severe PH. In the large majority of cases (86%), the correct ILD diagnosis/etiology was established clinically with MDD alone. Only 20% of severe PH cases were classified as IPF, with the most common subtype identified as autoimmune-associated ILD. On histopathology, IPF patients with severe PH demonstrated a similar extent of usual interstitial pneumonia but markedly less normal lung and a greater burden of atypical pathology, particularly nonspecific interstitial pneumonia, compared to IPF patients without PH. Conclusions Our study illustrates the low prevalence of IPF in severe PH-ILD, describes a novel finding of distinct histopathologic features of IPF patients with severe PH versus no PH, and demonstrates the diagnostic utility of MDD without explant pathology.

items.title: The Heart Transplant Alimony- Prior scars causing future strain
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Heart and Lung Transplantation
items.abstract: Background Primary heart transplantation for hypoplastic left heart syndrome (HLHS) has been limited by the scarcity of neonatal donors. Although hypothermic oxygenated machine perfusion (HOPE) enables donation after circulatory death (DCD) heart transplantation, previous cannulation techniques sacrificed the donor aortic arch, precluding the reconstruction required for HLHS. Methods A neonatal-sized porcine DCD heart was recovered with the entire thoracic aorta preserved en-bloc using a novel split-cannulation strategy compatible with HOPE. Following 304 minutes of ex situ preservation, the heart–aorta graft was transplanted into a recipient after reconstruction designed to replicate HLHS anatomy. Graft function, haemodynamics, myocardial oedema, and systemic outflow were assessed. Results The split-cannulation strategy enabled stable HOPE preservation of the intact heart–thoracic aorta graft throughout ex situ perfusion. Myocardial oedema was minimal (8% weight increase during preservation, 2% above baseline after transplantation). Successful implantation was demonstrated by spontaneous recovery of electrical activity, restoration of sinus rhythm, progressive improvement in cardiac output, and satisfactory ventricular contraction on epicardial echocardiography. No significant pressure gradient was detected across the reconstructed aortic arch. Conclusions This study demonstrates the technical feasibility of recovering, preserving, and transplanting an intact neonatal-sized DCD heart–thoracic aorta graft using a novel split-cannulation HOPE strategy. By preserving the donor thoracic aorta for arch reconstruction, this technique overcomes a key anatomical barrier to primary DCD heart transplantation for HLHS and provides the technical foundation for clinical translation.

items.title: Unintended Shifts in High-Priority Adult Heart Transplant Listings after the OPTN’s September 2025 Policy Change
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Heart and Lung Transplantation
items.abstract: The Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network amended Status 2 heart allocation criteria in September 2025, requiring documented failure of high-dose inotropes before candidates could qualify via intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP) or percutaneous endovascular ventricular assist device (PEVAD) support. Using OPTN data, we compared seasonally matched pre-policy (September 2024-June 2025, n=4,206) and post-policy (September 2025-June 2026, n=4,231) adult candidates. While standard Status 3 high-dose inotrope listings increased 2.0% to 4.1% and standard Status 2 IABP/PEVAD listings decreased 18.2% to 11.0%, Status 1 listings and Status 2 exceptions increased 7.7% to 10.6% and 17.5% to 21.5%, respectively (all p<0.001). Consequently, combined initial Status 1/2 listings were unchanged (44.5% vs 44.0%, p=0.71). Furthermore, overall transplant volume remained similar, but status at transplant shifted from standard Status 2 toward Status 2 exceptions and Status 1. Tightening standard Status 2 eligibility was associated with redistribution across high-priority pathways rather than reduced high-priority listings.

items.title: Menstrual Health in Children, Adolescents, and Young Adults with Cardiac Disease: An Underrecognized Component of Heart Failure, Mechanical Circulatory Support, and Transplant Care
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Heart and Lung Transplantation
items.abstract: Background Menstrual abnormalities, including heavy menstrual bleeding, amenorrhea, and dysmenorrhea, are frequently encountered among children, adolescents, and young adults with congenital and acquired heart disease, yet remain underrecognized in routine cardiovascular care. Anticoagulation, thrombosis risk, heart failure physiology, and limited high-quality evidence complicate management and contribute to substantial variation in practice. Methods The Advanced Cardiac Therapies Improving Outcomes Network convened a multidisciplinary working group of cardiologists, hematologists, gynecologists, adolescent medicine specialists, and allied health providers. Following a literature search, the group met monthly via virtual meetings to synthesize current evidence and clinical experience and develop consensus guidance. Results The consensus emphasizes routine, developmentally appropriate menstrual screening and recognition that traditional definitions of heavy menstrual bleeding may underestimate its clinical impact in patients with heart disease. Management requires individualized assessment of bleeding risk, thrombotic risk, cardiac physiology, and patient preferences. Menstrual abnormalities may warrant broader evaluation for changes in overall health, cardiac status, or energy availability. Conclusions Menstrual health is integral to comprehensive cardiovascular care. Integrating screening and individualized management into cardiology practice may reduce morbidity, improve quality of life, and support equitable, sex-informed care. Further research and culturally responsive, multidisciplinary implementation are needed to strengthen the evidence base and improve care consistency.

items.title: Heart Transplantation in Adult Fontan Patients: New Insights from Fontan-Associated Liver Disease Beyond Traditional Predictors
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Heart and Lung Transplantation
items.abstract: Structured Abstract Background Fontan patients are considered high risk for heart transplantation (HT) owing to their complex anatomy, multiple prior chest entries, and universal Fontan-associated liver disease (FALD). The impact of FALD and other preoperative factors remains, however, uncertain. Objectives We sought to identify factors associated with 90-day mortality after isolated HT in adults with Fontan circulation, with particular focus on the relationship between liver-related parameters and post-transplant outcomes. Methods A retrospective cohort study of all adult Fontan patients undergoing isolated HT was conducted. Factors associated with 90-day mortality were assessed using appropriate univariate analyses and penalized multivariable logistic regression. ROC analysis was used to derive liver size cut-offs and compare the discriminative performance of selected variables. A descriptive analysis of adult Fontan patients undergoing combined heart-liver transplantation (CHLT) was also performed for contextual comparison. Results Thirty-seven patients (mean age 30 years) underwent isolated HT; 19% (n=8) died within 90 days. Factors associated with increased 90-day mortality were >4 previous chest entries, major perioperative bleeding, and small liver size [total liver volume (TLV) ≤1366 mL, total liver volume indexed to body surface area (TLVi) <786 mL/m 2 and liver transverse dimension (LTD) <21 cm]. Multiple chest veno-venous collaterals, >4 previous chest entries, and small liver were strongly associated with bleeding and subsequent fatal complications including sepsis, graft dysfunction, and bowel ischaemia. Within the study period, five other patients had undergone CHLT. All had biopsy confirmed advanced liver disease with features of clinically significant portal hypertension or hepatocellular carcinoma. One patient died within 90 days following prolonged cardiopulmonary bypass, major bleeding, graft dysfunction and sepsis, culminating in multiorgan failure. Conclusions In Fontan patients undergoing isolated HT, >4 previous chest entries, major bleeding, and small liver volume were associated with increased 90-day mortality. Objective liver metrics (TLV ≤1366 mL, TLVi <786 mL/m 2 , TLD <21 cm) may provide adjunctive risk stratification for Fontan patients considered for isolated HT; however, these measures and proposed thresholds remain exploratory and require external validation. CHLT is a viable option, although non-liver related transplant risk factors may similarly influence outcomes. Detailed liver assessment and management at experienced, high-volume congenital transplant centres are important to optimizing outcomes in this complex population.

items.title: Reanimationless Rapid Recovery Versus Thoraco-Abdominal Normothermic Regional Perfusion for Donation After Circulatory Death Heart Transplantation Following Prolonged Asystolic Warm Ischemia
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Heart and Lung Transplantation
items.abstract: Background Donation after circulatory death (DCD) heart transplantation has expanded the donor pool, yet contemporary recovery strategies remain constrained. Rapid Recovery with Extended Ultra-Oxygenated Preservation (REUP) is a non-reanimation DCD recovery strategy that eliminates the need for donor heart reperfusion prior to transplantation. As prolonged asystolic warm ischemic time (AWIT) during circulatory arrest has raised ongoing concerns, whether REUP achieves outcomes comparable to TA-NRP in DCD donors with prolonged AWIT remains unknown. Methods We performed a retrospective single-center study of DCD heart transplant recipients whose donor hearts were recovered using either TA-NRP or REUP and preserved with 10°C static cold storage. Donors with AWIT Results Eighty-two DCD heart transplant recipients met inclusion criteria, including 55 TA-NRP and 27 REUP recipients. Compared with TA-NRP donors, REUP donors were older (42.0 vs 33.7 years) and experienced longer total ischemic times (285 vs 219 minutes). Severe PGD occurred in 4 TA-NRP recipients (7.3%) and no REUP recipients (0.0%). Ninety-day mortality was 12.7% versus 7.4%, respectively. In weighted bootstrap analyses, REUP was associated with a directional signal toward lower severe PGD (OR 0.22, 95% CI 0.09-1.02; directional consistency 97.4%) and lower 90-day mortality (OR 0.56, 95% CI 0.09-2.57; directional consistency 76.3%), although confidence intervals were wide. Conclusions Among DCD heart transplant recipients with AWIT ≥10 minutes, REUP demonstrated early graft function and short-term survival comparable to TA-NRP despite a more challenging donor profile. These findings support further prospective multicenter evaluation of REUP as a broadly deployable non-reanimation DCD heart recovery strategy.

items.title: Impact of donor care unit opening and use on lung donation from deceased organ donors after brain death
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Heart and Lung Transplantation
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Deceased donors after brain death (DBD) transferred to donor care units (DCUs) have higher rates of lung donation than donors remaining in hospitals, but contributions of regional DCU availability and donor transfer to lung donation remain unknown. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Cohort study using Organ Procurement & Transplantation Network (OPTN) deceased donor registry files, including adult DBDs managed in donation regions with operating DCUs, 2017-2024. Multivariable logistic regression and G-computation were used to test the hypothesis that individual donor transfer to DCU, rather than regional DCU availability, is associated with a higher likelihood of lung donation (primary outcome). RESULTS: Among 27,795 DBDs managed by 28 OPOs, lung donation rate was 28.6% (7,958 donations). After adjustment for donor characteristics, predicted lung donation rates were similar before (29.1%, 95% CI 27.9-30.2) and after (28.9%, 95% CI 28.3-29.6) regional DCU adoption. Despite wide variation in regional transfer rates (5.2-96.7%), greater regional transfer was not associated with lung donation. After adjustment for donor factors, organ recovery year, and organ procurement organization, donor transfer to DCUs (vs. hospitals) remained associated with higher odds of lung donation overall (aOR 1.32, 95% CI 1.20-1.46) and for each DCU type (independent (aOR 1.41, 95% CI 1.21-1.65) and hospital-based (aOR 1.27, 95% CI 1.12-1.44)). CONCLUSIONS: Superior lung donation rates were seen only for donors transferred from regional hospitals to DCUs. There was no observable association between the proportion of donors transferred and lung donation, suggesting that superior donation outcomes may reflect the selection of donors for transfer rather than system-wide effects of DCU availability.

items.title: En Bloc Heart-Lung Transplantation in the Modern Donor Era: Dual-Organ Recovery and Preservation Challenges
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Heart and Lung Transplantation
items.abstract: Combined heart-lung transplantation remains a rare but essential therapy for selected patients with end-stage cardiopulmonary disease that cannot be addressed by isolated heart or lung transplantation. Modern donor allocation, increasing recipient acuity, donation after circulatory death, and longer transport distances have made graft preservation a critical determinant of whether scarce en bloc grafts can be used safely. Unlike isolated organs, the intact heart-lung bloc presents competing preservation requirements: the heart and lungs differ in ischemic tolerance, optimal storage temperature, perfusate chemistry, airway management, and tolerance of pressure and volume during recovery. Across conventional static cold storage, controlled hypothermic transport, regulated airway-pressure devices, 10°C storage, and emerging donation after circulatory death recovery pathways, this review integrates contemporary approaches for donation after brain death and donation after circulatory death while distinguishing direct en bloc evidence from single-organ extrapolation. The evidence base remains observational and constrained by procedural rarity. Future progress will require multicenter preservation-specific data collection and graft-specific systems that treat the heart-lung bloc as an integrated physiologic unit rather than as two isolated organs transported together.
