Effectiveness of Continuous Automatic Endotracheal Cuff Pressure Monitoring in Preventing Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia in the Pediatric Intensive Care Unit: A Randomized Controlled Trial
items.abstract: Background Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) is a major healthcare-associated infection in critically ill children, primarily driven by microaspiration around the endotracheal tube cuff. Research question Does continuous automatic cuff pressure monitoring (CACPM) reduce the incidence of VAP compared to intermittent manual cuff pressure monitoring (IMCPM) in critically ill pediatric patients requiring mechanical ventilation? Study design and methods In this open-label, randomized controlled superiority trial, pediatric patients requiring mechanical ventilation for ≥48 hours were randomly assigned (1:1) to either CACPM or IMCPM. The target cuff pressure was strictly maintained at 20-25 cmH 2 O. The primary outcome was the proportion of patients developing VAP within 28 days following intubation, evaluated in the intention to treat population. Secondary outcomes included time to VAP diagnosis and target pressure compliance. Statistical approaches included Kaplan-Meier survival analysis and multivariable Cox proportional hazard regression. Results Among 241 randomized patients, ITT analysis showed lower VAP with CACPM than IMCPM (13.3% vs 24.0%; risk difference, -10.6 percentage points; 95% CI, -20.3 to -0.8; P=0.034), with similar PP findings (15.0% vs 26.6%; P=0.044). ITT incidence density was 15.7 vs 27.1 per 1,000 ventilator-days (IRR, 1.73; 95% CI, 0.94-3.18; P=0.080). Unadjusted time-to-VAP was nonsignificant (HR, 1.80; 95% CI, 0.976-3.321; P=0.060), whereas adjusted Cox analysis narrowly indicated a higher VAP hazard with IMCPM (HR, 1.90; 95% CI, 1.024-3.510; P=0.042). Target-pressure compliance was higher with CACPM (P Interpretation CACPM significantly reduces the proportion of critically ill pediatric patients developing VAP compared with IMCPM. This preventive effect appears directly linked to improved target pressure compliance, suggesting that automated regulation could be a valuable addition to pediatric VAP prevention strategies. Clinical trial registration ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT05918172.

items.title: Dominant lung involvement and heterozygous IFIH1 variants
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Heterozygous gain-of-function (GoF) variants in IFIH1 are associated with rare autoinflammatory diseases characterized by heightened interferons-stimulated gene (ISG) signatures. These include Aicardi-Goutières syndrome, presenting with slowly progressive spastic paraparesis of the lower limbs, intracerebral calcifications, and neuroinflammation, and Singleton-Merten syndrome, defined by tooth loss, bone demineralization, and vascular calcification. RESEARCH QUESTION: Do rare IFIH1 GoF variants contribute to an interstitial lung disease phenotype, thereby expanding the spectrum of IFIH1-related disorders? STUDY DESIGN AND METHODS: Among 559 children with interstitial lung disease (chILD) and exome sequencing as part of their diagnostic work-up, 12 rare heterozygous IFIH1 variants were identified. Of these, 10 were missense variants of unknown significance, which were functionally assessed in vitro using luciferase assay and ISG-expression profiling. Genome-wide RNA analysis was performed on available patient samples to explore broader transcriptional effects. RESULTS: Four variants with increased basal IFNβ transcription in vitro and elevated ISG expression in vivo indicating GoF behaviour were identified. Disease severity correlated with GoF potential of the respective variant. Two patients harbouring IFIH1 variants with strong GoF activity displayed multisystem involvement and died from respiratory failure at 3 and 4 months of age, respectively. Two additional patients showed milder phenotypes with chronic lung disease stabilizing by the age of 8 and 10 years, respectively. Lung biopsies showed alveolar hypoplasia and alveolar macrophage pneumonia (=desquamative interstitial pneumonia) of varying severity. INTERPRETATION: We report a dominant interstitial lung disease phenotype in individuals harbouring novel IFIH1 variants, expanding IFIH1-related disease to the group of type I interferonopathies with pulmonary manifestations like STING-associated vasculopathy with onset in infancy (SAVI) and COPA syndrome.

items.title: High-Frequency Chest Wall Oscillation in Acute Respiratory Failure With Bronchial Hypersecretion: A Randomized Controlled Trial
items.abstract: Background Airway secretion retention is common in patients with acute respiratory failure (ARF), particularly in those requiring noninvasive respiratory support (NIRS). High-frequency chest wall oscillation (HFCWO) may improve airway clearance but critical care evidence remains limited. Research question Does adding HFCWO to standard care improve clinical outcomes in patients with bronchial hypersecretion and ARF requiring NIRS? Study design and methods We conducted a single-center randomized controlled trial in a RICU. Patients with ARF requiring NIRS, including high-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) and/or noninvasive ventilation (NIV), bronchial hypersecretion, and ineffective cough (peak cough expiratory flow Results Eighty-eight patients were enrolled (44 HFCWO, 44 control), with comparable baseline characteristics. Bronchoscopy was required in 6 patients (13.6%) versus 14 (31.8%) (unadjusted p=0.042); after adjustment the association did not retain statistical significance (adjusted OR 0.336, 95% CI 0.111-1.021; p=0.055). Secondary outcomes, analyzed without correction for multiple testing, are exploratory. Hospital stay (12 [10-15.5] vs 16.5 [13-21] days) and RICU stay (8 [7-10.5] vs 12 [9-17] days) were shorter, with adjusted reductions of 4.5 and 3.6 days. HFNC duration was shorter (6 [4-8] vs 9.5 [6-11.5] days) and remained significant after adjustment, whereas the reduction in NIV duration did not (adjusted p=0.166). No patient required intubation and mortality did not differ. Interpretation In this exploratory trial, HFCWO did not significantly reduce the need for therapeutic bronchoscopy after adjustment. Associated reductions in LOS and HFNC duration are hypothesis-generating and require confirmation in adequately powered multicenter trials. Clinical trial registration ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT05751707; Tuscany Ethics Committee (Protocol: 21987-10/17/2022).

items.title: Effect of clarithromycin on the circulating inflammatory proteome in community-acquired pneumonia: a secondary analysis of the ACCESS trial
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: The ACCESS randomized double-blind controlled trial in hospitalized adults with community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) showed that adding clarithromycin to standard-of-care therapy accelerated clinical recovery within the first 72 hours after the commencement of treatment and reduced progression to organ dysfunction. RESEARCH QUESTION: Does clarithromycin treatment modulate the circulating inflammatory protein profile in CAP, and can inflammatory endotypes identify patient subgroups with distinct clinical responses? STUDY DESIGN AND METHODS: Serum samples obtained from ACCESS trial patients at baseline and 72 hours were profiled using the Olink Target 96 Inflammation panel. Patients were grouped by treatment arm and by achievement of the trial's composite primary endpoint. After quality control, 70 proteins from 394 paired samples across 197 patients were analyzed to assess differential expression within and between groups over time, evaluate associations with clinical outcomes, and identify immune endotypes using unsupervised clustering. RESULTS: IL6 was selectively downregulated on day 4 in the clarithromycin arm, whereas IFN-γ, CXCL9, CXCL10, and SCF decreased over time across both treatment arms, consistent with resolution of inflammation. Among patients achieving the primary endpoint, IL6, CXCL9, CXCL10, and IFN-γ were suppressed only in clarithromycin-treated individuals. Clustering consistently identified two inflammatory endotypes with comparable SOFA, but distinct RSS scores. The endotype with lower RSS demonstrated higher IFN-γ and globally elevated inflammatory protein expression; in that endotype 90-day mortality was decreased with clarithromycin treatment. INTERPRETATION: Clarithromycin exerts measurable immunomodulatory effects in CAP, characterized by attenuation of pro-inflammatory cytokines, particularly IL6. The identification of distinct inflammatory endotypes suggests biological heterogeneity in CAP and supports future investigation of endotype-guided approaches to identify patients most likely to benefit from immunomodulatory therapies. CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04724044, EudraCT 2020-004452-15.

items.title: Lung Cancer Screening Rates Remain Low Among Adults Aged 50–54 Years Despite Updated USPSTF Recommendations
Striving for Equity in Cystic Fibrosis Research: Perspectives from Black and Hispanic/ Latino(a) Individuals with CF
items.abstract: Background Black and Hispanic people with cystic fibrosis (PwCF) experience worse health outcomes. Health disparities are exacerbated by clinical research that does not adequately represent the diversity of the CF population. Research questions How do Black/African American and Hispanic/Latino(a) PwCF perceive clinical research? What are the barriers and facilitators to participation in research? Are there viable solutions to improve inclusion? Study design and methods Semi-structured, individual interviews were conducted with PwCF aged ≥18 years who identify as Black/African American race and/or Hispanic/Latino(a) ethnicity. Participants were recruited from six geographically diverse CF centers and through CF Foundation Community Voice, a CF community partner organization. The interview guide was created by a committee that included minoritized PwCF, research coordinators, and physician-scientists. Thematic analysis with inductive and deductive coding was used to analyze interview transcripts. Results Twenty PwCF were interviewed from 2024 to 2025. Drawing from a race-conscious adaptation of the Behavioral Model for Vulnerable Populations, we used domains of predisposing, need-based, and healthcare environment factors, as well as emergent themes relating to information and support needs. Participants discussed barriers to research participation that included narrow eligibility criteria (e.g., genotype requirements, health status) and logistical challenges such as time and cost. PwCF described a sense of isolation as persons of color with CF, which impacted sense of trust in CF care and research studies. They highlighted that racialized experiences, especially doubt surrounding their CF diagnosis, significantly impact willingness to participate. Solutions center around providing community support to address feelings of isolation and information needs to provide transparency about study design and intent. Interpretation Participation in clinical research is strongly influenced by an interplay of social, cultural, health, and systemic factors. Solutions to improve inclusion in trials center the needs of marginalized communities across all phases of study design and implementation.

items.title: Fertility, pregnancy, and women’s health in bronchiectasis: a multicenter study and ELF-EMBARC patient survey
items.abstract: Background Bronchiectasis in women of reproductive age is increasingly recognized, yet data on fertility and pregnancy outcomes remain limited. Research question What are fertility characteristics, pregnancy outcomes, and patient-reported reproductive health experiences in women with bronchiectasis? Study design and methods We conducted a multicenter, retrospective cohort study across EMBARC-affiliated centers including women with bronchiectasis and pregnancy between 2012 and 2023. Clinical, pulmonary, obstetric, and neonatal data were collected. In parallel, an international patient survey assessed fertility, pregnancy, and hormonal influences on disease. Statistical analyses included comparative and correlation testing. Results Eighty-three women contributed data from 121 pregnancies and 123 neonates. Mean age at conception was 29.5 years. Assisted reproductive technologies were used in 32.1% of pregnancies, more frequently in primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD) than other etiologies (48.5% vs. 8.7%, P=0.004). Lung function remained stable during and after pregnancy. Exacerbations occurred in 58.6% of pregnancies. Mean gestational age was 38 weeks and mean birth weight was 2.99 kg. Pre-pregnancy FEV1 correlated with birth weight (ρ=0.42, P=0.001) and gestational age (ρ=0.25, P=0.042). Neonatal outcomes were generally favorable. Survey data (n=629) demonstrated an early onset of menopause in women with bronchiectasis diagnosed before age 50 years compared to after 50 years. Women with PCD reported difficulties conceiving more often than women with early onset bronchiectasis without PCD. Interpretation Pregnancy in women with bronchiectasis is frequently complicated by exacerbations and low neonatal birth weight. Subfertility is primarily driven by PCD, while non-PCD bronchiectasis shows rates similar to the general population. Pre-pregnancy lung function is associated with neonatal outcomes, supporting the importance of pulmonary optimization and multidisciplinary care before and during pregnancy.

items.title: Dyspnea during resting breathing and carbon dioxide rebreathing in adult patients with congenital central hypoventilation syndrome
items.abstract: Background Congenital central hypoventilation syndrome (CCHS) is an ultra-rare genetic disorder caused by PHOX2B mutations. Patients lack central CO2 chemosensitivity and require ventilatory support during sleep. Children with CCHS have been reported to lack CO2-induced air hunger, but respiratory sensations and dyspnea have not been characterized in adults. Research question Do genetically characterized adult CCHS patients experience respiratory sensations and dyspnea during unassisted resting breathing and CO2 rebreathing, and along which dimensions? Study design and methods This was a prospective controlled observational study conducted on a convenience sample derived from a national cohort of an ultrarare disease. Thirteen adult CCHS patients carrying PHOX2B mutations underwent Multidimensional Dyspnea Profile (MDP) assessment during unassisted resting breathing and at the end of CO2 rebreathing. Healthy controls were studied under the same conditions. Results Before the study, none of the patients had spontaneously reported dyspnea or bothersome respiratory sensations. When prompted with the MDP during resting breathing, 9/13 patients described breathing unpleasantness (non-zero MDP-A1) versus 0/18 controls (p Interpretation Adult CCHS patients can experience conscious unpleasant breathing awareness at rest and retain a perceptual response to CO2 despite abolished or nearly abolished central chemosensitivity. These findings suggest respiratory interoceptive pathways beyond canonical brainstem chemosensitive circuits and support active multidimensional assessment of dyspnea in adult CCHS patients.

items.title: Diagnostic Contribution of Endobronchial Optical Coherence Tomography in the Multidisciplinary Diagnosis of Interstitial Lung Disease
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Less-invasive, lower-risk alternatives to surgical lung biopsy (SLB) have emerged for interstitial lung disease (ILD) diagnosis, such as transbronchial lung cryobiopsy (TBLC) and Envisia Genomic Classifier (EGC), but suffer from limited sampling and simplified binomial classification, respectively. Endobronchial optical coherence tomography (EB-OCT) is a low-risk, large-volume bronchoscopic imaging modality with microscopic resolution, which accurately detects features and patterns for ILD diagnosis as previously validated against SLB. RESEARCH QUESTION: How does EB-OCT contribute to ILD diagnosis and diagnostic confidence at multidisciplinary discussion (MDD) when paired with clinically indicated TBLC and EGC? STUDY DESIGN AND METHODS: Patients with low-confidence ILD diagnosis clinically referred for both TBLC with EGC were enrolled to undergo concurrent EB-OCT imaging. Each modality was interpreted independently by blinded pathologists. Separate MDD sessions were conducted at two independent sites, including one without prior EB-OCT experience. RESULTS: Fifteen patients were included (9 male; mean age: 70.6 years) with final diagnoses of UIP/IPF (n=5), secondary UIP (n=2), and various non-UIP ILDs (n=8) in agreement at both MDDs. EB-OCT provided diagnostic data that was in agreement with final MDD diagnosis for 100% of subjects (15/15), including in the 40% of subjects (6/15) where TBLC was non-diagnostic. In the subjects where TBLC yielded diagnostic data (60%, 9/15), EB-OCT diagnosis was in agreement. EB-OCT combined with TBLC/EGC increased diagnostic confidence and/or narrowed the differential diagnosis from baseline clinical/radiologic data review in all subjects, with replication across both independent MDDs. INTERPRETATION: In this pilot study, we demonstrate EB-OCT is a safe, large-volume imaging method that detects microscopic features and patterns for ILD diagnosis, which increases diagnostic confidence in the context of MDD and complements TBLC and EGC. Future multicenter studies are needed to further validate these findings.

items.title: Determinants of lung cancer screening follow-up care in community care settings: A qualitative multi-case study in the ACCELL trial
items.abstract: Background Adherence to lung cancer screening (LCS) follow-up is essential to achieve mortality benefits from screening. However, population-based studies demonstrate follow-up is Research question What are determinants of LCS follow-up in community settings? Study design and methods This qualitative multi-case study informed a pre-post intervention trial, testing pragmatic interventions to address LCS follow-up in community settings. We conducted rapid ethnographic assessments (REA) through virtual and in person site visits of LCS delivery in three community-based healthcare systems in Washington state. Additionally at the two future intervention sites, we conducted provider and patient interviews. Interview transcripts were analyzed using Rapid Group Analysis Process. All data were triangulated according to Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research and National Institute on Minority Health and Health Disparities Research Framework domains. Results Twenty-eight organizational leaders, providers, and staff participated in REA. Thirty-one patients and 15 providers from the future intervention sites participated in interviews. Determinants of LCS follow-up in the intervention domain included role of primary care, LCS complexity and care process standardization. In the inner setting domain (organization and clinic), screening prioritization, EHR use, radiology support, and context of wellness visits affected LCS. The main theme in the outer setting domain was the influence of social determinants of health on LCS. In the individuals domain, shared beliefs in LCS and LCS education and information sharing were key. In the process implementation domain, clinical champions and use of data and metrics were crucial. Interpretation Integrated findings suggest determinants related to LCS complexity, care fragmentation, socioeconomic status and language, and limitations of PCPs could be overcome through more centralized approaches. However, increased use of EHR tools, increased education and standardizing LCS performance metrics may enable follow-up in decentralized settings. Clinical trials registration NCT06324110.

items.title: Non-Diagnostic Does Not Mean Non-Malignant: Outcomes and Predictors of Malignancy Following Nondiagnostic Robotic-Assisted Bronchoscopy
Adherence to Non-Invasive Ventilation in a Provincial Cohort of Children
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Non-invasive ventilation (NIV) adherence is critical to its effectiveness, yet no standardized pediatric definition of "optimal" adherence exists, and population-level data are scarce. RESEARCH QUESTION: What are adherence patterns to NIV in children, and which factors are associated with adherence in a provincial longitudinal cohort? STUDY DESIGN AND METHODS: Canadian retrospective longitudinal cohort study linking records from the Ontario Ventilator Equipment Pool to health administrative databases. We identified children <18 years prescribed NIV with telemonitoring (2020 to 2022) and ≥1 month of data. The adherence definitions explored were the adult definition of ≥4 hours/day (primary) and measures of any daily use, daily NIV hours, and data missingness ("days not used" = 0 hours recorded; "days no data" = no signal). Mixed-effects regression models were used to explore adherence factors. RESULTS: We included 237 children (mean age 12.9 years; 61% male) with 3,685 person-months of NIV data (median 13 [IQR 8-24]). Across person-months, mean adherence by the ≥4-hours/day definition was 69.6%. Child-level monthly mean (SD) adherence was 59% (32%) by this definition, and 68% (26%) for any use. Mean (SD) daily use when used was 7.5 (3.2) hours. Monthly "days not used" and "no data" averaged 5.1 (6.4) and 4.4 (5.0) days, respectively. Greater adherence was associated with younger age (2-percentage-point decrease per year increase; 95% CI, 1-3), having ≥3 complex chronic conditions vs none (14 percentage-points higher; 95% CI, 3-26), and longer time prescribed NIV (2-percentage-point increase per year; 95% CI, 1-3). INTERPRETATION: NIV adherence was moderate across definitions, with higher adherence among younger children, greater medical complexity, and those using therapy longer, highlighting the need for pediatric-specific adherence targets and home NIV support strategies.

items.title: Clinical Phenotypes and Prognostic Heterogeneity of Mild-to-Moderate Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease: A Prospective Community-Based Cohort Study
items.abstract: Background The clinical phenotypes, prognosis, and heterogeneity of mild-to-moderate chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) have not been systematically evaluated. Research question Do different clinical phenotypes of mild-to-moderate COPD have different prognoses? Study design and methods We analysed the baseline and 3-year follow-up data of participants with mild-to-moderate COPD from a prospective community-based cohort study. Mild-to-moderate COPD was defined as a forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV 1 ) / forced vital capacity ratio of 1 ≥ 50% of the predicted value. The clinical phenotypes included respiratory symptoms, exacerbation history, emphysema, air trapping, and airway remodelling. Respiratory health outcomes included exacerbations and lung function decline over the 3-year follow-up. Results Overall, 806 participants with mild-to-moderate COPD were included, of whom 712 (88%) completed the 3-year follow-up. Participants with mild-to-moderate COPD had more severe emphysema, air trapping, and airway remodelling; increased exacerbation risk; and faster annual FEV 1 decline than those with preserved spirometry. The severity of airflow obstruction, respiratory symptoms, emphysema, and air trapping, as well as the eosinophilic phenotype, had low overlap in mild-to-moderate COPD. There was significant individual variation in the annual FEV 1 decline rate and exacerbation incidence among participants with mild-to-moderate COPD. Emphysema and air trapping were associated with faster FEV 1 decline and higher exacerbation risk. Respiratory symptoms and exacerbations in the previous year were associated with a higher acute exacerbation risk but not with faster lung function decline. Interpretation Mild-to-moderate COPD exhibited distinct clinical phenotypes with significant prognostic heterogeneity. Accurate phenotype identification is essential for targeted intervention, clinical precision management, and prognostic improvement.

items.title: Subspecialty ILD Clinic Care is Associated with More Guideline-Concordant Evaluation and Improved Outcomes Compared to Other Ambulatory Settings: A Retrospective Cohort Study
items.abstract: Background Subspecialty interstitial lung disease (ILD) clinics are associated with improved outcomes, yet access remains uneven. Even within tertiary health systems, patients with ILD are managed across diverse ambulatory settings, with unclear implications for care and outcomes. Research question Within a single academic health system, do patient characteristics, care delivery, and outcomes differ between individuals with ILD managed in a subspecialty ILD clinic versus other ambulatory settings? Study design and methods We conducted a retrospective cohort study of adults with ILD at a large academic medical center. Identified patients were stratified by care in a subspecialty ILD clinic versus non-specialty setting. Demographic, diagnostic testing, treatment, health care utilization, and survival data were extracted from the electronic health record. Diagnostic and treatment measures were analyzed using multivariable logistic regression. Hospitalization, emergency department visit, and death were analyzed as time-to-event outcomes. Results Among 6,637 patients with ILD, 4,371 (66%) were seen in the subspecialty ILD clinic. The 2,266 patients (34%) managed in non-specialty settings were more likely to identify as Black or Latinx, reside in more socioeconomically deprived neighborhoods, and have an unspecified ILD diagnosis (all p Interpretation Within a single health system, subspecialty ILD clinic care was associated with more guideline-concordant care and improved outcomes. Differences in access to subspecialty expertise may contribute to inequities in care delivery, underscoring the need for scalable strategies, referral optimization, telemedicine, and clinical decision support, to extend ILD expertise and improve outcomes.

items.title: Azithromycin Exposure and Incident Nontuberculous Mycobacterial Isolation in Bronchiectasis and COPD: A Nationwide Nested Case-Control Study
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Azithromycin reduces exacerbations in chronic airway disease, but whether it alters the risk of nontuberculous mycobacterial (NTM) isolation is unresolved. RESEARCH QUESTION: Is azithromycin exposure in the preceding year associated with incident respiratory NTM isolation in non-cystic fibrosis bronchiectasis and in COPD? STUDY DESIGN AND METHODS: Two nationwide register-based nested case-control analyses in Denmark. Case patients had a first positive respiratory culture for NTM; controls, alive and free of prior NTM isolation on the index date, were matched 1:20 on age, sex, and comorbidity index. The prespecified exposure was at least 3,000 mg of azithromycin with at least two prescriptions redeemed in the preceding 12 months, with a 3-month lag. Conditional logistic regression was adjusted for inhaled and oral corticosteroids. Exploratory analyses examined an active comparator at matched thresholds, recency, and outcome stringency. RESULTS: The analyses comprised 173 cases and 3,409 controls (bronchiectasis) and 365 and 7,300 (COPD). Under the prespecified definition, azithromycin was not associated with incident NTM isolation (bronchiectasis: OR, 1.31; 95% CI, 0.79-2.18; COPD: 1.29; 0.78-2.13). In COPD, the OR was 1.61 (1.14-2.28) for one or more prescriptions and 1.29 (0.78-2.13) for two or more. The COPD association was concentrated within 90 days of the index date (2.55; 1.73-3.76) and attenuated with microbiological stringency (definite isolates: 0.77; 0.27-2.20). Non-macrolide antibacterials were more strongly associated than azithromycin at every matched threshold in bronchiectasis (one or more prescriptions: 1.90 [1.36-2.65] vs 1.15 [0.75-1.75]), and at the two higher thresholds in COPD (two or more: 1.48 [1.17-1.86] vs 1.24 [0.75-2.05]). INTERPRETATION: Azithromycin was not associated with NTM isolation under the prespecified definition. Associations under broader definitions were not dose-dependent and clustered close to the index date, more consistent with indication-driven testing than a drug effect, although in COPD an association with any exposure persisted after accounting for other antibacterials.

items.title: Recurrent primary sclerosing cholangitis after liver transplantation: Impact of inflammatory bowel disease on graft outcomes in a Southern European multicenter cohort
items.abstract: Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) is an established indication for liver transplantation (LT), but disease recurrence (rPSC) and the course of associated inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) may influence post-transplant outcomes. This study aimed to determine the prevalence of rPSC and evaluate associated risk factors in a Mediterranean population. We conducted a multicenter retrospective study including PSC patients who underwent LT across 14 transplant centers in Southern Europe. Clinical characteristics, IBD phenotype and activity, immunosuppressive therapy, colectomy status, and post-LT outcomes were analyzed. rPSC was defined according to established diagnostic criteria based on imaging and/or histology after exclusion of secondary causes of biliary injury. A total of 143 patients were included. rPSC occurred in 19.6% of recipients, a prevalence comparable to Northern European cohorts. The presence of IBD was independently associated with increased risk of rPSC in multivariable analysis (HR 4.26; 95% CI: 1.27–14.23; p =0.02), whereas recurrence was more frequently observed among patients with ulcerative colitis. De novo IBD developed in 6.9% of patients and was more frequent among those with rPSC. Post-LT IBD activity worsened in 25% of cases, requiring therapeutic escalation, although it was not significantly associated with recurrence. Neither pre- nor post-transplant colectomy significantly influenced recurrence risk. rPSC was not associated with overall patient survival but was linked to impaired graft survival and a higher need for retransplantation. In this large Mediterranean cohort, IBD was independently associated with increased recurrence risk, whereas ulcerative colitis and de novo IBD were more frequently observed among patients with rPSC. Recurrent PSC was associated with impaired graft outcomes, including reduced graft survival and increased retransplantation. These findings highlight the importance of careful IBD monitoring after LT and support structured long-term surveillance strategies.

items.title: Graft-to-Recipient weight ratio, graft inflow modulation, and small-for-size syndrome: A multicenter prospective study from the LDLT registry
items.abstract: Introduction: Graft-to-recipient weight ratio (GRWR) is widely used to guide graft selection in living donor liver transplantation (LDLT), however its role as an independent predictor of postoperative outcomes and small-for-size syndrome (SFSS) remains debated. Graft inflow modulation (GIM) has been increasingly adopted to allow the safe use of smaller grafts. This study evaluated the impact of GRWR and GIM on short-term outcomes using data from a prospective international registry. Methods: An analysis of prospectively collected data from the International Living Donor Liver Transplant Registry (LDLTregistry.org) was conducted, including 1,944 consecutive LDLT performed at 55 centers (Sep 2023-Feb 2025). Recipients were stratified by GRWR (<0.60%, 0.60%-0.80%, >0.80%). Primary outcomes included major postoperative complications (Clavien-Dindo ≥3a), SFSS and 90-day mortality. Results: Lower GRWR was associated with higher rates of major complications, SFSS, and GIM use. Overall SFSS incidence, classified according to the ILTS-iLDLT-LTSI Consensus Conference Guidelines, was 36.9%, Grade B in 17.0%, and Grade C in 4.0%. SFSS of any grade increased progressively with lower GRWR: 33.4% in GRWR >0.80%, 43.7% in GRWR 0.60%-0.80%, and 63.1% in GRWR <0.60% ( p <0.001). Grade A SFSS was similar across groups ( p =0.12), whereas clinically significant SFSS (Grade B and C) was highest in the GRWR<0.6% (47.6%, p <0.001). 90-day mortality remained low (<5%) across all groups. Nearly half of small grafts were unexpectedly small, without worse short-term outcomes. On multivariable analysis, GRWR was not associated with major complications. Conclusions: GRWR influences short-term outcomes after LDLT but does not fully explain SFSS risk, which appears multifactorial. These findings support a shift away from graft size as the sole determinant of risk, toward a physiology-based, lobe-specific, and standardized intraoperative approach in LDLT.

items.title: Long-term graft and patient survival of patients with portal vein stenosis after pediatric liver transplantation; results from the multicenter multinational PORTAL registry
items.abstract: Background and aims: Pediatric liver transplantation (pLT) has become a standard treatment, but it is still burdened by complications such as portal vein stenosis (PVS). PVS can result in compromised graft function and portal hypertension if left untreated. We aimed to assess long-term patient and graft survival after PVS diagnosis after pLT. Methods: Our study analyzed data from the Portal vein Obstruction Revascularisation Therapy After Liver transplantation (PORTAL) registry, which contains retrospective data from 21 centers, across 18 countries, over a 20-year period. Graft- and patient survival rates were determined after PVS diagnosis. Results : This study included 239 patients (53% female; median age at pLT 1.1 years) diagnosed with PVS. The median age at diagnosis was 2.7 years. The overall ten-year graft survival was 90%, and the ten-year patient survival was 96%. One-year graft and patient survival was lowest in patients with PVS diagnosed ≤7 days after pLT (80% and 92%, respectively). Initial treatment strategies comprised of mostly endovascular procedures (87%), followed by conservative (11%) and surgical treatment (3%). Patient outcome did not differ between these treatment groups. Within the endovascular group, graft survival in patients treated with stent (n=26) was significantly lower compared to those with percutaneous transluminal angioplasty (n=181) (88% vs 98%, respectively, p =0.01). Conclusions: Our findings indicate excellent graft and patient survival after PVS diagnosis and its treatment. Further research is needed to determine the safety and efficacy of optimal management strategies, especially in early-onset PVS.

items.title: Letter to the Editor: Pre-LT sphincterotomy and post-transplant biliary complications—a radiological perspective on anastomotic geometry and biliary anatomy
Changing national practice patterns in living donor BMI and liver biopsy utilization from 2000-2024
items.abstract: Background: Living donor liver transplantation (LDLT) remains an important alternative to deceased donor transplantation amid organ shortages. However, rising obesity may limits its growth through increased steatosis and decreased donor approval. We evaluated trends in donor and recipient BMI, liver biopsy utilization, and the association between donor obesity and recipient outcomes from 2000-2024. Methods: Adult transplant recipients and donors from 2000-2024 were identified using the UNOS STAR file. Temporal BMI trends were assessed using annual percent change (APC). Liver biopsy utilization was evaluated overall and stratified by donor obesity status (BMI ≥30 kg/m 2 ), center volume, and UNOS region. Secondary outcomes included length of stay and post-operative complications. Post-transplant survival was assessed using Cox proportional hazard models, with multivariable regression adjusting for a priori selected covariates. Results: Among 7,942 donor-recipient pairs, recipient median BMI increased from 25.9 to 26.8 kg/m 2 , (APC 0.1%, p =0.01), while donor BMI increased from 24.6 to 27.6 kg/m 2 (APC 0.4%, p <0.001). Despite increasing BMI, liver biopsy utilization declined from approximately 45%-50% in the mid-2000s to 6% by 2024 (APC −8.3%). Biopsy utilization remained higher among obese donors and declined more slowly (APC −5.8%). Donor BMI was not associated with transplant length of stay, post-operative complications (reoperation, vascular/biliary complications, readmissions), or post-transplant recipient survival (OR 1.00, 95% CI 0.99-1.01, p =0.42). Conclusions: Donor and recipient BMI have both increased since 2000, yet donor obesity was not associated with inferior recipient outcomes. Liver biopsy utilization has declined substantially, with persistent regional and center-level variation. Standardization of steatosis assessment may help expand the living donor pool without compromising outcomes. Future studies should assess graft-specific outcomes and long-term steatosis recurrence.

items.title: Letter to the editor: pretransplant exercise prehabilitation or posttransplant nutritional support for better outcomes in living donor liver transplantation
Letter to Editor: Peripheral limitation as main factor for reduced cardiorespiratory fitness and no beta-blockers effects in patients with cirrhosis
Reply: Pre-LT sphincterotomy and post-transplant biliary complications—a radiological perspective on anastomotic geometry and biliary anatomy
Letter to the Editor: Initial outcomes and global demand for liver transplant mentorship—the international liver transplantation society experience
Letter to the Editor: How to indicate liver transplantation for improving long-term survivals with intensive management of frailty
External validation of the SNAPP score for hepatocellular carcinoma recurrence after living donor liver transplantation
items.abstract: Background: Binary morphologic criteria cannot capture biologic heterogeneity among living donor liver transplantation (LDLT) recipients. SNAPP score (tumor size, number, AFP, PIVKA-II, PET/CT) yields a graded recurrence-risk estimate but lacks independent validation. We externally validated SNAPP for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) recurrence after LDLT. Methods: SNAPP was applied without refitting in 230 LDLT recipients with HCC at two Korean centers and benchmarked against Milan, French-AFP, Metroticket 2.0, MoRAL, RETREAT, and three LDLT-derived selection systems (Kyoto, Medanta LDLT, and National Cancer Center Korea). Discrimination, calibration, Brier score, and reclassification were assessed using IPCW-weighted methods with bootstrap 95% CIs. Results: Among 230 patients (median follow-up, 91.5 mo), 49 (21.3%) recurred. SNAPP achieved discrimination comparable to the best pretransplant tool, MoRAL (Harrell C-index, 0.756; 95% CI, 0.690–0.821), and exceeded Milan (0.503; Holm-adjusted p =0.01). Discrimination was numerically higher than Metroticket 2.0 (0.605) and three LDLT-derived systems (C-index difference, 0.10-0.15), but none of these differences survived correction for multiplicity (Holm-adjusted p =0.24). RETREAT, a posttransplant benchmark, reached 0.807. Calibration-in-the-large was −0.068; slope, 0.59 (95% CI, 0.43–0.77). Within Milan-eligible patients (n=217), SNAPP resolved a monotonic, approximately 5.9-fold gradient in 5-year cumulative recurrence (11.9%, 48.8%, 70.0%). Reclassification favored SNAPP over Milan, French-AFP, and Metroticket 2.0; the center-adjusted hazard ratio per point 1.79 (95% CI, 1.51–2.14). Conclusions: SNAPP showed discrimination comparable to MoRAL and exceeded Milan, with numerically higher but not definitively superior discrimination compared with Metroticket 2.0, French-AFP, and three LDLT-specific selection systems, while resolving biologic heterogeneity within Milan-eligible candidates using only pretransplant variables. With near-zero calibration-in-the-large but a slope below unity, SNAPP supports risk stratification at listing, though individualized probability estimates require recalibration.

items.title: A tale of two cholangiopathies: Divergence, parity, and paradox

Differences in donation after circulatory determination of death (DCD) liver donor management. An international survey initiated by the international liver transplantation society (ILTS), society for the advancement of transplant anesthesia (SATA), and liver intensive care group of europe (LICAGE)
items.abstract: We conducted a survey to evaluate variability in determination of death and management of Donation after Circulatory Determination of Death (DCD) liver donors across different countries. 153 centers from 17 countries were included (48.4% US, 51.6% non-US). Most reported using onset of hemodynamic instability, rather than withdrawal of life-sustaining therapy (WLST), as the beginning of the waiting time for decision making related to organ acceptance (76.1% US vs. 47.1% non-US). Actual and maximum acceptable waiting times were comparable between groups (43.7 vs. 50.2 and 50.8 vs. 60.3 min, respectively), frequently exceeding limits defined by national policies. Onset of hemodynamic instability was most commonly defined using systolic blood pressure (SBP) alone (51.4% US vs. 31.6% non-US) or a combination of SBP and oxygen saturation (SpO2) (41.6% US vs. 56.6% non-US). Less commonly, centers used SpO2 (4.2% vs. 3.9%) or arrythmia alone (1.4% US vs. 0.0% non-US). Thresholds for SBP and SpO2 were similar between US and non-US centers (SBP 80 mmHg; and 80% for both). Sedation and analgesia for donor comfort was used less frequently in US centers compared to non-US centers (27.8% vs. 48.1%, p =0.02). Decision-making regarding waiting time was more commonly performed by a multidisciplinary team outside the US (26.1% vs. 52.0%). Over half of US and non-US centers reported using machine perfusion in over 50% of DCD grafts (64.9% vs. 51.9%). When used, normothermic regional perfusion cannulation was more commonly initiated after declaration of death (71.6% US vs. 62.0% non-US). These findings demonstrate substantial variability in DCD donor management. Standardization of definitions and practices, particularly with regard to exclusion of hemodynamic stability period from Warm Ischemic Time (WIT), may improve consistency in decision-making related to organ acceptance.

items.title: Benefits and risks of induction immunosuppression in pediatric autoimmune liver disease from SPLIT Registry
items.abstract: The optimal induction regimen for pediatric liver transplantation (LT) in patients with Autoimmune Liver Disease (AILD) is not well-defined. This study compared outcomes between corticosteroids only, anti-thymocyte globulin (ATG), and IL-2 receptor antagonists (IL2RA; Basiliximab/Daclizumab). A retrospective review of 445 pediatric LT recipients with AILD (Autoimmune hepatitis, primary sclerosing cholangitis, or autoimmune sclerosing cholangitis) was conducted using the SPLIT database. Re-transplants were excluded. Primary outcomes included biopsy-confirmed rejection, culture-proven infection, graft loss, and mortality. Baseline demographics were comparable across groups. At 30 days post-LT, the IL2RA group demonstrated a significantly lower rate of biopsy-confirmed rejection (11.2%) compared to corticosteroids only (20.9%) and ATG (28%; p =0.05). Conversely, the ATG group experienced a significantly higher incidence of culture-proven infections between days 30–90 (42.9%) compared to corticosteroids only (10.2%) and IL2RA (17.9%; p =0.03). In multivariable-adjusted models, ATG induction was associated with a 10-fold higher risk of sub-acute culture-proven infection at 30–90 days (aOR=10.0, 95%CI: 1.4–71.8, p =0.02) compared to corticosteroids alone. However, neither ATG (aOR=0.47) nor IL-2RA (aOR=0.63) significantly altered the odds of early acute rejection at 0–30 days ( p >0.30). No significant differences were observed in graft loss, mortality, disease recurrence, or post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder up to five years post-transplant. In pediatric AILD, induction with IL2RA significantly reduces early acute rejection without increasing infection risks or compromising long-term graft and patient survival.

items.title: Letter to the editor: a more urgent case for building the hybrid living and deceased donor liver transplant pathway
Serum ammonia improves early risk stratification beyond West Haven criteria in acute liver failure
items.abstract: Background & Aims: The prognosis of patients with acute liver failure (ALF) presenting with low grade hepatic encephalopathy (HE) defined by the West Haven criteria (WHC) is difficult to establish. We studied the association between HE severity, assessed by WHC and serum ammonia, with outcomes across different age groups. Methods: Retrospective analysis of the prospective multicentre United States ALF Study Group registry (2000-2016). Exposures were WHC and serum ammonia on day 1 post inclusion. Endpoints were transplant-free survival (TFS) and mortality due to cerebral events on day 21. Findings were validated in a different and more recent (2010-2023) European cohort. Results: Among 1092 patients, median age was 39 years and 526 (48.2%) had acetaminophen toxicity. On day 1, 968 (88.6%) patients were in the intensive care unit and 669 (61.3%) were receiving any specific organ support (ventilation vasopressors, or renal replacement therapy). TFS and cerebral mortality on day 21 were 45.2% and 6.3%, respectively. Patients with hyperammonemia (≥50 µmol/L) on day 1 had lower TFS on day 21 than others, both for WHC grades 1-2 (53.0% vs. 65.2%) and 3-4 (31.8% vs. 60.9%). Higher ammonia on day 1 was independently associated with lower TFS on day 21, irrespective of WHC grade (odds ratio of 0.958 per each 10 µmol/L increment). Ammonia on day 1 of ≥100 µmol/L showed a significant threshold effect for TFS or cerebral mortality on day 21. Patients with <40 years had the highest probability of cerebral mortality on day 21. Conclusions: In ALF, serum ammonia may help to define HE and assess prognosis earlier, irrespective of WHC grade. Patients with early serum ammonia of ≥100 µmol/L require optimized monitoring and treatment.

items.title: The pre-transplant cystatin C-to-serum creatinine ratio is associated with key clinical outcomes following liver transplantation
Development and internal validation of the Laboratory-based Liver Frailty Index (Lab-LFI)—a prediction model for frailty in patients with cirrhosis
items.abstract: Background and Aims: Frailty, as measured by the Liver Frailty Index (LFI), is a well-established predictor of outcomes in cirrhosis, but testing requires in-person encounters. We sought to develop a blood-based biomarker index that correlates with frailty. Approach and Results: Seven serum/plasma analytes (myostatin, IL-6, growth differentiation factor-15 [GDF-15], testosterone, leucine-rich alpha-2 glycoprotein [LRG1], fetuin-A, and IGF-1) were measured by ELISA in 527 ambulatory cirrhosis patients. “Frail” was defined as LFI≥4.4. The cohort was split in half; the “Lab-LFI” was developed using LASSO regression in the training set and validated in the test set. Other machine learning methods (generalized additive model [GAM], Random Forest, and XGBOOST) were considered to compare discrimination. Of 527 patients (median age 59, MELD 14), 114 (21.6%) were frail. All seven biomarkers were associated with frailty. In the test set, Lab-LFI’s c-statistic was 0.80 (95% CI 0.74-0.87) for frailty. The GAM, random forest, and XGBOOST approaches produced similar discrimination (c-statistics 0.79-0.82); as such, the LASSO model was chosen for maximum interpretability. Addition of clinical variables to the LASSO model, including MELD labs and sex, did not improve discrimination (c-statistic 0.79, 95% CI 0.72-0.85). Patients were stratified by Lab-LFI using a cutpoint maximizing Youden’s index; after adjusting for MELD and liver disease etiology, the high-risk group had higher pre-transplant death/waitlist dropout (HR 1.77, 95% CI 1.17-2.68, p =0.007). Conclusions : We developed and internally validated the Lab-LFI, a frailty prediction model consisting of 7 laboratory-based biomarkers. Lab-LFI enables blood-based assessment of physical function, as MELD does with liver function.

items.title: Work-life chaos: Enhancing mental health during times of strife
items.abstract: The practice of medicine can be both be professionally fulfilling and inherently demanding. Physicians are often perceived as invincible, yet recurrent exposure to patient suffering, high-stakes decision-making, and institutional pressure can profoundly impact mental health. These challenges may be particularly pronounced in organ transplantation, where transplant teams navigate life-and-death decisions, complex longitudinal care, and the responsibility of stewarding scarce organs. Using narrative reflection, this article highlights the dialectic that is inherent in the culture of medicine but seldom discussed: the expectation that physicians not only “do well” by delivering high-quality care and also “be well” themselves. Personal experience with complicated grief, functional impairment, and subsequent recovery is discussed within broader literature indicating increased rates of depression, anxiety, and burnout among physicians compared to the general population. Barriers to seeking support, including stigma, unclear institutional pathways, and concerns over professional repercussions are outlined. Evidence-based interventions, including values exercises, physician-coaching, confidential support programs, and structured return to work policies are discussed as strategies to facilitate early identification of distress and foster sustainable recovery.

items.title: A randomized controlled trial of normothermic versus dual-hypothermic oxygenated ex-situ perfusion in DCD liver transplantation
items.abstract: DCD liver transplantation has expanded worldwide but remains associated with an increased risk of complications. Sequential use of normothermic regional perfusion (NRP) followed by ex-situ machine perfusion (MP) is increasingly adopted but the choice of MP technique remains controversial. This randomized controlled trial compares outcomes of dual-hypothermic oxygenated perfusion (D-HOPE) versus normothermic machine perfusion (NMP) following NRP in DCD liver transplantation. After NRP, 50 grafts (44 controlled and 6 uncontrolled DCD) were randomized 1:1 to D-HOPE or NMP using concealed allocation with sequentially numbered sealed envelopes. Ex-situ perfusion was not performed for additional assessment. The primary endpoint was 1-year incidence of serious adverse events (SAE), including graft or patient loss and biliary or vascular complications. Secondary endpoint included other perioperative outcomes. We have also performed an exploratory analysis to identify predictive factors of graft loss and SAE. No case of primary non-function or vascular complication occurred. One-year graft and patient survival were both 88% in the D-HOPE group and 100% in the NMP group ( p =0.07). One-year SAE rate was similar (16%vs.20%, p =0.31). Biliary leakage and postoperative dialysis rate were comparable between the two groups (16%vs.0%, p =0.12). Blood pH variation, lactate and IL-6 levels during NRP, perfusate lactate trend, portal flow, IL-6, IL-10 and TNF levels during D-HOPE and perfusate pH variations and IL-10 levels during NMP were related to graft loss. Conclusions: When applied after NRP, D-HOPE and NMP provide comparable mid-term clinical outcomes in DCD liver transplantation. Differences in specific complications may require individualized selection of ex-situ MP. The limited sample size and number of events preclude definitive conclusions regarding differences in individual complications or the relative efficacy of either ex-situ perfusion strategy. The observed differences in specific complications and exploratory associations with perfusion parameters warrant evaluation in larger prospective studies.

items.title: Reply: Day-7 thresholds in a moving target—separating small-for-size physiology from early allograft dysfunction in LDLT
Letter to the Editor: Day-7 thresholds in a moving target—separating small-for-size physiology from early allograft dysfunction in LDLT
AUD care is transplant care: Lessons from the LIFT clinic
Pre-transplant vulnerability and clinically consequential osteonecrosis after liver transplantation
items.abstract: Osteonecrosis of the femoral head (ONFH) after liver transplantation (LT) frequently progresses to joint collapse and surgical intervention. Although corticosteroids have traditionally been implicated in its pathogenesis, their independent contribution under contemporary immunosuppressive protocols remains uncertain. We aimed to identify factors associated with clinically consequential ONFH, with particular attention to pre-transplant disease burden and systemic vulnerability. This retrospective cohort study included 1,836 adults who underwent first-time LT between 2000 and 2023. To minimize time-dependent bias, corticosteroid exposure was assessed as cumulative dose over a fixed 3-month post-transplant period and examined using risk-set percentile analysis and an adjusted Cox model. Additional candidate factors were screened using covariate-balancing approaches and evaluated in a full-cohort multivariable Cox model. ONFH developed in 64 patients (3.5%) at a mean of 5.86±4.58 years after LT, and 71.9% of affected patients subsequently underwent surgical intervention. Corticosteroid exposure was not significantly associated with ONFH after adjustment for baseline covariates ( p =0.47), and findings were consistent across analyses accounting for time-dependent bias. In contrast, other diagnoses including primary biliary cholangitis or Wilson disease (HR 4.21; 95% CI, 1.19–14.91; p =0.03) and preoperative enteral nutrition requirement (HR 2.98; 95% CI 1.03–8.64; p =0.04) were associated with increased risk. Cumulative smoking exposure ( p =0.08) and time-weighted average MELD score ( p =0.07) demonstrated suggestive associations with ONFH risk. Clinically consequential ONFH after LT may be influenced more by pre-transplant vulnerability and nutritional frailty than by corticosteroid exposure alone. These findings support a vulnerability-based framework for post-transplant ONFH and may help identify recipients who could benefit from heightened clinical awareness and timely diagnostic evaluation when compatible symptoms develop.

items.title: Letter To The Editor: Who should receive a graft for unresectable colorectal liver metastases? Lessons from real-world TransMet validation for living-donor programs
Reply: Who should receive a graft for unresectable colorectal liver metastases? Lessons from real-world TransMet validation for living-donor programs
Can robotic living donor hepatectomy be safely offered to all donors? evidence, experience, and program development
items.abstract: Robotic living donor hepatectomy (R-LDH) aims to improve the safety and experience of healthy donors by combining three-dimensional visualization, wristed instrumentation, precision, and stable ergonomics with the benefits of minimal access. This review article summarizes current evidence and offers a pragmatic approach for centers to transition from open to routine robotic donation. Available evidence from retrospective feasibility series, matched cohorts, multicenter analyses, and registry data suggests that R-LDH may reduce donor morbidity compared to open and some evidence of fewer recipient biliary complications, although current evidence remains heterogeneous and largely non-randomized. Available comparative data, including single-center and international registry analyses, suggest lower morbidity with the robotic approach than with laparoscopy, although these comparisons remain limited and would benefit from confirmation in prospective multicenter studies. Learning-curve studies and prospective series suggest that with standardized technique, simulation, and early proctorship, proficiency appears achievable within a limited number of cases, with reduced complications over time. A center-readiness structure focused on “People” (trained team), “Process” (protocolized pathways with explicit conversion criteria), “Platform” (reliable robot access, ICG, ERAS), and “Proof” (prospective audit and external validation) supports phased adoption from standard to complex anatomy. Persistent barriers include limited robotic platform access, scheduling constraints, heterogeneity in reporting, and incomplete cost data, though shorter hospital stay, less pain, and faster return to normal daily activities may partially or potentially offset procedural costs in high-volume programs. In appropriately prepared centers, routine consideration of R-LDH for eligible donors may represent a reasonable donor-centered strategy. Concrete steps are outlined that surgeons and hospital leaders can undertake to implement R-LDH safely, monitor outcomes, and improve equitable access.

items.title: Are we over-immunosuppressing liver transplant recipients?
Autoimmune hepatitis and primary biliary cholangitis are among a subset of autoimmune diseases defined by profound co-prevalence and genetic risk association with the IL12 pathway
items.abstract: Background and Aims: Distinct autoimmune diseases can share symptoms and autoantibodies, but the molecular pathways underlying this shared etiology remain poorly understood. We assessed genetic support for IL12 signaling across 27 diseases. Approach and Results: We identified a rare variant upstream of IL12A with large risk-increasing effects on autoimmune hepatitis [AIH; per-allele odds ratio (OR)=2.98, p =3×10 −9 ], primary biliary cholangitis (PBC; OR=2.80, p =2×10 −8 ), systemic sclerosis (SSc; OR=2.64, p =2×10 −11 ), Sjogren's disease (SjD; OR=1.94, p =10 −11 ), systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE; OR=1.83, p =5×10 −10 ) and multiple sclerosis (OR=1.79, p =10 −11 ). Lifetime risk for developing at least one of these conditions increased 6-fold in homozygote carriers (OR=5.73, p =0.003). We then evaluated genetic support for all 4 IL12 signaling genes and found that: (i) a non-coding variant downstream of IL12A (linked to lower gene expression) protected against 5 of the 6 diseases; (ii) an intronic variant in IL12RB2 (linked to higher gene expression) increased risk of all 6 diseases; and (iii) heterozygote carriers of rare predicted loss-of-function or missense variants in IL12RB2 had 18% lower odds of SLE (OR=0.82, p =2×10 −5 ). IL23 signaling, which shares ligand and receptor subunits with IL12, was not associated with these conditions. In epidemiologic analyses of co-prevalence, 5 of the 6 diseases strongly co-occurred with each other: AIH, PBC, SSc, SjD and SLE. Conclusions: AIH, PBC, SSc, SjD and SLE represent a distinct subset of autoimmune diseases that share genetic associations with the IL12 pathway, as well as profound co-prevalence, suggesting they may have a shared etiology and may respond to the same targeted therapeutic intervention(s).

items.title: Erratum: Circular RNA sequencing identifies CircASAP1 as a key regulator in hepatocellular carcinoma metastasis
Beyond the primary endpoint: Learning from “negative” AIH trials
Cinderella no more: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency–associated liver disease steps into the ballroom
Upholding telomeres prevents hepatic stellate cell transdifferentiation and liver fibrogenesis
items.abstract: Background & Aims: Hepatic stellate cells (HSCs) are principal drivers of liver cirrhosis. Whether and how telomere dysfunction affects HSC function remain unclear. This study was undertaken to investigate the role of telomere maintenance in HSCs during fibrogenesis and to evaluate its therapeutic potential by genetic and pharmacological means. Approach & Results: Liver fibrosis was established in mice treated with carbon tetrachloride (CCl 4 ) or bile duct ligation (BDL), and characterized by tissue and molecular pathology and biochemistry, followed by HSC isolation using flow cytometry. Animals were engineered for HSC-specific overexpression of the telomerase reverse transcriptase (TERT) gene or Acd (encoding the shelterin component TPP1). Alternatively, mice were intraperitoneally injected with telomere dysfunction inhibitor (TELODIN), a D-amino acid octapeptide that stabilizes the telomerase activator TPP1. HSC-specific TERT expression alleviated hepatic fibrosis by suppressing HSC activation, proliferation, and transdifferentiation. Likewise, HSC-specific TPP1 overexpression mitigated hepatic fibrosis by preventing telomere dysfunction and shortening. Pharmacological stabilization of TPP1 by intraperitoneal administration of TELODIN counteracted hepatic fibrogenesis while maintaining HSC quiescence. Mechanistically, TELODIN stabilized TPP1, reduced telomere dysfunction, and decreased HSC transdifferentiation into profibrotic myofibroblasts. Conclusions: Telomere dysfunction mediates HSC transdifferentiation during experimental hepatic fibrogenesis. Targeted interventions – that increase telomerase activity or TPP1 mediated telomerase recruitment and activation – alleviate HSC-mediated fibrosis. Pharmacological administration of TELODIN effectively attenuates experimental liver fibrosis by restoring telomere homeostasis in HSCs.

items.title: Saroglitazar improves hepatic steatosis and liver enzymes in women with polycystic ovary syndrome and MASLD: A multicenter, double-blind, placebo-controlled study
items.abstract: Background and Aims: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is the leading endocrine disorder in reproductive-age women. Metabolic dysfunction–associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is common in women with PCOS, but they are underrepresented in MASLD therapeutic trials. We evaluated the safety and efficacy of saroglitazar, a novel peroxisome proliferator–activated receptors α/γ agonist, for the treatment of hepatic steatosis in women with PCOS and MASLD. Methods: In this multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2A trial, 60 women (18–45 y) with PCOS and MASLD were randomized 1:1 to either saroglitazar 4 mg or placebo for 24 weeks. The primary endpoint was relative (percent) change in hepatic fat content, measured by MRI proton density fat fraction. Primary analysis was performed in the per-protocol population (saroglitazar: 25; placebo: 23). Results: Participants in the saroglitazar group showed a significant reduction in percent hepatic fat content at 24 weeks from baseline compared to placebo ([least squares mean±SE]: −14.81±5.52 vs. 1.96±5.75, p =0.041). When controlled for baseline HbA1c imbalance, the beneficial effect of saroglitazar was more pronounced ([least squares mean±SE]: −18.93±4.83 vs. 6.43±5.04, p <0.009). A higher proportion in the saroglitazar group achieved ≥30% reduction in magnetic resonance imaging-proton density fat fraction (36.0% vs. 8.7%; p =0.025). Saroglitazar also significantly reduced aminotransferase levels, lipid parameters, and the FibroScan AST score. Adverse events were comparable between the groups, and none were serious. One pregnancy in the saroglitazar arm resulted in uneventful maternal and neonatal outcomes. Conclusions: In women with PCOS and MASLD, saroglitazar significantly improved hepatic steatosis, liver enzymes, lipid profile, and FibroScan AST score. These findings support further evaluation of saroglitazar in larger studies in women with PCOS.

items.title: A gentler squeeze: A first signal from OCE-205, a selective V1a mixed agonist–antagonist for hepatorenal syndrome–acute kidney injury
Featured video: Complications of chronic liver disease
Turning down the ammonia dial: Phase 2a evidence for YAQ007 in cirrhosis
Rethinking albumin after paracentesis: It’s not just about the volume
Present but not prescient: Cardiometabolic risk factors in alcohol-associated hepatitis
AASLD AGA clinical Practice Guideline on management of primary biliary cholangitis
items.abstract: Background & Aims: Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) is a chronic cholestatic liver disease associated with progressive fibrosis, cirrhosis, liver transplantation, and premature mortality. Despite effective therapies, important challenges remain in the diagnosis and management of PBC, including identification of antimitochondrial antibody–negative disease, assessment of response to ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA), risk stratification, treatment of patients with inadequate response, management of cholestatic pruritus, and prevention of recurrent disease after liver transplantation. The aim of this guideline was to develop evidence-based recommendations addressing these key areas of clinical care. Methods: The American Gastroenterological Association (AGA) and the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases (AASLD) convened a multidisciplinary panel to develop clinical practice recommendations for adults with PBC. Systematic reviews were performed for 6 prioritized clinical questions. The Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation framework was used to prioritize clinical outcomes and assess evidence, and its Evidence to Decision Framework was used to develop recommendations. Results: The guideline panel agreed on 6 recommendations. These recommendations address the use of PBC-specific antinuclear antibodies in antimitochondrial antibody–negative suspected PBC, UDCA as first-line therapy, liver stiffness measurement for prognostication, peroxisome proliferator–activated receptor agonists for patients with inadequate response or intolerance to UDCA, linerixibat for moderate to severe pruritus, and UDCA prophylaxis post-transplantation to reduce disease recurrence. The certainty of evidence ranged from moderate to very low. Conclusions: The guideline emphasizes early diagnosis, optimization of first-line therapy, risk-based treatment escalation, symptom management, and prevention of post-transplantation disease recurrence to improve patient outcomes and quality of life.

items.title: Two diseases, one trial: Designing integrated treatments for alcohol-associated hepatitis and alcohol use disorder
Apolipoproteins in hepatitis B virus infection: ApoC1 links HBV entry, morphogenesis, and cholesterol homeostasis
Baveno VI criteria validation and development of a new non-invasive strategy for varices rule-out in patients with HCC (SAPHE-R: Stiffness, ALBI, Platelets, HEpatocellular carcinoma Rule)
items.abstract: Background and Aims: Accuracy of Baveno criteria for avoiding endoscopy in patients with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is uncertain, and systematic upper gastrointestinal endoscopy (UGE) may not be necessary. We evaluated Baveno VI criteria performance in this population and developed an alternative non-invasive rule to exclude esophagogastric varices of any grade, rather than high-risk varices (HRV). Methods: Patients with BCLC 0-C HCC and compensated advanced chronic liver disease (cACLD) from Italian Liver Cancer (ITA.LI.CA) database, with available liver stiffness measurement (LSM), UGE, and blood tests within six months of diagnosis, were included. Independent predictors of varices identified by logistic regression were combined through grid-search to derive a rule-out strategy (SAPHE-R), validated by bootstrap-resampling and in an independent cohort (Vienna). Results: The derivation cohort comprised 598 patients (age, 69 years; male sex, 75.3%; viral etiology, 69.3%; BCLC 0/A, 77.9%; ALBI 1, 54.2%; varices, 33.4%; HRV, 11.2%). Baveno VI criteria missed 8.5% of varices and 6.0% of HRV, sparing 31.1% of UGE. Independent predictors of varices were incorporated into SAPHE-R (LSM≤16 kPa, platelet count ≥160×10⁹/L, ALBI grade 1), which missed 4.0% of varices (HRV 3.0%, spared UGE 17.6%). In the validation cohort (n=149), SAPHE-R missed 4.8% of varices (HRV 3.1%, spared UGE 14.8%). Results remained consistent in sensitivity analyses. In an exploratory analysis, no HVPG-defined CSPH was observed among SAPHE-R rule-out patients (0/22). Conclusions: Baveno VI criteria showed suboptimal performance in patients with HCC and cACLD, whereas SAPHE-R provided a reliable non-invasive strategy to rule out varices, facilitating variceal risk assessment in patients with HCC.

items.title: Single-cell landscape of alcohol-related hepatitis reveals serum amyloid a hepatocytes as key drivers of disease pathogenesis
items.abstract: Background & Aims: Alcohol-related hepatitis (AH) is a severe form of alcohol-related liver disease (ALD). The cellular subpopulations that contribute to AH and dynamics remain poorly understood. This study aimed to identify key cellular subpopulations and their interactions in AH and explore key mechanisms contributing to disease pathogenesis. Approach & Results: Single-cell RNA sequencing was performed starting from liver biopsies from patients with AH, early-stage ALD, and healthy individuals. Immunofluorescence was used to validate protein expression of selected markers. Liver biopsy-derived organoids were generated and exposed to a conditioned medium recapitulating AH (AH-medium) to assess serum amyloid A (SAA) secretion by ELISA. Circulating SAA levels were measured in plasma samples obtained from patients at different stages of ALD. Our analysis revealed an atlas of several cell subpopulations of AH, including hepatocytes expressing SAA, scar-associated (SA) endothelial cells, Fibulin-3 + mesenchymal cells, SA-macrophages expressing MMP19, activated CD4+ and stressed/effector CD8+ T cell subsets, and hyperactivated neutrophils expressing FPR2. Cell-communication analysis predicted a strong SAA-FPR2 interaction between hepatocyte and neutrophil subpopulations in AH. We confirmed that AH-hepatocytes secreted SAA in organoid cultures after stimulation with AH-medium. We also found out that circulating SAA levels were elevated in AH and were associated with reduced survival. Conclusions: The SAA-FPR2 pathway emerges as a potential mediator of inflammation in AH, offering potential therapeutic targets for this severe disease. This study provides new insights into the cellular heterogeneity and dynamics in ALD progression, dissecting AH at a single-cell level.

items.title: Trends in the etiologies and outcomes of idiosyncratic drug-induced liver injury in the united states: The DILIN prospective registry, 2004 to 2024
items.abstract: Background & Aims: Idiosyncratic drug-induced liver injury (DILI) is an infrequent cause of liver disease. The aim of this study is to report on temporal changes in the etiology and outcomes of idiosyncratic DILI in the United States DILIN Prospective study. Methods: The presenting clinical features and outcomes of consecutive high causality DILI cases followed for 6 months at multiple DILIN sites from 2004 to 2024 were compared over time and by suspect drug class, age, sex, and prior chronic liver disease (CLD) status. Results: Amongst the 1983 high causality cases, median age was 52 years, 59% were female, 54% had hepatocellular injury and antibiotics (41%) were the leading drug class. The median peak total bilirubin, INR and severity scores decreased significantly over time, as did the proportion of cases attributed to antimicrobials, including isoniazid and nitrofurantoin, and to central nervous system agents. In contrast, the proportion of herbal and dietary supplement (HDS) and antineoplastic drug cases (including checkpoint inhibitors), increased significantly. Patients with CLD had higher mortality compared to non-CLD patients. Pediatric patients presented more frequently with hepatocellular injury but had a lower overall and liver related mortality compared to adults. Oncology DILI patients had a 6-month mortality rate of 30% with most deaths attributed to non-liver related causes. Conclusions: Over the past 20 years, a decreasing proportion of DILI cases are attributed to antibiotics while an increasing proportion are attributed to HDS products and antineoplastics. Oncology patients and those > 65 years old have significantly higher overall and liver-related mortality.

items.title: A phase 2b/3 trial of saroglitazar in primary biliary cholangitis
items.abstract: Background: Saroglitazar, a dual PPAR alpha/gamma agonist, improved serum alkaline phosphatase (ALP) levels in patients with primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) in a phase 2a clinical trial. Methods: EPICS-III is a phase 2b/3 adaptive, double-blind, randomized controlled trial in patients with PBC who had an inadequate response to or were intolerant of ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA). In phase 2b, 37 participants received placebo or saroglitazar magnesium 1 or 2 mg for 16 weeks. Saroglitazar magnesium 1 mg (0.97 mg of saroglitazar) was selected for phase 3, which randomized 148 patients to saroglitazar (n=97) or placebo (n=51) for 52 weeks. The primary endpoint was biochemical response at week 52, defined as ALP <1.67 x ULN with ≥15% reduction from baseline and total bilirubin below ULN; the key secondary endpoint was ALP normalization. Results: Baseline characteristics in the phase 3 efficacy population were comparable except for higher baseline ALP and other liver biochemistries in the saroglitazar group. Biochemical response was achieved in 56.7% versus 9.8% with placebo (difference, 48.0%; 95% CI, 35.3 to 60.8; p <0.001). Among participants with baseline ALP ≤3xULN, biochemical response rates were 79.0% versus 14.3%, and 83.1% versus 14.7% in the per-protocol analysis. ALP normalization occurred in 8.2% with saroglitazar versus 0% with placebo (difference, 8.5%; 95% CI, 2.9 to 14; p =0.016). Among participants with baseline 5-D Itch score ≥12, the week-24 treatment difference was −3.2 points (95% CI, −5.66 to −0.82) but was not maintained at week 52. Adverse events occurred in 81.1% with saroglitazar versus 90.5% with placebo, and serious adverse events occurred in 6.3% and 11.1%, respectively. Conclusion: Saroglitazar 0.97 mg significantly improved biochemical response and ALP normalization and was well tolerated over 52 weeks.

items.title: Phase 1b study of miricorilant in patients with presumed metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH)
items.abstract: Background and Aims: Miricorilant, an oral nonsteroidal selective glucocorticoid receptor modulator, is being investigated as a therapy that modulates hepatic cortisol activity in patients with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH). This phase 1b study evaluated miricorilant’s efficacy and safety. Approach and Results: Seventy patients with presumed MASH received oral miricorilant daily (30–150 mg) or intermittent (100–200 mg once, twice, or thrice weekly) dosing regimens for 12 or 24 weeks. Across dosing regimens, reductions in relative liver fat content (LFC) ranged from 10.1% to 76.6%. Improvements in MASH liver function markers and the enhanced liver fibrosis (ELF) score were observed across regimens. Treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAE) leading to drug interruption/discontinuation occurred in 12.9% of patients (n=9) each; most were due to aminotransferase elevations during an excessively rapid drop in LFC (up to 70.2% at week 6) and in patients receiving daily dosing. Intermittent dosing enabled more patients to complete 12 weeks of treatment without discontinuation due to TEAEs. Intermittent dosing with miricorilant 100 mg twice weekly had the best benefit-risk profile; this cohort demonstrated a mean LFC reduction of 28.2% at week 12, with a corresponding decline in liver enzymes (ALT, −3.8 U/L; AST, −6.0 U/L). Patients in this cohort also had numerical improvement in lipid profiles, glycemic markers, and fibrosis biomarkers. Conclusions: Intermittent miricorilant dosing of 100 mg twice weekly achieved meaningful reductions in LFC and improved liver health markers with a favorable safety profile. This regimen is being evaluated in the phase 2b MONARCH study (NCT06108219).

items.title: Government digital maturity and liver-related mortality: A multinational ecological study
A pivotal Phase 2 study of derazantinib for previously-treated, locally advanced or metastatic cholangiocarcinoma with FGFR2 aberrations: FIDES-01
items.abstract: Background & Aims: To evaluate safety and efficacy of FGFR1–3 kinase inhibitor derazantinib, in advanced intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (iCCA) harboring FGFR2 fusions or rearrangements ( FGFR2 F ), mutations ( FGFR2 M ), or amplifications ( FGFR2 A ), previously treated with chemotherapy. Approach & Results: Open-label, non-controlled Phase 2 trial. Patients with advanced iCCA, ≥1 prior chemotherapy, and FGFR2 F (Substudy 1) or FGFR2 M /FGFR A (Substudy 2), received once-daily oral derazantinib 300 mg until disease progression, unacceptable toxicity, consent withdrawal or investigator decision to stop. Efficacy was assessed by central radiology review using RECIST v1.1. Primary endpoints were objective response rate (ORR; Substudy 1) and 3-month progression-free survival (PFS3; Substudy 2). Other endpoints were PFS, ORR (Substudy 2), disease control rate (DCR), duration of response (DOR), and overall survival (OS). In Substudy 1, ORR and DCR were 22.3% (23/103 partial responses) and 75.7%, respectively; median (95% CI) PFS was 8.1 (5.5,8.3) months, DOR was 6.5 (4.6,9.2) months, and OS was 17.2 (12.5,22.4) months. In Substudy 2, PFS3 was 63% (27/43), ORR was 9.3% (3 partial, 1 complete response), DCR was 69.8%, and OS was 11.9 (8.4,15.9) months. There were no Grade 4 or 5 drug-related events. FGFR inhibitor class-specific toxicities included drug-related hyperphosphataemia (38%, Grade 3: 3%) and dry eye (36%). Nail disorders (10%, any grade or causality), stomatitis (5%), retinal events (5%), and palmar-plantar erythrodysesthesia (1%) were infrequent. Conclusions: In previously chemotherapy treated, FGFR-inhibitor-naïve patients with iCCA harboring FGFR2 fusions, mutations, or amplifications, derazantinib showed clinically meaningful efficacy with durable objective responses, and a manageable safety profile.

items.title: Acute-on-chronic liver failure: A global multisociety consensus on definitions
items.firstAuthor: American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases (AASLD)
items.abstract: The acute-on-chronic liver failure (ACLF) multisociety harmonisation initiative represents a global collaborative effort to establish a unified, evidence-based framework for the definition, diagnosis, grading, and management of ACLF. Building on the strengths of existing regional definitions and integrating diverse international perspectives, this consensus provides a pragmatic, globally applicable foundation for clinical practice, research, and education. It also establishes a common framework for patient stratification, organ dysfunction and failure assessment, critical care management, liver transplantation, and the design of future phase II/III trials. Standardised, regulatory-aligned endpoints are expected to improve cross-study comparability, strengthen collaboration, and accelerate development of effective ACLF therapies.
