items.title: Perceived inappropriateness of care among ICU clinicians is associated with burnout and intention to leave the job
Principles of drug dosing for obese patients in the intensive care unit
items.abstract: Purpose The increasing prevalence of severe obesity in intensive care unit (ICU) patients has led to several challenges with medication dosing. Doses listed in product labels or tertiary references typically do not account for the pharmacokinetic or pharmacodynamic variability encountered with obesity, leading to the potential for treatment failure or an adverse effect. The purpose of this review is to provide guidance for ICU clinicians when crafting pharmacotherapy regimens in critically ill patients with extreme obesity. Methods A literature search was performed to identify relevant articles pertaining to the pharmacokinetics or pharmacodynamics of medications in obese patients. Articles describing both general treatment principles and medication specific assessments were retrieved. Bibliographies were searched for additional publications. Results Evidence guiding medication use in critically ill obese patients is limited by the small number of patients with more extreme forms of obesity, the lack of clinical outcome measurements, and the few studies that are specific to the ICU. Obesity-related alterations in pharmacokinetic parameters, such as apparent volume of distribution and drug clearance, may hinder attainment of pharmacodynamic targets. Individualized dosing strategies are essential to optimize therapeutic outcomes. This review provides dosing recommendations for selected ICU medications and proposes a practical framework to guide medication dosing decisions in this patient population. Conclusion Drug dosing in critically ill obese patients should be individualized by assessing pharmacokinetic variability and whether pharmacodynamic goals can be achieved. Selecting the correct weight for weight-based calculations or dose for fixed regimens is paramount for achieving these goals. Consultation with a clinical pharmacist may be beneficial.

European Society of Intensive Care Medicine consensus statement on human-centred partnership in the intensive care unit
items.abstract: A human-centred partnership in the intensive care unit (ICU) aims to integrate person-centred care, communication, emotional support, equity, and collaboration into ICU environments. The European Society of Intensive Care Medicine (ESICM) developed a consensus statement on human-centred partnership in the ICU following a systematic, multi-phase, evidence-informed methodology incorporating the views of ICU professionals, academics, and patient and family representatives. This international multidisciplinary panel of 46 members conducted rapid reviews addressing 20 Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcomes (PICO) questions across six domains: person-centred care; communication and transparency; emotional well-being; equity, diversity, and inclusion; ICU environment; technology and innovation. Based on the evidence synthesis, 53 draft statements were developed and evaluated through a two-round eDelphi study. The final set of statements was discussed and ratified at an expert consensus meeting with the initial panel of experts and with patients and family representatives. A total of 201 international stakeholders participated in round 1 and 149 in round 2. Members of the expert consensus meeting ultimately endorsed 43 consensus statements. Key recommendations supported flexible family visitation, structured interdisciplinary communication, empathy-based staff training, psychological support for patients and ICU professionals, culturally responsive care, environmental interventions to improve sleep and reduce delirium, and the integration of digital supported technologies. The consensus statement on human-centred partnership in the ICU provides a comprehensive framework for clinicians with evidence-informed directions to deliver high-quality practice across diverse ICU settings. By prioritising person-centred care, communication, inclusivity, and well-being alongside responsible technological innovation, the experiences and outcomes of patients, families, and ICU professionals may improve.

Ventilator-associated pneumonia after traumatic brain injury: a timing-sensitive ecological framework of neuroimmune–pulmonary vulnerability
items.abstract: Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) is frequent after traumatic brain injury (TBI), but its biological meaning and outcome impact remain incompletely defined. Traditional models emphasise mechanical ventilation, aspiration, colonisation, endotracheal tube biofilm, and hospital pathogens. These mechanisms remain essential, but they do not fully explain the early clustering, heterogeneous susceptibility, changing bacteriology, and variable mortality effect observed after TBI. Severe brain injury creates an early vulnerable host state through impaired consciousness and airway protection, neuroimmune dysregulation, autonomic and endocrine activation, altered pulmonary immune surveillance, and, in many patients, extracranial trauma, shock, transfusion, or thoracic injury. These processes interact with ventilation, antibiotic pressure, and rapid respiratory microbiome disruption. Early VAP may reflect abrupt loss of control after injury and intubation, whereas late VAP may reflect persistent or secondary failure driven by biofilm maturation, antibiotic selection, multidrug-resistant pathogens, and intensive care unit (ICU)-acquired immune dysfunction. Clinically, VAP consistently prolongs ventilation, ICU stay, antibiotic exposure, and resource use, while its independent effect on mortality is phenotype- and context-dependent. This model proposes a timing-sensitive ecological framework in which established mechanisms may converge early and with particular clinical intensity after severe TBI, creating a vulnerable host-microbe state that may lower the threshold for clinically apparent infection. Future studies should distinguish isolated TBI from polytrauma, compare TBI with other acute brain injuries and non-neurological ventilated populations, and incorporate dynamic immune, microbial, and trajectory-based outcomes. VAP after TBI should be viewed as a timing-sensitive interaction between ventilator exposure and early host vulnerability, not as a distinct disease entity or as a pneumonia pathway unique to traumatic brain injury. The TBI-focused contribution lies in the early convergence of otherwise non-unique mechanisms: impaired airway control, aspiration risk, neuroimmune-endocrine activation, treatment exposure, dysbiosis, and extracranial injury burden, rather than in any single TBI-specific mechanism. Isolated TBI and TBI with polytrauma are biologically different phenotypes and should be separated in future studies. Early and late VAP may represent different phases of loss of pulmonary host–microbe containment; this distinction is probabilistic rather than TBI-specific in itself and requires validation in TBI-stratified cohorts. Mortality remains clinically relevant but context-dependent; VAP more consistently modifies recovery trajectory, ventilator dependence, ICU stay, antibiotic exposure, and possibly neurological recovery.

Immunological signatures of sepsis in abdominal solid organ transplant recipients: A multilayer and multicentric prospective cohort study
items.abstract: Sepsis is defined as life-threatening organ dysfunction resulting from a dysregulated host response to infection. Patients with prior abdominal solid organ transplantation (SOT) are highly susceptible to infection due to chronic immunosuppression, yet exhibit improved survival once sepsis occurs. The underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. We conducted a post hoc analysis within a prospective multicenter cohort of septic patients (SepsisDataNet.NRW; n = 538). Clinical outcomes were assessed using Kaplan-Meier analysis and multivariable Cox regression. Immune profiling included serum cytokines, flow cytometric immunophenotyping, plasma proteomics, and intracellular signaling using proximity ligation assays (PLA) in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs). To reduce clinical confounding, complementary exploratory analyses were performed in a non-septic kidney transplant cohort (e:KID). SOT patients demonstrated improved 30-day survival compared with non-SOT patients (84% vs. 66%; adjusted HR 0.49, 95% CI 0.26–0.95). Cytokine analysis revealed lower IL-6 and TNF-α levels alongside higher IL-18 concentrations, indicating an altered inflammatory profile. Flow cytometry showed reductions in adaptive immune cells but relatively preserved innate immune function, reflected by higher monocytic HLA-DR expression. Proteomics identified enrichment of innate immune, complement, and lipid metabolic response networks. PLA-based cellular analyses revealed increased GLUT1 expression and enhanced TFAM/TFB2M interaction in SOT patients, indicating a distinct immunometabolic marker profile. In e:KID patients paired serum metabolomics demonstrated higher glucose and lower lactate concentrations 12 months after transplantation, accompanied by broader alterations in lipid and branched-chain amino acid profiles. In patients with sepsis, abdominal SOT is associated with significant better survival than in non-SOT patients. Septic abdominal SOT patients display a distinct immune phenotype characterized by attenuated systemic inflammation, relative preservation of selected innate immune readouts, and alterations in immunometabolic markers.

items.title: The Easiest Decision in the Room: Continuous Renal Replacement Therapy in Cirrhosis
Pediatric Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation Ventilation Rates and Outcomes
items.abstract: Objectives: Evaluate the association between cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) ventilation rates and survival to hospital discharge, and identify novel ventilation targets. Design: Multicenter prospective ancillary observational cohort study of the ICU-RESUS trial (NCT02837497). Setting: A total of 18 ICUs from 10 U.S. clinical sites from October 2016 to March 2021. Patients: Hospitalized children (≤ 18 yr) with endotracheal or tracheostomy tubes and evaluable intra-arrest end-tidal carbon dioxide data to calculate ventilation rate. Interventions: None. Measurements and Main Results: Among 234 included events, 86 events (36.8%) had guideline-recommended (20–30 beats per min [bpm]) average ventilation rates during CPR. The association between guideline-recommended CPR ventilation rate and survival to hospital discharge was evaluated with Poisson regression using generalized estimating equations, controlling for a priori covariables (initial pulse status, immediate cause of arrest). We found no association between guideline-recommended ventilation rates and survival to hospital discharge (adjusted relative risk [aRR], 0.95; 95% CI, 0.75–1.21; p = 0.68). In exploratory analyses, novel age-stratified ventilation rates were identified using natural cubic splines and subsequently evaluated in multivariable models. We identified potential thresholds (< 8 yr, ≥ 26 bpm; ≥ 8 yr, < 26 bpm). For children younger than 8 years, average CPR ventilation rate greater than or equal to 26 bpm was associated with improved survival to hospital discharge compared with less than 26 bpm (aRR, 1.32; 95% CI, 1.00–1.73; p = 0.048). Conclusions: CPR ventilation rates in the currently recommended range (20–30 bpm) were not associated with survival in children with in-hospital cardiac arrest. In exploratory analyses in children younger than 8 years, higher ventilation rates (≥ 26 bpm) were associated with improved survival and warrant confirmation in future studies.

items.title: Tools Measuring Health Literacy in Critically Ill Patients and Their Caregivers: A Scoping Review
items.abstract: Objectives: Health literacy, the ability to understand and use health information, is important for critically ill patients and their caregivers in the neonatal ICU (NICU), PICU, and adult ICU to make informed decisions and navigate complex care. This review aimed to identify and summarize tools used to assess health literacy in critically ill patients or their caregivers. Data Sources: We searched MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, and PsycINFO through July 24, 2025. Study Selection: Included articles reported on tools to assess health literacy in critically ill patients or their caregivers. Two reviewers independently performed screening and data extraction. Data Extraction: Two independent reviewers extracted data in Covidence. Data items included study characteristics (country in which the study was conducted, study funding, study setting) and health literacy tool characteristics (tool user, types of questions in the tool, method of tool administration, if the tool was created by the study team, and if a full version was available in the publication). Data Synthesis: We included 92 articles describing 84 health literacy tools. Tools measured: 1) topic-specific clinical knowledge (e.g., organ donation, cardiopulmonary resuscitation; n = 24/84, 29%; NICU: n = 9; PICU: n = 1; ICU: n = 14); 2) ICU prognosis, diagnosis, and treatment ( n = 23/84, 27%; NICU: 6; PICU: 3; ICU: n = 15); 3) neonatal and parenting ( n = 13/84, 15%; all NICU); 4) general health literacy abilities ( n = 11/84, 13%; NICU: n = 6; PICU: n = 2; ICU: n = 7); 5) information needs ( n = 4/84, 5%; NICU: n = 1; PICU: n = 0; ICU: n = 3); 6) readiness for discharge ( n = 3/84, 4%; all NICU); 7) decision-making ( n = 3/84, 4%; all NICU); 8) health-related behaviors ( n = 2/84, 2%; NICU: n = 1; ICU: n = 1); and 9) research participation ( n = 1/84, 1%; NICU). Conclusions: Although several health literacy tools exist, they often focus on individual knowledge of specific aspects of ICU care, with less attention to how understanding is produced within the clinical context through interactions among patients, caregivers, and healthcare providers. This may limit their ability to reflect how health literacy functions in critical illness. Assessment of health literacy requires pairing the appropriate tools with interaction-focused approaches to guide communication and support informed decision-making in ICU settings.

items.title: New Insights Into U.S. Pediatric Critical Care Epidemiology
Association of Oliguria With Acute Kidney Injury, Chronic Kidney Disease, and Mortality: Determining the Optimal Threshold in Critically Ill Patients
items.abstract: Objectives: Oliguria is a key prognostic indicator of acute kidney injury (AKI), yet the consensus definition (< 0.5 mL/kg/hr) is increasingly questioned. We aimed to determine thresholds of lowest mean diuresis (LMD) associated with AKI, chronic kidney disease (CKD), and mortality. Design: Retrospective observational study. Setting: Uppsala University Hospital ICU, Sweden. Patients: A total of 4999 adults (≥ 18 yr) without preexisting CKD admitted to the ICU between 2017 and 2024. Interventions: None. Measurements and Main Results: LMD was calculated over 3, 6, 12, and 24 hours (LMD3h–LMD24h). Generalized additive models were used, adjusting for Simplified Acute Physiology Score 3 estimated mortality ratio and gender. Outcomes were AKI within 7 days of LMD (Kidney Disease Improving Global Outcomes creatinine criteria), incident CKD after ICU discharge, and 90-day mortality. All LMD time frames were significantly associated with AKI, CKD, and death ( p < 0.0001). Thresholds for AKI were 0.43, 0.41, 0.42, and 0.53 mL/kg/hr; for CKD, 0.21, 0.21, 0.31, and 0.43 mL/kg/hr; and for mortality 0.16, 0.18, 0.24, and 0.39 across LMD3h–LMD24h. Conclusions: The risk of mortality or persistent kidney injury, reflected by incident CKD, increases at a lower urine output threshold than the current AKI definition. These findings support the idea of filtration deficit, urine output, and tissue injury as different dimensions of AKI and should influence future AKI definitions.

items.title: Long-Lasting Mental Disorders in Caregivers of ICU Sepsis Survivors and Their Association With Patients’ Post-Intensive Care Syndrome: A Prospective Multicenter Cohort Study
items.abstract: Objectives: To investigate the prevalence of long-term mental disorders in caregivers of ICU sepsis survivors and examine associations with post-intensive care syndrome (PICS) in patients. Design: Prospective observational study. Setting: Twenty-one mixed ICUs. Patients: Caregivers (the next of kin) of the patients diagnosed with sepsis between November 2020 and April 2022. Interventions: None. Measurements and Main Results: Caregivers and patients were assessed at 3, 6, and 12 months after hospital discharge by telephone and mail. The primary outcome was caregiver mental disorders (mental post-intensive care syndrome-family [PICS-F]). Mixed-effects logistic regression analyses were performed to evaluate the association between caregiver PICS-F and patient PICS. Ninety-four caregiver-patient dyads were analyzed. Caregivers were a median of 67 years old (55–79 yr old), 31 (33.0%) were male, and 41 (43.6%) were spouses. Patients were a median of 74 years old (69–82 yr old), and 54 (57.4%) were male. The prevalence of mental PICS-F did not decrease from 3 to 12 months (43% vs. 42%, respectively), whereas the presence of PICS symptoms in patients decreased from 82% to 62%. In mixed-effects logistic regression, the presence of PICS symptoms in patients was significantly associated with PICS-F (adjusted odds ratio, 3.00; 95% CI, 1.54–5.88; p < 0.01). Among the individual patient PICS domains, only mental PICS was significantly associated with PICS-F (3.71; 2.03–6.77; p < 0.01), whereas physical and cognitive impairments in patients were not. Conclusions: The prevalence of mental PICS-F in caregivers of ICU sepsis survivors was frequent and long-lasting over the first year after hospital discharge. Since it was most strongly associated with patients’ mental disorders rather than physical or cognitive impairments, the mental PICS domain in patients may be an important indicator of PICS-F and should be considered in future studies.

items.title: Open Visiting Policy and Delirium in Adult Patients in ICUs: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Clinical Trials
items.abstract: Objectives: To critically evaluate the comparative effects of open or flexible family presence policies vs. restricted or traditional family presence policies on the occurrence of delirium and other major outcomes among adult patients admitted to ICUs. Data Sources: We conducted a comprehensive electronic search of MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, CINAHL, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials from inception to November 21, 2025. Study Selection: We included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing open or flexible vs. restricted ICU visiting policies in adult patients. Data Extraction: The primary outcome extracted was delirium occurrence. Secondary outcomes included the duration of invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV), ICU length of stay, hospital-acquired infections, and ICU mortality. Data Synthesis: Thirteen RCTs comprising 3861 patients were included. Random-effects models showed that compared with restricted policies, open/flexible family presence reduced delirium occurrence (risk ratio [RR], 0.48; 95% CI, 0.29–0.81; low certainty) and IMV duration (mean difference [MD], –0.36 d; 95% CI, –0.46 to –0.26 d; low certainty). The intervention did not affect the ICU length of stay (MD, 4.21 d; 95% CI, –4.65 to 13.07 d; very low certainty), the rates of hospital-acquired infections (RR, 1.00; 95% CI, 0.81–1.23; low certainty), or ICU mortality (RR, 0.88; 95% CI, 0.72–1.08; very low certainty). Conclusions: Open/flexible ICU family presence may reduce delirium and shorten the duration of IMV slightly, without increasing infections or ICU mortality, although the certainty of evidence is low and heterogeneity remains substantial.

items.title: Weaning Strategies for High-Flow Nasal Cannula in Critically Ill Adults: A Randomized Clinical Trial
items.abstract: Objectives: This study evaluated the efficacy of different high-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) weaning protocols in critically ill adults. Design: This multicenter, randomized controlled trial was conducted from December 1, 2022, to August 31, 2024, based on the suggested protocol (SLOWH trial). Experts reviewed the trial between October 2, 2024, and April 15, 2025. Setting: Randomization was performed by a research coordinator using a sequence of random numbers generated by an independent statistician blinded to both researchers and participants. Patients: Adults (≥ 18 yr old) in the ICU who met the weaning criteria after receiving HFNC were included. Among 102 patients from three tertiary care hospitals, 15 were excluded. Interventions: The remaining patients were randomized into three intervention groups: flow reduction (FR) first, F io 2 reduction (OR) first, or simultaneous reduction (SR). The primary outcome was the HFNC weaning success rate, defined as successful transition to conventional oxygen therapy without the need for HFNC reapplication, noninvasive ventilation, or endotracheal intubation within 24 hours. Measurements and Main Results: A total of 87 adults completed the trial (FR, n = 31 [male, 52%]; OR, n = 26 [male, 77%]; SR, n = 30 [male, 53%]). The weaning success rates in the FR, OR, and SR groups were 94%, 81%, and 77%, respectively ( p = 0.15). The median [interquartile range] weaning duration was 31.0 hours (29.0–45.8 hr), 29.5 hours (28.0–60.4 hr), and 29.5 hours (26.5–45.0 hr) in the FR, OR, and SR groups, respectively, with no statistically significant difference among groups ( p = 0.87). Conclusions: In this randomized trial, no statistically significant differences were observed among the three HFNC weaning strategies in terms of weaning success or duration.

items.title: Association of Tele-Critical Care Capability With Interhospital Transfers and Potentially Low-Value Transfers Among Critically Ill Medicare Beneficiaries
items.abstract: Objectives: Interhospital transfer is essential for accessing specialized critical care services, yet it poses clinical risk and substantial burden for patients and the healthcare system. Tele-critical care (TCC) programs extend expertise to resource-limited hospitals and may influence transfer decisions by identifying patients requiring escalation or supporting local management. We examined the association between TCC capability at index ICU hospitalizations, interhospital transfer, and post-transfer outcomes. Design: Nationwide retrospective cohort study using 2021–2023 Medicare claims linked to the American Hospital Association Annual Survey Database (AHAASD). Setting: U.S. acute care hospitals. Patients: Medicare fee-for-service beneficiaries with ICU hospitalizations between 2022 and 2023. Interventions: None. Measurements and Main Results: TCC capability was identified by AHAASD reporting and/or the presence of five or more TCC claims annually. The primary outcome was interhospital ICU transfer. Exploratory post-transfer outcomes included receipt of specialty procedures, death or hospice discharge within 1 day of transfer, in-hospital and 30-day mortality, and discharge disposition. Hierarchical logistic regression adjusted for patient demographics, comorbidities, acute organ failures, and transferring/accepting hospital characteristics, with transferring hospitals as random intercepts. Among 2,140,919 ICU hospitalizations, 33.4% occurred at 1,066 TCC-capable hospitals. Absolute transfer rates were similar (2.5% vs. 3.0%), but TCC capability was associated with higher adjusted odds of transfer (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 1.08; 95% CI, 1.01–1.14). In exploratory post-transfer analyses, transferred patients from TCC hospitals had greater illness severity yet were less likely to die or be discharged to hospice within 1 day of transfer (4.6% vs. 6.6%; aOR, 0.86; 95% CI, 0.76–0.97) and more likely to be discharged home within 2 days (4.7% vs. 3.7%; aOR, 1.17; 95% CI, 1.03–1.33). Conclusions: TCC capability was associated with modestly increased transfer rates, fewer potentially low-value transfers, and improved post-transfer outcomes, suggesting improved transfer selection.

items.title: Developing Models for Complicated Outcomes in Acutely Intoxicated ICU Patients With and Without Toxicity Information
items.abstract: Objectives: To assess the prognostic value of the mean Lethality Risk Score (LRS), reflecting the toxicity of substances involved in an exposure, and to develop prediction models for complicated outcomes in ICU patients with acute intoxication. Design: Multicenter prospective cohort study. Setting: Seventy-eight ICUs in Europe, Australia, and the Eastern Mediterranean (2020–2023). Patients: A total of 2265 adult patients were admitted to the ICU with acute intoxication as the main reason for admission for at least 4 hours. Intervention: None. Measurements and Main Results: The primary outcome was defined as ICU complications or death (22.5%). Clinical data were collected in an electronic capture system. We developed two prediction models: one incorporating laboratory variables (“Laboratory Model”), and one including the mean LRS (“Expo Model”). The mean LRS was calculated as the average of the individual LRS values assigned to the toxicants involved in the exposure. Key predictors were age, severity at presentation, systolic blood pressure, Glasgow Coma Scale score, and hospital type. The mean LRS remained significant only when laboratory variables were not considered. Model performance was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic (AUROC), calibration plots, likelihood ratio tests, and decision curve analysis. Internal validation demonstrated good performance for both models (AUROCs of 0.79 and 0.77; calibration slopes of 0.94 and 0.95; intercepts of −0.06 and –0.06), with minimal overfitting. Decision curve analysis revealed clinically relevant threshold probability ranges of 0–50% for the Laboratory Model and 0–40% for the Expo Model. Conclusions: The mean LRS had prognostic value only in the absence of laboratory test results. Both models may aid decision-making regarding the management of acutely intoxicated patients in the ICU.

items.title: Ventilatory Management in Neurocritical Versus Non-Neurocritical Care Patients: A Pooled Analysis From the PRIME Database
items.abstract: Objectives: To describe ventilatory management in neurocritical care and non-neurocritical care patients and determine whether specific ventilator settings are associated with development of acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) and mortality in neurocritical care patients. The primary endpoint was a diagnosis of ARDS after initiation of invasive ventilation; one secondary endpoint was ICU mortality. Data Sources: Post hoc pooled analysis of harmonized individual patient data from three recent prospective observational studies combined into the PRIME database. Study Selection: PRIME is a harmonized pooled database comprising individual patient data from three recent prospective observational studies on ventilatory management in critically ill patients: “PRactice of VENTilation in critically ill patients without ARDS” (PRoVENT), “PRactice of VENTilation in critically ill patients in Middle-income Countries” (PRoVENT-iMiC), and “Extubation strategies in Neuro-ICU patients and associations with Outcomes” (ENIO). We excluded patients with ARDS at the start of ventilation. Data Extraction: Demographic and clinical characteristics, ventilator settings, respiratory variables, arterial blood gas values, and clinical outcomes were extracted from the harmonized PRIME database. Derived ventilation parameters included tidal volume normalized to predicted body weight, driving pressure, respiratory system compliance, mechanical power, ventilatory ratio, and Pao 2 /Fio 2 ratio. Data Synthesis: This analysis included 3848 patients, including 1702 neurocritical care and 1920 non-neurocritical care patients. Based on recorded ventilatory variables, neurocritical care patients received lower median tidal volumes (V t s), positive end-expiratory pressure, and F io 2 . They had lower median driving pressure (ΔP), mechanical power (MP) of ventilation, and ventilatory ratio, as well as higher respiratory system compliance compared with non-neurocritical care patients. These differences were consistently observed at both assessed time points. ARDS was diagnosed more frequently in neurocritical care patients than in non-neurocritical care patients (8.7% vs. 3.9%; p < 0.001), while ICU mortality was lower (14.3% vs. 22.8%; p < 0.001). Among neurocritical care patients, those who developed ARDS were ventilated with lower median V t and higher F io 2 and had higher median ΔP and MP. V t normalized for predicted body weight in neurocritical care patients was independently associated with the development of ARDS. Conclusions: In this cohort, ventilatory management at the initial and 48-hour assessments differed between neurocritical care and non-neurocritical care patients, particularly with respect to key ventilator settings like V t , positive end-expiratory pressure, and F io 2 . In neurocritical care patients, ARDS was more often diagnosed than in non-neurocritical care patients.

items.title: A Quality Improvement Initiative to Achieve Provincial Implementation of a Web-Based Family Satisfaction in ICU (FS-ICU) Survey to Inform Patient-Centered Care
items.abstract: Objectives: To review the web-based Family Satisfaction in ICU (FS-ICU) survey across all adult level 3 Ontario ICUs to capture patient and family experiences with critical care, and to evaluate feasibility, participation, and satisfaction scores. Design: A province-wide, multisite quality improvement study using an electronic, key-based FS-ICU survey with prospectively collected anonymous data linked to encounters through a centralized database. Setting: All 83 adult level 3 ICUs (52 community, 31 academic) in ON, Canada, from July 1, 2019, to May 31, 2024. Patients: The population comprised adult ICU patients, family members, or substitute decision-makers, with one survey per ICU encounter regardless of length of stay or number of family members. Interventions: ICUs implemented a web-based FS-ICU using a unique seven-digit key in three formats (Staff-Provided, Quick Response-Driven, Website-Code), supported by training, resources, and tablets, with no clinical care interventions beyond routine practice. Measurements and Main Results: Feasibility metrics included onboarding (keys generated per ICU admission), opening, participation, and completion rates, calculated for different centers using provincial data. Over the study period, 24,679 unique keys were generated for 353,400 ICU admissions (onboarding rate, 7.0%), 13,596 keys were opened (opening rate, 55.1%), and 7,542 surveys met the greater than or equal to 70% completion threshold (completion rate, 57.6% among opened surveys; reflection rate, 2.1% of ICU encounters). Survey initiation was highest with the Staff-Provided format (88.4% of keys initiated), and overall satisfaction was high, with mean FS with Care, 87.8; FS with Decision-Making, 84.4; and FS-TOTAL 86.5 on a 0–100 scale, with nursing care rated highest and adequacy of time for questions rated lowest. Conclusions: A provincial, web-based FS-ICU was implemented across all adult level 3 Ontario ICUs, producing a large dataset with high satisfaction scores. A small proportion completed the survey, highlighting feasibility and workflow barriers. Future efforts should improve activation and completion rates and integrate FS-ICU data into routine quality improvement to enhance patient- and family-centered care.

items.title: ICU Physical Environments Used for Family Conferences: A Multimodal Qualitative Evaluation with ICU Team Members
items.abstract: Objectives: Family-clinician communication is central to high-quality care for critically ill patients. Although previous work has focused on improving how and what is communicated, little is known about where this high-stakes communication takes place and how it is shaped by the physical environment. Our objectives were to characterize ICU spaces typically used for family conferences and identify modifiable environmental features that influence communication. Design: We conducted a multimodal qualitative study of 17 spaces typically used for family conferences across four adult ICUs in a U.S. academic medical center. Healthcare design and architecture experts independently assessed architectural plans and photographs to characterize spatial features. Then, we conducted semi-structured interviews with 23 ICU team members (nurses, social workers, case managers) to elicit perspectives on and experiences within these spaces. We conducted qualitative content analysis using a combined inductive and deductive approach. Setting: A total of 17 family conference spaces across four adult ICUs in a U.S. academic medical center. Participants: A total of 23 ICU team members. Interventions: None. Results: The 17 analyzed spaces included designated family-communication rooms ( n = 2), multipurpose rooms ( n = 6), visitor lounges ( n = 4), and public areas ( n = 5; lobbies/hallways). Study participants preferred designated spaces, as they provide privacy, prevent interruption, and facilitate emotional support. Conversely, multipurpose and public areas are prone to distractions and interruptions from conflicting uses. We identified key environmental features that support communication: proximity to patients, flexible furniture layout, and nonclinical ambiance. Conclusions: Family conferences occur in a variety of physical environments in and around adult ICUs, ranging from intentionally designed rooms to elevator lobbies. ICU team members perceive that physical environments have an important influence on communication quality, and we identified pragmatic opportunities to improve existing spaces.

items.title: Infections Acquired in the ICU Among Cancer and Other Immunosuppressed Patients: A Nationwide Cohort Study
items.abstract: Objectives: To compare the cumulative incidence of ICU-acquired infections (ICU-AIs) across distinct immunosuppression diagnostic categories (solid cancer, hematological cancer, other immunosuppression) and nonimmunosuppressed patients, accounting for competing risks of death and discharge. Design: Retrospective cohort study using prospectively collected data. Setting: A total of 50 participating ICUs in Brazil. Patients: A total of 38,126 adult patients admitted between October 2019 and December 2021 with an ICU stay exceeding 48 hours and no infections diagnosed within the first 48 hours. Interventions: None. Measurements and Main Results: The primary outcome was the incidence of the first ICU-AI during the ICU stay, evaluated using Fine-Gray subdistribution hazard ratios (sHR). In the multivariable competing-risk analysis, patients with hematological malignancies (sHR, 1.64; 95% CI, 1.01–2.65) and other immunosuppressive conditions (sHR, 1.61; 95% CI, 1.02–2.54) were associated with an increased cumulative incidence of ICU-AI, while solid malignancy was not significantly different from non-immunosuppressed patients (sHR, 0.88; 95% CI, 0.68–1.14). Conclusions: Patients with hematological malignancies and other immunosuppressive conditions face a significantly higher risk of ICU-AIs.

items.title: Assessment of Tidal Volume in Patients Undergoing Noninvasive Ventilation: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.abstract: Objectives: Noninvasive ventilation (NIV) is widely used in acute respiratory failure (ARF), yet the association between high tidal volume (V t ) and clinical outcomes remains incompletely defined. We evaluated the association between V t and NIV failure overall and by ARF type, and its relationship with respiratory and clinical outcomes. Data Sources: MEDLINE, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, Web of Science, and Latin American and Caribbean Health Science Literature (1976 to September 2025). Study Selection: Observational studies of adults with ARF treated with NIV reporting V t or V t normalized to predicted body weight (V t /PBW) in NIV success and failure groups. Data Extraction: Three pairs of reviewers identified studies and extracted data independently. Random-effects meta-analysis was performed. Risk of bias and certainty of evidence were assessed using Risk of Bias In Nonrandomized Studies of Interventions and Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation. Data Synthesis: Eleven studies (1136 patients) were included. V t /PBW was higher in NIV failure vs. success (mean difference [MD], 1.02 mL/kg [95% CI, 0.60–1.45 mL/kg]), whereas absolute V t did not differ (MD, 1.30 [–33.31 to 35.91]). In hypoxemic ARF, V t /PBW remained higher in NIV failure (MD, 0.89 mL/kg [95% CI, 0.04–1.73 mL/kg]); no data were available for hypercapnic ARF. Post hoc analyses showed that higher V t /PBW was associated with increased mortality (odds ratio, 9.11; 95% CI, 3.88–21.37), higher respiratory rate (RR; MD, 3.14 breaths/min [95% CI, 1.36–4.92 breaths/min]), and lower Pa co 2 (MD, –2.38 mm Hg [95% CI, –4.16 to –0.5938 mm Hg]), but no with pressure support (PS) level (MD, 0.24 [95% CI, –0.81 to 1.29]). Certainty of evidence ranged from very low to moderate. Conclusions: In adults with ARF treated with NIV, higher V t /PBW was associated with NIV failure and worse outcomes. These findings reflect prognostic associations rather than causality, and interventional studies with systematic V t monitoring are needed. Importantly, elevated V t /PBW, higher RR, lower Pa co 2 , and increased mortality, without differences in PS, collectively implicate elevated respiratory drive as a driver of increased mortality (PROSPERO [CRD42024584977]). Findings: Higher V t /PBW was associated with NIV failure, particularly in hypoxemic respiratory failure; post hoc analyses showed associations with increased mortality, higher respiratory rate, and lower Pa co 2 .

items.title: Role of Mitochondrial Impairment in Sepsis-Induced Platelet Activation
items.abstract: Objectives: Sepsis-induced mitochondrial impairment has been described in different organs, in both animal models and humans. Excessive radical oxygen species (ROS) could be involved in this phenomenon. As a result, antioxidants have been proposed as a potential therapeutic strategy, although results remain controversial. Platelet hyperactivation is considered a central pathogenic mechanism in the development of sepsis-induced organ damage. In this study, we aimed to determine whether mitochondrial dysfunction contributes to platelet hyperactivation during sepsis. We also evaluated the effect of ROS scavenging using the mitochondria-targeted antioxidant MitoTEMPO. Design: Laboratory investigation. Setting: University Hospital. Patients and Subjects: Patients with sepsis/septic shock ( n = 3/7), nonseptic burn patients ( n = 10), and healthy control subjects ( n = 10). Interventions: Platelet mitochondria and isolated platelets from healthy donors were treated in vitro with plasma from patients with sepsis/septic shock and healthy subjects, before and after preincubation with MitoTEMPO. Measurements and Main Results: We measured platelet oxygen consumption rates in isolated human platelets using the Seahorse Extracellular Flux Analyzer. Platelet mitochondrial respiratory chain enzyme activity was measured in mitochondria-enriched fractions by spectrophotometry. Platelet aggregation in platelet-rich plasma was analyzed using light-transmission aggregometry, and leukocyte-platelet adhesion in whole blood by flow cytometry. We found that incubating platelets with septic plasma significantly reduced basal, maximal, and adenosine triphosphate-linked oxygen consumption rate. Incubation of platelet mitochondria with septic plasma also reduced platelet Complex I activity, compared with healthy plasma or plasma from nonseptic burn patients. This decrease was associated with an increase in Epinephrine-induced platelet activation. Preincubating platelets with the mitochondria-selective ROS scavenger MitoTEMPO significantly reversed these effects. Conclusions: Our results show that the mitochondria-selective ROS scavenger MitoTEMPO prevents mitochondrial dysfunction and enhances platelet activation induced by septic plasma in human platelets in vitro. This may help in designing new therapeutic approaches to prevent sepsis-induced organ damage mediated by mitochondrial dysfunction and platelet hyperactivation.

items.title: Rethinking Oliguria in the ICU: From Threshold to Trajectory
Music Therapy During Weaning From Invasive Mechanical Ventilation in the ICU: A Randomized Controlled Trial
items.abstract: Objectives: The study examined the effect of daily music therapy on weaning from invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV) in the ICU, with a primary focus on weaning duration. Secondary agitation, sedation, and analgesia doses, pain, delirium, and perceived stress after 90 days were assessed. Additionally, total IMV and ICU stay durations and tracheostomy rates were studied. Physiologic parameters were assessed in the music therapy group (MG). The study also aimed to promote the humanization of critical care through a biopsychosocial and creative music therapy approach. Design: Randomized controlled trial with two parallel groups: control group receiving standard care during weaning and MG receiving music therapy additionally. Setting and Patients: Adult critically ill patients ( n = 100) admitted to a general ICU who received IMV for at least 48 hours. Interventions: MG received daily, individualized music therapy sessions averaging 25 minutes, based on patient needs and musical preferences, which included music relaxation, music listening, and clinical improvisation. Measurements and Main Results: No significant difference in weaning duration was observed between groups ( p = 0.97). Patients in the MG group showed significant improvements in agitation and sedation levels (Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale) on days 1 and 3 ( p = 0.048, 0.005, and 0.024) and a lower percentage required propofol ( p = 0.028). No significant difference in perceived pain (Visual Analog Pain Scale). The MG obtained lower Perceived Stress Scale-14 scores ( p = 0.24). Additionally, MG significantly reduced tracheostomy rates (14%; p = 0.025). Median total IMV and ICU stay duration were shorter in the MG group, but not significantly ( p = 0.206 and 0.203). Heart rate, respiratory rate, blood pressure, and oxygenation showed no significant difference before and after music therapy. Conclusions: Music therapy may serve as a nonpharmacological complementary adjunct during weaning by reducing agitation, sedation, and tracheostomy rate. It may potentially decrease perceived stress and IMV and ICU stay durations. Further research is warranted.

items.title: Delay From Hypotension Onset to Appropriate Antifungal Therapy Initiation Is the Critical Determinant of Outcome in Candida Septic Shock
items.abstract: Objectives: To determine the effect of delays in initiation of appropriate antifungal therapy from the initial onset of persistent hypotension to the outcome of Candida septic shock. Design: Retrospective cohort study. Setting: A total of 32 academic and community hospitals in Canada, the United States, and Saudi Arabia (July 1989 to June 2018). Patients: A total of 850 adult patients with culture-positive Candida septic shock. Interventions: None. Measurements and Main Results: Out of 850 patients with Candida septic shock, 69.2% patients (589) received appropriate antifungal therapy after the onset of persistent hypotension. A strong relationship was observed between the delay in initiation of pathogen-appropriate antifungal (PAA) therapy and hospital survival. The adjusted odds ratio of death was 1.045 per hour of delay (95% CI, 1.035–1.056; p < 0.0001). The survival rate was 86% when an appropriate antifungal for the isolated pathogen was administered within 2 hours of the initial documentation of persistent hypotension. Thereafter, hospital survival decreased an average of 5.0% per hour for each hour of delay to 10–12 hours of delay. In a multivariate analysis, which included the Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation II score and epidemiologic/therapeutic variables, the time to initiation of appropriate antifungal therapy emerged as the single strongest predictor of outcome. Sensitivity analysis further demonstrated that the adverse effects of delayed antifungal treatment were consistent across various subgroups, including different types of infections, pathogens, and antifungal drug classes. Median time to appropriate antifungal therapy was 32.3 hours (interquartile range, 11.2–66.0 hr), with only 16.9% receiving therapy within 6 hours of hypotension onset. Conclusions: Administration of PAAs within the first hours of documented hypotension significantly improved hospital survival. Less than 20% of patients received appropriate antifungals within 6 hours of documented hypotension.

items.title: Ketamine as an Opioid-Sparing Adjunct During Mechanical Ventilation: Feasible and Ready for a Larger Trial
Scientific Output in Septic Shock According to Country Income and Gender: A Meta-Epidemiological Study
items.abstract: Objectives: We aimed to assess trends in septic shock publications by country income and author gender. Data Sources: We systematically searched PubMed, Embase, and Web of Science for articles indexed with “septic shock” between January 2014 and December 2024. Study Selection: All peer-reviewed publication types were eligible. Conference abstracts and non–peer-reviewed material were excluded. Data Extraction: Bibliographic data, first and last author affiliations, country income level (World Bank classification: low- and middle-income countries [LMICs] and high-income countries [HICs]), and journal prestige (SCImago Journal Rank [SJR]) were extracted. Author gender was inferred using the NamSor application programming interface (API). Data Synthesis: Of 10,352 eligible publications, LMIC-affiliated first authors increased over time (+2.13% per year; 95% CI, +1.66 to +2.61; p < 0.001) from 18% in 2014 to 37% in 2024. Women represented 35.6% of first authors and 25.0% of last authors (with around 20% of authors not classifiable by the NamSor API), with higher proportions in LMICs than HICs ( p < 0.001) for both first authors (44.5% vs. 32.5%) and last authors (35.2% vs. 21.5%). Gender concordance was more frequent, with female first authors more often paired with female last authors than male first authors (31.7% vs. 21.1%). Cross-income collaborations, especially involving LMIC last authors, remained rare. Articles led by men in HICs were more often published in higher-SJR journals compared with those led by women ( p < 0.001), whereas no gender differences were observed among LMIC-affiliated authors. Conclusions: Despite encouraging growth in LMIC contributions and female representation, major inequities persist. Strengthening equitable collaborations and supporting underrepresented groups would broaden participation and enhance the global applicability in critical care research.

items.title: Cluster Versus Individual Randomization in Prehospital, Emergency and Critical Care Trials: A Meta-Epidemiological Study
items.abstract: Objectives: Cluster-randomized clinical trials (cRCTs) are pooled with individually randomized clinical trials (iRCTs) in meta-analyses. However, cRCTs are associated with methodological characteristics potentially inducing systematic differences compared with iRCTs. In acute settings, trial inclusion is time-sensitive, exacerbating inclusion-based biases. We conducted a meta-epidemiological study to assess deviations in effect estimates between cRCTs and iRCTs in these settings. Data Sources: A systematic literature search was conducted in PubMed and Embase. Data Selection: We screened and identified all meta-analyses in prehospital, emergency, or critical care within the last decade that included at least one cRCT and one iRCT. Data Extraction: Data were extracted in duplicate from the meta-analyses. If overlapping trials were identified, results were pooled. The primary outcome was mortality; the secondary outcome comprised length-of-stay- or days-alive-type outcomes. Data Synthesis: Using absolute ln(odds ratio [OR]) for mortality and absolute Hedges’ g for the secondary outcome, mean differences (MDs) in effect estimates between cRCTs and iRCTs were analyzed using mixed regression models, presented with 95% CIs. We identified 94 eligible meta-analyses; 44.7% reported on randomization type (cRCT or iRCT). We included 65 meta-analyses in quantitative analyses, encompassing 212 randomized clinical trials (39 cRCTs and 173 iRCTs) and 315,276 patients. No statistically significant difference in absolute ln(OR) for mortality between cRCTs and iRCTs was found (MD, –0.110; 95% CI, –0.093 to 0.313). For length-of-stay- or days-alive-type outcomes, a significant difference in absolute Hedges’ g was found (MD, –0.202; 95% CI, –0.392 to –0.012). Conclusions: A systematic difference between cRCTs and iRCTs in length-of-stay- or days-alive-type outcomes, but not mortality, was identified, with cRCTs reporting smaller effect size magnitudes than iRCTs. With under half of identified meta-analyses reporting on randomization modality, these results highlight the need for improved transparency and statistical consideration of randomization type in future meta-analyses in prehospital, emergency, and critical care.

items.title: Furosemide Stress Test in Adults and Children With Acute Kidney Injury: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.abstract: Objectives: To evaluate the diagnostic accuracy and therapeutic utility of the furosemide stress test (FST) for acute kidney injury (AKI) management in critically ill adults and children. Data Sources: PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials were searched from inception to March 3, 2026. Study Selection: Studies evaluating the standardized FST protocol in critically ill adults or children with AKI were eligible. Outcomes included AKI stage 3 progression (Q1), kidney replacement therapy (KRT) initiation (Q2), short-term mortality (Q3), successful KRT liberation (Q4), and FST-guided vs. standard KRT initiation in randomized trials (Q5). Data Extraction: Two reviewers independently extracted data and assessed risk of bias using Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies 2 and Risk of Bias 2. Certainty of evidence was assessed using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) framework. Data Synthesis: Twenty studies ( n = 1979; 11 countries; 2013–2025) were included. For AKI progression (nine studies; n = 501), pooled sensitivity was 0.69 and specificity was 0.88 (area under the curve [AUC], 0.89; GRADE: low). For KRT initiation (nine studies; n = 952), sensitivity was 0.81 and specificity was 0.75 (AUC, 0.79; GRADE: very low). For mortality (six studies; n = 487), sensitivity was 0.56 and specificity was 0.76 (AUC, 0.75; GRADE: very low). For KRT liberation (three studies; n = 177), sensitivity was 0.81 and specificity was 0.87 (AUC, 0.89; GRADE: low for sensitivity, very low for specificity). The effect of FST-guided early KRT initiation on short-term mortality was uncertain (pooled risk ratio, 1.00; 95% CI, 0.79–1.27; two randomized controlled trials, n = 212; GRADE: very low). Pediatric analyses yielded AUC values of 0.81 and 0.63 for KRT initiation and mortality, respectively. Conclusions: Based on low to very low certainty evidence, the FST may support risk stratification for AKI progression and KRT liberation in critically ill adults. Its impact on mortality when guiding early KRT initiation remains uncertain. As a low-cost bedside test, the FST can be a useful tool in resource-limited settings where novel biomarkers are inaccessible.

items.title: Association of Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome Radiographic Findings Identified by Machine Learning and Outcomes of Patients Receiving Invasive Mechanical Ventilation
items.abstract: Objectives: To determine whether predictions from a deep learning model that identifies acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) findings on chest radiographs (CXRs) can also predict clinical outcomes beyond traditional indicators of hypoxemia and illness severity. Design: Retrospective cohort study. Setting: Single academic medical center. Intervention: None. Patients: Adult patients with CXRs performed at the time of invasive mechanical ventilation initiation. Methods and Main Results: We applied a deep learning model that was previously trained to identify bilateral airspace opacities consistent with ARDS to CXRs of 6591 patients receiving invasive mechanical ventilation. The resulting ARDS-CXR scores were evaluated for their ability to discriminate risk of 28-day mortality and their association with 28-day mortality and time to extubation after adjusting for a patient’s Pa o 2 /F io 2 or Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation-IV. The median ARDS-CXR score was –2.09, corresponding to an ARDS probability of 15%, and 1089 (17%) patients had a positive score, corresponding to an ARDS probability above 50%. Twenty-eight-day mortality was 35.1% among patients with a positive score and 13.5% among patients with a negative score. ARDS-CXR scores below the ARDS threshold also stratified risk, with mortality increasing from 12.8% at a score of –2 to 19.9% at –1 and 27.5% at 0. The ARDS-CXR score area under the receiver operating characteristic (AUROC) curve was 0.68 (95% CI, 0.66–0.70) for predicting 28-day mortality, whereas the Pa o 2 /F io 2 AUROC was 0.64 (95% CI, 0.62–0.66). After adjusting for either the patient’s Pa o 2 /F io 2 or Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation-IV, a 1-point increase in the ARDS-CXR score was significantly associated with higher 28-day mortality or prolonged time to extubation. Conclusions: A deep learning–derived ARDS-CXR score quantifying radiographic findings of ARDS independently predicted mortality and ventilator outcomes beyond hypoxemia and illness severity. Algorithmically derived markers of lung injury severity from chest imaging could be used to support clinical care decisions, predictive enrichment in research studies, or incorporated into a future ARDS definition.

items.title: Brachial-to-Radial Pressure Gradient in Critically Ill Patients Treated With Vasoactive Agents: A Prospective Observational Study
items.abstract: Objectives: To determine the incidence of a significant noninvasive brachial-to-radial arterial pressure gradient (NIBR-APG) and its clinical associations in critically ill patients receiving vasoactive agents. Design: Prospective, multicenter, observational study. Setting: Thirteen ICUs in Poland. Patients: Adult ICU patients with radial arterial catheters receiving vasoactive agents hospitalized between April 2025 and July 2025. Interventions: None. Measurements and Main Results: Invasive radial mean arterial pressure (MAP) and noninvasive brachial MAP were measured twice and averaged. A NIBR-APG greater than 11 mm Hg was predefined as clinically significant. Baseline characteristics, hemodynamic variables, and outcomes were recorded. Among 303 patients, 49.5% were surgical admissions and 33.3% had septic shock. The median NIBR-APG was 4.5 mm Hg (interquartile range, 0.0–10.0 mm Hg). Fifty-six patients (18.4%) exhibited a NIBR-APG greater than 11 mm Hg. Compared with patients without a significant gradient, these patients received higher norepinephrine-equivalent doses (0.23 vs. 0.10 µg/kg/min), had higher Sequential Organ Failure Assessment scores (11 vs. 10), prolonged capillary refill time (3.0 vs. 2.5 s), and higher lactate concentrations (2.7 vs. 1.3 mmol/L). In multivariable analysis, only vasoactive drug dose was independently associated with NIBR-APG greater than 11 mm Hg (odds ratio, 1.68; 95% CI, 1.12–2.52). ICU mortality was higher in patients with significant gradients (48.0% vs. 30.1%). Conclusions: Nearly one in five critically ill patients receiving vasoactive agents demonstrated a clinically significant NIBR-APG. The presence of this gradient was independently associated with higher vasoactive drug requirements and was accompanied by greater illness severity and higher ICU mortality.

items.title: Comparative Analysis of Tracheal Intubation–Associated Cardiac Arrest in 2015–2023: A Report From the National Emergency Airway Registry for Children Multicenter Registry
items.abstract: Objectives: To determine the contemporary incidence of tracheal intubation–associated cardiac arrest (TI-CA) in critically ill children and identify potentially modifiable factors to prevent TI-CA in PICUs and pediatric cardiac ICUs (PCICUs). Design: Retrospective cohort study Setting: Seventy international PICUs and PCICUs Patients: Critically ill children requiring tracheal intubation in PICUs and PCICUs Interventions: Tracheal intubation data were prospectively collected for all initial intubations in 68 PICUs and PCICUs from January 2015 to December 2023 using the National Emergency Airway Registry for Children registry. Measurements and Main Results: TI-CA was defined as CA occurrence or receipt of chest compressions for at least 1 minute within 20 minutes of endotracheal tube placement. TI during ongoing cardiopulmonary resuscitation was not considered TI-CA. A total of 27,773 TIs were evaluated, with TI-CA reported in 1.2% ( n = 331). Pre-TI oxygenation failure and shock were associated with higher odds of TI-CA (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 2.29; 95% CI, 1.81–2.89 and aOR, 4.67; 95% CI, 3.68–5.92, respectively). Each additional TI attempt required was associated with increased odds of TI-CA (aOR, 1.70; 95% CI, 1.56–1.85, for each attempt). Use of ketamine (aOR, 0.64; 95% CI, 0.49–0.82), propofol (aOR, 0.44; 95% CI, 0.27–0.72), neuromuscular blockade (aOR, 0.67; 95% CI, 0.49–0.91), and video laryngoscopy (aOR, 0.76; 95% CI, 0.6–0.97) were associated with lower odds of TI-CA. Mediation analysis indicated that 13% of video laryngoscopy’s protective effect was due to a reduction in TI attempt counts. The protective effects of ketamine, propofol, and neuromuscular blockade were minimally mediated by reduced TI attempt counts (5%, 4%, and 7%). Conclusions: TI-CA occurred in 1.2% of TIs performed in the PICUs. Odds of TI-CA increased incrementally with successive TI attempts. Video laryngoscopy was protective against TI-CA. Mediation analysis revealed that reduced TI attempts accounted for 13% of the protective benefit associated with video laryngoscopy.

items.title: Candida Septic Shock: If Every Hour Matters, Who Requires Empiric Therapy?
Beyond 28-Day Mortality: The Unfinished Story of Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation Survivorship

Variation in Pediatric Extracorporeal Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation Survival After In-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: Development and Validation of a Survival Model for Risk-Standardized Survival Rates: An Analysis of the Extracorporeal Life Support Organization Registry
items.abstract: Objectives: To develop and internally validate a multivariable prediction model for survival to hospital discharge after pediatric extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) for in-hospital cardiac arrest (IHCA), and to use this model to derive risk-standardized survival rates (RSSRs) and quantify between-hospital variation in outcomes. Design: Retrospective multicenter cohort study. Setting: Hospitals contributing to the Extracorporeal Life Support Organization (ELSO) registry between 2020 and 2023. Patients: Children (< 18 yr) treated with ECPR for IHCA. Interventions: None. Measurements and Main Results: Eligible patients were identified from the ELSO Registry and split into derivation ( N = 1060) and validation ( N = 317) cohorts using a hospital-stratified split to preserve within-hospital clustering. Survival prediction models were derived using penalized logistic regression with the least absolute shrinkage and selection operator. A full-event model incorporating 14 routinely available clinical variables demonstrated fair discrimination (area under the curve, 0.728 in the derivation cohort and 0.678 in the validation cohort) and good calibration (observed-to-expected ratio, 0.995; Brier score, 0.222 in the validation cohort). This model was embedded in a multilevel logistic regression model to generate hospital-level RSSRs for centers reporting five or more ECPR cases. Between-hospital variation was quantified using the median odds ratio, which was 1.30 (95% CI, 1.11–1.93), indicating significant differences in survival likelihood between centers after adjusting for patient-level risk. Conclusions: In a large, international cohort of pediatric ECPR patients, we developed and internally validated a clinically interpretable model for survival to hospital discharge. The model performance as a discriminator likely limits its use as a standalone tool for clinical decision-making. However, strong internal calibration allowed for determination of hospital-level RSSRs, which revealed significant inter-hospital variability. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of developing a risk-adjustment model capable of estimating hospital-level RSSRs. Additional external validation and evaluation of residual case-mix differences are needed before such models can be used for benchmarking across pediatric ECPR centers.

items.title: Geo-economic variations in structure and organization of intensive care units: the ISOREA survey
items.containerTitle: American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine
items.abstract: Purpose Little is known on critical care services globally. This study aimed to describe ICU resources and organization across countries and assess variability by income group, between countries, and within countries. Methods Participating centers provided structured data on hospital and ICU characteristics via electronic case report form (January 2018 to July 2020). Questionnaire included 237 items covering general characteristics (2 topics) and ICU resources and organization (18 topics). We computed standardized functional domain scores (ISOREA score), classified ICUs using Marshall criteria, and readiness for essential emergency and critical care using a modified Schell score. Results A total of 1,426 ICUs from five continents were recruited, and 1,225 were analyzed, from high-income countries (HICs, 58%), upper-middle-income (20%), and low/lower-middle-income countries (LLMICs, 22%). Most ICUs were in referral centers (90%) and large urban areas (80%). Most variables (93%) were significantly associated with income group, Most variables (93%) were significantly associated with income group, with 88% showing higher levels in HICs and lower levels in LLMICs. Six domains showed major disparities: extracorporeal support, respiratory support, emergency access to interventional radiology and surgery, neurology and trauma care, patient file and general monitoring, and cardiovascular and hemodynamic monitoring. According to the Marshall classification, 79% of ICUs in HICs were classified as level III, whereas 55% of ICUs in LLMICs were classified as level I. Domains with higher ISOREA scores varied primarily between countries, whereas lower-performing domains exhibited greater variability across ICUs within the same country. Adjustment for income group reduced, but did not eliminate, country-level clustering. Conclusion Substantial disparities exist in ICU resources and organization across income groups, countries, and ICUs. ICU capacities appeared multidimensional, extending beyond resource limitations.

items.title: Therapeutic Targeting of the Macrophage YTHDC1/TIGAR/NF-κB Axis Mitigates Pulmonary Hypertension
items.containerTitle: American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine
items.abstract: Rationale Immune dysregulation is a pivotal driver of pulmonary hypertension (PH) pathogenesis, yet therapeutic targeting of inflammation has yielded limited clinical success. Although cytosolic RNA-binding proteins are known to regulate immune responses in PH, the specific role of the nuclear m⁶A reader YTHDC1 remains undefined. Objectives To elucidate the function of macrophage YTHDC1 in orchestrating inflammatory vascular remodeling during PH. Methods Expression profiles of YTHDC1 and TP53-induced glycolysis and apoptosis regulator (TIGAR) were evaluated in human and rodent PH specimens. The mechanistic and therapeutic roles of this axis were assessed using myeloid-specific knockout mice and pharmacological inhibitors (YL-5092, 5Z-7-oxozeaenol) across hypoxia-, SU5416/hypoxia-, and monocrotaline-induced PH models. Measurements and Main Results In patients with idiopathic or connective tissue disease-associated PAH, YTHDC1 and TIGAR expression levels were elevated in pulmonary and circulating macrophages, correlating with disease severity. In murine models, myeloid-specific deletion of Ythdc1 or Tigar conferred profound protection against hypoxia- and SU5416/hypoxia-induced PH. Mechanistically, hypoxia upregulated Ythdc1, which directly bound and stabilized Tigar mRNA. The subsequent accumulation of Tigar protein operated non-enzymatically via a specific domain (residues 152-161) to interact with Tak1, thereby activating the NF-κB cascade, augmenting pro-inflammatory cytokine release, and driving pulmonary artery smooth muscle cell proliferation. Pharmacological inhibition of YTHDC1 (YL-5092) or disruption of the TIGAR-TAK1 interaction (5Z-7-oxozeaenol) effectively attenuated vascular inflammation and mitigated PH progression in diverse rodent models. Conclusions The macrophage YTHDC1/TIGAR/NF-κB signaling axis acts as a critical determinant of inflammation and vascular remodeling in PH, representing a potential biomarker and therapeutic target for this disease.

items.title: The Future of AI in Critical Care: An Exploration in Ten Parables
items.containerTitle: American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine
items.abstract: We cannot know how artificial intelligence (AI) will ultimately change critical care, only that it is driving substantial change quickly. Through ten parables, we describe plausible benefits, harms, and trade-offs involving prognosis, monitoring, liability, research, clinical work, data governance, education, and triage. These parables are not predictions. They are intended to help clinicians, institutions, and regulators envision a range of potential scenarios and think broadly about which applications to pursue, which risks to consider, and which rules to establish before AI systems become entrenched. Each parable reveals how the outlook for AI in critical care is characterized by uncertainty. This includes uncertainty about what a single prediction means for the patient in front of us, how an application built and tested in one setting performs in another, accountability frameworks, professional practice and learning, patient privacy and autonomy, and more. Within each parable we try to keep visible what current evidence already supports and what remains speculative. We close with a set of questions designed to focus that speculation among the interested parties who will shape the future of AI in critical care.

items.title: Clinician-guided digital CBT-I improves sleep quality and apnea severity in patients with co-morbid insomnia and OSA: A Double-Blind, Randomized Clinical Trial
items.containerTitle: American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine
items.abstract: Rationale Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is the accepted first-line treatment for insomnia, but its scalability and safety in patients with co-morbid insomnia and obstructive sleep apnea (COMISA) remain unclear. Clinician-guided digital CBT-I (D-CBT-I) is a potential treatment option that may address these limitations in COMISA. Objective To evaluate the effectiveness of clinician-guided D-CBT-I versus sleep hygiene education (SHE) in patients with COMISA. Methods This randomized trial (n = 88) compared clinician-guided D-CBT-I (6 weekly online sessions: sleep restriction, sleep hygiene, stimulus control, cognitive restructuring, relapse prevention) with SHE alone. Blinded outcome assessments were conducted at baseline, posttreatment (6 weeks), and 3-month follow-up. Primary outcomes were Insomnia Severity Index (ISI) and Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) scores at posttreatment and 3-month follow-up. Secondary outcomes included daytime sleepiness, sleep parameters, OSA severity, neurocognitive function, and adverse events. Measurements and Main Results At 3-month follow-up, intention-to-treat analysis showed significantly greater improvements with D-CBT-I versus SHE on ISI (−9.5 vs. −4.0 points; d = −1.18, P = 0.001) and PSQI (−4.9 vs. −1.8 points; d = −0.87, P = 0.001); D-CBT-I also reduced subjective sleepiness (Epworth Sleepiness Scale; -3.4 vs. -1.0 points; d = -0.68, P < 0.001). At posttreatment, D-CBT-I reduced the apnea–hypopnea index (attended in-laboratory polysomnography; −6.0 vs. +2.0 events/h; d = -0.64, P = 0.019). Although transient increases in ESS occurred at weeks 2-4, no functional impairment or sleepiness-related adverse events were reported. Additional benefits were observed in metacognition and executive function. Conclusion Clinician-guided D-CBT-I improved insomnia and OSA severity, and enhanced cognitive function in COMISA patients. Trial registration Chinese Clinical Trial Registry; NO.: ChiCTR2500099854; URL: https://www.chictr.org.cn/showproj.html?proj=267457

items.title: Pragmatic trial of a self-directed intervention for weight loss in obstructive sleep apnea (POWER)
items.containerTitle: American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine
items.abstract: Rationale Self-directed lifestyle interventions may improve access to weight loss care in obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), but effectiveness in routine practice is unknown. Objective Test whether a proactively delivered self-directed lifestyle intervention improves weight and sleep-related quality of life versus usual care. Methods POWER enrolled patients with OSA and body mass index of 30-45 kg/m2, recruited from Veteran Affairs (VA) sites nationwide, and randomized participants to a self-directed intervention based on the Diabetes Prevention Program with video-based sessions, readings, and regular coaching reminders or usual care. Co-primary outcomes were change in Functional Outcomes of Sleep Questionnaire (FOSQ) and clinical weight in kilograms (kg) from baseline to 12 months post-randomization. Given two primary outcomes, we defined significance at p = 0.025. Measurements and Main Results This trial randomized 696 participants. Mean age was 56.2 years (SD 12.2), with 19.7% identifying as female. Clinical weights at 12 months were available for 81.9% of intervention and 83.6% of control participants. Unadjusted weight declined 2.1 kg (SD 6.8) in intervention and 0.9 kg (SD 5.9) in control (adjusted between-group difference: -1.1 kg, 95%CI -2.0, -0.1; p = 0.037). FOSQ measures were available at 12 months for 78.2% of intervention and 90.5% of control participants. From baseline to 12 months, unadjusted FOSQ improved 1.4 (SD 2.7) points in intervention and 0.9 (SD 2.9) points in control (adjusted between-group difference: 0.6 points, 95%CI 0.2, 1.0; p = 0.001). Conclusion and Relevance Among participants with OSA and obesity, a self-directed lifestyle intervention did not improve weight loss and led to improvements in sleep-related quality of life that are of limited clinical importance. Trial Registration Clinicaltrials.gov NCT05104450, registered 10/19/2021

items.title: YesReCan software-based capillary refill time measurement improves reproducibility compared with clinician assessment in critically ill patients
items.abstract: Capillary refill time (CRT) is a simple marker of peripheral perfusion but suffers from limited reproducibility when assessed visually. We evaluated the performance of the YesReCan software platform for video-based CRT measurement. In this single-center observational study, 126 standardized CRT videos from 34 critically ill patients were analyzed by trained clinicians and using a semi-automated software approach. Reproducibility was assessed using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC). Agreement, measurement precision, and diagnostic performance for detecting prolonged CRT (> 3 s) were also evaluated. Semi-automated CRT demonstrated excellent reproducibility, with intra- and inter-observer ICCs of 0.945 (95% CI, 0.837–0.995) and 0.992 (95% CI, 0.985–0.997), respectively, compared with 0.640 (95% CI, 0.474–0.765) and 0.603 (95% CI, 0.428–0.736) for clinician assessment. Measurement precision was substantially improved, with a relative least significant change of 40.7% (95% CI, 11.7%–66.9%) versus 74.7% (95% CI, 56.1%–89.1%) for single measurements. Agreement with clinician assessment was moderate (CCC 0.689, 95% CI, 0.533–0.772), and discrimination for prolonged CRT was excellent (AUC 0.885, 95% CI, 0.785–0.962). Video-based CRT analysis substantially improves reproducibility and measurement precision compared with clinician assessment while maintaining excellent diagnostic performance. These findings support the potential of automated CRT measurement to standardize peripheral perfusion assessment in clinical practice and research, although external validation in larger multicenter cohorts is required before widespread implementation. Not applicable.

items.title: Feasibility and bedside visual evaluation of lymphatic dysfunction in sepsis using indocyanine green lymphography
items.abstract: Previous studies have suggested that lymphatic dysfunction contributes to organ injury during sepsis, yet clinical features of peripheral lymphatic drainage remain poorly characterized among septic patients. We performed a prospective observational cohort study enrolling adult patients fulfilling Sepsis‑3 diagnostic criteria and non‑septic critically‑ill controls. Subcutaneous indocyanine green (ICG) injection was delivered to intact upper extremities within 24 h of diagnosis. A portable laser lymphatic imager was used for image acquisition and calculation of lymphatic flow velocity. Clinical data and 28‑day survival outcomes were collected. We enrolled 47 participants, including 34 patients with sepsis (28‑day all‑cause mortality 35.3%) and 13 non‑septic controls. Lymphatic flow velocity was 0.24 cm/s (IQR, 0.14‑0.36 cm/s) in non‑septic patients, 0.08 cm/s (IQR, 0.01‑0.25 cm/s) in sepsis survivors, and 0.02 cm/s (IQR, 0.00‑0.14 cm/s) in sepsis non‑survivors; overall between‑group difference was statistically significant ( P = 0.014). Among patients with sepsis, 9 participants had zero lymphatic flow velocity, of whom 55.6% died within 28 days. The complete examination was finished within 10 min, with no hypersensitivity, local infection or other adverse events reported. Bedside ICG lymphography enables safe and rapid visual and quantitative assessment of peripheral lymphatic drainage in adults with sepsis. Reduced peripheral lymphatic flow velocity is associated with poor prognosis, which may serve as a potential prognostic biomarker for sepsis. These findings require validation in larger‑sample cohorts.

items.title: Negative-pressure ICU rooms and pulmonary aspergillosis: room conversion matters
Timing and dose do not tell the same story: a reply to Wieruszewski and Khanna
The fragility of randomized controlled trials in critical care
items.abstract: Studies conducted in the field of critical care medicine often investigate short-term binary outcomes that require large sample sizes to reach statistical power. The Fragility Index is a statistical measure of the number of events needed to convert a statistically significant difference between groups into a difference that is no longer statistically significant. This study aimed to systematically review the robustness of published randomized clinical trials (RCTs) in critical care and the methodological pitfalls that contribute to a lower Fragility Index. We used Ovid/MEDLINE and PubMed to identify all RCTs in the top ten critical care medicine journals from January 1, 2020 to May 31, 2025. Eligible studies reported a statistically significant primary binary outcome. Our search yielded 815 studies, of which 59 studies were eligible and included in the analysis. We calculated the Fragility Index, extracted other trial methodological characteristics (expected and observed event rates, attrition rates, effect sizes, and sample size), including methods used by the authors to reduce risks to internal validity. We then analyzed the relationships between these characteristics and the Fragility Index. The median Fragility Index was 6 (range, 0–73; interquartile range, 2–10). The median expected relative risk reduction was 50% (IQR, 36%-65%). 23/53 (43%) studies that reported expected event rates, achieved an event rate in the experimental arm at or above the expected rate used for planning. 28/59 (47%) studies had a Fragility Index less than or equal to the number of participants lost to follow-up. The median Fragility Index in the critical care literature has increased, but differences in outcome selection may explain this finding. The Fragility Index is a simple and conservative starting point to evaluate the robustness of the findings of a trial. In addition to threats to validity, other threats to robustness include overestimating the expected effect size during the planning phase of the trial, recruiting a sample with too few events, and suffering a high rate of attrition.

Diagnostic immunothrombosis biomarkers for distinguishing sepsis from non-septic infection at emergency department presentation: a prospective observational pilot study
items.abstract: Distinguishing sepsis from non-septic infection at emergency department (ED) presentation is a diagnostic challenge, yet existing biomarkers are almost exclusively inflammatory. Immunothrombosis, the coupling of coagulation and innate immunity, is central to the early pathogenesis of sepsis, and alterations in the enzymes governing this response are largely unexplored as diagnostic markers. We evaluated ADAMTS13 antigen, activity, and ADAMTS13 activity: antigen ratio, alongside protein C antigen, for this purpose and as additions to measures already available at triage. Prospective observational cohort study at two tertiary-care EDs with derivation ( n = 207; 98 septic, 109 non-septic infected) and validation ( n = 56; 28 septic, 28 non-septic infected) cohorts. Adults with suspected sepsis were adjudicated into three groups by two blinded independent physicians using Sepsis-3 criteria. Biomarker levels were compared by Mann-Whitney U test and diagnostic performance by receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis, with areas under the curve (AUROC) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) by the DeLong method. Incremental values beyond the baseline of Hamilton Early Warning Score and lactate was assessed via logistic regression, with optimism correction by bootstrap resampling. ADAMTS13 antigen was modestly discriminatory in derivation (AUROC 0.60, 95% CI 0.52–0.68) but did not replicate in validation (AUROC 0.49, 95% CI 0.33–0.65). ADAMTS13 activity performed best in validation (AUROC 0.68, 95% CI 0.54–0.83), significantly outperforming antigen (DeLong p = 0.03).
