At its optimal threshold, ADAMTS13 activity achieved 96.4% specificity and 39.3% sensitivity (LR + 11.00). ADAMTS13 activity and protein C antigen separated septic from non-septic infected patients ( p = 0.018 and p = 0.008). ADAMTS13 antigen and ADAMTS13 activity: antigen ratio did not ( p = 0.93 and p = 0.13). In this pilot study no single or combination biomarker improved model fit significantly beyond clinically available assessment. In our validation cohort, ADAMTS13 activity and protein C antigen distinguished septic from non-septic infected patients, indicating that the choice of assay determines whether the diagnostic signal is detected. Our discovery that these two mechanistically distinct immunothrombosis proteins separated these groups supports the pathway as a diagnostic target, although thresholds for both were derived within the validation cohort and these estimates are exploratory. Whether these markers add to early warning scores, which performed well in this population, warrants further investigation.

items.title: Advanced assisted ventilation modes for weaning from invasive mechanical ventilation in adult patients: a systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
items.abstract: Liberation from invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV) is a key objective in critically ill patients. Pressure support ventilation (PSV)is the most commonly used and may be associated with patient–ventilator asynchrony and suboptimal assistance. Advanced ventilatory modes, including neurally adjusted ventilatory assist (NAVA), proportional assist ventilation (PAV), adaptive support ventilation (ASV), and SmartCare/pressure support (SmartCare/PS), may improve patient–ventilator interaction and facilitate weaning. We performed a systematic review and network meta-analysis (NMA) comparing these modes with PSV in adult ICU patients undergoing IMV weaning. MEDLINE, Scopus, and ClinicalTrials.gov were searched from inception to March 27, 2026 (PROSPERO CRD420251268880) for parallel-group randomized controlled trials enrolling adult ICU patients undergoing IMV weaning and comparing NAVA, PAV, ASV, SmartCare/PS, and PSV. The primary outcome was weaning success. Secondary outcomes included weaning duration, IMV duration, patient–ventilator asynchrony index (AI), severe AI, 28-day ventilator-free days, reintubation, and ICU, hospital, and 28-day mortality. A frequentist random-effects NMA was performed, with treatment ranking based on P-scores. Certainty of evidence was assessed using CINeMA. Twenty-three RCTs involving 3,755 patients were included. Compared with PSV, NAVA significantly increased weaning success (RR 1.13, 95% CI 1.00–1.27), reduced weaning duration (MD − 0.58 days, 95% CI − 0.99 to − 0.18), decreased AI (MD − 7.77%) and severe asynchrony (MD 0.38), shortened IMV duration, increased ventilator-free days, and reduced hospital mortality (RR 0.59, 95% CI 0.40–0.86). PAV (RR 1.12, 95% CI 1.00–1.25), ASV (RR 1.05, 95% CI 0.87–1.26), and SmartCare/PS (RR 1.04, 95% CI 0.91–1.19) showed non-significant trends toward higher weaning success. ASV significantly shortened weaning duration (MD − 0.65 days, 95% CI − 1.06 to − 0.24) and reduced severe asynchrony. No significant differences were observed in reintubation, ICU mortality or 28-day mortality. NAVA may have improved weaning success, reduced asynchrony and hospital mortality, shortened IMV duration, increased ventilator-free days, compared with PSV. ASV reduced weaning duration and severe asynchrony. These findings suggest NAVA, and to a lesser extent ASV, as preferred weaning modes, particularly in patients at high risk of asynchrony or prolonged ventilation.

items.title: Clinical prediction models in cardiac surgery-associated acute kidney injury: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.abstract: Cardiac surgery-associated acute kidney injury (CSA-AKI) is a frequent postoperative complication associated with substantial morbidity and mortality. Clinical prediction models (CPM) may identify high-risk patients enabling targeted preventive interventions and improved outcomes. The objective of the study was to identify available CPMs for the risk of developing CSA-AKI and summarize their performance. A systematic search of studies published in Pubmed, Scopus, the Chocrane Library and Web of Science was conducted, including studies that developed or validated CPMs for CSA-AKI in adult patients undergoing cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass. Data were extracted by two independent reviewers. Summary measures of diagnostic performance were calculated when feasible using random-effects models. Calibration and sensitivity analyses were also performed. The pooled incidence of CSA-AKI was 26.3% (95% CI, 26.0-26.4), whereas CSA-AKI requiring renal replacement therapy (CSA-AKI RRT) occurred in 2.2% of patients (95% CI, 2.1–2.2). Among validated CPMs, Thakar 2005 demonstrated the best predictive performance for CSA-AKI RRT: pooled AUC 0.80 (95% CI, 0.77–0.82), sensitivity of 0.87, and a specificity of 0.49 at a threshold of ≥ 3 points. Calibration analyses indicated underestimation of risk. The Mehta 2006 and Wijeysundera 2007 models also demonstrated good discrimination. Discrimination for the prediction of milder stages of CSA-AKI was poorer, but newer models such as the Demirjian 2022 model showed promising performance. Accurate and well-validated CPMs can facilitate risk stratification for CSA-AKI which can influence clinical practice and research. Thakar 2005 demonstrated very good discrimination for predicting CSA-AKI RRT, whereas more validation studies for the prediction of milder stages of CSA-AKI are warranted. Cardiac surgery-associated acute kidney injury is common, and clinical prediction models may improve risk stratification and support future clinical research. This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated validated CPMs and pooled their diagnostic performance. Thakar 2005 had the most extensive validation and demonstrated good discrimination for CSA-AKI requiring renal replacement therapy, whereas newer CPMs targeting milder stages show promising discriminatory performance but remain supported by limited validation evidence.

items.title: Weeks alive and out of hospital among adult ECMO survivors: a multicentre registry-based study
items.abstract: To describe the one-year clinical trajectories and healthcare utilisation of adult patients receiving extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO). Retrospective, multicentre, population-based cohort study, including adult patients (≥ 18 years) who received venovenous (VV-) ECMO, venoarterial (VA-) ECMO, or extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (eCPR) in public hospitals in Hong Kong between January 2010 and August 2024. Patients were followed for one year from ECMO initiation. The primary outcome was time alive and out of hospital. A total of 1,617 patients (635 VV-ECMO, 616 VA-ECMO, 366 eCPR) were included. The median (interquartile range [IQR]) age was 56 (45–64) years. Survival to hospital discharge varied by ECMO modality: 66.5% for VV-ECMO, 46.9% for VA-ECMO, and 28.1% for eCPR. Notably, survival was sustained after hospital discharge across ECMO modalities, with one-year survival rates of 64.6%, 45.1%, and 27.3%, respectively. Among the 814 hospital survivors, the median (IQR) time spent alive and out of hospital in the year after ECMO initiation was 45.3 (38.7–48.3) weeks (VV-ECMO), 45.4 (39.1–48.4) weeks (VA-ECMO), and 46.3 (37.7–48.7) weeks (eCPR). However, among hospital survivors, 29.5% had at least one unplanned readmission, and patients attended a median (IQR) of 13 (7–23) outpatient clinic visits during the one-year follow-up period. Patients who received ECMO and who survived to hospital discharge had reasonable one-year survival. Despite a median of > 45 weeks spent alive and out of hospital, this was accompanied by a significant ongoing healthcare burden, highlighting the need for robust ECMO survivorship care.

items.title: Unsupervised clustering to classify patients with candidemia in intensive care: algorithmic tautology or the generation of highly anticipated new data?
items.limitations: We have already acknowledged the limitations of our study, including its retrospective design and the absence of external validation. However, this analysis demonstrates that our phenotypes are not merely a statistical artifact of SAPS II weighting but reflect genuine patient heterogeneity. The observation that excluding SAPS II increases heterogeneity within the catheter-related cluster (through merging with cirrhotic patients) and obscures clinically meaningful differences in mortality supports the validity of our original phenotypes.We agree with Yang and Zhang that future studies should explore clustering without composite severity scores to identify more granular, biology-driven endotypes, and that transcriptomic, proteomic, or metabolomic biomarkers would enrich phenotype characterization.However, we maintain that illness severity is an intrinsic component of the clinical presentation in critical care and should not be dismissed as a “bias” when the goal is to characterize the entire clinical syndrome. We propose a pragmatic compromise: future studies could be performed with two-layer clustering: a first clustering on biological and microbiological variables (excluding severity scores) to identify disease-specific signatures, and a second clustering to stratify these clusters by severity. We believe that our framework constitutes a meaningful step toward precision medicine in the context of candidemia in the ICU.

items.title: Rethinking diaphragmatic ultrasound for AECOPD weaning prediction: considerations on parameter selection, thresholds, and outcome definitions
items.limitations: Although a WIND-stratified analysis is not feasible within the present dataset, we suggest explicitly stating this interpretive limitation in the discussion: the pooled sensitivity and specificity reflect a broad outcome that mixes several weaning trajectories rather than a specific weaning phenotype. Second, DCV was evaluated in only four cohorts and was not entered into meta-regression; D-RSBI, with eight cohorts, likewise offers limited statistical power. With such small samples, a negative meta-regression result for the reference-standard covariate should be interpreted as an absence of evidence rather than evidence of absence. Third, the authors did not perform a stratified subgroup or sensitivity analysis by reference-standard type (SBT failure versus post-extubation reintubation/NIV). We understand that “weaning-failure definition” was entered as a covariate in meta-regression.

items.title: Early adequate empiric antifungal therapy and 28-day mortality in ICU patients with candidemia: a pooled patient-level analysis of EUROBACT-1 and EUROBACT-2 cohorts
items.abstract: Background The optimal timing of empiric antifungal therapy in patients with suspected candidemia remains uncertain. In practice, many antifungal treatments initiated empirically are eventually found to be unnecessary, exposing patients to potential toxicity, selection of non- albicans Candida species, emergence of resistance, and additional costs. The objective of the study was to evaluate whether adequate empiric antifungal therapy initiated within 2 days after blood culture draw was associated with 28-day mortality. Methods We performed a pooled secondary analysis of two prospective worldwide observational cohorts (EUROBACT-1 and EUROBACT-2) including adult patients with Candida bloodstream infection. The exposure was defined as receipt of adequate antifungal therapy within 2 days after blood culture draw. Propensity scores for receiving early adequate antifungal therapy were estimated using prespecified covariates, and inverse probability of treatment weights were applied in a weighted Cox proportional hazards model to assess the association with 28-day mortality. Prespecified subgroup analyses were conducted according to study cohort, Candida species, and presence of hypotension at the time of bloodstream infection. As a sensitivity analysis, a frailty Cox proportional hazards model including a random center effect was performed. Results The final study population included 272 patients with candidemia from 158 centers, including 81 from EUROBACT-1 and 191 from EUROBACT-2. One hundred and ten patients received early adequate antifungal therapy and 162 did not. Overall, 38.6% of patients (105/272) died within 28 days, including 40.9% (45/110) in the early adequate therapy group and 37.0% (60/162) in the non-early adequate therapy group. In the weighted Cox model, early adequate antifungal therapy was not significantly associated with 28-day mortality (HR 1.23, 95% CI 0.82–1.83, p = 0.314). Results were consistent across subgroup analyses according to study cohort, Candida species, the presence of hypotension at the time of bloodstream infection, as well as in the frailty Cox sensitivity analysis. Conclusions Early adequate antifungal therapy was not independently associated with improved 28-day survival in ICU patients with candidemia. These findings support a more targeted approach to early empirical antifungal treatment and underscore the need to identify patient subgroups most likely to benefit from immediate therapy.

items.title: Decision volume and temporal workload structure as dissociable correlates of fatigue and mood in intensive care physicians: a real-time observational study
items.abstract: Background Intensive care physicians make hundreds of decisions per shift under sustained cognitive and emotional demands. Decision fatigue, the tendency towards less effortful choices as cumulative decision load increases, may affect clinician wellbeing and decision processes. However, the associations of decision volume and temporal workload structure with within-shift fatigue and mood in intensive care unit (ICU) physicians remain unclear. This study explored whether decision volume and temporal clustering show distinct associations with fatigue, sleepiness, mood, and post-shift decision responses. Methods Five physicians (two residents, three consultants) at a surgical ICU of a German university hospital were shadowed during 38 twelve-hour shifts (456 hours) between October and December 2025. Clinical decisions were classified by severity using a study-specific, non-validated Decision Severity Score. Because recruitment was feasibility-based and involved only five physicians, all analyses were considered exploratory and hypothesis-generating. Psychometric assessments of decision fatigue, sleepiness, and mood (Decision Fatigue Scale, Karolinska Sleepiness Scale, Profile of Mood States – Short Form) were administered at morning, midday, and shift end. Following each shift, physicians completed a standardised scenario task requiring three binary treatment decisions. Temporal workload structure was quantified using the burstiness metric; shifts were classified into four types by median split of decision density and burstiness (quiet-smooth, quiet-clustered, busy-smooth, busy-clustered). Linear and binomial mixed-effects models with physician as random intercept were used throughout. Results Across 17,953 recorded decisions (median 474 per shift; range 366–589), a higher mean decision rate was associated with greater end-of-shift decision fatigue: an increase of 0.5 decisions per 5-minute interval corresponded to a 2.1-point higher decision-fatigue score (95 % CI 0.6 to 3.6). Higher burstiness was associated with less mood disturbance, with a 0.10 increase in burstiness corresponding to a 6.3-point lower mood score (95% CI −10.2 to −2.3). Averaged across all shifts, changes between morning and evening were small and not statistically significant for any of the three scores. Within-shift trajectories differed by shift type, however, with mood disturbance increasing over the shift in quiet-smooth shifts only, a difference already apparent at midday. Quiet-smooth shifts, the least objectively demanding, showed the least favourable psychometric values. Response certainty in the post-shift scenario task was lower after shifts with more task interruptions, with each ten additional interruptions corresponding to a 0.29-point lower certainty score (p = 0.012), whilst a descriptive trend towards more conservative scenario responses was observed in busy-clustered shifts (odds ratio 2.25, p = 0.555). Conclusions Decision volume and temporal workload structure showed different associations with psychometric outcomes: higher decision rates were associated with greater end-of-shift decision fatigue, whereas greater temporal clustering was associated with lower mood disturbance, already apparent from midday onwards. That more quiet, uniformly paced shifts showed the least favourable psychometric values suggests that reducing decision volume alone may not improve physician wellbeing; this observation requires replication. Mitigation strategies may therefore need to extend beyond reducing decision volume to protecting concentrated, meaningful clinical activity and minimising hindrance stressors such as interruptions. Future multicentre studies should determine whether these associations are reproducible and whether temporal workload structure is related to objective decision quality or patient-safety outcomes. Trial registration German Clinical Trials Register, DRKS00037564. Registered 27th August 2025.
items.limitations: Our study has several limitations. Only five physicians contributed data, and high intraclass correlations indicate that stable between-physician differences dominated the variance, leaving low power at the shift level. The single-centre design and direct recruitment limit generalisability and introduce volunteer bias, and observer presence may have influenced behaviour. The Decision Severity Score was developed de novo, was not externally validated, and incorporates physician experience, rendering score-based analyses exploratory; experience levels were not compared inferentially. The median-based shift types formed small, unevenly distributed subgroups, and the mood-score advantage of busy over quiet-smooth shifts did not survive a rank-based sensitivity analysis.

items.title: Validating the 2025 ERC/ESICM neuroprognostication algorithm using a restricted predictor set in a minimal WLST cohort
items.abstract: Background The 2021 European Resuscitation Council (ERC)/European Society of Intensive Care Medicine (ESICM) neuroprognostication guidelines were highly specific but limited by strict entry criteria (Glasgow Coma Scale-Motor [GCS-M] ≤ 3), leaving nearly half of patients with an “indeterminate” prognosis. The updated 2025 guidelines introduced an expanded entry (GCS-M < 6) and a two-tiered sequential algorithm integrating favorable and unfavorable criteria to resolve this clinical uncertainty. This study validated the real-world performance of the 2025 algorithm using a pragmatic, restricted core predictor set in a cohort with a low frequency of withdrawal of life-sustaining therapy (WLST). Methods This retrospective observational study included adult comatose out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) survivors treated with targeted temperature management who remained unconscious (GCS-M < 6) at 72 h between 2020 and 2025. Six-month functional outcomes were categorized using the modified Rankin Scale (poor: 4–6). The 2025 algorithm was applied using four unfavorable predictors (absent pupillary/corneal reflexes, status myoclonus, neuron-specific enolase [NSE] > 60 µg/L, gray-to-white matter ratio on brain computed tomography ≤ 1.10 via automated software) and two favorable predictors (GCS-M 4–5 on day 4, NSE ≤ 17 µg/L). Results Among 400 OHCA survivors, 129 were excluded due to early awakening ( n = 90) or death within 72 h ( n = 39). Of the 271 included patients, 233 (86.0%) had poor outcomes, and the withdrawal of life-sustaining therapy rate was low (5.5%). The integrated 2025 algorithm predicted poor outcomes with 76.2% sensitivity (95% CI, 68.4–82.9), 97.1% specificity (95% CI, 85.1–99.9), a 99.1% positive predictive value (95% CI, 95.0–100.0), and a 50.0% negative predictive value (95% CI, 37.6–62.4). Step 2 favorable criteria reclassified 48.9% (68/139) of patients who remained unclassified after Step 1, reducing the unclassified proportion from 55.8% (139/249) to a final indeterminate rate of 28.5% (71/249). Among patients with indeterminate outcomes, 97.2% (69/71) ultimately had poor outcomes. Among 22 patients with discordant favorable and unfavorable predictors, 6 (27.3%) had good outcomes. Conclusions In a cohort with a low frequency of WLST, the 2025 ERC/ESICM algorithm maintained high specificity, while Step 2 substantially reduced the proportion of unclassified patients. However, the restricted predictor set may have limited sensitivity and contributed to persistent indeterminate classifications.

items.title: When pupillometry indices disagree: does QPi add prognostic information beyond NPi?
Distinct serum cholesterol and lipoprotein signatures in sepsis and major elective surgery: a lipid-focused NMR study
items.abstract: Background Low circulating cholesterol is a recognised feature of sepsis, but whether the serum lipid signature of sepsis differs from that of sterile (non-infectious) inflammation is unclear. Methods Targeted serum proton nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) metabolomics (250 metabolites) was used to compare 34 patients with sepsis, 21 patients before and after major elective surgery, and 89 healthy controls. Results Compared with healthy controls, 199 metabolites differed in sepsis and 150 after surgery. 127 changes were common to both states, 23 specific to surgery and 72 to sepsis. Both states lowered total, LDL and HDL cholesterol, cholesteryl esters, phospholipids and several fatty acids. Surgery alone reduced apolipoprotein B, remnant cholesterol and LDL particle number, whereas triglyceride-rich VLDL and the inflammatory marker GlycA were higher in sepsis only. Triglyceride-rich lipoproteins fell after surgery but rose in sepsis, and the sepsis-specific signature was dominated by a coordinated rise across the VLDL subclasses with a fall across the large HDL subclasses. No metabolite distinguished sepsis survivors from non-survivors. Conclusions Low cholesterol was common to both post-operative and septic states, whereas a rise in triglyceride-rich VLDL was detected in sepsis but not after surgery. These exploratory differences require confirmation in matched cohorts, and illustrate how lipid-focused NMR spectroscopy can provide a detailed analysis of cholesterol and lipoprotein signatures in critical illness.

items.title: Towards personalised protein prescription in critically ill patients during metabolic stress and recovery: a narrative review and proposed future research directions
items.abstract: Protein provision in critically ill patients has traditionally been guided by population-based, body weight-derived targets and the assumption that higher delivery may attenuate catabolism, muscle wasting and functional decline. Recent large, randomised trials comparing higher versus lower protein delivery have not demonstrated benefit on their primary patient-centred outcomes. Renal subgroup analyses have raised additional safety concerns, but these findings do not establish that patients without acute kidney injury (AKI) benefit from higher protein exposure. This narrative review critically appraises randomised trials, systematic reviews and meta-analyses, together with selected mechanistic and non-randomised evidence, and proposes future research directions for personalised protein prescription throughout critical illness and recovery. The capacity to receive and metabolically handle administered protein is unlikely to remain constant, such that protein dose should be prescribed according to metabolic phase and direction of clinical trajectory rather than intensive care unit (ICU) day alone. Conventional weight-based dosing may be imprecise because patients with similar body weight can differ substantially in fat-free mass, skeletal muscle mass and adiposity. Computed tomography (CT), muscle ultrasound and bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA) may identify low muscularity or structural change, but require careful interpretation because of limitations related to timing, fluid status, methodology and measurement variability; none has been validated to determine an individual protein requirement. Monitoring should distinguish prescribed protein targets, actual protein delivery, gastrointestinal capacity to receive enteral nutrition, organ constraints and metabolic response. Personalised protein prescription should not be regarded as an alternative to evidence generated by adequately designed randomised controlled trials (RCTs). Future research should prioritise phase-specific and phenotype-enriched RCTs, prospective testing of body-composition- and response-informed strategies, and outcomes reflecting muscle health, physical function, independence and quality of life while appropriately accounting for death. A phase-, phenotype- and response-informed approach is biologically plausible and testable but is not yet a validated dosing algorithm.

items.title: Hydroxyethyl starch for prehospital fluid resuscitation: results of two helicopter emergency medical service operators in Germany
Prone positioning redirects exhaled aerosol and changes bedside staff exposure during respiratory support
Modulating metabolism to mitigate reperfusion injury induced by resuscitation from cardiac arrest: a narrative review
items.abstract: Cardiac arrest remains a leading cause of mortality and morbidity. Overall survival rates remain below 10%, with many survivors suffering from persistent neurological and cognitive impairment. A major contributor to these poor outcomes is reperfusion injury resulting from the necessary restoration of a spontaneous circulation. This restoration triggers a further cascade of metabolic disturbances and tissue injury, predominantly driven by an abrupt surge in reactive oxygen species production. Metabolic modulation offers a promising avenue to limit secondary injury by mitigating reperfusion injury. Strategies include suppression of metabolic demand such as hypothermic temperature control and mitochondrial electron chain inhibition, mitochondrial-targeted antioxidant therapies, and administration of specific energy substrates during the critical early post-resuscitation period. While laboratory studies have demonstrated encouraging results, translation into routine clinical practice has been hindered by a lack of positive outcomes from controlled trials. This reflects challenges in prompt delivery of the strategy, identifying effective therapeutic windows and optimising dosing regimens. This review describes strategies employed to mitigate reperfusion injury after cardiac arrest, their mechanisms of action, outcomes in non-clinical models, the limited human data available to date, and challenges in trial design.

items.title: Much of the excess mortality in immunocompromised patients with viral severe acute respiratory infection occurs after ICU discharge
Response to: “MAPSE in critical illness: from prognostic association to clinical utility”
72-hour hemodynamic and urine output trajectories predict renal recovery in continuous kidney replacement therapy: a machine learning approach
items.abstract: Abstract Background: Predicting renal recovery in patients receiving continuous kidney replacement therapy (CKRT) remains challenging. Conventional single-time-point hemodynamic assessments at CKRT initiation have shown limited prognostic value. We investigated whether 72-hour hemodynamic and urine output (UO) trajectories, analyzed through machine learning, could improve prediction of 28-day renal recovery. Methods: This single-center retrospective cohort study included 331 CKRT episodes (318 patients). Renal recovery was defined as successful CKRT discontinuation with no kidney replacement therapy for at least 72 hours within 28 days of initiation. Phase 1 employed Cox proportional hazards regression to evaluate day-0 variables. Phase 2 developed machine learning models (logistic regression, XGBoost, bidirectional LSTM) using 105 engineered features from 72-hour MAP, SBP, DBP, heart rate (HR), and UO time-series data. Model performance was assessed using 5-fold stratified cross-validation with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals. SHAP analysis was used for model interpretability. Results: Of 331 episodes, 71 (21.5%) achieved renal recovery. In Phase 1, day-0 UO was non-significant in both univariable (HR=1.010 per 100 mL/day; p=0.146) and multivariable Cox regression (HR=1.003 per 100 mL/day; p=0.703), even when forced into a model with clinically important covariates. The multivariable model (C-index=0.768) identified CCI (HR=0.749; p<0.001) and SOFA (HR=0.805; p<0.001) as the strongest independent predictors. In Phase 2, incorporating 72-hour trajectories significantly improved prediction: XGBoost Combined (day-0 + 72h features) achieved an AUC of 0.848 (95% CI, 0.765–0.890), compared with 0.762 for baseline-only XGBoost (AUC difference=+0.086, DeLong p=0.035). SHAP analysis revealed late-phase (36–72h) UO variability (UO_late_std) as the dominant predictor (mean |SHAP|=1.311), exceeding the second-ranked feature by four-fold. The 72-hour UO trajectory features occupied two of the top three positions in feature importance. Conclusions: Day-0 hemodynamic variables fail to predict renal recovery in CKRT patients when assessed as single-time-point measurements. However, 72-hour trajectories—particularly late-phase UO variability—are powerful predictors when captured through machine learning. These findings support integrating temporal hemodynamic patterns into clinical decision-making for CKRT patients.

items.title: Temporal dissociation of physiological adaptations during speaking valve training in tracheostomized patients: a wearable device-based study
items.abstract: Background Speaking valve (SV) training facilitates communication and ventilator weaning for tracheostomized patients, yet the dynamic, multi-system physiological responses and their temporal trajectories remain poorly characterized. This study aims to comprehensively evaluate the cardiopulmonary adaptations during and following SV training using wearable sensing technology. Methods A prospective observational study was conducted on 120 tracheostomized patients. Continuous physiological monitoring was performed using a wearable sensor across three phases: baseline (T0), SV intervention (T1), and recovery (T2). A multidimensional panel of 86 parameters was extracted across four domains: macro vital signs, respiratory cycle structure, respiratory complexity, and heart rate variability (HRV). Results SV training was well-tolerated, with no participants meeting predefined safety stopping criteria. Analysis revealed a distinct temporal decoupling in physiological responses—that is, respiratory mechanical and autonomic adaptations occurred immediately during valve use, whereas oxygenation improvements emerged only after valve removal. During the intervention (T1 vs. T0), patients exhibited immediate respiratory mechanical adaptation and significantly enhanced respiratory complexity (increased multiscale entropy at scales1–5; adjusted p < 0.05), reflecting active neural compensatory regulation by the respiratory controller. This was accompanied by acute cardiovascular stress, evidenced by vagal withdrawal (decreased RMSSD, HF power, and total power). However, oxygenation metrics remained unchanged during T1. Notably, significant improvements in oxygenation (increased minimum SpO₂ and reduced desaturation burden) emerged exclusively during the recovery phase (T2 vs. T0; adjusted p < 0.05). Furthermore, autonomic recovery was delayed: the LF/HF ratio rose significantly from training to recovery ( p = 0.02), indicating persistent sympathetic predominance after valve removal. Conclusions SV training triggers an immediate respiratory regulation response and acute cardiovascular stress, whereas the beneficial effects on oxygenation manifest as a delayed phenomenon during recovery. This temporal decoupling underscores the necessity of incorporating monitored recovery periods into SV clinical protocols and highlights the value of multidimensional wearable monitoring in revealing covert physiological dynamics in critically ill patients.

items.title: Acute exacerbation of systemic autoimmune rheumatic disease-associated interstitial lung disease: integrated pathophysiology and respiratory care
items.abstract: Acute exacerbation of systemic autoimmune rheumatic disease-associated interstitial lung disease (AE-SARD-ILD) is an uncommon but severe cause of acute respiratory failure, frequently requiring intensive care. Although commonly managed according to paradigms derived from acute exacerbation of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis or acute respiratory distress syndrome, AE-SARD-ILD encompasses heterogeneous pathological processes with distinct respiratory mechanics, pulmonary vascular involvement, reversibility, and treatment response. Management based solely on the underlying rheumatic disease or radiological pattern may therefore be inadequate. This Perspective reviews current evidence on the diagnosis and critical care management of AE-SARD-ILD and proposes an integrated clinical–radiological–mechanical framework for physiology-guided decision-making. Moving beyond conventional disease- and imaging-based fibrotic classifications, the framework identifies four dominant, potentially overlapping physiological phenotypes arising from the interaction between the chronic pulmonary substrate and the superimposed acute insult: fibrotic/UIP-like, inflammatory/ARDS-like, pulmonary hypertension-dominant, and diffuse alveolar haemorrhage-dominant. These phenotypes provide a physiological rationale for selecting, titrating, and escalating non-invasive and invasive respiratory support, controlling excessive respiratory drive, and integrating immunomodulatory, pulmonary vascular, and extracorporeal strategies. Although prospective validation is required, physiological phenotype-based assessment may support individualized respiratory management, dynamic prognostication, and time-limited intensive care trials in AE-SARD-ILD.

items.title: Answer to: “Left ventricular longitudinal function and hyperkinetic profile: a new echo world to explore?”
From equipment availability to effective organ support: critical care capacity and capability for the future of intensive care
items.abstract: Intensive care unit (ICU) bed and equipment counts describe installed resources but can overstate the support available to patients. Reliable organ support also requires infrastructure, staff, supplies, maintenance and clinical coordination. This Perspective defines effective organ-support capacity as the amount of clinically appropriate support a service can reliably deliver over a specified period, given its clinical capability and available resources. It distinguishes capacity from readiness, capability, observed quality of care and the contextual conditions influencing access and delivery. Five features describe this capacity: it is dynamic, multidisciplinary, longitudinal, context-sensitive and outcome-oriented. Six enabling conditions support organ-support delivery, including staffing, monitoring, governance and continuity. The framework is intended primarily for facility teams undertaking quality improvement and operational planning. Candidate indicators are linked to published measurement precedents, with explicit separation of established measures from proposed extensions. A hypothetical ventilation example illustrates data collection, interpretation and action. A staged validation agenda addresses feasibility, reliability, validity and the risks of premature comparison. Reporting deliverable organ support alongside equipment inventories could improve critical care planning. The framework remains a conceptual proposal; its indicators require testing before accreditation or comparisons between services.

items.title: GDF15 and risk heterogeneity within the hypoinflammatory phenotype
Preserved anabolic skeletal muscle capacity in response to exercise and protein intake after critical illness
items.abstract: Background Low muscle mass and persistent weakness are common after critical illness, but the mechanisms behind impaired recovery are incompletely understood. The aim of this study was to investigate the skeletal muscle anabolic response to combined resistance exercise and protein intake in intensive care unit (ICU) survivors, compared to matched controls without a history of critical illness. We hypothesised that residual anabolic resistance limits muscle regeneration after ICU stay. Methods Former patients were enrolled within 3 to 6 months of intensive care unit discharge. Muscle biopsies were obtained before and after resistance exercise using a flywheel leg extension ergometer, combined with ingestion of 24 g hydrolysed protein. Muscle protein fractional synthetic rate was determined from the incorporation of [ring-²H₅]phenylalanine into mixed-muscle protein during a primed continuous intravenous infusion. Anabolic and proteolytic pathways were measured using standard assays. Group-by-time differences were analysed using linear mixed models. The primary comparison was the between-group difference in pre-to-post change in muscle protein synthesis. Results Twenty ICU survivors (60 ± 12 years, 30% female, BMI 26.9 (IQR 22.9–28.7), SAPS 3 62.3 ± 15.8) and 20 age- and sex-matched controls were included. ICU survivors had significantly lower quadriceps muscle thickness ( p = 0.02) and handgrip strength ( p = 0.04) than controls. In ICU survivors, muscle protein synthesis from plasma precursor amino acids was higher at baseline than in controls (0.041%/hour vs. 0.030%/hour, p = 0.009), but increased less (Δ 0.031 vs. Δ 0.040%/hour, p = 0.04). Post-intervention muscle protein synthesis was similar between groups (0.071%/hour vs. 0.070%/hour, p = 0.70). At baseline, ICU survivors showed lower activation of the autophagy-lysosomal pathway. In both groups, the intervention increased anabolic signalling, decreased initiation of autophagy and increased parts of the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway. Conclusions In ICU survivors with persistent muscle loss and weakness, the increase in muscle protein synthesis after combined resistance exercise and protein intake was smaller than in controls, in the context of a higher baseline fractional synthetic rate. Post-intervention muscle protein synthesis rates were similar between groups. These findings provide the first mechanistic support for structured exercise-nutrition rehabilitation to promote muscle recovery after critical illness. Trial registration This study was prospectively registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05261984), 2022-02-20.
items.limitations: Several limitations should be considered. Participation in the study was time-consuming and included potentially painful procedures. Despite systematic screening, this introduced the risk of selection bias, as participants may have had unmeasured baseline physical and/or mental characteristics not representative of the target population. However, RAND-36 physical and mental component summary scores were nearly identical to those observed in a recent nationwide cohort study of ICU patients with sepsis. Differences in muscle mass and strength were also similar to those described in a one-year follow-up of critically ill patients using age-matched controls.

items.title: Extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation strategies for refractory out-of-hospital cardiac arrest
items.abstract: Background Refractory out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) is almost invariably fatal. Extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) has emerged as a feasible rescue treatment and may improve outcomes in highly selected patients. On-scene and hospital-based ECPR each have distinct strengths and limitations, but a real-world comparison of their association with survival is lacking. Methods We analysed a multicentric prospective registry of 52,505 OHCAs in the Greater Paris area (France), from May 2011 to August 2024. We quantified the association between an on-scene ECPR strategy and survival to hospital discharge with favourable neurological outcome (defined as a Cerebral Performance Category 1 or 2), compared to a hospital-based ECPR strategy, adjusting for established prognostic factors, with multivariable and propensity score methods. Results A total of 1,031 patients treated with ECPR were included (16% were female, median age 50 years). Of them, 256 patients received on-scene ECPR, with favourable neurological outcome in 13%, compared to 6% in 775 patients with hospital-based ECPR ( P < 0.01). The time from CPR to ECPR initiation was shorter with the on-scene strategy (70 min [60–84] vs. 93 min [75–113], P < 0.01). In multivariable analysis, the on-scene ECPR strategy was independently associated with favourable neurological outcome (OR, 2.3; 95% CI, 1.4–3.9; P < 0.01). These findings were consistent in propensity score–matched analyses (OR, 2.1; 95% CI, 1.1–4.1; P = 0.03). For IPTW, OR 2.3, 95%CI 1.4–3.9, P<0.01). At one year of follow-up, there was a significant association between the on-scene ECPR strategy and overall survival, (log-rank test, P < 0.01). Conclusions In this large, population-based registry of refractory OHCA, the on-scene ECPR strategy was associated with a significantly shorter time to ECPR initiation and favourable neurological outcome at hospital discharge when compared with the hospital-based ECPR strategy. These findings highlight the potential interest of an on-scene ECPR strategy in selected patients, but further investigations are warranted. Large, randomized controlled trials and studies conducted in diverse healthcare systems are needed to clarify its role more precisely, particularly regarding long-term neurological recovery, cost-effectiveness, and broader system-level impact.

items.title: Capillary refill time prolongation in sepsis and septic shock: supported and potential mechanisms from a pathophysiological perspective
items.abstract: Capillary refill time (CRT) has evolved from a bedside sign into a resuscitation target in septic shock. Although simple to measure, CRT reflects restoration of cutaneous microvascular blood flow after transient external compression and therefore integrates multiple physiological processes. This narrative review proposes a framework for understanding the principal pathophysiological mechanisms that may prolong CRT in sepsis and septic shock. Six non-mutually exclusive mechanisms are considered, broadly ordered according to the strength and directness of the supporting evidence. First, reduced effective tissue perfusion may trigger sympathetically mediated redistribution of blood flow away from the skin through precapillary vasoconstriction and closure of thermoregulatory arteriovenous shunts. Second, inadequate upstream flow generation may result from hypovolemia, ventricular dysfunction, adverse ventriculo-arterial coupling, arrhythmias, or excessive afterload. Third, inflammatory endothelial and microvascular injury may impair reactive hyperemia through glycocalyx degradation, edema, capillary derecruitment, microvascular obstruction, altered hemorheology, and flow heterogeneity. Fourth, loss of coordinated myogenic, neurogenic, and endothelial vasomotor regulation may uncouple systemic pressure from effective capillary recruitment. Fifth, severe vasoplegia may alter the arterial closing-pressure boundary and vascular-waterfall behavior, potentially increasing the pressure dependence of microvascular flow. CRT-specific observational associations support this proposal, but its causal contribution to CRT prolongation remains unproven. Sixth, elevated venous and interstitial pressures could impair microvascular perfusion; their proposed contribution to CRT prolongation remains hypothesis-generating because direct CRT-specific evidence is lacking. These mechanisms may coexist, with their relative contributions varying according to hemodynamic phenotype, disease severity, treatment, and timing of assessment. CRT should therefore be interpreted dynamically and integrated with preload responsiveness, cardiac output, arterial pressure, vasopressor exposure, skin temperature, mottling, venous congestion, and complementary perfusion markers. Responses to controlled hemodynamic interventions may help characterize peripheral perfusion responsiveness, although they cannot, by themselves, establish the underlying mechanism. This framework supports contextual interpretation of CRT and generates testable hypotheses about its prolongation, while distinguishing established physiology and observational associations from unproven causal mechanisms.

items.title: Interpreting weaning success and ventilation duration in PRiVENT
Selective coronary hypoxemia during VA-ECMO: limitations of peripheral oxygenation monitoring
items.abstract: Differential hypoxemia during peripheral veno-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) is fundamentally a spatial, not merely temporal, monitoring problem. When native left ventricular ejection coexists with severely impaired pulmonary gas exchange, poorly oxygenated blood may preferentially occupy the aortic root, the most proximal arterial territory, while oxygenated extracorporeal blood returning from a femoral cannula may supply more distal territories. This possibility is not new. Previous computational, experimental, and clinical observations have demonstrated the potential for inadequate myocardial or aortic-root oxygenation during VA-ECMO [ 1 , 2 , 3 ], and contemporary nomenclature of dual circulation has emphasized the limitations of peripheral measurements in defining oxygenation across vascular territories [ 4 ]. Our contribution is therefore not to define a new syndrome, but to frame selective coronary hypoxemia as a clinically relevant monitoring blind spot and to propose an exploratory physiological framework for its recognition and investigation. Importantly, reduced coronary arterial oxygenation, reduced myocardial oxygen delivery, and myocardial ischemia are related but distinct phenomena: myocardial oxygen delivery also depends on coronary blood flow and hemoglobin concentration, whereas ischemia reflects the balance between oxygen supply and myocardial demand.
items.limitations: Previous computational, experimental, and clinical observations have demonstrated the potential for inadequate myocardial or aortic-root oxygenation during VA-ECMO, and contemporary nomenclature of dual circulation has emphasized the limitations of peripheral measurements in defining oxygenation across vascular territories. Our contribution is therefore not to define a new syndrome, but to frame selective coronary hypoxemia as a clinically relevant monitoring blind spot and to propose an exploratory physiological framework for its recognition and investigation. Importantly, reduced coronary arterial oxygenation, reduced myocardial oxygen delivery, and myocardial ischemia are related but distinct phenomena: myocardial oxygen delivery also depends on coronary blood flow and hemoglobin concentration, whereas ischemia reflects the balance between oxygen supply and myocardial demand. Each monitoring modality interrogates a specific anatomical or vascular compartment. Cerebral NIRS reflects regional cerebral tissue oxygenation, whereas radial NIRS has been investigated as a non-invasive approach to detecting differential upper-body oxygenation during VA-ECMO. Increasing sampling frequency improves temporal surveillance but cannot correct this spatial limitation. The risk may increase during myocardial recovery. As native ejection rises, the mixing zone may migrate distally while severely impaired pulmonary gas exchange persists. Although coronary perfusion occurs predominantly in diastole, the oxygen content of coronary arterial blood depends on the blood occupying the aortic root. Thus, as native ejection increases, oxygenated extracorporeal blood may be progressively displaced from the proximal aorta while pulmonary gas exchange remains impaired. Selective coronary hypoxemia highlights an important limitation of peripheral oxygenation monitoring during VA-ECMO: satisfactory oxygenation at sampled systemic sites does not necessarily establish adequate oxygenation of blood reaching the coronary ostia. This distinction is particularly relevant when native ejection increases while pulmonary gas exchange remains severely impaired. However, coronary arterial hypoxemia should not be equated with myocardial ischemia, which depends on the broader balance between myocardial oxygen supply and demand. ScsO₂ may provide an exploratory physiological signal of this balance, but its relationship with coronary arterial oxygenation requires mechanistic validation before it can be considered a diagnostic tool. The clinical challenge is therefore not only how frequently oxygenation is measured, but whether the sampled vascular territory adequately represents the organ at risk.

items.title: Assessment of creatinine production rate as a predictive biomarker to individualize nutrition in the ICU: a secondary analysis of the EPaNIC-RCT
items.abstract: The creatinine-production-rate (CPR) was suggested as integrative indicator of muscle-status, which may identify patients upon intensive-care-unit (ICU) admission benefiting from certain treatments. Initiating supplemental parenteral nutrition early to reach caloric targets (early-PN) harmed ICU-patients as compared with omitting PN for one week (late-PN). We investigated whether CPR can identify patient subgroups who could benefit from early-PN. In this EPaNIC-RCT ( n = 4640) secondary analysis, we studied the impact of early-PN vs. late-PN on CPR and body-size-corrected CPR-index profiles from ICU-day 2–14, excluding patients on renal-replacement-therapy. We investigated whether day-2 CPR or CPR-index statistically interacted with the randomized intervention for impact on duration of mechanical-ventilation as surrogate for muscle-weakness, adjusting for baseline risk factors. Finally, impact of early-PN vs. late-PN was assessed in patients with high (> mean) or low (≤ mean) day-2 CPR or CPR-index. Significance was set at P < 0.05, except for interaction- P < 0.1. Day-2 CPR was available for 1322 early-PN and 1382 late-PN patients. Early-PN patients had a higher CPR and CPR-index than late-PN patients from day 4–11. Day-2 CPR ( P = 0.067) and CPR-index ( P = 0.058) interacted with randomization for impact on mechanical-ventilation. A lower likelihood of earlier live ventilator-weaning was observed with early-PN vs. late-PN in patients with high CPR (adjusted-hazard-ratio 0.871 (0.778–0.981), P = 0.022) or CPR-index (0.858 (0.764–0.963), P = 0.0095), unlike in patients with low CPR ( P = 0.60) or CPR-index ( P = 0.73). Early-PN affected CPR and CPR-index profiles in the former group only. The day-2 CPR and CPR-index did not identify ICU-patients who could benefit from intensive nutritional therapy with early-PN. ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00512122, registered July 31, 2007.

items.title: Development and evaluation of a blood transfusion prediction algorithm tailored for precision and utility in civilian and military trauma patients
items.abstract: Early decisions regarding blood transfusion in trauma are time-critical and made under substantial uncertainty. Existing prediction models typically classify patients using fixed thresholds and do not estimate the volume or timing of transfusion. This limits their utility for real-time clinical decision-making and resource planning. We developed and validated a Bayesian network model, informed by domain knowledge and clinical data, to predict transfusion requirements in trauma using injury and physiological variables available early after injury. The model estimates transfusion volume across multiple timeframes (2, 6, 12, and 24 h). It was developed using data from a prospective civilian cohort and military trauma registries ( n = 2361) and evaluated using internal cross-validation and external validation in an independent dataset ( n = 13,347). The model achieved AUROC values of 0·82–0·94 for binary outcomes across timeframes. For ordinal volume predictions, Ranked Probability Scores were 0·07 for 0–12 h predictions and 0·04 for 12–24 h predictions. In scenario-based evaluation, agreement with model predictions was observed in 213 of 225 (95%) expert assessments. Prediction models based on binary thresholds may have limited impact on clinical decision-making despite good performance. A decision-support approach that estimates transfusion requirements by volume and timing, using early-available clinical data, may provide more clinically useful decision support in trauma care.

items.title: The tyranny of a number: why a pressure reading cannot carry the weight of the injured brain
Discordance between pupillometry indices: a matter of scale and sedation
items.limitations: The within-patient analysis of discordant episodes proposed by Dr Xu is attractive, but our dataset has two limitations that would make its results difficult to interpret. Resting pupil diameter was not recorded in brain-injured patients, and sedation depth and cumulative drug doses were not collected with enough precision to be used as covariates. Without these variables, a discordant episode attributable to miosis cannot be distinguished from one attributable to neurological dysfunction, which is precisely the question at stake. In addition, because abnormal NPi values were rare, almost all abnormal QPi measurements fell into the discordant category, so such an analysis would largely reproduce the QPi model already reported. Finally, testing the incremental value of the QPi would require both indices, sedation exposure and pupil size in the same model, which our number of outcome events does not allow without a substantial risk of overfitting.

items.title: Long-term outcomes of sepsis survivors in Indian sepsis registry: the LOSS study
Association of inter-clinician diagnostic disagreement with increased mortality among patients with septic shock: a retrospective cohort study
items.abstract: Background Septic shock mortality remains high despite dissemination of Surviving Sepsis Campaign guidelines. These guidelines recommend early treatment with antibiotics, fluids, and vasopressors. A prerequisite for early treatment is early identification of sepsis as the shock etiology. We hypothesized that early disagreement between clinical teams regarding shock etiology would be associated with treatment delays and increased mortality among septic shock patients. Therefore, we aimed to quantify the association between inter-clinician disagreement regarding shock etiology and mortality in septic shock patients, and to determine whether delays in septic shock treatment mediate this relationship. Methods Multicenter, retrospective cohort study of 2,233 septic shock patients meeting Sepsis-3 organ-dysfunction criteria across eight acute care hospitals (2018–2023). Shock etiologies documented by clinicians within the first 48 ICU hours were identified using regular expressions and compared using Cosine Similarity Scores. Disagreement was defined as a score < 1. An inverse-probability-of-treatment-weighted multivariable logistic regression tested the association between disagreement and mortality adjusting for demographics, comorbidities, SOFA score, blood culture positivity, and ICU specialty. Multivariable Fine-Gray models assessed whether disagreement affected administration of antibiotics, bolus fluids, or vasopressors. Mediation analysis assessed whether differences in time to antibiotics, bolus fluids, or vasopressors explained any relationship between disagreement and mortality. Results Two hundred and thirteen patients (9.5%) had inter-clinician disagreement on shock etiology. Disagreement was present for 13.3% of patients at the academic medical center and 7.2% at community sites ( p < 0.001). Effect modification of the association between disagreement and mortality by blood culture positivity was significant (OR 2.37, 95% CI 1.03–5.45, p = 0.042), with a stratified 1.99-fold increased adjusted odds of ICU mortality in positive blood culture patients (95% CI 0.98–4.01, p = 0.056; linear-probability delta-risk + 16.9% points, 95% CI + 1.1 to + 32.7, p = 0.036). Notably, disagreement was not associated with different rates of antibiotic, fluid, or vasopressor administration in the blood culture-positive subgroup. Disagreement-associated mortality was not mediated by time to antibiotics, fluids, or vasopressors in the subgroup. Conclusion Early inter-clinician disagreement on shock etiology is a prognostic marker of increased ICU mortality among Sepsis-3 septic shock patients with positive blood cultures. The association is not mediated by timing of antibiotics, fluid boluses, or vasopressors.

items.title: Recalibrating the urine output criteria for acute kidney injury: stage-specific thresholds matched to creatinine-stage-derived mortality
Association between human serum albumin for fluid resuscitation and acute kidney injury in intensive care: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.abstract: Fluid resuscitation is frequently used in intensive care unit (ICU). However, impact of human serum albumin on acute kidney injury (AKI) remains uncertain. We therefore conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) to assess whether albumin resuscitation has an incidence on AKI in critically ill patients. MEDLINE, EMBASE, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials and clinical trial registries were systematically searched from January 2004 to April 30, 2026 for RCTs assessing albumin as a resuscitation fluid in critically ill patients. The primary outcome was the occurrence of AKI. Two reviewers independently identified trials, extracted data and assessed risk of bias. Random-effects meta-analyses were conducted to calculate risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). We used the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) to assess the quality of evidence. Trial sequency analysis (TSA) was performed to assess the robustness of evidence. Nine RCTs including 11,778 patients were selected. Albumin administration did not significantly reduce the incidence of AKI (RR: 1.00 [0.91–1.11], I² =47.2%), with a low quality of evidence. In four trials, all using 20% albumin, albumin was associated with a higher rate of RRT (RR: 1.26, [1.07–1.48]; low certainty of evidence). Albumin also increased ICU length of stay (MD: 0.33 days, [0.12–0.55]), without affecting mortality (RR: 0.98, 95%CI [0.92–1.05]). TSA showed that the cumulative Z-curve crossed the futility boundary, suggesting that further trials are unlikely to change the primary conclusion. Albumin administration did not significantly reduce the incidence of AKI in ICU patients with a low quality of evidence. In this first meta-analysis focussing on renal outcomes, albumin administration does not significantly reduce the risk of AKI in critically ill patients with a low quality of evidence and may increase the need for renal replacement therapy with a low-certainty signal that requires confirmation. These findings do not support the routine use of albumin in critically ill patients for the prevention of AKI.

items.title: Chlorhexidine within a standardized oral-care bundle for the prevention of ventilator-associated pneumonia: a pragmatic cluster-randomized crossover trial in six medical intensive care units
items.abstract: Chlorhexidine (CHX) has been a long-standing component of oral-care bundles for preventing ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP), but recent evidence has questioned its benefit in non-cardiac-surgery ICU. We evaluated whether adding 0.12% CHX to standardized oral-care bundle provides incremental benefit in a mixed medical ICU. We conducted a prospective, pragmatic cluster-randomized crossover (AB/BA) trial in six adult medical ICUs of a single tertiary-care academic hospital in Bhubaneswar, India. ICUs were randomized as three ICUs of two Period of 9 months with the multicomponent oral-care bundle without chlorhexidine and three with the same bundle plus 0.12% chlorhexidine with a 1-month wash-in and re-training interval. Consecutive adults ventilated for ≥ 48 h were included. The primary outcome was VAP incidence density (Clinical Pulmonary Infection Score (CPIS) > 6) as per 1,000 ventilator-days. Secondary outcomes were 28-day all-cause mortality, duration of mechanical ventilation, ICU length of stay, 28- day ventilator-free days, Beck Oral Assessment Scale (BOAS) and Critical-Care Pain Observation Tool (CPOT) scores. The primary model was a population-averaged Poisson generalized estimating equation (GEE) and adjustment for treatment, period, sequence, age, sex, APACHE II, and SOFA. A total of 1,035 patients (637 No CHX, 398 CHX) accrued 10,024 ventilator-days (5,918 vs. 4,106). Groups were well balanced at baseline (mean age ≈ 55 years; APACHE II ≈ 19.6; SOFA ≈ 13.4). VAP occurred in 100/5,918 ventilator-days (16.9 per 1,000) vs. 77/4,106 (18.8 per 1,000) (No CHX vs. CHX). The adjusted Poisson incidence rate ratio was 1.08 (95% CI 0.84–1.38; p = 0.56). 28-day mortality was 28.7% vs. 26.4% (no CHX vs. CHX) (adjusted OR 0.87, 95% CI 0.65–1.15; p = 0.33). ICU length of stay was longer in the CHX arm (adjusted mean difference + 0.89 days, 95% CI + 0.19 to + 1.58; p = 0.013). BOAS and CPOT scores did not differ. In this trial, adding 0.12% chlorhexidine to a standardized oral-care bundle did not reduce VAP incidence density or 28-day mortality and was associated with a modest increase in ICU length of stay. Routine CHX use provided no clear incremental benefit in a mixed medical ICU population. Clinical Trials Regisrty- India (CTRI) identifier [CTRI/2024/02/062201], registered [01 February 2024].

items.title: ICU-led remote vital sign trends monitoring of selected non-ICU-patients: a first year experience
Nocturnal intravenous gamma-hydroxybutyrate and sleep architecture in non-sedated intensive care unit patients: a polysomnographic experience
South Africa shifts away from salbutamol-only asthma relief
Interstitial lung diseases in a changing climate: emerging risks and opportunities to improve care
items.abstract: Although climate change represents one of the greatest public health challenges of our time, its impacts on patients with interstitial lung disease (ILD) remain unclear. This Personal View synthesises the evidence surrounding established, emerging, and postulated climate change health effects on patients with ILD, who are especially vulnerable to disease due to older age, reduced lung function, and sensitivity to inhaled exposures. Established risk factors for ILD such as air pollution might worsen with climate change, whereas other exposures such as extreme heat, viral illnesses, residential water intrusion, pollen, natural disasters, and desertification could pose novel threats to this population. Knowledge gaps exist across multiple domains, including wildfire smoke effects, the effects of climate on occupational ILD, and disaster preparedness. The incorporation of multiple research modalities, including patient-centred approaches, is crucial to address these gaps. Clinicians, scientists, and professional societies can lead climate-health research, the adoption of mitigation and adaptation strategies, and drive global policy actions to address this growing challenge.

items.title: When a vulnerable lung meets a changing climate
Efzofitimod versus placebo in patients with pulmonary sarcoidosis (EFZO-FIT): a multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial
items.abstract: Background Oral corticosteroids are currently standard-of-care therapy for pulmonary sarcoidosis, but they are associated with substantial toxicity and reduced health-related quality of life (HRQoL). The EFZO-FIT trial aimed to assess the efficacy and safety of efzofitimod, a novel immunomodulatory fusion protein targeting the neuropilin 2 receptor, as a steroid-sparing agent in pulmonary sarcoidosis. Methods In this multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial, adults aged 18-75 years with pulmonary sarcoidosis requiring treatment were enrolled at 85 study centres across nine countries (Brazil, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, Netherlands, Spain, UK, and USA). Participants were randomly assigned 1:1:1 using stratified block randomisation to receive monthly intravenous infusions of efzofitimod 3 mg/kg, efzofitimod 5 mg/kg, or placebo over a 48-week treatment period, including a 12-week oral corticosteroid taper targeting 0 mg per day (starting on day 15). Oral corticosteroid dose could be adjusted upwards in the event of worsening sarcoidosis. The primary endpoint was change from baseline in mean daily oral corticosteroid dose at week 48. Outcome and safety analyses were done in participants who received at least one dose of the study drug and had at least one post-baseline efficacy assessment. This study was registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05415137) and is complete. Findings Between Sept 22, 2022, and Aug 14, 2025, 331 patients were screened for inclusion. 63 were excluded and 268 participants were randomly assigned to receive placebo (n=91), efzofitimod 3 mg/kg (n=89), or efzofitimod 5 mg/kg (n=88). Four patients were excluded after random assignment (one in the placebo group and three in the efzofitimod 3 mg/kg group). 264 patients who received at least one dose of study treatment and had at least one post-baseline assessment were included in the outcome analysis and safety population (90 in the placebo group, 86 in the efzofitimod 3 mg/kg group, and 88 in the efzofitimod 5 mg/kg group). Among the 264 participants, the mean age was 53·8 years (SD 10·6); 114 (43%) of 264 patients were female and 150 (57%) were male. 168 (64%) identified as White. Mean steroid dose was 10·7 mg per day (SD 4·4) at baseline and 2·9 mg per day (4·5) at week 48. No difference was seen in the magnitude of oral corticosteroid taper between the active and placebo dose groups; the placebo-adjusted change from baseline was 0·02 mg per day in the efzofitimod 3 mg/kg group (95% CI -1·49 to 1·52, p=0·98) and -0·73 mg per day in the efzofitimod 5 mg/kg group (-2·21 to 0·75, p=0·33). The percentage of participants with serious treatment-emergent adverse events was similar between groups. Malaise was more common in the placebo group (five [6%] of 90 patients vs zero in both efzofitimod groups). TEAEs that were more common in the efzofitimod groups included headache (17 [19%] of 88 patients in the efzofitimod 5 mg/kg group, 11 [13%] of 86 patients in the efzofitimod 3 mg/kg group, and four [4%] of 90 patients in the placebo group), sinusitis (nine [10%], six [7%], and two [2%] patients, respectively), wheezing (seven [8%], two [2%], and zero patients, respectively), and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) increased (five [6%], one [1%], and zero patients, respectively). Most adverse events were grade 1 or 2. Two participants died, both in the efzofitimod 3 mg/kg group (one respiratory failure and one incarceration of a pre-existing inguinal hernia). Neither event was considered to be causally related to the treatment. Interpretation Efzofitimod was well tolerated but did not result in lower steroid doses at week 48 compared with placebo. The results from steroid tapering indicate that oral corticosteroid doses can be more aggressively reduced in many patients with pulmonary sarcoidosis. Funding aTyr and Kyorin.

items.title: Corticosteroid reduction and the endpoint challenge in sarcoidosis: striving for the lowest dose of uncertainty
Diagnostic labels, GETomics, and biostates in airway diseases
Twice-yearly depemokimab: beyond dosing convenience

Long-term safety and efficacy of twice-yearly depemokimab in type 2 asthma with an eosinophilic phenotype: 2-year integrated analysis of the phase 3a SWIFT-1 and SWIFT-2 studies and AGILE open-label extension
items.abstract: Background Depemokimab is the first ultra-long-acting biologic, with enhanced interleukin-5 binding affinity, high potency, and extended half-life, enabling twice-yearly dosing. The double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3a SWIFT-1 and SWIFT-2 studies demonstrated depemokimab efficacy and safety over 52 weeks in patients with asthma with type 2 inflammation and an eosinophilic phenotype. Here, we present long-term safety and efficacy outcomes over the 52-week, phase 3a open-label extension (OLE) of SWIFT-1 and SWIFT-2 (AGILE) alongside an integrated post-hoc analysis of the 104-week SWIFT and AGILE period. Methods In SWIFT-1 and SWIFT-2, patients (aged ≥12 years) with asthma with type 2 inflammation, an eosinophilic phenotype (≥150 cells/μL at screening or ≥300 cells/μL during the previous 12 months), and a history of at least two exacerbations in the previous 12 months despite receiving medium-dose or high-dose inhaled corticosteroids were randomly assigned (2:1) to subcutaneous depemokimab 100 mg or placebo every 26 weeks in addition to standard of care for 52 weeks. Patients who completed SWIFT-1 or SWIFT-2 could join the single-arm, 52-week AGILE OLE study, conducted at 156 centres across 14 countries. Patients continued depemokimab (depemokimab-depemokimab group) or switched to depemokimab from placebo (placebo-depemokimab group). The primary endpoints for the 52-week AGILE OLE period were the incidence of adverse events and serious adverse events, and immunogenicity as measured by the presence of anti-drug antibodies and neutralising antibodies. Secondary efficacy outcomes, including exacerbation rate, St George's Respiratory Questionnaire (SGRQ) total score, Asthma Control Questionnaire-5 (ACQ-5) score, and pre-bronchodilator forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV 1 ), were also assessed. Additional post-hoc analyses were carried out to assess safety and efficacy over the 104-week integrated SWIFT and AGILE analysis period. AGILE OLE is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT05243680. The SWIFT-1 and SWIFT-2 trials are registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT04719832 and NCT04718103. Findings Between March 1, 2022, and May 19, 2025, 629 patients were included in the AGILE OLE study (419 patients in the depemokimab-depemokimab group and 210 patients in the placebo-depemokimab group). During the 52-week AGILE OLE period, adverse events occurred in 297 (71%) of 419 patients in the depemokimab-depemokimab group and 146 (70%) of 210 patients in the placebo-depemokimab group; serious adverse events were infrequent (37 [9%] of 419 in the depemokimab-depemokimab group and 19 [9%] of 210 in the placebo-depemokimab group), with no treatment-related or fatal serious adverse events reported. In the depemokimab-depemokimab group, the reduced annualised exacerbation rate was sustained over 2 years (0·51 [95% CI 0·43-0·61] in the 52-week SWIFT-1 and SWIFT-2 period and 0·56 [0·47-0·66] in the AGILE OLE). Improvements in SGRQ total score, ACQ-5 score, and FEV 1 were maintained over 2 years. In the placebo-depemokimab group, improvements in clinical outcomes were observed after the switch to depemokimab during the AGILE OLE. Interpretation Twice-yearly depemokimab was well tolerated and demonstrated sustained efficacy over the 2-year SWIFT and AGILE period, supporting its long-term therapeutic benefit and safety profile. Funding GSK.

items.title: Reshaping COPD care in China: bridging geographical divides and empowering health-care workers
The present and future of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease prevention, diagnosis, and management in China: a Lancet Respiratory Medicine Commission
From coverage to equitable reach: addressing social inequalities in COPD in China
Corrigendum to “European Resuscitation Council Guideline 2025 Adult Advanced Life Support” [Resuscitation 215(Supplement 1) (2025) 110769]
Mechanical versus manual bag-valve ventilation during cardiopulmonary resuscitation in adults with cardiac arrest: a systematic review and Bayesian meta-analysis
items.abstract: Background/objective Optimal ventilation delivery during cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) remains uncertain. Current resuscitation guidelines do not recommend mechanical ventilation (MV) over manual bag-valve ventilation (BV). We evaluated the association between MV use during CPR and clinical outcomes in adults with cardiac arrest compared with manual BV. Methods We searched 6 bibliographic databases from inception through May 31, 2026. Included studies compared MV and BV ventilation CPR in adult cardiac arrest patients. Patients receiving MV at any moment during CPR were classified as the MV group; those receiving only BV comprised the BV group. Primary outcomes included return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC), survival to hospital admission, survival to hospital discharge, and good neurological outcome. Secondary outcomes included physiologic variables and pneumothorax. We calculated pooled risk ratios (RRs) and mean differences with 95% credible intervals (CrIs) using Bayesian random-effects meta-analyses. Results Eight studies involving 6847 patients were included. For the primary outcome, MV use during CPR was associated with a higher rate of ROSC than BV use (pooled RR, 1.20; 95% CrI, 1.04-1.42), with a 99% posterior probability of benefit. Posterior probabilities favoring MV for survival to admission, survival to discharge, and good neurological outcome were 92.3%, 93.6%, and 92.2%, respectively. Pneumothorax incidence was similar between groups. Conclusion In adult cardiac arrest, MV use during CPR was associated with higher ROSC compared with manual BV. Evidence for improved survival and neurological outcomes remains imprecise and inconclusive.

items.title: Translating the R-EDByUS score into clinical decisions after cardiac arrest
Where are the female manikins? Representation of female anatomy across two European resuscitation congresses
Beyond Selection Bias: Post-Event Video Deletion and Trust in Healthcare
Making blood work: Toward precision care after cardiac arrest
Association between capnographic changes during pulse checks of varying durations and clinical outcomes during cardiopulmonary resuscitation: a multicenter study from Türkiye (CaPTuRe)
items.abstract: Aim To investigate the association between capnographic changes during pulse checks of different durations and cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) outcomes. Methods This multicenter, prospective, controlled, quasi-randomized study categorized patients according to pulse check duration: Group A (≤5 s) and Group B (>5-≤10 s). Five measurements were obtained during the first six CPR cycles. Four capnographic parameters were evaluated for each measurement: Post-CPR end-tidal carbon dioxide (ETCO 2 ), Pre-CPR ETCO 2 , loss rate (percentage decrease between Post- and Pre-CPR ETCO 2 ), and recovery time (time required to regain the previous cycle's Post-CPR ETCO 2 ). Results The study included 252 cardiac arrest patients (Group A, n = 124; Group B, n = 128). In Group A, patients with return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) had markedly lower loss rates and shorter recovery times than non-survivors, together with higher pre- and post-CPR ETCO 2 values (all p 2 was strongly negatively correlated with loss rate (ρ = -0.770), whereas Pre- and Post-CPR ETCO 2 values (ρ = 0.96) and loss rate and recovery time (ρ = 0.89) were strongly positively correlated. Conclusion Pulse checks completed within 5 s were associated with more favorable capnographic dynamics and higher ROSC rates than those lasting 6-10 s. These findings are hypothesis-generating and warrant prospective validation.

items.title: Fatigue, Anxiety and Depression 12 Months After Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: A Population Based Cohort Study
items.abstract: Aim To determine the prevalence and factors associated with fatigue, anxiety, and depression 12 months after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA); examine their associations with health-related quality of life (HRQoL) and functional recovery; and compare symptom burden with population norms. Methods This prospective, population-based cohort study included adults (≥18 years) who received EMS-attempted resuscitation and survived to hospital discharge following non-traumatic OHCA in Victoria, Australia, between July 2019 and June 2022. Survivors were identified from a statewide OHCA registry and completed a 12-month telephone interview. Primary outcomes were fatigue (Modified Fatigue Impact Scale), anxiety and depression (Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale). Secondary outcomes included HRQoL (EQ-5D, SF-12), functional recovery (GOSE), living arrangement, and return to work. Results Of 1068 eligible 12-month survivors, 728 (68.2%) completed follow-up (median age 61 years; 555 [76.2%] male). Fatigue was reported by 35.8% (250/699), anxiety by 22.6% (162/716), and depression by 18.0% (129/716). Higher symptom burden was associated with lower EQ-5D and SF-12 scores, worse GOSE outcomes (all p Conclusions Fatigue, anxiety, and depression were common at 12 months after OHCA and are associated with poorer recovery. Fatigue exceeded population norms and may be an under-recognised component of cardiac arrest survivorship.

items.title: Association between burst-suppression with identical bursts and multimodal measures of cerebral oxygenation after cardiac arrest
items.abstract: Objective Burst-suppression with identical bursts (BSIB) is an electroencephalographic (EEG) pattern associated with severe post-cardiac arrest brain injury (PCABI). Whether modifiable mechanisms of brain injury underlie BSIB is unknown. We hypothesized BSIB is associated with impaired cerebral oxygen metabolism, reflected as pathologically elevated jugular bulb venous oxygen saturation (SjvO 2 ), higher brain tissue oxygen tension (PbtO 2 ), normal jugular bulb venous-to-arterial carbon dioxide gradient (PbCO 2 gap, and lower intracranial pressure (ICP) compared to other EEG patterns. Methods This single-center retrospective study included patients resuscitated from cardiac arrest who underwent EEG and SjvO 2 or PbtO 2 monitoring. We categorized EEG patterns as BSIB, malignant without BSIB, and non-malignant. Using mixed effects linear regression, we examined associations between EEG and SjvO 2 , PbCO 2 gap, PbtO 2 , and ICP. Results The SjvO 2 and PbtO 2 cohorts included 109 and 33 patients, respectively. SjvO 2 did not differ between BSIB and malignant EEGs (β=3; 95% CI, -0.6 to 7.0), butwas higher with BSIB compared to non-malignant patterns (β=12; 95% CI, 7.0 to 16.0). BSIB was associated with lower PbCO 2 gap compared to malignant (β=-1.4; 95% CI, -2.6 to -0.3) and non-malignant (β=-2.6; 95% CI, -4.1 to -1.0) patterns. PbtO 2 was highest with BSIB, but not significantly higher compared to malignant patterns in our adjusted model (β=4.0; 95% CI, -4.7 to 13.0). ICP was lower in those with BSIB compared to malignant patterns (β=-19.0; 95% CI, -32.5 to -5.6). Interpretation BSIB may represent a distinct subtype of PCABI characterized by impaired oxygen metabolism with preserved oxygen delivery and diffusion.
