items.title: Intrahepatic Cholangiocarcinoma
items.abstract: Importance Intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (iCCA) is the second most common primary liver malignancy, and incidence is increasing worldwide. Despite advances in multimodal therapy, 5-year overall survival remains approximately 9%, underscoring the urgent need for improved therapeutic strategies and comprehensive understanding of current management approaches. Observations Surgical resection with regional lymphadenectomy remains the cornerstone of curative therapy, with adjuvant capecitabine established as standard of care after resection. Neoadjuvant chemotherapy may be strongly considered for patients with iCCA with high-risk features, including at least 1 of the following: tumor size larger than 5 cm, multifocal disease, vascular invasion, lymph node involvement, and elevated carbohydrate antigen 19-9. For unresectable, liver-confined disease, locoregional therapies, including transarterial chemoembolization, Y-90 radioembolization, hepatic artery infusion pump chemotherapy, thermal ablation, and radiotherapy, may provide meaningful survival benefits. Liver transplant is emerging as a viable option in highly selected patients with very early iCCA or sustained response to neoadjuvant therapy. In advanced disease, chemoimmunotherapy with gemcitabine/cisplatin plus durvalumab or pembrolizumab has become the first-line treatment. Comprehensive molecular profiling identifies actionable targets in 30% to 40% of patients, including FGFR2 fusions/rearrangements, IDH1 variants, and other alterations amenable to targeted therapies approved by the US Food and Drug Administration. Conclusions and Relevance The management of iCCA has evolved substantially with neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy for high-risk resectable disease, enhanced locoregional strategies for liver-confined tumors, chemoimmunotherapy as first-line systemic therapy for advanced disease, and precision oncology approaches targeting recurrent molecular alterations. Multidisciplinary evaluation and comprehensive genomic profiling are essential for optimal patient outcomes.

items.title: Best Practices for Tribal Surgical Health Services Research
Days at Home After Gastrointestinal Cancer Surgery as a Patient-Centered Outcome
items.abstract: Importance Traditional postoperative outcomes may not fully reflect recovery after gastrointestinal (GI) cancer surgery. Days at home (DAH) is a patient-centered metric that integrates survival, complications, and health care use. Objective To characterize and identify an optimal postoperative observation window and validate DAH after elective GI cancer surgery. Design, Setting, and Participants This was a population-based retrospective cohort study from 2003 to 2021 in Ontario, Canada. Included were adults 18 years and older who underwent elective surgery for GI cancer. Patients were excluded if they were long-term care residents at baseline, underwent emergency surgery, or had another cancer diagnosis within a 2-year lookback. Study data were analyzed from April to November 2025. Exposures Covariates explored were age, sex, frailty, comorbidity burden, income quintile, cancer site, histology, metastatic disease, neoadjuvant therapy, procedure type, operative approach, and hospital volume. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome was DAH, defined as days alive and out of health care institutions and assessed at 30, 90, 180, and 365 days. Death during the observation window resulted in a DAH = 0. DAH after surgery at 90 days (DAH-90) was established as an optimal window, based on the proportion of zeros and variability, while considering clinical pathways in GI cancer. Exploratory multivariable quantile regression examined patient, cancer, and treatment factors associated with DAH-90. Quantile plots evaluated these associations across the distribution of DAH-90. Validity was explored through associations with major morbidity (construct validity) and 1-year mortality (criterion validity). Results Among 91 270 operations in 89 378 participants (mean [SD] age, 67.3 [12.2] years; 51 343 male [56.2%]), median (IQR) DAH-90 was 82 (77-85) days. DAH-90 varied across cancer site, histology, and procedure. Median (IQR) DAH-90 was lowest for esophageal cancer (76 [63-80] days) and highest for small-bowel cancer (84 [80-86] days). In multivariable quantile regression, preoperative frailty was associated with 2.6 fewer DAH-90 (95% CI, 2.3-2.9 fewer days), whereas laparoscopic approach was associated with 3.0 more DAH-90 (95% CI, 2.9-3.1 more days). DAH-90 was lower among patients with major morbidity (median [IQR], 70 [41-79] days vs 83 [80-85] days; P &lt; .001) and among patients who died within 1 year (median, 62 [0-80] days vs 83 [78-85] days; P &lt; .001). Conclusions and Relevance Results of this study suggest that DAH-90 was found to be a valid and clinically meaningful outcome after GI cancer surgery. These findings support the use of DAH-90 in patient counseling, quality assessment, and future GI cancer surgery research.

items.title: Quantifying Risk Tolerance in Kidney Xenotransplant—From Clinical Trials to Clinical Practice
items.abstract: This Viewpoint explores the benefits of stated-preference methods for quantifying risk tolerance in kidney xenotransplantation.

items.title: Defining Surgical Margins in Nonrhabdomyosarcoma Soft Tissue Sarcoma
The Future of Precision Hepatopancreatobiliary Surgery—Beyond Anatomy
items.abstract: This Viewpoint proposes that the future of hepatopancreatobiliary surgery lies in layering molecular profiling, artificial intelligence, and liquid biopsy onto the traditional anatomic framework to individualize every phase of surgical care.

items.title: Surgical Margin and Risk of Local Recurrence in Children and Young Adults With Nonrhabdomyosarcoma Soft Tissue Sarcoma
items.abstract: Importance The extent of negative margin necessary to achieve a high rate of local tumor control in children and young adult patients with nonrhabdomyosarcoma soft tissue sarcomas (NRSTS) is unknown. Objective To evaluate the impact of negative margin extent on local tumor control in children and young adult patients with NRSTS undergoing R0 resection as part of risk-adapted multimodality treatment. Design, Setting, and Participants This multicenter prospective clinical trial was conducted at Children’s Oncology Group (COG) member sites from February 2007 through February 2012. Analysis was performed on the final dataset June 30, 2018, with a median follow-up of 6.2 years. Reviewers of margin status/extent were blinded to local control outcomes. Patients included 266 eligible/evaluable individuals younger than 30 years with nonmetastatic NRSTS who were enrolled in the COG ARST0332 trial and underwent upfront or delayed R0 resection as part of treatment. Patients who underwent an amputation or did not receive protocol-specified radiotherapy were excluded. These data were analyzed from January 2023 through July 2026. Intervention Risk-adapted treatment included 3 patient groups with upfront or delayed surgery with or without radiation therapy with or without ifosfamide/doxorubicin chemotherapy, based on the extent of initial resection, surgical margin status, tumor size, and histologic grade. Main Outcomes Cumulative incidence of local recurrence based on treatment approach and surgical margin extent and outcomes after local recurrence. Results Of 266 patients (median age 13.7 [range, 2.1-27.6] years; 138 female [52%] and 128 male [48%]) who underwent upfront (n = 207) or delayed (n = 59) R0 resection, 132 had measured surgical margins: 1 mm (n = 56), 2 to 5 mm (n = 50), or 6-mm or larger (n = 26). The 5-year cumulative incidence of local recurrence overall was 4.4%. Local recurrence occurred in 10 of 178 patients treated with surgery alone (5.6%) and 2 of 88 patients treated with surgery and chemoradiotherapy (2.3%). Among the 132 patients with measured surgical margins, the 5-year cumulative incidence of local recurrence was 4.9% for 1-mm margins, 2.0% for 2- to 5-mm margins, and 0% for 6-mm or larger margins. Local recurrence occurred in 10 of 178 (5.6%) patients with tumors smaller than 5 cm treated with margin-negative surgery alone, 1 of 29 (3.4%) patients with tumors larger than 5 cm treated with margin-negative surgery followed by chemoradiotherapy, and 1 of 59 (1.7%) patients with initially unresectable disease treated with neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy. Five of 12 patients with local recurrence were alive without further disease progression. Conclusions and Relevance In this study, the local recurrence rate after R0 resection among children and young adult patients treated with risk-based therapy for nonmetastatic NRSTS was low, and some patients underwent successful salvage therapy with durable long-term disease control. Wider (&gt;1 mm) negative margins further decrease local recurrence risk. Close surgical margins may be adequate in some clinical settings, particularly in the context of chemoradiotherapy, according to a risk-adapted approach. Trial Registration ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT00346164

items.title: Error in Figure 2
Rethinking Risk in Ventral Hernia Repair—Sex as a Signal, Not a Cause
Comparison of Outcomes Between Men and Women Undergoing Ventral Hernia Repair
items.abstract: Importance Sex-based differences in ventral hernia repair (VHR) outcomes remain incompletely characterized. Objective To compare short-term clinical outcomes, recurrence through 3 years, and patient-reported outcomes between female and male patients undergoing VHR. Design, Setting, and Participants This cohort study included patients undergoing VHR from January 2012 through December 2023, with follow-up through 3 years. Data were from the Abdominal Core Health Quality Collaborative (ACHQC), a prospective, multi-institutional clinical registry. Participants were adults undergoing primary or incisional VHR whose data were recorded in the ACHQC database. Data analysis was performed from May to September 2026. Exposures Sex (female vs male). Main Outcomes and Measures Primary outcomes included 30-day wound morbidity, comprising surgical site infection (SSI), surgical-site occurrence (SSO), and SSO requiring procedural intervention (SSO-PI), readmission, and length of stay. Secondary outcomes included pragmatic recurrence at 30 days, 1 year, 2 years, and 3 years and patient-reported quality of life and pain. Multivariable logistic regression assessed associations between sex and outcomes. Results Among 31 358 patients, 14 303 (45.6%) were female and 17 055 (54.4%) were male. Women were younger than men (mean [SD] age, 55.0 [14.6] vs 56.5 [13.0] years, respectively) and had higher body mass index (mean [SD], 32.1 [7.6] vs 31.7 [5.9], respectively). Women presented with more complex hernia phenotypes, including higher rates of incisional, recurrent, and larger hernias. Compared with men, women experienced higher 30-day readmission (483 [3.4%] for women vs 428 [2.5%] for men), SSI (370 [2.6%] vs 284 [1.7%], respectively) SSO (1323 [9.2%] and 1286 [7.5%], respectively), and SSO-PI (517 [3.6%] vs 434 [2.5%], respectively; all P &lt; .001), with no differences in reoperation or mortality. Female sex was independently associated with higher odds of SSI (odds ratio [OR], 1.40; 95% CI, 1.17-1.67) and SSO-PI (OR, 1.21; 95% CI, 1.04-1.40) after incisional hernia repair. Clinical outcomes and recurrence were similar at 1 year; however, women had higher recurrence at 2 years (444 [19.3%] vs 406 [15.7%] men) and 3 years (351 [20.9%] vs 320 [17.6%] men). Women reported worse baseline quality of life and pain but greater improvement after 1 year. Conclusions and Relevance This study found that women undergoing VHR presented with greater hernia complexity and experienced higher early wound morbidity and increased late recurrence, while achieving substantial patient-reported benefit. These findings may inform sex-specific risk stratification and counseling, although further studies with more longitudinal follow-up are needed.

items.title: What Factors Drive Female Surgeons to Change Jobs or Leave Medicine Altogether?
items.abstract: Objective: To explore reasons female surgeons change jobs or leave medicine entirely. Summary of Background Data: Only a quarter of physicians in surgical specialties are female. Identifying reasons for career dissatisfaction is crucial to improve retention. Methods: An anonymous survey was distributed via private female physician social media groups (physician credentials required) and email communication from 2/2024 to 5/2024. Respondents’ demographics, personal and professional characteristics, and job transitions were collected. Respondents who have not changed jobs or left medicine were excluded. Respondents were categorized into female surgeons or female nonsurgeons, and responses were compared between the 2 groups. Results: A total of 593 surveys were included: 170 (28.7%) female surgeons and 423 (71.3%) female nonsurgeons. Among surgeons, 10 (5.9%) left medicine and 167 (99.4%) changed jobs at least once. Compared with nonsurgeons, surgeons were more frequently non-Hispanic/Latino ethnicity (97.6% vs. 92.3%, P =0.016), more frequently completed fellowship training (58.8% vs. 40.4%, P <0.001), and a higher proportion currently worked in an academic clinical job (44.1% vs. 30%, P =0.002). All other demographics, personal and professional characteristics were comparable between the 2 groups. Surgeons more frequently identified pay inequity (5.3% vs. 1.2%, P =0.005) and harassment/bullying/discrimination (15.3% vs. 6.4%, P <0.001) as the primary reasons for their job change, while nonsurgeons more frequently cited long hours (39.5% vs. 28.7%, P =0.015). Conclusions: Pay inequity and harassment/bullying/discrimination emerged as primary factors driving job changes among female surgeons compared with nonsurgeons. Nearly half of all surgeons indicated an improved work environment and culture could have prevented them from leaving. Efforts are needed to address these concerns and improve retention. Level of evidence: Level III.

items.title: De-escalation of Axillary Surgery in Early Breast Cancer
items.abstract: Objective: To prospectively evaluate how often axillary staging can successfully be omitted in postmenopausal HR+/HER2- patients. Background: Three randomized trials showed no difference in recurrence or survival outcomes with omission of sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) in cT1-T2N0 patients with a negative axillary ultrasound (AUS) undergoing breast-conserving surgery (BCS). We prospectively evaluated applicability of this approach. Methods: From 3/1/24 to 9/1/25, SLNB was omitted in postmenopausal women age 50–70 years with unicentric or multifocal, clinical stage 1, grade 1/2, HR+/HER2- cancers and a normal AUS undergoing BCS. After the results of INSEMA were reported, tumors up to 2.5 cm were included. Patients with pathology showing grade 3, T≥3 cm, or HR- or HER2+ underwent multidisciplinary discussion regarding the need for SLNB. Results: In 437 patients with 442 cancers, the median patient age was 63 years, median mammographic tumor size was 0.9 cm, and 74% were grade 2. A total of 34 patients (8%) had high-risk features on final pathology (grade 3, n=20; T≥3 cm, n=11; HER2+, n=3) and 14 (3.2%) had SLNB. Of these, 2 had SLN metastases. A total of 96% of patients received radiotherapy (40% whole breast, 56% partial breast), 415 (95%) received adjuvant endocrine therapy, and 31 (7%) received chemotherapy. At 7.7-month median follow-up, there have been no axillary recurrences. Conclusion: Adoption of the SOUND, INSEMA, and BOOG 13-08 data allowed omission of SLNB in 97% of postmenopausal patients age ≤70 years with cT1-2N0, grade 1/2, HR+/HER2- cancers and a normal AUS, reducing the burden of treatment.

items.title: Rethinking Education in Acute Care Surgery
SETI—The Semi-Elective Transplant Initiative
items.abstract: Objective: To evaluate whether formal integration of preservation strategy with predictable operating room access was associated with measurable changes in transplant timing, preservation practice, the logistical profile of transplanted grafts, and early clinical outcomes. Summary Background Data: Deceased donor kidney transplantation remains a reactive process requiring urgent mobilization of hospital resources. As volumes increase and hospitals operate near capacity, this creates operational barriers that limit organ utilization. We report a retrospective evaluation of a prospectively implemented operational redesign; the design does not support causal inference. Methods: Adult deceased-donor kidney transplants (January 2022–June 2025) were grouped into pre-SETI, SETI-1 (expanded machine perfusion), and SETI-2 (morning operating room access). A contemporaneous SRTR cohort (N=12,302) served as the comparator. Results: Among 936 transplants, mean cold ischemia time (CIT) increased after SETI (20.2→21.9 h, P =0.0039). Donation after circulatory death (DCD) kidneys with CIT >30 hours increased from 0.5% pre-SETI to 7.7% after full implementation ( P <0.0001). Overnight perfusion increased more than 3-fold, and operative starts shifted toward 8–10 AM. Kidney Donor Profile Index rose across eras (median: 29→33→43, P <0.001). No significant differences were observed in DGF (41.4→38.2%, P =0.071) or graft failure (5.4→3.2%, P =0.34); these comparisons were underpowered and do not establish equivalence. Donor hypertension predicted graft failure, whereas CIT, DCD status, and SETI era did not. Conclusions: Systems-based operational redesign transformed reactive deceased-donor kidney transplantation into a proactive model, enabling transplantation of a greater proportion of logistics-sensitive grafts, including DCD kidneys and organs with prolonged CIT, within existing healthcare resources. Whether this increases net organ utilization was not established by these data.

items.title: Caregiving in Surgery: Insights on Measurement, Inclusivity, and Policy
Preoperative Injection of Botulinum Toxin Into the Sphincter of Oddi Does Not Prevent Pancreatic Fistula After Distal Pancreatectomy: The Randomized Controlled PREBOTPilot Trial
items.abstract: Objective: To investigate whether preoperative injection of botulinum toxin (BTX) into the sphincter of Oddi (SO) is a safe and feasible strategy to prevent postoperative pancreatic fistula (POPF) after distal pancreatectomy (DP). Summary Background Data: POPF remains a common and potentially serious complication following DP, affecting up to 30% of patients. Pharmacologically induced sphincter relaxation by endoscopic injection of BTX into the SO has been described as a new approach to prevent POPF after DP by improved drainage of pancreatic fluid towards the duodenum. Methods: Patients scheduled for elective primary distal pancreatectomy (DP), irrespective of the underlying disease, were included in this monocenter, randomized controlled, open-label, phase-II trial with 2 parallel arms. Patients randomly assigned to the intervention group received an endoscopic injection of BTX (100 units) into the SO 3–10 days before surgery. Patients in the control group did not undergo any preoperative intervention. The combined primary endpoint was defined as the occurrence of clinically relevant postoperative pancreatic fistula (POPF grades B/C) and/or death due to any cause within 30 days following DP. Results: From March 2020 to August 2023, 50 patients were included in the trial. Subsequent to the analysis of the primary endpoint, which revealed no tendency of a beneficial effect on the rate of POPF after DP following BTX injection, even with the most favorable outcome upon further inclusion of the remaining 10 patients planned for recruitment, the recruitment was prematurely terminated. All 26 patients in the intervention group underwent successful SO BTX injection within a median of 6 (IQR of 5–8) days before surgery. DP was performed in 41 patients (82%). Postinterventional pancreatitis was not detected. Within 30 days, POPF grade B/C occurred in 6 patients in the intervention and 3 patients in the control group (28.6% vs. 15%, P =0.294). One patient in the intervention group died during the trial due to POPF-induced postpancreatectomy hemorrhage (PPH). Conclusion: Preoperative injection of BTX into the SO did not reduce clinically relevant POPF or 30-day mortality following DP, and the trial was prematurely terminated for futility. Although the intervention was safe and feasible, these findings do not support its use for the prevention of POPF after DP.

items.title: Patient-reported Outcomes According to Mesh Position After Elective Incisional Hernia Repair
items.abstract: Objectives: The aim of this study was to investigate the association between mesh position and patient-reported outcomes, including prevalence of severe chronic pain, foreign body sensation, self-reported recurrence, and physical impact score in patients undergoing elective incisional hernia repair. Background: Patient-reported outcomes are increasingly recognized as important measures of treatment success following incisional hernia repair, yet the impact of mesh position remains uncertain. Methods: This nationwide Danish survey- and register-based cohort study was conducted within the AFTERHERNIA Project and based on the Abdominal Hernia questionnaire. All patients undergoing elective incisional hernia repair in Denmark between January 1, 2014, and March 31, 2024, were eligible for inclusion. Survey responses were linked with operative data from the Danish Ventral Hernia Database. Adjusted prevalences and means were estimated using g-computation. Results: Of 2827 eligible patients, 2348 patients responded, corresponding to a response rate of 83%. Among these, 28% of patients received onlay, 28% retromuscular, 13% preperitoneal, and 31% intraperitoneal mesh position with defect closure. Onlay was associated with a higher prevalence of foreign body sensation compared with retromuscular position (adjusted prevalence, 37.1% vs. 30.3%; difference, 6.8%; 95% CI, 0.9–12.8). No differences were observed across mesh positions regarding the prevalence of severe chronic pain, self-reported recurrence, and physical impact score. Conclusions: Onlay position was associated with a higher prevalence of foreign body sensation compared with retromuscular position, while no differences were observed regarding the prevalence of severe chronic pain, self-reported recurrence, or physical impact score.

items.title: Anti-DEI Policies and Academic Surgery
items.abstract: Importance: The January 2025 federal executive orders (EOs) restricting diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) programming in government-funded and private institutions represent a structural inflection point for academic surgery. The effects extend beyond institutional compliance and directly threaten workforce sustainability, research enterprises, and editorial freedom. Objective: To evaluate the immediate and projected effects of January 2025 federal EOs on research, editorial freedom, and workforce recruitment and retention in academic surgery, and to propose adaptive strategies for mission preservation. Design: A narrative synthesis of the literature and multi-institutional experience presented during a 2026 Academic Surgical Congress Committee panel session evaluated across multiple domains: workforce, scientific research/education, patient care, and editorial ecosystems. Results: Anti-DEI EOs produced measurable disruptions across the domains examined. Regarding the workforce, survey data indicate that 50% of faculty in affected states are seeking positions elsewhere, and underrepresented-in-medicine trainees are redistributing away from institutions with policy climates perceived as hostile. In research, federal grant withdrawals and self-censorship constrain equity-focused scientific inquiry and threaten surgeon-scientist career trajectories. In publishing, editorial leaders report early signals of declining submissions addressing disparities, reflecting investigators’ concerns for possible retaliation rather than actual changes in editorial policy. Across domains, a false binary of “doubling down” versus “pivot” obscures a potentially more viable path: adaptive reframing that modifies language and programmatic infrastructure, while sustaining core missions. Conclusions: Academic surgery should preserve its mission to train a diverse surgical workforce, advance rigorous science, and deliver equitable patient care. Adaptive reframing, by embedding equity-oriented work within quality improvement, workforce sustainability, and patient safety frameworks, offers a principled strategy for navigating evolving legal constraints, without abandoning institutional missions or scientific integrity.

items.title: Technical Complications and Salvage of Hepatic Artery Infusion Pumps
items.abstract: Objective: Describe the technical complications of hepatic artery infusion pump (HAIP) placement and characterize salvage rates. Summary Background Data: HAIP chemotherapy is an effective tool used in the treatment of hepatic malignancies and has become increasingly adopted at select centers. Much of the safety data is reported from small, newer programs or older, large series. Methods: Retrospective analysis of all patients who underwent HAIP placement at our institution between 2000 and 2022 was conducted. Pump salvage was defined as the ability to receive HAIP chemotherapy after a pump-associated complication. Pump failure was defined as an HAIP-related complication permanently stopping ongoing HAIP chemotherapy. Results: Over the study period, 2935 patients had an HAIP placed for colorectal liver metastases (n=2582, 88%), intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (n=294, 10%) or another malignancy (n=59, 2%). Of all patients, 759 (26%) had an HAIP-related complication, with 404/759 (53%) having their pump salvaged. The most common complications were abnormal perfusion (n=360 [12%], 285/360 [79%] salvaged), arterial pseudoaneurysm and/or hemorrhage (n=117 [4%], 7/117 [6%] salvaged), and pump-pocket infection (n=115 [4%], 60/115 [52%] salvaged). The complications with the highest salvage rates were pump-pocket seroma (n=15/16, 94%), pump-flipping (n=41/44, 93%), and pump-pocket hematoma (n=45/49, 92%). Unsalvaged complications were catheter dislodgement from vessel (n=0/47, 0%), catheter erosion into bowel (n=0/25, 0%), and arterial thrombosis (n=0/19, 0%). The cumulative incidence of pump failure at 1 year in patients receiving adjuvant therapy was 6.6%, and 4.5% among those receiving palliative therapy. Conclusions: HAIP-related complications occur in about one quarter of patients, predominantly perfusion and pump-pocket complications. These are salvageable in the majority of cases with multidisciplinary interventions.

items.title: Multimodal Prediction in Robotic Surgery: The Incremental Value of Task-Level Kinematic Data
items.abstract: Objective: To determine whether multimodal predictive models incorporating task-level objective performance indicators (OPIs) alongside preoperative clinical variables improve prediction of surgeon experience, case complexity, and outcomes in robotic cholecystectomy. Background: OPIs from robotic platforms enable automated assessment of intraoperative performance, but prior multimodal analyses have suggested limited incremental value beyond clinical variables. Whether this conclusion holds when OPIs are computed at task level and target specifically curated endpoints remains untested. Methods: We retrospectively analyzed 234 Calot’s triangle dissections, 198 by attending surgeons and 36 by trainees. Three feature sets per target—clinical-only (10 preoperative variables), OPI-only (10 target-specific kinematic features), and combined—were evaluated using nested 5-seed×5-fold cross-validation across 5 algorithms (logistic regression, support vector machine, random forest, XGBoost, LightGBM). Discriminative performance was compared by paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests on fold-level area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC). Feature contributions were quantified with SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis. Results: For surgeon experience and case complexity, OPIs alone matched the combined model (AUROC: 0.967 vs. 0.964; 0.791 vs. 0.792; both P >0.05) and outperformed clinical variables alone ( P <0.001 and P =0.006). For outcomes, the combined model significantly exceeded both single-modality models (AUROC: 0.753 vs. 0.720 clinical and 0.720 OPI-only; P =0.015 and 0.005). OPIs contributed 90.7%, 73.3%, and 51.7% of total absolute SHAP value across the 3 targets, decreasing with distance from intraoperative kinematics. Conclusions: Task-level, target-specific OPIs carry independent discriminative information beyond routine preoperative clinical variables. Their incremental value is target-dependent, with multimodal integration offering statistically significant but modest gains for outcomes.

items.title: Prior Biliary Drainage Procedure Is a Near-universal Risk Factor for Postoperative Hepatic Abscess After Liver Resection
Out in the Match
items.abstract: Objective: To explore LGBTQ+ general surgery resident experiences during the Match process. Summary Background Data: General surgery (GS) applicants negotiate the residency match process through the lens of their identities, but little is known about LGBTQ+ applicant experiences. This study explored how current LGBTQ+-GS residents navigated their identity and evaluated programs for psychological safety and belonging during the Match. Methods: This qualitative study utilized semistructured interviews with current US LGBTQ+-GS residents recruited using purposive and snowball sampling from Oct to Dec 2025. Interviews focused on LGBTQ+ identity, experiences throughout medical school, recruitment, and residency, and how psychological safety was assessed. Interviews were audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, and analyzed using a deductive-inductive approach to identify themes. Results: Of 17 participants, mean age was 30.7±1.8 years, and most identified as male (52.9%) and White (76.5%). Five themes were identified: (1) Participants strategically disclosed identity: disclosing as a “ litmus test ” to filter for identity-affirming programs or concealing identity in fear “ that’s the reason why I don’t get ranked .” (2) Participants relied on subtle micro-signals to indicate psychological safety (eg, pronouns, pride symbols). (3) Participants scrutinized the manner and tone of responses to LGBTQ+-related questions in addition to the content. (4) Representation of LGBTQ+ residents/faculty reduced belonging uncertainty. (5) Participants “used geography as a proxy for acceptance , ” weighing regional sociopolitical climates when assessing their potential to thrive. Conclusions: LGBTQ+ trainees assessed a variety of micro- and macro-signals to evaluate residency programs. Residency programs can design their programs around these signals to enhance recruitment of LGBTQ+-GS applicants.

items.title: Surgeon Perspectives on Disclosure of Artificial Intelligence in the Operating Room
Endoscopic Classification of Fundoplication Integrity Predicts Pathologic Reflux
items.abstract: Objective: We aimed to validate individual endoscopic parameters against clinical and functional testing and to build a simple classification of fundoplication integrity. Summary Background Data: Endoscopy is the main tool to assess the gastroesophageal valve after antireflux surgery (ARS), but existing classifications are complex and have never been validated against objective pathophysiologic data. Methods: This was a single-center, two-phase cohort study of adults undergoing endoscopy, high-resolution manometry (HRM), and reflux monitoring after ARS. Retroflexed videoclips were reviewed blinded to functional results. In the development cohort (2018–2024), endoscopic parameters were tested against pathologic GERD (Lyon 2.0 criteria); those correlating with reflux were included in the classification and the population was stratified according to the number of impaired mechanisms (0–3). In the second phase, the classification was validated prospectively (2024–2026). Results: Of 122 patients, 73 formed the development and 49 the validation cohort. Three parameters were associated with pathologic GERD: intrathoracic valve, disrupted valve, and visible hiatus. Clinical, manometric, and reflux metrics worsened stepwise with the number of impaired mechanisms, and pathologic GERD rose from 11.8% to 37.5% to 85.7%. The new classification discriminated pathologic GERD with an area under the curve of 0.860 in the development and 0.870 in the validation cohort (0.869 overall). Conclusions: A simple endoscopic classification based on valve location, disruption, and hiatal opening reliably identifies fundoplication failure and correlates with symptoms, manometric features, and reflux burden.

items.title: Reappraising Liver Transplantation for Combined Hepatocellular-cholangiocarcinoma
items.abstract: Objective: To determine whether liver transplantation (LT) confers durable oncologic benefit in combined hepatocellular-cholangiocarcinoma (cHCC-CCA) and to identify predictors of recurrence that may guide transplant candidacy. Background: cHCC-CCA is a rare primary liver malignancy with aggressive biological behavior. LT has traditionally been contraindicated due to concerns regarding recurrence. We evaluated long-term outcomes of LT versus liver resection (LR) and compared LT outcomes for cHCC-CCA with those for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Methods: Patients with cHCC-CCA who underwent LT or LR between 2010 and 2024 were identified from a prospective database. Survival outcomes, recurrence patterns, and risk factors for recurrence were analyzed. Outcomes of LT for cHCC-CCA were additionally compared with HCC. Results: A total of 79 patients underwent LT (diagnosed on explant) and 32 underwent LR for cHCC-CCA. 5-year overall survival (OS) and recurrence-free survival (RFS) were superior following LT compared with LR (OS: 89.9% vs. 65.6%, P =0.007; RFS: 84.8% vs. 53.1%, P =0.001). This benefit was maintained for tumors within UCSF criteria [overall survival (88.7% LT vs. 65.6% LR, log rank P 0.014) and RFS (89.8% LT vs. 51.6% LR, P <0.001)]. Among LT recipients, OS for cHCC-CCA was comparable to HCC (89.9% vs. 86%, P =0.721). Within the LT cohort, macrovascular invasion (HR 25.01, P =0.003) and poor tumor differentiation (HR 7.29, P =0.004) independently predicted recurrence. Conclusion: In carefully selected patients, cHCC-CCA within UCSF criteria can achieve transplant outcomes comparable to HCC. Macrovascular invasion and poor tumor differentiation are major predictors of recurrence and may inform candidate selection for LT.

items.title: Hospital-level Variation in Medical Debt After Acute Traumatic Injury
items.abstract: Objective: To determine whether the treating hospital contributes to patients’ medical debt following injury. Summary Background Data: Trauma patients often have little or no choice in where they receive care. However, variation in hospital billing and collection practices, and their association with patient medical debt, remains poorly characterized. Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of adult trauma patients hospitalized from January 2019 to December 2020 at 29 Level I and II trauma centers within a statewide quality collaborative. Trauma registry data were linked to quarterly consumer credit reports from 12 months preinjury through 18 months postinjury. The primary outcome was change in medical debt in collections from baseline to months 9–18 postinjury. Hierarchical mixed-effects models with empirical Bayes shrinkage and reliability adjustment estimated risk-adjusted hospital-level changes, adjusting for demographics, injury severity, and treatment intensity. Hospitals were classified as outliers if 95% confidence intervals for observed-minus-expected differences excluded zero. Results: Among 20,613 patients (mean age 63 y; 49% female; 82% non-Hispanic White), mean change in medical debt was $314 (SD $3464). Four hospitals (14%) were high outliers, generating $365–$566 more debt per patient than expected, while 4 (14%) were low outliers, generating $292–$676 less. Low-outlier hospitals cared for younger, lower-income, and higher-risk patients yet produced less debt than predicted. Findings were robust across sensitivity analyses. Conclusions: Substantial hospital-level variation in postinjury medical debt persists after adjustment for clinical and demographic factors. Billing, financial assistance, and collection practices may represent modifiable targets to reduce financial hardship after trauma.

items.title: Surgeon Perspectives on Pregnancy Loss
items.abstract: Objective: To voice surgeons’ experiences with pregnancy loss during training and identify current gaps in support structures within training programs. Summary Background Data: Previous literature emphasizes the prevalence of pregnancy loss among female surgeons, frequently reporting a rate of more than double that of the general population. Despite this, little has been done to voice the personal experiences behind this data and to identify solutions to support trainees through these events. Methods: Semistructured focus groups and individual interviews were conducted between June and August of 2025. Surgeons within 5 years of general surgery residency graduation and current surgical fellows and general surgery trainees who identify as female and as having had a pregnancy loss during surgical training were recruited through targeted social media platforms. Transcripts were individually coded, and emerging codes were iteratively refined into themes related to the pregnancy loss experience and gaps in support resources. Results: Participants described the multidimensional impact of pregnancy loss during general surgery training. Mental health, physical, and professional impacts were pervasive. Five barriers to seeking support were identified: burden to colleagues, privacy concerns, reputation concerns, guilt and isolation, and rigidity of training. Facilitators to seeking support, though fewer, were greatly beneficial. These thematic categories informed critical gaps in general surgery program support structures and important components of a pregnancy loss policy designed to reduce stigma, promote trainee well-being, and mitigate attrition from the field. Conclusions: This study highlights the pregnancy loss experience among current and former general surgery trainees and uses these experiences to propose necessary support structures to be implemented within training programs.

items.title: Reductions in PTSD symptom clusters among perinatal and postnatal survivors of intimate partner violence participating in the Heartbeats program
items.containerTitle: Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Intimate partner violence (IPV) remains a leading cause of injury among women, especially during pregnancy and the postpartum period. Experiencing IPV increases the risk of mental health disorders, including post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). PTSD during the perinatal period is associated with poorer maternal mental health and adverse early child outcomes. Heartbeats (HB) is a hospital-based, community-linked violence intervention program designed to reduce morbidity and mortality among perinatal and postnatal survivors of IPV. HB provides crisis intervention, intensive case management, and counseling to pregnant patients up to 2 years postpartum who have experienced IPV. Given the high burden of mental health concerns in this population, a primary goal of HB is to reduce PTSD symptoms. METHODS: This study was conducted at a Level 1 trauma center. Participants were identified through IPV-related injury presentations, routine hospital screening, or referrals. Seventy-four participants completed the PTSD Checklist for DSM-5 (PCL-5) at intake (baseline) and 4 months postbaseline (follow-up). Total PTSD and subscale scores were calculated for intrusion (re-experiencing), avoidance, negative alterations in cognition and mood, and alterations in arousal and reactivity (hyperarousal). Paired-samples t tests assessed changes from baseline to follow-up. RESULTS: Significant reductions were observed in total PTSD symptoms (M=9.16, SD=23.64, p =0.003) and across all subscales: intrusion (re-experiencing; M=2.76, SD=6.19, p <0.001), avoidance (M=1.18, SD=2.90, p <0.001), negative alterations in cognition and mood (M=3.82, SD=8.83, p <0.001), and alterations in arousal and reactivity (hyperarousal; M=2.33, SD=7.25, p =0.008). CONCLUSIONS: HB program participation was associated with significant reductions in overall PTSD severity and each DSM-5 symptom cluster. These findings support the potential of integrated hospital-based, community-linked programs to improve trauma recovery outcomes among perinatal survivors of IPV. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Prognostic/Epidemiological; Level III.

items.title: Western Trauma Association critical decisions in trauma: Traumatic hemothorax
items.containerTitle: Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery
items.abstract: Traumatic hemothorax is a common consequence of thoracic injury, with management strategies ranging from observation to tube thoracostomy and operative intervention. This Western Trauma Association algorithm provides a practical framework for the evaluation and management of patients with traumatic hemothorax. Recommendations were developed through review of the available literature, including randomized and observational studies, supplemented by expert consensus where high-quality evidence is limited. The proposed pathway incorporates patient physiology, hemothorax size, adequacy of pleural drainage, and evidence of ongoing hemorrhage to guide management decisions. Because clinical circumstances, institutional resources, and local practice patterns vary, the algorithm is intended to support rather than replace individualized clinical judgment. It may be used as a bedside reference and as a framework for the development of institution-specific protocols. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Consensus algorithm from the Western Trauma Association; Level V.

items.title: A clinically relevant porcine model of flail chest: Development and multimodal validation
items.containerTitle: Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Flail chest has high mortality, but large-animal models with thoracic anatomy comparable to humans are lacking. The objective of this study was to develop a clinically relevant porcine flail chest model that preserves pleural, pulmonary, and neurovascular integrity, and to validate it using multimodal assessment including computed tomography (CT) imaging and physiologic parameters. METHODS: Twelve male Landrace pigs were randomly assigned to a flail chest (FC) group and a multiple single rib fracture (MRF) group (n=6 per group). Under general anesthesia, controlled osteotomies were performed on the fifth to eighth ribs. The intercostal neurovascular bundle was protected, and the parietal pleura was bluntly separated before each osteotomy to preserve pleural integrity. In the FC group, each rib was transected at two sites to create a four-rib flail segment; in the MRF group, a single transection was made per rib. Paradoxical chest wall motion was visually confirmed in the FC group before layered closure. Invasive arterial pressure, heart rate, pulse oxygen saturation (SpO₂), and end‑tidal carbon dioxide tension (ETCO₂) were monitored throughout. Chest CT was performed on Day 7. RESULTS: All surgeries were successful, with no mortality. Paradoxical chest wall motion was confirmed in all FC animals after emergence. The SpO₂/FiO₂ ratio declined postoperatively in both groups, with a significantly greater decrease in the FC group than in the MRF group (221.0±1.4 vs. 260.2±1.9, P <0.001). Heart rate and mean arterial pressure increased in both groups and were significantly higher in the FC group ( P <0.001). CT confirmed the intended fracture patterns and flail-segment displacement, with no evidence of pleural breach, pulmonary injury, pneumothorax, or hemothorax. CONCLUSIONS: A standardized porcine flail chest model was established that preserves pleural, pulmonary, and neurovascular integrity, allowing the isolated study of rib fracture pathophysiology. This model will facilitate future research on fixation materials and surgical techniques. STUDY TYPE: Basic Science/ Animal Study.

items.title: Contemporary management of traumatic abdominal wall hernias: What you need to know
items.containerTitle: Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery
items.abstract: Traumatic abdominal wall hernia (TAWH) is an uncommon but clinically important consequence of both blunt and penetrating abdominal trauma. It is defined by disruption of the abdominal wall musculature and fascia with herniation of intra-abdominal or retroperitoneal contents through the defect. Although penetrating abdominal wall defects are usually apparent and can often be primarily closed during operative exploration, blunt TAWH is significantly more heterogeneous and challenging. The skin may remain intact while the muscle, fascia, neurovascular supply, and bony attachments are disrupted. The reported incidence of TAWH varies according to imaging strategy and trauma population, but frank herniation remains rare, occurring in <1% of blunt trauma patients in most contemporary series. The major management challenge is deciding whether the patient requires immediate trauma laparotomy or laparoscopy, acute abdominal wall repair, staged management with same-admission repair, or delayed hernia repair/abdominal wall reconstruction. Evidence remains primarily dominated by retrospective single-center series, multicenter registry studies, and systematic reviews with heterogeneous definitions and follow-up. Although traditional dogma had taught that these repairs should always be performed in a delayed fashion, recent multicenter data, systematic reviews, and surgeon experience suggest that timing of repair, type of repair, and mesh use must be individualized; bowel injury, contamination, defect location, and patient physiology are more important than a universal early-versus-delayed algorithm. This article summarizes the practical issues the trauma and acute care surgeon needs to know: diagnosis, classification, associated injuries, indications for exploration, repair timing, operative strategy, management of lateral and posterior defects, mesh use in contaminated fields, and associated outcomes.

items.title: Multicompartmental hemorrhage: A high-risk pattern associated with increased risk for progression in TBI patients
items.containerTitle: Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) with intracranial hemorrhage (ICH) often requires repeat head computed tomography (CT) imaging to monitor for bleed progression. While prior literature has explored patient-level factors, data on the impact of ICH morphologies (subdural [SDH], epidural [EDH], intraparenchymal [IPH], intraventricular [IVH], and multicompartment hemorrhage [MCH]) on radiographic ICH progression remains unclear. We hypothesized that MCH and IVH would have an increased associated risk of progression. METHODS: This retrospective (2021–2023) single-center cohort included adults (≥18 y) with TBI-related ICH who underwent initial and repeat head CT. Patients were stratified into radiographic progression versus no-progression cohorts, with progression defined as new or enlarging hemorrhage on attending radiologist interpretation of follow-up head CT. The primary outcome was the rate of radiographic progression for each ICH type. MCH was defined as the presence of two or more ICH types. Multivariable logistic regression was performed to evaluate the association between each ICH type and radiographic progression, adjusting for age, mechanism of injury, Injury Severity Score, Glasgow Coma Scale on arrival, trauma-bay intubation, and preinjury antithrombotic exposure. RESULTS: Of the 817 patients with ICH on initial head CT and documented repeat CT, 401 (49.1%) had radiographic progression. Patients with progression were younger (58 vs. 62 y, p =0.027), more frequently male (71.3% vs. 63.7%, p =0.020), and had similar antithrombotic exposure (15.2% vs. 14.2%, p =0.678). Craniotomy/craniectomy was more frequent among those with progression (21.2% vs. 8.2%, p <0.001). On multivariable analysis, MCH demonstrated the strongest associated risk for progression (odds ratio [OR] 5.60, 95% confidence interval [CI] 3.36–9.33, p <0.001), whereas IPH (OR 2.02, CI: 0.86–4.75, p =0.108), SDH, EDH, and IVH were not independently associated with radiographic ICH progression. CONCLUSIONS: MCH was independently associated with radiographic ICH progression. This higher-risk hemorrhage pattern may warrant closer neurological monitoring. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Prognostic/Epidemiologic; Level III.

items.title: Trends in mortality rates in hypotensive pediatric trauma patients undergoing emergent trauma laparotomy
items.containerTitle: Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Massive hemorrhage remains the leading cause of preventable death after pediatric trauma. Emergent trauma laparotomy (ETL) is a common operation to obtain hemorrhage control. Mortality rates for adult patients in hemorrhagic shock requiring ETL remain high and unchanged. Information on mortality rates after ETL in pediatric patients is limited. We sought to evaluate trends in mortality rates for pediatric ETL patients. METHODS: The National Trauma Data Bank (NTDB) was queried from 2007 to 2023. Patients aged 0 to 18 years old were included if they underwent ETL. ETL was defined as laparotomy within 1 hour of arrival. Hypotension was defined as a systolic blood pressure <90 mm Hg on arrival. The primary outcome was annual hospital mortality rates for hypotensive patients requiring ETL. Secondary outcomes included annual 24-hour mortality rates for both hypotensive and all patients requiring ETL. Mortality rates were compared in 5-year cohorts to reduce annual variability. RESULTS: A total of 11,374 patients underwent ETL. The majority of patients were male (79%; n=78,963/11,374). Most patients were between the ages of 12 and 17 (84%; n=9,565/11,374), followed by ages 5 to 11 (11%; n=1,227/11,374), then ages 0 to 4 (5%; n=582/11,374). Penetrating injuries predominated (69%; n=7,866/11,374). The hospital mortality rate for all patients was 18.3% (n=2,079/11,374). Of patients who died, 74% were within 24 hours of arrival (n=1,533/2,079). Overall, 19% (n=2,125/11,374) were hypotensive on arrival. For hypotensive patients, the 24-hour and hospital mortality rates were 30% (n=641/2,125) and 45.9% (n=976/2,125). There was year-to-year variability in rates of hospital mortality of hypotensive patients through the study period ( p <0.001). However, the average mortality rates from 2007 to 2011 (45%; n=293/645) and 2019 to 2023 (42%; n=266/638) were unchanged ( p =0.95). CONCLUSIONS: Pediatric trauma patients with exsanguinating hemorrhage requiring ETL continue to suffer high rates of mortality. These findings underscore the urgent need for targeted research and performance improvement. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Prognostic and Epidemiological; Level III.

items.title: In older adults, “mild” by GCS does not mean low risk: Multicenter study of 1,157 patients with mild TBI and acute subdural hematoma
items.containerTitle: Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Acute traumatic subdural hematoma (SDH) is the most common intracranial injury in mild TBI (mTBI), particularly in older adults. However, the relationship of patient and brain computed tomography (CT) characteristics with outcomes remains poorly described in a contemporary cohort. This study aims to characterize outcomes in younger and older adults with mTBI and isolated acute SDH. METHODS: This was a 10-center, retrospective cohort study of adult traumas with emergency department Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) 13 to 15 and acute traumatic SDH on initial brain CT (’22–’23). Trauma registry, EHR, and Picture Archiving and Communication System (PACS) data were collected through automated and manual methods. The primary outcome was total mortality (TM=death+hospice discharge); the sample was stratified by 18 to 64 versus older than or equal to 65 years. Multivariable backward selection logistic regression examined 21 demographic, injury, and brain CT covariates. RESULTS: In total, 1,157 patients were included (18–64 y: 28%; ≥65 y: 72%; 58% transferred in). Median [IQR] non-head ISS was 1 [1–5] in 18 to 64 years, and 1 [1–2] in older than or equal to 65 years. Ten percent had neurosurgical intervention (18–64 y: 8%; ≥65 y: 11%). TM was higher in older than or equal to 65 years than 18 to 64 years (10% vs. 3%). Compared with older than or equal to 65 years, 18 to 64 years were discharged home more frequently (78% vs. 51%) and to hospice less frequently (2% vs. 7%). In 18 to 64 years, factors associated with TM were race, advance directive, functional dependence, ISS, more midline shift, and thicker SDH (too few TMs for adjusted models). In older than or equal to 65 years, factors independently associated with TM were advance directive (aOR [95% CI]: 11.8 [2.9–49.0]), male sex (3.0 [1.3–7.0]), midline shift (1.8 [1.3–2.6]), shock index (1.5 [1.1–2.1]), and worsening SDH on follow-up CT (2.9 [1.3–6.6]). CONCLUSIONS: Despite presenting as “mild”, these data highlight that older adults with SDH have high TM and should continue to receive the highest-level care with timely goals-of-care discussions. The association between advance directives and TM should be interpreted within the context of baseline vulnerability and preinjury treatment preferences, not as a biological mortality predictor. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III, prognostic/epidemiological.

items.title: Opioid prescribing and hospital outcomes after trauma in patients with substance use disorder: An analysis of the michigan trauma quality improvement project
items.containerTitle: Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Trauma patients frequently have comorbid substance use disorders (SUD), which may complicate pain management and increase the risk of opioid-related adverse outcomes after discharge. We hypothesized that trauma patients with SUD would be prescribed more opioids at discharge than those without SUD. METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed a cohort of adult trauma patients across the state from 2022 to 2025 using a statewide collaborative database. Primary outcomes were opioid prescription at discharge (yes/no) and amount prescribed standardized to oxycodone 5 mg pills. A multivariable approach assessed risk-adjusted differences in outcomes among patients with SUD versus without SUD. RESULTS: Among 29,805 total patients, 8,672 (29.1%) had a diagnosis of SUD. 71.2% of patients with SUD received a discharge opioid prescription, compared with 59.6% of patients without SUD ( p <0.001). After adjustment, the predicted probability of receiving an opioid prescription at discharge was 64.2% (95% CI, 63.1%–65.2%) for patients with SUD and 62.5% (95% CI, 62.0%–63.1%) for those without. Among patients that received a prescription, those with SUD were prescribed 21.2 pills of 5 mg oxycodone, corresponding to an adjusted difference of 1.6 additional pills (95% CI, 0.89–2.31; p <0.001) compared with those without. Prescribing patterns also differed by race and ethnicity: Hispanic or Latino patients were 5.4-percentage points more likely to receive an opioid prescription than non-Hispanic or Latino patients, while, among prescription recipients, Black patients received 3.56 fewer pills than White patients. CONCLUSIONS: Our findings demonstrate that patients with SUD received opioids more frequently and in greater amounts at discharge, yet absolute differences were small in magnitude and may not represent clinically meaningful differences. Differences in prescribing by race and ethnicity were larger in magnitude and warrant further investigation. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Prognostic and epidemiological; Level III.

items.title: Wrong hospital, wrong outcome: Impact of care fragmentation following trauma laparotomy
items.containerTitle: Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Care fragmentation (CF), defined as readmission to a nonindex hospital, has been identified as a potential predictor of poor outcomes after traumatic injury. Trauma laparotomy (TL) is a common procedure with perioperative risk of complications and readmission. Incidence of CF following TL, its risk factors, and its effects on outcomes are unknown. We hypothesized that CF after TL is associated with increased mortality during hospital readmission compared with continuity of care (CC). METHODS: The Nationwide Readmissions Database (2016–2022) was queried for hospitalized adult (≥18) patients with traumatic injury and open surgery of gastrointestinal or genitourinary systems during index admission, and unplanned readmission within 90 days. Demographics, comorbidities, injury severity, procedures, and disposition data were collected for patients with CF and compared with patients with CC. The primary outcome was in-hospital death during readmission. Univariate comparisons and multivariable logistic regression were performed. RESULTS: A total of 14,773 TL patients were included in the analysis. From these, 2,059 (13.9%) were readmitted within 90 days. The average age of readmitted patients was 43 years, and the majority (68.6%) were male. Of the readmissions, 441 (21.4%) experienced CF. Discharge home from the index admission was associated with lower odds of CF (OR 0.52, 95% CI: 0.32–0.84, p =0.008). On multivariable regression analysis, CF was significantly associated with in-hospital death during readmission (OR 5.09, 95% CI: 1.22–21.16, p =0.03). CONCLUSIONS: CF is common following TL and is associated with an increased risk of death on readmission, even after adjustment for baseline comorbidities and other hospital characteristics. Patients who are discharged home are less likely to experience CF. TL survivors may represent a patient population that would benefit from targeted efforts to reduce CF. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Therapeutic; Level III.

items.title: Trauma Quality Programs Mortality Reporting System Case Reports: Unanticipated Mortality Due to Prolonged Operative Course
items.containerTitle: Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery
items.abstract: The American College of Surgeons Trauma Quality Programs Mortality Reporting System is an online anonymous case reporting system designed to share experiences from rare events that may have contributed to unanticipated mortality at contributing trauma centers. This report analyzes cases, summarizes opportunities for truncated operating room time, and offers a defined framework to assess the need for a damage control strategy.

items.title: Weathering the storm: Predictors and resource burden of paroxysmal sympathetic hyperactivity after severe traumatic brain injury
items.containerTitle: Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Reported incidence of paroxysmal sympathetic hyperactivity (PSH) after severe traumatic brain injury (TBI) approaches one-third, largely from cohorts that excluded early deaths. Predictors and resource consequences remain unclear. We identified predictors of PSH development and associations between diagnosis, PSH Assessment Measure (PSH-AM) subscores [clinical features scale (CFS) and diagnosis likelihood tool (DLT)], and resource utilization. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of adults with severe TBI admitted to a tertiary care center intensive care unit (ICU) (October 2020–September 2025), stratified by PSH diagnosis. Two reviewers assigned PSH-AM scores. PSH cannot be diagnosed until the syndrome declares itself over days, so exposure is conditioned on survival; mortality is reported descriptively. Multivariable logistic regression identified predictors of PSH diagnosis. Log-transformed linear regressions estimated associations of PSH diagnosis and subscores with hospital length of stay (LOS), ICU LOS, and ventilator days. Thirty-day composite outcomes, inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW), and landmark analysis evaluated robustness. RESULTS: Of 509 patients with severe TBI, 86 (17%) developed PSH. Younger age [odds ratio (OR): 0.97 (95% CI: 0.96–0.98); P <0.001) and higher ISS [1.05 (1.02–1.07); P <0.001] independently predicted PSH. PSH was associated with longer hospital LOS (372.9%), ICU LOS (278.3%), and more ventilator days (266.4%; all P <0.001). Mortality was 11.6% (PSH) versus 35.9% (non-PSH). IPTW demonstrated PSH had fewer days alive and out of hospital (−46.8%; P <0.001) and landmark analysis highlighted fewer ventilator-free days (−40.2%; P =0.0097) and ICU-free days (−46.9%; P <0.001). Higher DLT subscores were associated with longer hospital (36.3%; P =0.001) and ICU (23.3%; P =0.005) stays, whereas the CFS subscore showed no associations. CONCLUSIONS: The PSH diagnosis is contingent on survival. Younger patients with severe TBI who survive their initial injuries are more likely to develop PSH and occupy hospital beds meaningfully longer. The diagnosis likelihood tool, not the clinical features scale, tracks with that burden. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III, prognostic/epidemiological.

items.title: The impact of presentations in scientific conferences: Publication and citation rates in trauma surgery
items.containerTitle: Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Understanding the publication rates and citation patterns of conference abstracts is critical for program committees and investigators alike. However, the downstream scholarly outcome of conference abstracts remains poorly characterized. We hypothesized that across contemporary US trauma-related scientific meetings, a substantial proportion of conference abstracts would not progress to peer-reviewed publications, and that publication rates and citation patterns would vary by presentation format and conference. METHODS: We conducted a cross-sectional study of abstracts presented at four major US trauma surgery conferences from 2017 to 2019. We identified peer-reviewed manuscripts associated with conference abstracts via Google Scholar and PubMed. We collected presentation format, publishing journal, 2024 journal impact factor, and citation count. A cohort of directly submitted peer-reviewed manuscripts was also analyzed. Mixed-effects Poisson regression models assessed the association between presentation and citation counts, adjusting for publication timing. RESULTS: Of 1,157 abstracts, 762 (66%) were published as peer-reviewed manuscripts. Most manuscripts were published in the Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery ( JTACS ) (55%), with 5 in journals with a higher-impact factor than JTACS . On regression analysis, abstracts presented as oral presentations, and published in journals with an impact factor higher than JTACS , were associated with a greater number of citations. When comparing manuscripts presented as abstracts to directly submitted peer-reviewed manuscripts, abstract presentation was associated with 22% more citations (incidence rate ratio: 1.22; 95% CI [1.16–1.29]; p <0.001). CONCLUSIONS: This cross-sectional study of four trauma societies found that approximately a third of presented abstracts did not progress to peer-reviewed publication, with publication rates varying by conference and presentation format. Exploratory analyses found that among those published in JTACS , published manuscripts originating from presented abstracts demonstrated a modestly higher citation count compared with directly submitted manuscripts. Our findings highlight an opportunity to better understand how conference time and investigator effort translate into downstream scholarly output. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Prognostic/Epidemiological; Level IV.

items.title: β-Blockade reprograms trauma-induced changes in bone marrow exosomal microRNAs
items.containerTitle: Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Severe trauma produces sustained sympathetic activation that contributes to bone marrow dysfunction, impaired hematopoiesis, and persistent injury-associated anemia. Although β-adrenergic blockade improves bone marrow recovery after injury, the downstream mechanisms remain incompletely defined. We hypothesized that propranolol reprograms trauma-induced bone marrow extracellular vesicle (EV) microRNA (miRNA) expression toward restoration of hematopoietic homeostasis. METHODS: Sprague-Dawley rats were randomized to naïve, polytrauma (PT), PT plus propranolol (PT+BB), PT with chronic restraint stress (PTRS), or PTRS plus propranolol (PTRS+BB) groups (n=6–8 per group). Propranolol (10 mg/kg intraperitoneally) was administered daily. On day 7, complete blood counts were obtained, and bone marrow–derived EV miRNAs were profiled using the NanoString nCounter platform. Differentially expressed miRNAs were identified using an absolute log2 fold change ≥1.5 and p <0.05. Predicted pathways were assessed using Ingenuity Pathway Analysis, and miR-125b-5p was validated by quantitative PCR. RESULTS: PT altered 45 EV miRNAs compared with naïve animals, including suppression of miRNAs involved in hematopoietic stem cell maintenance and erythropoiesis. Chronic restraint stress amplified this response, with 93 differentially expressed miRNAs following PTRS. Propranolol altered 12 miRNAs after PT and 43 after PTRS, increasing hematopoietic regulatory miRNAs, including miR-125b-5p, while suppressing several stress- and inflammation-associated miRNAs. Pathway analysis identified alterations in NOTCH, RUNX1, PTEN, thyroid receptor/retinoid X receptor, and histone modification signaling. Quantitative PCR confirmed a 2.4-fold increase in EV miR-125b-5p following propranolol in PTRS animals ( p =0.018). CONCLUSIONS: Trauma and persistent adrenergic stress broadly remodel bone marrow EV miRNA signaling. β-Adrenergic blockade selectively reprograms these networks toward pathways associated with hematopoietic recovery, identifying EV miRNAs as potential mediators of posttraumatic bone marrow dysfunction. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Not applicable—Animal research.

items.title: An anti-inflammatory melanocortin fusion polypeptide augments whole blood resuscitation of hemorrhagic shock in a rodent polytrauma model
items.containerTitle: Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Severe trauma induces a cytokine storm that is associated with impaired resuscitation and recovery. We investigated the impact of AQB-565, an anti-inflammatory melanocortin fusion polypeptide, as a novel treatment adjunct for whole blood resuscitation of hemorrhagic shock using a rat polytrauma shock model. METHODS: Hemorrhagic shock with polytrauma was induced in 64 Sprague-Dawley rats. The rats were randomized to receive one of four intravenous treatments at 15 minutes posthemorrhage (T15): saline control, AQB-565, tranexamic acid (TXA), or combined AQB-565+ TXA. The rats were given autologous transfusion of shed whole blood at 60 minutes and as needed thereafter to achieve mean arterial pressure (MAP) of 60 mm Hg for up to 3 hours. Survival, hemodynamics, cytokine profiles, and hemorrhage volumes were compared between groups. RESULTS: There was a significant overall effect of treatment group on MAP (two-way rmANOVA p =0.02) that coincided with blood transfusion. MAP was significantly increased at T105 with AQB-565+TXA versus saline control ( p =0.046). Inflammatory plasma cytokines, including interleukin-6, were significantly decreased with AQB-565 versus control groups (ANOVA p values ≤ 0.01). Seventeen (26.6%) rats died before 3 hours. There was a trend towards increased survival for treatments containing AQB-565 versus controls that was not statistically significant (Kaplan-Meier log rank p =0.06). CONCLUSIONS: A melanocortin pathway-activating polypeptide suppressed inflammation and improved hemodynamic response to whole blood transfusion in this hemorrhagic shock model.

Publications
A variety of publications and other educational resources are available through the Society and contain the latest information in cardiovascular anesthesiology. Discount subscriptions to the publications listed below are available for those who are members of both the SCA and the IARS.

SCA Newsletter
The SCA newsletter serves as a valuable resource for its members, offering updates on the latest advancements, educational events, and leadership messages relevant to cardiovascular anesthesiology. Each edition typically includes previews of upcoming conferences, such as the annual Echo and Thoracic Anesthesia Symposiums, important policy and guideline changes, and opportunities for professional development through hands-on workshops and scientific discussions. The newsletter also features announcements of society activities, member achievements, and committee updates, helping practitioners stay informed and engaged within the SCA community.
Read more

Anesthesia and Analgesia
The official journal of the International Anesthesia Research Society hosts three sections of interest to SCA membership: Cardiovascular Anesthesiology, Hemostasis, and Perioperative Echocardiography and Cardiovascular Education.
Discount subscriptions are available for those who are members of both the SCA and the IARS.
Free Access Articles
Read more

Journal of Cardiothoracic and Vascular Anesthesia
Aimed primarily at anesthesiologists who deal with patients undergoing cardiac, thoracic, or vascular surgical procedures.
The Red Journal features a multidisciplinary approach, with contributions from cardiac, vascular and thoracic surgeons, cardiologists, and other related specialists.
Emphasis is placed on rapid publication of clinically relevant material.
The journal is international in scope and encourages innovative submissions from all continents.
Read more

OpenAnesthesia
Sponsored by the IARS, this comprehensive resource for anesthesiology residents and physicians offers online and mobile education resources.
Read more

A&A Practice
The official clinical companion e-journal to A&A Practice is published semi-monthly and available online or via your mobile device.

Guideline FAQs
How do I obtain copyright permission to use a table/figure from an ASE Guideline?Expand
To use images or tables from any ASE guideline (or JASE article) you must apply for permission to the JASE publisher, Elsevier. This is done via CCC RightsLink(opens in new tab).
A shortcut is to find the guideline or article you need on JASE (onlinejase.com) and then select the “get rights” link (which looks like a copyright symbol) and it will take you to the CCC RightsLink form for that specific guideline or article. Note that you may request more than one image/table from a guideline on the same form, but you will need separate forms for each guideline or article.
How do I submit an idea for an ASE Guideline?Expand
ASE members may become involved in proposing an ASE Guideline through participation in one of the ASE Councils(opens in new tab) or ASE Specialty Interest Groups(opens in new tab). ASE members may also login to the member portal to download the ASE Guideline Development Manual (updated June 2023) and download the ASE Guideline Proposal Template (see instructions here(opens in new tab)) for more information. Note that guideline proposals are reviewed, prioritized, and approved by ASE leadership depending on topic.
What is ASE’s Endorsement Policy? Expand
ASE supports collaboration with other medical societies and organizations that develop clinical practice guidelines, appropriate use criteria, position statements, and other communications related to echocardiographic imaging. ASE views collaboration as an opportunity to harmonize clinical recommendations, improve the delivery of patient care, and advance cardiovascular ultrasound to improve lives.
Guidelines and other clinical guidance documents developed by external organizations may be considered for ASE endorsement when they address topics relevant to ASE and its membership and meet the basic criteria for review, including:
Medical and scientific soundness.
Alignment with ASE policies.
Alignment with the ASE strategic plan.
At the discretion of the ASE Executive Committee, a request for review of a submitted clinical guidance document may not be accepted. Submission and review do not guarantee endorsement, and ASE endorsement does not guarantee publication in the Journal of the American Society of Echocardiography (JASE).
ASE Endorsement Process
ASE endorsement requires:
Formal review by the ASE Guidelines and Standards Committee to assess the appropriateness of endorsement.
Approval by the ASE Executive Committee.
External organizations may approach ASE to request review and endorsement of guidelines developed without ASE involvement. Although such documents may be considered, the likelihood of consideration is increased when ASE has been involved in, and has knowledge of, the development process.
Organizations seeking ASE endorsement must submit the guideline to ASE Guidelines staff for consideration and complete ASE’s Endorsement Letter of Agreement (LOA). The requesting organization should submit the final manuscript along with the endorsement request.
Categories of ASE Recognition
Clinical guidelines developed by external organizations that are relevant to patient care in cardiovascular ultrasound may be categorized as follows:
Endorsed
The guideline meets ASE’s criteria for endorsement, and ASE fully endorses the document.
Whenever feasible, ASE’s involvement in the development and review of an endorsed document should include one or more of the following:
ASE representation on the writing committee, with at least one member appointed by the ASE Executive Committee.
ASE participation in peer review of the final document.
The sponsoring organization’s written response to ASE peer-review comments and provision of the final document to ASE for review.
Affirmation of Value
The guideline does not meet the requirements for full endorsement, or ASE cannot endorse all of the recommendations. However, ASE determines that the guideline provides value in improving patient care as it relates to the advancement of cardiovascular ultrasound.
Not Endorsed
ASE does not endorse the guideline.
Dissemination of Endorsed Documents
If ASE fully endorses a document:
ASE may disseminate the document to its members with permission from the primary organization.
ASE may request permission to publish the full document, a portion of the document, or a summary on the ASE website, or to provide a link to the article after publication by the primary organization.
The requesting organization should submit the endorsement request and final manuscript to ASE Guidelines staff for consideration.

Clinical Practice Documents and Policies
Scroll to top
The Society of Thoracic Surgeons Workforce on Evidence Based Surgery develops clinical practice documents including clinical practice guidelines, expert consensus documents, and expert opinion/white papers to provide practical assistance to the STS membership. These documents are intended to assist physicians and other health care providers in clinical decision-making by describing a range of generally acceptable approaches for the diagnosis, management, or prevention of specific diseases or conditions.
Clinical practice guideline documents are thoroughly reviewed, and the conclusions and recommendations are based on a systematic review of scientific evidence published in medical literature.
Expert consensus documents represent the collective opinions of an expert panel on a clinical topic. The opinions expressed in the statement(s) are not generally developed in accordance with the formal evidence review process outline for clinical practice guidelines. The authors may suggest treatment strategies based on their collective knowledge and clinical experience.
An expert opinion/white paper is authored by leading experts on clinical topics with scarce data and significant uncertainty. These documents are intended to synthesize existing scientific literature, divergent opinions, and other treatment strategies, rather than provide recommendations.

AATS/STS Position Statement on Developing Clinical Practice Documents
Clinical practice guidelines are intended as one element of the physician’s armamentarium and should not be considered inclusive of all proper methods of care or exclusive of other methods of care reasonably directed at obtaining the same results. Moreover, these guidelines are subject to change over time, without notice. The ultimate judgment regarding the care of a particular patient must be made by the physician in light of the individual circumstances presented by the patient.
STS clinical practice guidelines may be printed or downloaded for individual and personal use only. Guidelines may not be reproduced in any print or electronic publication or offered for sale or distribution in any format without the express written permission of The Society of Thoracic Surgeons.

The aim of clinical guidelines are to help clinicians to make informed decisions about their patients. However, adherence to a guideline does not guarantee a successful outcome. Ultimately, healthcare professionals must make their own treatment decisions about care on a case-by-case basis, after consultation with their patients, using their clinical judgement, knowledge and expertise. These guidelines do not take the place of physicians’ and other health professionals’ judgment in diagnosing and treatment of particular patients. These guidelines are not intended to and should not be interpreted as setting a standard of care, or be deemed inclusive of all proper methods of care nor exclusive of other methods of care reasonably directed to obtaining the same results. The ultimate judgment must be made by the physician and other health professionals and the patient in light of all the circumstances presented by the individual patient, and the known variability and biological behavior of the clinical condition. These guidelines reflects the data at the time the guidelines were prepared; the results of subsequent studies or other information may cause revisions to the recommendations in these guidelines to be prudent to reflect new data, but ELSO is under no obligation to provide updates.
